Volume Eight
The Book of Divine Decree

In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Bestower of Mercy. All praise belongs to Allah alone, and may blessings and peace be upon him after whom there is no prophet.

Shaykh al-Islām Ahmad ibn Taymiyyah—may Allah bless his resting place—said:

Section on “The Power of the Lord,” the Almighty and Majestic (*)

Muslims and the adherents of all other religions agree that Allah has power over all things, as the Quran declares in very many places. I have refuted those who deny the Lord’s power at length in several places, including what we have written on al-Arbaʿīn and al-Muhassal, in the commentary on al-Asbahāniyyah, and elsewhere. We have also discussed what al-Rāzī and others have said

## Page 3723

on “the question of the Lord’s possessing power and acting by choice,” and the considerable shortcomings in its treatment—matters that are not our subject here.

(The purpose here is to discuss the matter among adherents of religions who affirm the truth of the messengers. We therefore say: There are several questions here.

The first question:

Allah has stated that He has power over all things. People hold three views on this:

“One group” says that this is general in scope and includes what is intrinsically impossible, such as combining two contraries; this, too, therefore falls within the scope of divine power. A group that includes Ibn Hazm holds this view.

“Another group” says that this is a general statement subject to an exception: what is intrinsically impossible is excluded. Although it is a thing, it does not fall within the scope of divine power. Ibn ‘Atiyyah and others have stated this view.

Both views are mistaken. The correct view is the third, held by the great majority of those engaged in rational inquiry: what is intrinsically impossible is not a thing at all. Although they disagree concerning the nonexistent, what is intrinsically impossible cannot be realized in external reality, nor can the mind conceive of it as actually existing externally. Rather, the conjunction of the two contraries is mentally postulated and then judged impossible in external reality, since it can neither be realized externally nor conceived in the mind, except by way of analogy, as when one says: “There may be a conjunction of

---

## Page 3724

motion and rest in a thing. Is it then possible, in external reality, for blackness and whiteness to coexist in a single subject, just as motion and rest coexist?”

The answer is: This is impossible. Thus, a conjunction analogous to a possible one is postulated and then judged impossible. But the actual conjunction of whiteness and blackness in a single subject is neither possible nor conceivable. It is therefore not a thing, either in external reality or in the mind, and so does not fall within His statement:

“And He has power over all things.”

The second question:

According to the majority, what does not exist is not a thing in external reality, and this is correct. They may also state without qualification that a thing is something that exists.

It may then be objected: It follows that He has power only over what exists, and that He has no power over what He has not created. This is the position of some adherents of innovation, who say that He has power only over what He wills, not over what He does not will. This view is reported from a pupil of al-Nazzām.

Those affirmationist thinkers who say that a thing is something that exists—such as al-Ash‘arī and those who agree with him among the followers of the imams, Ahmad and others, including Judge Abū Ya‘lā, Ibn al-Zāghūnī, and others—say that He has power over what exists. It may then be said: These thinkers have affirmed something that the verse does not affirm. The verse affirms His power over what exists, whereas they say that He has power over both what exists and what does not exist.

The precise account is that “thing” is a designation for both what exists in external reality and what is conceived in the mind. Thus, whatever Allah has decreed and knows will come to be is a thing in His decree, His knowledge, and the Record, even if it is not

---

## Page 3725

a thing in external reality. An example is His saying:

“His command, when He wills a thing, is only to say to it, ‘Be,’ and it is.”

The word “thing” in the verse encompasses both senses. Thus, He has power over every thing that exists and everything the mind conceives as existing, provided that its existence is conceivable. Nothing is excluded from this, nor is anything added to it. As He, the Exalted, says:

“Yes, We are able even to restore his fingertips.”

And He says:

“Say: He has power to send punishment upon you from above you or from beneath your feet.”

It is established in the two Sahīh collections that when this was revealed, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said, “I seek refuge in Your Face.” When the words “or divide you into factions” were revealed, continuing the verse, he said, “These two are less severe.” Thus, He has power over the first two, even though He has not brought them about. He also says:

“And We sent down water from the sky in due measure and settled it in the earth, and We are certainly able to take it away.”

The Quran commentators said: We are certainly able to take it away, so that you die of thirst, your livestock perish, and your lands fall into ruin.

It is well known that He has not taken it away. This is like His saying:

“Have you considered the water that you drink?”

through to His saying:

“And do you repay your provision with denial?”

This shows that He has power to do what He does not do. For He has stated that, had He willed, He would have made the water bitterly salty, yet He has not done so. Similar examples are:

“Had We willed, We would have given every soul its guidance.”

“Had your Lord willed, those on earth would have believed.”

“Had Allah willed, they would not have fought one another.”

In more than one passage, He has stated that, had He willed, He would have done things that He has not done. If He did not have power over them, then even if He willed them, He could not do them.

The third question:

He has power over all things, and this includes

---

## Page 3726

the acts of His servants and everything other than their acts. Most of the Muʿtazilites say that a servant’s acts are not within His power.

(The fourth question:

This also includes His own acts. The revealed texts affirm both, as in His words, Exalted is He:

“Is not He who created the heavens and the earth able to create their like?”

“Is He not able to give life to the dead?”

“Yes, We are able even to restore his fingertips.”

There are many similar passages. Power over concrete entities is mentioned in passages such as His words:

“And We have certainly created man.”

“Does he think that no one will have power over him?”

It is also explicitly affirmed in the Quran and Sunnah. As for the Quran, He says:

“Even if We take you away, We will certainly exact retribution from them.”

He thus makes clear that He, glorified is He, has power over them themselves. This explicitly affirms His power over created entities. He also says:

“You are not set over them to compel them.”

And:

“You are not set over them as a controller.”

There are other similar passages. By implication, these indicate that the Lord is the One who compels them and exercises control over them, which necessarily entails His power over them. His words:

“And he thought that We would have no power over him”

—according to the interpretation of al-Hasan and others among the early generations who understood this as referring to power—are evidence that Allah has power over him and others like him. Similarly, there is the account of the man who left instructions to his family:

“‘If Allah has power over me, He will surely punish me as He has never punished anyone in all creation.’ When they had burned him, Allah, Exalted is He, restored him and asked him, ‘What prompted you to do what you did?’ He replied, ‘Fear of You, my Lord.’ So He forgave him.”

He was mistaken in saying, “If Allah has power over me, He will surely punish me,” as the hadith indicates, and Allah

---

## Page 3727

did have power over him. Yet because of his fear and faith, Allah forgave him for this ignorance and error.

Evidence may also be drawn from His words:

“Did We not create you from a lowly fluid?”

Through to His words:

“How excellent are We in power!”

This is according to the interpretation that takes the expression as referring to power, for it encompasses power over created beings, although He, glorified is He, also has power to create them. Power to create them entails power over them, and power over them entails power to create them.

This is also explicitly stated in hadith, such as the Prophet’s words, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, to Abū Masʿūd when he saw him beating his slave:

“Allah has greater power over you than you have over this slave.”

This makes clear the Lord’s power over the servant himself, and that He has greater power over him than he has over his own slave. It also affirms the servant’s power.

People have differed concerning “the power of the Lord and the servant.” One group maintains that both kinds encompass the act subsisting in the agent and the object of his power. This is the soundest view, and it is what the Quran and Sunnah affirm: each of the two kinds of power encompasses both the act subsisting in the one who possesses that power and the object of his power that is distinct from him. Some of the evidence for this concerning the Lord’s power has already been explained.

As for the servant’s power, references to his power to perform acts subsisting in him are numerous. This is agreed upon by those who affirm that the servant possesses power. Examples include His words:

“So fear Allah as much as you are able.”

“Then he must fast for two consecutive months before they touch one another. But whoever is unable must feed sixty needy people.”

“They will swear by Allah, ‘Had we been able, we would have gone forth with you.’ They destroy themselves”—and the rest of the verse.

And the Prophet’s words, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“Pray standing; if you are unable, then sitting; and if you are unable, then on your side.”

---

## Page 3728

As for things distinct from the possessor of power, examples include His words:

“Allah has promised you abundant spoils which you will take”—through to His words—“and other spoils over which you have not yet had power,” continuing to “All-Powerful.”

This indicates that they had power over the former, and that they may have power over the latter at another time. This is power over concrete entities.

And His words:

“They set out early, determined and able”—through to His words—“Perhaps our Lord will replace it for us with something better,” and the rest of the verse.

Abū al-Faraj said: “There are three interpretations of His words ‘able.’ The first is that they believed themselves to have power over their garden. This was stated by Qatāda.”

I say: This is the view of both Mujāhid and Qatāda, as Ibn Abī Hātim narrated from them. Mujāhid said: “Able, in their own estimation.” This is also what al-Baghawī mentioned: “Believing themselves to have power over their garden and its fruits, with no one to stand between them and it.” Qatāda said: “The people set out early, pressing on towards their garden, believing themselves able to do so.”

Abū al-Faraj said: “The second is that they had power over the poor. This was stated by al-Shaʿbī, meaning that they could withhold from them. It has also been said that they were able to give to them, but miserliness prevented them from giving. Allah knows best.

“The third is that they set out early while able—that is, possessing means. This was stated by Ibn Qutayba.”

I say: The verse describes them as having set out early, determined and able. Determination here refers to intent: they set out with firm resolve and power, but Allah rendered them powerless. The statement that they were ‘able, in their own estimation’ means that they thought matters would remain as they had been. Had that been so, their power would have been complete; instead, they were deprived of that power through the destruction of their garden.

---

## Page 3729

Al-Baghawī said:

“Linguistically, hard may mean intent, withholding, or anger. Al-Hasan, Qatāda, and Abū al-ʿĀliya said: ‘With earnestness and effort.’ Al-Qurtubī (*), Mujāhid, and ʿIkrima said: ‘With a common purpose upon which they had agreed among themselves.’”

He said:

“This takes it in the sense of intent, for someone intent on something pursues it earnestly and resolutely. Abū ʿUbayda and al-Qutaybī said: ‘They set out of their own accord with hard—that is, intending to withhold from the poor.’ One says hāradat al-sana (‘the year withheld’) when it has no rain, and hāradat al-nāqatu ʿalayya (‘the she-camel withheld from me’) when she has no milk. Al-Shaʿbī and Sufyān said: ‘With resentment and anger towards the poor.’ In al-Wālibī’s commentary, Ibn ʿAbbās is reported to have said: ‘With power.’”

I say: Hard conveys firm resolve; this is inherent in the word. Its use regarding a year or a she-camel reflects its sense of severity. Likewise, resentment and anger involve intensity. They thus firmly resolved to take the garden’s produce and deprive the poor. They set out with this resolve, possessing the power to do so, with nothing to render them powerless or prevent them. But a command from heaven came upon the garden and nullified all of that. It has also been said that hard means rage and anger. Allah knows best.

A similar passage, which explicitly establishes the point at issue—that power may be exercised over concrete entities—is His saying, exalted is He:

“The life of this world is only like water which We send down from the sky”—through to His words—“Our command came upon it by night or by day, and We left it mown down, as though it had not flourished the day before,” and the rest of the verse.

His words:

“And its people thought they had power over it”

show that, were it not for the calamity, their assumption would have been correct, and they would have had power over it. But when Allah’s command came upon it, their assumption proved mistaken. Had they possessed no power over it, whether it remained intact or was destroyed, Allah would not have disproved their assumption by what He brought about

## Page 3730

by way of destruction. These people had not gone out to harvest; rather, they were deprived of power over it—namely, full power. That power ceased because the object upon which it could act no longer existed, not because of any weakness in the agent. In that account, He said:

“With firm resolve, possessing power.”

He did not say, “Possessing power in their own estimation.” If it is as those who interpret it as “in their own estimation” say, the meaning is the same. If, however, their being capable means that there was nothing within themselves incompatible with power, such as illness or weakness, but that the object of their power had ceased to exist, then this is like someone who can pay and provide sustenance but has nothing at his disposal.

Allah, exalted is He, says:

“The deeds of those who disbelieve in their Lord are like ashes swept violently by the wind on a stormy day. They have no power over anything they have earned. That is far-reaching error.”

In this condition, they have no power over anything they have earned. This indicates that in other circumstances they do have power over what they have earned. Likewise, others have power over what they have earned. What is meant by that which is earned is earned wealth.

Allah, exalted is He, also says:

“Allah presents an example: an owned slave who has no power over anything, and someone whom We have granted good provision from Us, from which he spends secretly and openly.”

When He states that the owned slave has no power over anything, His point is that the other man is not like that: rather, he has power over what this slave has no power over. This establishes that good provision is something over which its possessor has power, and that its possessor has power over it. This is how people of sound reason generally speak. They say, “So-and-so has power over such-and-such, and so-and-so has power over such-and-such; this person’s power is less than that person’s.”

---

## Page 3731

Another point that clarifies this is that a king acts as a deputy for people with respect to what Allah has granted them to own. Ownership entails power: no one can be an owner unless he can exercise control, whether personally or through his guardian or agent. Landed and movable property belong to their owner, indicating that they are within his power. Moses said:

“My Lord, I have control over none but myself and my brother.”

Since he could exercise authority over his brother because his brother obeyed him, he described this as having control over him. Allah, exalted is He, says:

“So they have ownership of them.”

And He says:

“And say, ‘Glory be to Him who has subjected this to us, for we could not have mastered it ourselves.’”

That is, they would not have had the ability. This indicates that they became capable of mastering these creatures when He subjected them to them. This is the meaning of His words:

“So they have ownership of them.”

Allah, exalted is He, also says:

“They could neither scale it nor pierce it.”

This indicates that, had they pierced it, they would have possessed the ability to do so. Piercing is not merely the movement of their hands; rather, it is making a hole in something. This therefore indicates that such piercing is within people’s power.

Furthermore, the Quran indicates that external objects produced by people are their handiwork. Whatever they make is, self-evidently and by common agreement, within their power. Yet the opposing disputant says, “Nothing outside the locus of their power is made by them.” This contradicts the Quran. Allah, exalted is He, said to Noah:

“Build the Ark under Our watchful eyes and according to Our revelation.”

And He said:

“And he was building the Ark.”

He has stated that ships are created, even though they are made by the children of Adam, and has made them among His signs, saying:

“And a sign for them is that We carried their descendants in the laden ship.”

“He has subjected to you whatever is on earth, and the ships that sail through the sea by His command.”

“And He has made for you ships and livestock on which you ride.”

And He said:

“Do you worship what you carve,
when Allah created you and what you make?”

---

## Page 3732

Thus He described the idols as carved and made by them, and stated that He created them and is the Creator of what they made. Here, mā (“what”) means “that which”: the meaning is that He created the idols they made. Since He is the Creator of the finished product, which bears the effect of the act, this indicates that He is the Creator of His servants’ acts. As for the view that mā serves to form a verbal noun, it is very weak indeed.

Allah, exalted is He, says:

“And We destroyed what Pharaoh and his people had made and what they had erected.”

What He destroyed was what they had built and erected. As for the accidental properties that subsisted in them, these had ceased to exist before they drowned. His words, “and what they had erected,” indicate that the structures were their handiwork: they themselves carried out the construction embodied in them, namely, the joining of their parts. Similarly, His words:

“Do you build on every height a monument for idle amusement?”

indicate that they themselves built those structures, for He says, “Do you build.” Likewise, His words:

“And you carve houses out of the mountains”

are like His words:

“Do you worship what you carve?”

And His words:

“They hewed the rock in the valley”

indicate that they hewed—that is, cut—the rock. Another example is His saying, exalted is He:

“Then, when the sacred months have passed, kill the polytheists.”

He commanded that they be killed, and a command can concern only something within the servant’s power. This therefore indicates that killing is within his power: it is the act he performs upon a person, causing that person to die. It is like slaughtering. Further examples are His words:

“Except those you slaughter,”

and His words:

“Do not kill game,”

and His words:

“Whoever among you kills it deliberately must compensate with livestock equivalent to what he killed.”

This indicates that the game is killed by the human being who kills it, in contrast to His words:

“You did not kill them, but Allah killed them.”

For this is like His saying:

“And you did not throw when you threw

---

## Page 3733

but Allah threw.” For the believers’ killing of their enemies came about through factors beyond their power, such as the sending down of angels and the casting of terror into their enemies’ hearts. Likewise, when he threw, it was not within his power to make the dust reach all their eyes and strike terror into their hearts. Thus, the throwing that Allah placed beyond a servant’s ordinary power is the throwing that Allah denied was his doing.

Abū ʿUbayd said:
“You did not gain victory or strike the mark; rather, Allah granted you victory and supported you.”

Al-Zajjāj said:
“Your throwing a handful of dust or pebbles could not fill the eyes of that vast army. It was Allah who brought that about.”

Ibn al-Anbārī stated:
“You did not strike terror into their hearts when you cast dust at their faces.”

This was therefore beyond his power, and so was one of the signs of his prophethood.

Another view holds, instead, that the Lord, exalted is He, has power only over created things separate from Him, and that no act over which He has power subsists in Him; whereas the servant has power only over what subsists in his own being and has no power over anything separate from him. This is the position of al-Ashʿarī and those followers of the imams who agreed with him, such as Judge Abū Yaʿlā, Ibn ʿAqīl, Ibn al-Zāghūnī, and others.

Another view holds that the servant has power over both, whereas the Lord has power only over what is separate from Him. This is the position of the Muʿtazilah. Yet another view holds that each has power over what subsists in him, but not over what is separate from him. I know of no one who has said that both have power over what is separate from them but not over what is connected to them.

The fifth issue:
Power consists in one’s ability to act, and acts are of “two kinds”:

---

## Page 3734

intransitive and transitive. These “two kinds” occur in His words:

“He is the One who created the heavens and the earth in six days, then rose over the Throne.”

Rising over the Throne, coming, arriving, descending, and similar acts are intransitive: they do not extend to an object, but rather subsist in the agent. Creating, providing sustenance, causing death, giving life, granting, withholding, guiding, granting victory, sending down, and similar acts extend to an object.

People hold “three views” concerning these two kinds of acts. Some affirm no act subsisting in the agent, whether intransitive or transitive. In their view, intransitive acts do not exist. As for transitive acts, such as creating, they say that creating is the created thing itself, or something distinct from the created thing. This is the position of the Jahmiyyah, the Muʿtazilah, and those who followed them, such as al-Ashʿarī and his followers. It is also the earlier of Judge Abū Yaʿlā’s two positions and the position of Ibn ʿAqīl.

Many of the Muʿtazilah say that creating is the created thing itself. Others say that it is distinct from it, but maintain that creating itself requires another act of creating, as Maʿmar ibn ʿAbbād holds. They are called the proponents of an infinite regress of meanings.

Some say that creating is identical with willing, as do some of the Muʿtazilah of Basra.

The “second view” is that transitive acts, but not intransitive acts, subsist in His own being. They therefore say that creating subsists in His own being and is not the created thing itself. They in turn hold two views.

---

## Page 3735

Some of them hold that this act occurs in time, while others hold that it is beginningless, saying that creating and bringing into being are eternal and without beginning. Among the latter are those who regard the act of creating itself as a single, beginningless entity, with created beings as its material; yet it is eternal and without beginning. They affirm neither descent nor rising over the Throne as subsisting in His own being, because these are occurrences in time. This is the position of the Kullābiyyah, who say that His action is beginningless, like His speech, as the followers of Ibn Khuzaymah maintained. It is also the position of many Hanafīs, Hanbalīs, Mālikīs, and Shāfiʿīs.

Others hold that the kind is beginningless, while its individual instances occur in time. According to this view, the act itself is subject to His power. As for those who regard it as one particular entity, if they say that it is beginningless, they contradict themselves, and their position entails that a particular beginningless entity is subject to His power. If they say that it is not subject to His power, they contradict themselves, because an act must be subject to His power. Allah knows best.

The third view affirms both kinds of acts—intransitive and transitive—as indicated by the Quran. Thus we affirm, as He has told us of Himself, that He created the heavens and the earth in six days, then rose over the Throne. This is the position of the early generations and the imams of the Sunnah. It is also the position of those who say that attributes exercised by His choice subsist in Him, such as the followers of Abū Muʿādh, Zuhayr al-Bābī, and Dāwūd ibn ʿAlī, as well as the Karrāmiyyah and other groups—even though the Karrāmiyyah say that descending and coming are acts subsisting in Him.

They say that He has the power to come, arrive, descend, rise over the Throne, and perform other such acts, as He has told us of Himself. This is perfection.

---

## Page 3736

The leading authorities who hold this view have explicitly stated that He “moves,” as Harb al-Kirmānī reported from Ahl al-Sunnah wa-l-Jamāʿah, naming among them Ahmad ibn Hanbal, Saʿīd ibn Mansūr, Ishāq ibn Ibrāhīm, and others. Likewise, ʿUthmān ibn Saʿīd al-Dārimī reported this from Ahl al-Sunnah and counted the denial of movement with respect to Allah, the Almighty and Majestic, among the teachings of the Jahmiyyah that the early generations rejected. He said: “Every living being moves, and whatever does not move is not alive.” Some of them said: “If a Jahmī tells you, ‘I disbelieve in a Lord who moves,’ say, ‘I believe in a Lord who does whatever He wills.’”

Those who hold this view say that whoever considers these acts impossible for Him and beyond His power has placed Him below inanimate things. Although an inanimate thing does not move by itself, it can nevertheless undergo movement. Those who deny such acts, however, say that He, exalted is He, cannot admit of this in any respect and that movement is impossible for Him. Yet movement and action are attributes of perfection, like knowledge, power, and will. Those who deny these attributes have stripped Him of attributes of perfection, and so have these Kullābiyyah.

As for those “deniers of the attributes,” when they are told: If He were not living, knowing, hearing, seeing, and speaking, it would necessarily follow that He was dead, ignorant, deaf, blind, and mute. These are deficiencies from which He must be declared free, for He, glorified is He, has created beings that live, hear, see, speak, know, possess power, and move. He therefore has a greater right to these qualities, for every perfection found in a created being, which is an effect, derives from the perfection of the Creator, whom they call an efficient cause.

---

## Page 3737

Moreover, the eternal One, whose existence is necessary in itself, is more perfect than whatever has come into being. It is therefore impossible for what is deficient alone to possess perfection.

They reply: “An inanimate thing is called neither living nor dead.” We have answered this objection in several ways elsewhere.

First: Their statement, “An inanimate thing is not called living; only what is capable of life is called dead,” is a matter of terminological convention. Otherwise, the Quran has called inanimate things dead in several passages, as in His words, exalted is He:

“And those they invoke besides Allah create nothing, but are themselves created.”

“They are dead, not alive, and do not perceive”—to the end of the verse.

Thus, He called idols dead, although they are stones. He also said:

“And a sign for them is the dead earth: We gave it life.”

(Second response: We do not concede that inanimate things are incapable of receiving this life. Rather, the Lord, exalted is He, has made them capable of life, and their receiving it is not impossible. Allah, exalted is He, turned Moses’ staff into a swiftly moving snake, demonstrating that wood can become a living creature. When Moses bathed, he placed his garment on a stone, and the stone fled with it. Allah also brought back to life the roasted fish that was with him and his young attendant. Pebbles glorified Allah, as did food—even while it was being eaten. The principal argument of those who deny this is that, if He were capable of movement, He would never be devoid of it, which would entail the existence of an endless succession of events. is the One who spoke it and sent it down. He thus made it an Arabic Quran through an act subsisting in Him: He spoke it and chose to speak it in Arabic—rather than any other language—and sent it down in that language.

For this reason, Ahmad said that making, on Allah’s part, may be creation or may be something other than creation. Making is an act, and an act may extend to an object distinct from the agent, as with creation. An act may also be intransitive; even if it takes an object in grammatical usage, its object subsists in the act itself, as with speaking. Speaking is an act that subsists in the speaker, and speech itself also subsists in the speaker. Thus He, glorified is He, made it an Arabic Quran: the making subsists in Him, and the Arabic Quran subsists in Him.

“Speech” encompasses two things: the act of speaking, and the ordered letters and sounds produced by that act. Hence utterance is sometimes treated as a kind of action, and sometimes as a category distinct from action. These matters have been explained at length elsewhere. And Allah knows best.

I have mentioned elsewhere that whenever anyone adduces evidence from revelation or reason in support of falsehood, that very evidence—when given its due, and when what it establishes is distinguished from what it does not—proves to demonstrate the falsity of the position of the person invoking it. It proves instead to be evidence for the people of truth. Sound evidence can establish only truth, and truth does not contradict itself; rather, its parts confirm one another. And Allah knows best.

at the time of death without his soul finding relief in it.” This is the declaration he urged his uncle to utter at the time of death.

He, glorified be He, made night and day succeed one another for whoever wishes to reflect or to give thanks. A person reflects upon the signs that establish knowledge and faith; then, when he recognizes Allah’s blessings, he thanks Him for them. The two are inseparable: signs and blessings are inseparable, for every blessing is a sign, and every sign is a blessing. Likewise, gratitude and reflection are inseparable. A grateful person gives thanks by praising Allah, obeying Him, and doing what He has commanded. This requires reflecting upon what His signs reveal of His names and praiseworthy attributes, and of His commands and prohibitions. Thus, He is praised and His commands are obeyed: this is gratitude. Both require reflection. As for reflection, when a person reflects upon His signs, he recognizes the blessings and kindness they contain. His signs encompass all created things, and they are goodness, blessings, and kindness.

“We praise You with all that is good.”

And in the opening supplication of prayer:

In everything Allah has created, He has wisdom, as He says:

He, glorified be He, has no need of any of creation. Wisdom thus comprises two things. The first is a wisdom pertaining to Him, which He loves and with which He is pleased.

## Page 3751

And the second pertains to His servants: it is a blessing to them in which they rejoice and take pleasure. This applies both to what He commands and to what He creates.

As for what He commands, He loves obedience and is pleased with it. He rejoices at a penitent’s repentance with a joy greater than any people know: His joy exceeds that of someone who, having lost his provisions and mount in a perilous wilderness, finds them after losing all hope. Likewise, His jealousy is greater than that of His servants. His jealousy is aroused when a servant commits what He has forbidden him. Thus, He is jealous when a servant does what He has prohibited, and He rejoices when the servant repents and returns to what He has commanded.

Obedience leads to happiness in this world and the Hereafter, and this is something in which the obedient servant rejoices. Thus, the acts of obedience He has commanded have praiseworthy consequences pertaining both to Him and to His servants. They embody wisdom pertaining to Him and mercy for His servants. Allah Most High says:

“O you who believe, shall I direct you to a trade that will save you from a painful punishment?

Believe in Allah and His Messenger and strive in the cause of Allah with your wealth and your lives. That is better for you, if you only knew.

He will forgive your sins and admit you into gardens beneath which rivers flow, and pleasant dwellings in Gardens of Eternity. That is the supreme triumph.

And another blessing that you love: victory from Allah and an imminent conquest. And give glad tidings to the believers.”

Thus, striving in Allah’s cause brings people a praiseworthy outcome in this world that they love—victory and conquest—and Paradise in the Hereafter. It also brings deliverance from the Fire.

He has said at the beginning of the surah:

“Indeed, Allah loves those who fight in His cause in ranks, as though they were a solidly joined structure.”

He therefore loves this. It embodies wisdom pertaining to Allah Most High and mercy for His servants, namely, the blessings they receive in this world

## Page 3752

and the Hereafter. The same applies to everything else He has commanded. Likewise, whatever He has created, He has created for a wise purpose pertaining to Himself, which He loves, and as a mercy to His servants, from which they benefit.

When people discussed “the reason for creation and the wisdom behind it,” each group spoke according to its knowledge. They grasped one aspect of the truth, while other aspects remained hidden from them. This is generally the case with matters over which people dispute: one group possesses some of the truth but leaves some of it aside, and the same is true of the others. Pure falsehood does not deceive people; rather, it must be mixed with something of the truth. Hence, they continue to differ, except those upon whom your Lord has mercy. These are the ones who believe in the whole truth and affirm whatever truth each group has expressed. They bring the truth and affirm it, and thus do not differ.

On this matter, the speculative theologians hold “three views,” belonging to three well-known groups. Each group has been supported by some followers of the four imams: Abū Hanīfah, Mālik, al-Shāfi‘ī, and Ahmad.

The first view is “the view of those who deny that He acts for a wise purpose.” They said that this would entail need, and therefore maintained that He does whatever He wills, but not for a wise purpose. Thus, they affirmed His power and will, and that He does whatever He wills. This exalts Him, but they denied wisdom because they thought it necessarily entailed need.

This is the view of al-Ash‘arī, his followers, and those who agreed with them, such as al-Qādī Abū Ya‘lā, Ibn al-Zāghūnī, and al-Juwaynī

---

## Page 3753

and al-Bājī and others like them. This view was originally held by Jahm ibn Safwān and the determinists who followed him. The philosophers hold a view even further removed from the truth: the torment that souls undergo, and other forms of harm, cannot be averted.

They say that He necessarily produces His effects by virtue of His essence, and that everything that occurs follows necessarily from His essence. Had they said that He necessarily brings about what He does through His will and power, they would have been correct. They have also said that evil occurs in the world but is outweighed by the good that exists. This is correct; however, it entails that the Creator created for a known wise purpose that is preserved and does not recur. Otherwise, without these two things, the argument remains meaningless. Thus, each group’s view contains some truth and some falsehood. These, then, are “four views.”

The fifth view is that of the imams: He has a wise purpose in everything He has created; indeed, there is both wisdom and mercy in it.

The second view—that is, the second of the “three” held by the speculative theologians—is that He creates and commands for a wise purpose relating to His servants: to benefit them and show them kindness. He has created and commanded solely for that purpose. This is the view of the Mu‘tazilah and others. Some of them then discussed the details of this wisdom, denied divine decree, and laid down a law for their Lord, determining what is just and what is permissible. This is the view of the “Qadariyyah.” Others affirmed divine decree and said, “Allah has a wise purpose that is hidden from us.” This is the view of Ibn ‘Aqīl

---

## Page 3754

and others who affirm divine decree. They agree with the Mu‘tazilah in affirming a wise purpose relating to created beings, while also acknowledging divine decree.

The third view is that of those who affirm a wise purpose relating to the Lord Himself, but in accordance with His knowledge. They say:

“He created them to worship Him, praise Him, extol Him, and glorify Him. Those He created for this purpose are those who actually do these things: whoever does so was created for that purpose. These are the believers. Whoever does not do so was not created for it.”

They say:

“This is an intended wise purpose, and it is realized, unlike the wise purpose affirmed by the Mu‘tazilah. They affirm a wise purpose consisting in benefiting His servants, yet then say that He created those whom He knew would derive no benefit from being created, but would instead suffer harm through it. They thus contradict themselves. We, by contrast, affirm a wise purpose known to be realized, and it has been realized: His believing servants’ knowledge of Him, their praise of Him, their extolling Him, and their glorifying Him. This actually occurs among the believers.”

They say:

“He may create those who suffer harm through being created for the benefit of others. Bringing about a little evil for the sake of abundant good is wise, as when rain is sent down to benefit His servants, even though it entails harm to some people.”

They say:

“The creation of the disbelievers and their punishment provide lessons for the believers, opportunities for jihad, and other benefits.”

This is the view preferred by Judge Abū Khāzim, son of Judge Abū Ya‘lā. He mentioned it in his book Usūl al-Dīn (The Foundations of Religion), which he composed on the basis of the book of Muhammad ibn al-Haytham al-Karrāmī.

They say that His words, Most High,

“I did not create the jinn and mankind except to worship Me,”

apply specifically to those who actually worship Him. This is the view of a group among the early and later generations.

They said: “What is meant

---

## Page 3755

by this is whoever actually worships Him: such a person was created for worship, whereas whoever does not worship Him was not created for it.”

It is reported that Sa‘īd ibn al-Musayyib said: “I created those who worship Me only that they should worship Me.” Al-Dahhāk, al-Farrā’, and Ibn Qutaybah likewise said this—a statement referring specifically to those who obey Him. Al-Dahhāk said: “It refers to the believers.” This is also the position of the Karrāmiyyah, as mentioned by Muhammad ibn al-Haytham. He said:

“This is indicated by His preceding words, ‘So turn away from them.’ Then He said, ‘I did not create the jinn and mankind except to worship Me’—meaning these believers who benefit from the reminder.”

They said: “This is an intended end that is actually realized, for the believers have indeed worshipped Him.” This interpretation was preferred by Abū Bakr ibn al-Tayyib, Judge Abū Ya‘lā, and others who hold that He does not act for a reason. They said—the wording is Judge Abū Ya‘lā’s:

“This is specific in meaning, not general, because the simple-minded, children, and the insane are not included in the address, even though they are human beings. Likewise, the disbelievers are excluded, as indicated by His words, ‘We have certainly created for Hell many of the jinn and mankind,’ and the rest of the verse. Whoever was created for wretchedness and Hell was not created for worship.”

I say: Although the position of these Karrāmiyyah and those who agree with them is stronger than that of the Jahmiyyah and the Mu‘tazilah in what they affirm of Allah’s wisdom, their interpretation of the verse—even though they agree in it with some of the early generations—is weak. It contradicts the majority’s position and what the verse indicates. The verse plainly intends a general meaning and makes this unmistakably clear. Had only the believers been intended, there would have been no difference between them and the angels, for they have all done what they were created for.

---

## Page 3756

and He would not have mentioned mankind and jinn in general. Yet the angels are not mentioned, even though the angels have rendered obedience and worship, unlike many among mankind and jinn.

Moreover, the context of the verse indicates that it censures and rebukes those among them who do not worship Allah, because Allah created them for a purpose, yet they did not fulfil the purpose for which they were created. Hence He followed it with His words:

“I do not want from them any provision, nor do I want them to feed Me.”

Affirming worship while denying this makes clear that He created them for worship, and did not want from them what masters want from their slaves: assistance through providing sustenance and food. Hence He subsequently said:

“Indeed, those who have wronged will have a share”—that is, a portion—“like the share of their counterparts”—meaning the earlier disbelievers. That is, a portion of the punishment. This is a threat against those among mankind and jinn who do not worship Him. He thus mentioned this threat immediately after this verse. From beginning to end, the surah contains a threat against those who do not worship Him.

He mentioned His punishment of them in this world and the Hereafter, saying at its beginning:

“By the winds scattering dust,”

up to His words:

“Indeed, what you are promised is true, and indeed, the Judgment will surely come to pass.”

Then He mentioned His words:

“Indeed, you are of differing opinions. Turned away from it is he who is turned away.”

Then He mentioned the threat of the Hereafter, saying:

“May the conjecturers be destroyed, those who are immersed in heedlessness and oblivious. They ask, ‘When is the Day of Judgment?’ It is the Day when they will be tormented over the Fire.”

Then He mentioned His promise to the believers, saying:

“Indeed, the righteous will be amid gardens and springs,”

up to His words:

“And on the earth are signs for those of sure faith, and in yourselves. Will you not then see? And in heaven is your provision and whatever you are promised. Then by the Lord of heaven and earth, it is certainly true, just as surely as you speak.”

Then He related the stories of those who believed and benefited from their faith, and those who disbelieved and whom He punished for their disbelief. He mentioned the story of Abraham, Lot and his people, and their punishment,

## Page 3757

then He said:

“And We left therein a sign for those who fear the painful punishment.”

“And in Moses, when We sent him to Pharaoh with clear authority.”

That is, the story of Moses also contains a sign. This is the view of the majority; some, such as Abu al-Faraj, mention no other interpretation. It has also been said that “And in Moses” is coordinated with His words:

“And on the earth are signs for those of sure faith.”

This interpretation is weak, because the accounts of Pharaoh and ʿĀd are of the same kind as that of the people of Lot: they mention the prophets, those who followed them, and those who opposed them. These accounts establish prophethood and demonstrate the ultimate fate of the obedient and the disobedient. As for His words, “And on the earth” and “And in yourselves,” those are signs pointing to the Maker—majestic is His glory—and they have already been mentioned.

Furthermore, a coordinated phrase is not separated from the phrase to which it is joined by such a lengthy passage. Moreover, the preceding statement is unsuitable as the phrase to which it is joined, namely His words:

“And We left therein a sign for those who fear the painful punishment.”

Then He said:

“And in ʿĀd.”

“And in Thamūd.”

Then He mentioned that He built heaven with strength, spread out the earth, and created pairs of all things so that you might take heed. Having explained the signs indicating the obligation to believe and worship Him, He commanded this, saying:

“So flee to Allah. Indeed, I am a clear warner to you from Him.”

“And do not set up another god alongside Allah”—to the end of the verse.

Then He explained that these deniers are like those who preceded them, so that the Messenger and the believers might take comfort in their example and patiently endure the harm inflicted on them by the disbelievers. He said:

“Likewise, no messenger came to those before them without their saying, ‘A magician or a madman!’”

“Did they pass this saying down to one another? Rather, they are a transgressing people.”

All of this entails commanding mankind and jinn to worship Him, obey Him, and obey His messengers, and that those who act deserve punishment in this world and the Hereafter. Thus, when He says thereafter:

“And I did not create

---

## Page 3758

the jinn and mankind except to worship Me.”

“I desire no provision from them, nor do I desire that they feed Me.”

This accords with what preceded it and is consistent with it. That is: “These whom I have commanded, I created only to worship Me. I desire nothing else from them—neither provision nor food.”

If it is said that He meant only the believers, this contradicts what preceded it in the surah. It would become something like an excuse for those who do not worship Him, whom Allah has condemned and rebuked. Ultimately, such a person could say: “You did not create me to worship and obey You. Had You created me for that, I would have been a worshipper. You created only these people to worship You. As for me, You created me to disbelieve in You, associate partners with You, reject Your messengers, and worship and obey Satan. I have done what You created me for, just as those believers have done what You created them for. Thus, I bear no guilt and deserve no punishment.”

These and similar implications necessarily follow from this position, whereas Allah’s speech is far above such things. They adopted this view only because Allah Most High does whatever He wills. They said: “Had He willed that they obey Him, He would have made them obedient, just as He made the believers obedient.”

The Qadariyyah say: “He willed nothing but obedience from either group, but He did not make either group obedient. Rather, willing here means commanding: He commands both groups to obey. The former worshipped Him by bringing their own volition and obedience into being, while the latter disobeyed Him by bringing their own volition and disobedience into being.”

Those who held the first position recognized the falsity of the Qadariyyah’s view, since Allah is the Creator, Lord, and Sovereign of everything. Whatever He wills comes to pass, and whatever He does not will does not come to pass. Nothing occurs in His dominion except what He wills, and nothing exists in His dominion except through His power, creation, and will, as indicated by revelation

---

## Page 3759

and reason. This is the position of all the Companions, the leading scholars of the Muslims, and the majority of Muslims; it is the position of Ahl al-Sunnah.

For this reason, those mentioned above adopted a restrictive interpretation of the verse. They could not reconcile belief in divine decree with His having created them to worship Him when they did not worship Him. They said: “Those whom He brought into being for Hell, He did not create to worship Him.” Whoever says, “He created His creatures so that the believers among them would worship Him,” has followed this approach.

As for “those who deny wisdom,” such as al-Ashʿarī and his followers, including al-Qādī Abū Bakr, Abū Yaʿlā, and others, their fundamental principle is that Allah does not create anything for the sake of anything else. Thus, He did not create anyone for worship or for any other purpose. According to them, there is no lām indicating purpose in the Quran. They may, however, acknowledge a lām indicating outcome, as in His words:

“Then Pharaoh’s household picked him up, only for him to become their enemy and a source of grief.”

They say the same concerning His words:

“We have certainly created for Hell many of the jinn and mankind.”

They mean that Hell was the eventual outcome for those people, and worship the eventual outcome for the believers, without the Creator having intended to create them for either end. Rather, He willed the creation of everything He created, not for any further purpose. This is their position, and it is weak for several reasons:

(First, the lām indicating an outcome for the sake of which the action was not intended applies only to the action of someone who is ignorant or powerless. An example of ignorance is His statement:

“Then Pharaoh’s household picked him up, only for him to become their enemy and a source of grief.”

Pharaoh did not know that this would be the outcome. An example of powerlessness is the saying:

“Bear children for death, and build for ruin.”

They know this outcome, but they are powerless to prevent it. Allah Most High, however, is All-Knowing and All-Powerful. It therefore cannot be said that His action is like that of someone who is ignorant and powerless.

---

## Page 3760

Second: All parties agree that Allah intended this end. The worship for which creation was brought into being is something He intended, by common agreement, and they themselves concede that Allah intended it. Yet when the lām indicates an outcome, the agent did not intend that outcome. These people say that He created them, willed their actions, and willed their punishment for those actions. Thus, everything that happens is willed by Him.

According to them, however, He never brings about one thing He wills for the sake of another, because acting for a purpose necessarily implies need. This is a plainly weak position. Those who interpret the verse restrictively gave a similar answer.

Another group said: The verse is general in scope, but worship here means His subjugating them, exercising His irresistible power over them, and subjecting them to His power and will, and that He has brought them to the felicity or wretchedness for which He created them. This is the answer given by Zayd ibn Aslam and a group of others, and it is the second interpretation of the verse.

Ibn Abī Hātim narrated from Ibn Jurayj, from Zayd ibn Aslam, concerning His words:

“I did not create the jinn and mankind except to worship Me.”

He said: “He fashioned them for wretchedness and felicity.” Wahb ibn Munabbih said: “He fashioned them for obedience, and He fashioned them for disobedience.”

This resembles the interpretation given by some to the Prophet’s words, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“Every child is born upon the natural disposition.”

They understood this to mean the felicity or wretchedness decreed for the child. A group held this view, including Ibn al-Mubārak and Ahmad ibn Hanbal, according to one of the two reports from him.

Mālik was told: “The adherents of the Qadariyyah use this hadith as evidence against us.” He replied: “Use its ending as evidence against them,” referring to his words:

“Allah knows best what they would have done.”

This response is appropriate as an answer to those who denied divine knowledge, as did a group among the early generations. These are the people known as the Qadariyyah in Mālik’s terminology.

## Page 3761

He went on to say:

Those who interpret this verse as meaning that “to worship Me” refers to the felicity or wretchedness for which He fashioned them and which He decreed for them, and who understand the hadith in the same way, take “to worship Me” to mean: “They submit to My will and power, becoming subjugated and humbled, so that My judgment and will take effect upon them, without their escaping My decree and predestination.” This meaning is correct in itself, even though the Qadariyyah deny it. Their denial of it is what made them people of innovation. Rather, Allah is the Creator of all things; whatever He wills comes to pass, and whatever He does not will does not come to pass. Among the Prophet’s supplications for refuge, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, are these words:

“I seek refuge in the perfect words of Allah, which neither the righteous nor the wicked can go beyond, from the evil of what He has created and brought into being. And I seek refuge in the perfect words of Allah from His anger, His punishment, and the evil of His servants.”

His perfect words are those by which He brought things into being, as He, exalted is He, says:

“His command, when He wills a thing, is only to say to it, ‘Be,’ and it is.”

Neither the righteous nor the wicked can go beyond these words. No one escapes the destiny decreed for him or goes beyond what has been written for him in the inscribed Tablet. The Quran indicates this meaning in numerous places, such as His words:

“We have certainly created for Hell…”

And His words:

“They would not believe unless Allah willed.”

“Do you not know that Allah knows whatever is in heaven and earth? Indeed, that is in a Record. Indeed, that is easy for Allah.”

And His words concerning sorcery:

“But they cannot harm anyone through it except by Allah’s permission.”

“Whoever Allah wills to guide, He opens his heart to Islam; and whoever He wills to lead astray, He makes his heart tight and constricted.”

There are other passages to the same effect. However, His words:

“I did not create the jinn and mankind except to worship Me.”

do not convey the meaning they adopted and sought to express—that all created things are subject to His will and irresistible power

## Page 3762

and His judgment. All created things fall within this; nothing is excluded.

He, exalted is He, has said:

And so the verse continues.

And His words:

“And those who shun the worship of false gods and turn to Allah.”

“And those who take protectors besides Him say, ‘We worship them only that they may bring us nearer to Allah.’”

And He said:

Such passages are numerous in the Quran. By worshipping Allah, He means only the worship commanded by the messengers: worshipping Him alone, without any partner. The polytheists do not worship Allah; rather, they worship Satan and whatever they invoke besides Allah. Whether they worship angels, prophets and righteous people, or fashioned statues and idols, these polytheists have worshipped something other than Allah Most High, just as Allah has stated.

How, then, can it be said that all human beings and jinn have worshipped Allah merely because Allah’s decree takes effect upon them? There is a clear distinction between their worshipping Him willingly and by choice, devoting their religion sincerely to Him and obeying His Messenger, and His subjecting them to servitude and carrying out His will concerning them, while their worship of others—Satan and idols—is itself among the things decreed.

This resembles the statement of one of the later figures: “I disbelieve in a Lord who is disobeyed.” He thus treats everything that happens as obedience, just as these people treated it as worship of Allah Most High because they are subject to His will. One of their shaykhs used to say of Iblīs: “If he disobeyed the command, he nevertheless obeyed the will.” But these people are antinomians who set aside the divine command.

## Page 3763

As for Zayd ibn Aslam, Wahb ibn Munabbih, and others like them, far be it from them to hold such a view! They were among those who held the divine commands and prohibitions, promises and threats in the greatest reverence. Rather, they intended to refute those who denied divine decree, claiming that Allah wills what does not happen and that things happen which He does not will. Their position effectively amounts to saying that He is unable to subject them to servitude and direct them according to His will. Zayd and the others therefore sought to refute their position—and how commendable their intention was! The question, however, concerns what the verse means.

The position of those antinomians resembles the statement that when the gnostic beholds the divine will, he is no longer subject to blame, and that when he beholds the decree—meaning the divine will—its cause is judged neither good nor bad. These and similar statements resemble those of the polytheists who said:

“If Allah had willed, neither we nor our fathers would have associated partners with Him, nor would we have forbidden anything.”

This has already been discussed at length. It has been explained that affirming Allah’s prior decree is right, but that it concerns the state the servant eventually reaches, not the disposition upon which he was created. As the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Every child is born upon the natural disposition. Then his parents make him a Jew, a Christian, or a Zoroastrian, just as an animal gives birth to a sound, whole animal. Do you see any mutilation in it?”

Through this analogy, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, explained that an animal is born sound and is subsequently mutilated, although that mutilation had been decreed for it. Likewise, the servant is born sound upon the natural disposition, then becomes corrupted by being made a Jew or a Christian, although it had already been written that this would happen.

The proponent of this view stated it only to explain what they were created for. This was also the intent of a group

## Page 3764

who interpreted worship as a reality common to all, rather than as the worship enjoined through the messengers. Thus, in Ibn Abī Talha’s commentary attributed to Ibn ‘Abbās, it is explained as:

This servitude is like that mentioned in His words:

The correct interpretation, however, is their submission to His decree without their choosing to do so, as when they surrender in times of calamity, and their compliance with those of His religious rulings that they dislike. Everyone must inevitably submit to His decree and His religious rulings. This is a sound meaning, discussed at length elsewhere, but it is not worship.

Likewise, some said:

“Except to submit to Me and humble themselves.”

They said: “The linguistic meaning of worship is humility and submission. Every created being among the jinn and humankind is subject to Allah Most High’s decree and humbled before His will. No one has the power to escape what he was created for.”

Abū al-Faraj mentioned this statement of Ibn ‘Abbās. He said: “This is explained by His words:

‘If you ask them who created them, they will surely say, “Allah.”’”

This verse accords with the interpretation, “Except to know Me,” as will be discussed below. Those who acknowledged that Allah was their Creator did not acknowledge this unwillingly, unlike their submission and subjection to Him, which may be unwilling. As for the acknowledgment itself, it is innate: they were created with it and offered it willingly.

## Page 3765

A fourth view has also been advanced. Ibn Abī Hātim narrated from Zā’idah, from al-Suddī, concerning His words:

“I did not create the jinn and humankind except to worship Me.”

He said: “He created them for worship. Some worship is beneficial, and some is not. ‘If you ask them who created the heavens and the earth and subjected the sun and the moon, they will surely say, “Allah.”’ This acknowledgment on their part is worship, but it does not benefit them while they associate partners with Him.”

This meaning is sound. However, the polytheist worships Satan and whatever he sets up as an equal to Allah; Allah is not being worshipped. Merely acknowledging the Maker while associating partners with Allah is not called worship of Allah. Rather, one should describe it as He does:

“Most of them do not believe in Allah without also associating partners with Him.”

Their belief in the Creator is thus coupled with their association of partners with Him. As for worship, the hadith states: “Allah says: ‘I am utterly free of any need for partners. Whoever performs a deed in which he associates someone else with Me, I disavow him, and that deed belongs entirely to the one he associated with Me.’”

Thus, although the polytheists devote some of their worship to Allah, He accepts none of it. Rather, all of it belongs to those they associate with Him. They have therefore not worshipped Allah, glorified is He.

Similar to this is the interpretation of those who said: “Except to affirm My oneness. The believer affirms His oneness in both hardship and ease, whereas the unbeliever affirms His oneness in hardship and affliction, but not amid blessings and ease. This is illustrated by His words: ‘When they board a ship, they call upon Allah, devoting their worship sincerely to Him.’”

A fifth view has also been advanced. Ibn Abī Hātim related it from Ibn Jurayj, who said: “To know Me.” He said: “It was also reported from Qatādah.” Al-Baghawī attributed it to Mujāhid, saying: “Mujāhid said: ‘Except to know Me.’” He then said: “This is a sound interpretation, for had He not created them, His existence and oneness would not have been known. Its evidence is His words:

‘If you ask them who created the heavens and the earth and subjected the sun and the moon, they will surely say, “Allah.”’”

The response is: This meaning is sound; the fact that He was known only through His creation of them implies

---

## Page 3766

that their creation is a prerequisite for their knowing Him; it does not imply that the knowledge they acquired is the purpose for which they were created. This is similar to al-Suddī’s statement, for they remain polytheists despite this general acknowledgment, as He says:

“And when your Lord took from the children of Adam…”

But this is not worship. These “four views” represent the position of those who recognized that the verse is general and therefore sought to interpret it as referring to a form of worship encompassing all humans and jinn. They believed that interpreting it as worship in its familiar sense—obedience to Allah and obedience to His messengers—would necessarily imply that such worship actually occurred among them, whereas it did not. They therefore sought to interpret it as a form of worship that actually occurred. They thought that interpreting it as worship that did not occur would commit them to the position of the Qadariyyah: that He created them to worship Him, but they disobeyed Him independently of His will and power. Thus they sought to avoid the position of the Qadariyyah, and they are excusable for seeking to avoid it.

Yet they interpreted the verse in a way that was not intended. This happens to many people concerning verses whose apparent meanings the people of innovation invoke as evidence. For example, the Rāfidah invoke His words:

“And wipe your heads and your feet”

as evidence for wiping the tops of the feet. We then find their opponents advancing weak explanations. One says that “your feet” takes the genitive case through proximity to an adjacent word, as in the expression juhr dabbin kharib (“a ruined lizard’s burrow”), and other similarly weak explanations. The same applies to what they have said concerning the statement, “Thus Adam prevailed over Moses in argument,” and similar texts.

The “sixth view”—although Abū al-Faraj mentioned only four views concerning the verse—is the position held by the majority of Muslims: Allah created them to worship Him, meaning to do what they were commanded to do. Hence Muslims, past and present, are found citing this verse as evidence for this

meaning, even in their exhortations, reminders, and accounts, as in the account of Ibrāhīm ibn Adham: “You were not created for this, nor were you commanded to do this.” A report from the Israelite tradition states:

## Page 3769

Those who hold this view then divide into two groups: Ahl al-Sunnah, who affirm divine decree, and those who deny it. Thus, there are “seven” views concerning the verse and “five” concerning divine wisdom.

Ahl al-Sunnah, who affirm divine decree, say that His words:

“I did not create jinn and mankind except to worship Me”

do not necessarily mean that they will actually worship Him, as the proponents of the preceding views have maintained. Nor do they entail denying what is divinely decreed—that something should exist in His dominion which He does not will, or that He should will something which does not come to pass—as the Qadariyyah maintain. The latter say that the purpose for which He created them was not realized because He wills things that do not happen, and things happen that He does not will.

The former said: “If whatever He wills comes to pass, and whatever He does not will does not come to pass, then whatever has not occurred was not willed by Him. Thus, whatever worship has not occurred was not willed by Him.” This reasoning is sound. They then said: “Whatever He created them for, He must will to create. Since He did not will to create this, He did not create them for it.”

The fundamental error of both groups is their assumption that He wills the occurrence of whatever He created them for. The former say that He wills to create it, while the latter say that He wills it to occur on their part, meaning that He commands them to do it. They do not acknowledge any will of His concerning human actions apart from His command, which people disobey.

For this reason, they said: “Things happen that He does not will, and He wills things that do not happen,” just as they say: “People do what He has forbidden them and neglect what He has commanded them.” This meaning is correct if what is intended is His religious command.

However, the Qadariyyah, who deny divine decree, understand “He willed” only to mean “He commanded.” Thus, in their view, human actions that are not acts of obedience are things He does not

---

## Page 3770

will, for, in their view, He does not create them. If He does not create something, He has not willed it, for all Muslims agree that whatever He wills to create, He creates.

The Qadariyyah do not dispute this. They do not dispute that whatever He Himself wills to do, He does, and that He is able to do whatever He wills to do. However, in their view, human actions do not fall within His creation, His power, or His will, nor within what He wills to do Himself. Rather, His will concerning them means only His command. They therefore say: He created them to worship Him—that they themselves should perform this worship—and He has commanded them to do so. If they do not perform it, this amounts to disobeying His command.

Those who affirm divine decree, however, say: Whatever He wills comes to pass, and whatever He does not will does not come to pass. He, glorified be He, is the Creator of all things:

“Had your Lord willed, He would have made mankind one community.”

“Had Allah willed, they would not have fought one another.”

“Had your Lord willed, they would not have done it.”

And there are other similar passages. Thus, if He created them for the worship He has commanded, yet they do not perform it, He has not willed that it take place. For had He willed it to take place, He would have brought it about. Nevertheless, He has commanded them to perform it, loves and approves of their doing so, and wills that they do so in the religious sense—a will embodied in His command to worship.

This makes the meaning of the verse clear. His words:

“I did not create jinn and mankind except to worship Me”

are similar to His words:

“So that you may complete the prescribed period and glorify Allah for guiding you,”

and His words:

“Thus He has subjected them to you, so that you may glorify Allah for guiding you,”

and His words:

“So that it may not circulate solely among the wealthy among you,”

and His words:

“That is so you may know that Allah knows whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on earth

---

## Page 3771

and that Allah has knowledge of all things,”

and His words:

“Allah is the One who created seven heavens, and of the earth their like,”

and the rest of the verse. Likewise, His words:

“We sent no messenger except to be obeyed by Allah’s permission.”

He sent the messenger only to be obeyed, yet he may be obeyed or disobeyed. Likewise, He created them only for worship, yet they may worship or may not.

There are many similar passages in the Quran explaining that He did what He did so that they would magnify Him, act justly and not commit injustice, know His attributes, and fulfil the other things Allah has commanded His servants, loved for them, and approved of from them—things in which their happiness, perfection, well-being, and success lie if they do them. Yet some of them do so, while others do not.

He, glorified be He, did not say that He performed the first act so that He Himself would perform the second, or so that He would bring about the second in them. Thus, He did not state that He created them in order to make them worshippers. For when He brings about means to ends that He Himself is to accomplish, He must inevitably accomplish those ends. It is impossible for Him to do one thing in order to do a second, yet not do the second. Rather, He stated that He performed the first act so that they would perform the second. They would therefore be the ones performing it, and through their action they would attain their happiness and what He loves and approves for them. Thus, both what He loves and what they love would be attained. As explained earlier, the ultimate purpose of everything He creates and commands is beloved to Allah and His servants. It embodies wisdom on His part and mercy toward His servants.

Thus, had they done that for which He created them, it would have brought about both what He loves and what they love. But they did not do it, and so they deserved what is deserved by one who disobeys Him, opposes His command, and neglects to do that for which he was created: the punishment of

---

this world and the Hereafter. He, glorified be He, willed that those who worshipped Him should do so, and thus made them worshippers and Muslims through His will, His guidance of them, and His making faith beloved to them. As He, Most High, said:

“But Allah has endeared faith to you and made it beautiful in your hearts, and has made disbelief, defiance, and disobedience hateful to you. Those are the rightly guided.”

For these people, He willed their worship both in creation and in command: He commanded them to worship Him and, through His act of creation, made them do so. As for the second group, He did not will to create them as worshippers, although He commanded them to worship Him. And Allah, glorified be He, knows best.

## Page 3773

He—may Allah have mercy on him—was asked:

To explain the distinction, in “will,” “permission,” “writing,” “judgment,” “decree,” “prohibition,” and similar matters, between what pertains to religion and accords with Allah’s love, pleasure, and revealed command, and what pertains to creation and accords with His will concerning creation.

He replied:

Praise be to Allah.

These matters—will, permission, writing, judgment, decree, prohibition, and others such as commanding, raising up, and sending—fall into two categories in the Book of Allah:

The first concerns religious matters that Allah Most High loves and is pleased with. He rewards those who observe them, admits them to Paradise, and grants them victory in this worldly life and in the Hereafter. Through these matters, He supports His servants: His pious allies, His successful party, and His righteous servants.

The second concerns events within creation that Allah has ordained and decreed, which encompass believers and disbelievers, the righteous and the wicked, the people of Paradise and the people of Hell, Allah’s allies and His enemies, those who obey Him—whom He loves and who love Him, and upon whom He and His angels send blessings—and those who disobey Him, whom He hates and abhors, and whom Allah curses and those who curse also curse.

---

## Page 3774

Whoever considers these matters from this perspective perceives the reality of creation and existence: he sees all things as created by Allah, governed by His will, and subject to His wisdom. Whatever Allah wills occurs, even if people do not will it; and whatever He does not will does not occur, even if people will it. None can overturn His judgment or repel His command. He sees that Allah, glorified be He, is the Lord and Sovereign of everything; to Him belong creation and command.

Everything other than Him is subject to His lordship, governed and subdued, possessing no power over its own harm or benefit, death, life, or resurrection. Rather, it is a servant utterly in need of Allah Most High in every respect, whereas Allah has no need of it, just as He has no need of any created being. This perception is itself true. Yet “one group” has fallen short of it—the Magian Qadariyyah—while “another group” has stopped at it—the polytheistic Qadariyyah.

As for the former, they are those who claim that some created things, such as human actions, fall outside Allah’s power, will, and creation. The extremists among them denied His eternal knowledge and His prior recording of events. These were the first of the Qadariyyah to arise in this community, and the Companions and the early generations of the community refuted them and disavowed them.

As for “the second group,” they are worse than the former. They comprise various groups devoted to spiritual wayfaring, aspiration, worship, Sufism, spiritual poverty, and the like. They perceive this reality and recognize that Allah is the Creator of all created things, and thus the Creator of human actions, and that He wills everything that occurs. Yet beyond this, they make no distinction between faith and disbelief, recognition and denial, truth and falsehood, the rightly guided and the misguided, the upright and the wayward, a prophet and a pretender to prophethood, or an ally of Allah and an enemy; nor

---

## Page 3775

between one with whom Allah is pleased and one who incurs His displeasure; nor between one whom Allah loves and one whom He detests; nor between justice and injustice, dutifulness and disobedience, the deeds of the people of Paradise and those of the people of Hell, or the righteous and the wicked. For they perceive what all beings share: the prior decree, the unfailingly effective will, the all-encompassing power, and the creation of all things. They perceive what created beings have in common but are blind to what distinguishes them.

Thus they become among those addressed by His words, Most High:

“Shall We then treat the Muslims like the criminals?”

“What is the matter with you? How do you judge?”

And His words, Most High:

“Or shall We treat those who believe and do righteous deeds like those who spread corruption on earth? Or shall We treat the God-fearing like the wicked?”

And His words, Most High:

“Or do those who commit evil deeds think that We will make them like those who believe and do righteous deeds?”

“And your Lord’s gracious word was fulfilled for the Children of Israel because of their patience.”

Another example is the saying of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“I seek refuge in the perfect words of Allah, beyond which neither the righteous nor the wicked can pass, from the evil of what He has created, brought forth, and fashioned; from the evil of what descends from heaven and what ascends into it; from the evil of what He has brought forth in the earth and what emerges from it; from the evil of the trials of night and day; and from the evil of every visitor by night, except one who comes with good, O Most Merciful.”

The words beyond which neither the righteous nor the wicked can pass are not His commands and prohibitions in religious law, for the wicked have disobeyed His commands and prohibitions. Rather, they are the words through which things come into being.

As for the words pertaining to religion, which contain His commands and prohibitions in religious law, these include the divine scriptures: the Torah, the Gospel, the Psalms, and the Quran. And He said:

## Page 3777

He—may Allah Most High have mercy on him—was asked:

“Some people say, ‘Allah’s will applies to both the past and the future,’ while others say, ‘The will applies to the future, not the past.’ Which is correct?”

He replied:

The past unfolded by Allah’s will, and the future will not come to pass unless Allah wills it.

Whoever says concerning the past, “Allah created the heavens, if Allah wills,” or “He sent Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, if Allah wills,” is mistaken. Whoever says, “Allah created the heavens by His will and sent Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, by His will,” or something similar, is correct.

Whoever says that anything comes into existence without Allah’s will is mistaken. Whoever says, “Whatever Allah wills comes to pass, and whatever He does not will does not come to pass,” is correct.

Everything that has already occurred has certainly occurred by Allah’s will. Allah certainly created the heavens by His will and certainly sent Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, by His will. Every human being in existence has certainly been created by Allah through His will. If Allah wills to change a created being from one state to another, He is able to do so. Thus, whatever He has created has certainly come into being by His will; and if Allah wills to change it, He certainly changes it by His will.

And Allah knows best.
