## Page 3778

What do the esteemed imams of the Muslims say concerning a group who disagree about Allah’s decree and predestination, both its good and its evil? Some of them hold that good comes from Allah Most High, whereas evil comes solely from one’s own self. Give us a ruling, and may you be rewarded.

The shaykh—may Allah be pleased with him—replied:

The doctrine of the people of the Sunnah and the community is that Allah Most High is the Creator, Lord and Sovereign of all things (*). There is no Lord besides Him and no Creator other than Him. Whatever He wills comes to pass, and whatever He does not will does not come to pass. He has power over all things and knowledge of all things.

The servant is commanded to obey Allah and His Messenger and forbidden to disobey Allah and His Messenger. If he obeys, that is a blessing; if he disobeys, he deserves blame and punishment. Allah has the conclusive argument against him, while no one has any argument against Allah Most High. All of this occurs by Allah’s decree, predestination, will and power. Yet He loves obedience, commands it, rewards those who practise it for doing so, and honours them. He hates disobedience, forbids it, punishes those who commit it, and humiliates them.

Whatever blessings come to the servant, Allah has bestowed them upon him; and whatever evil befalls him is because of his sins

and acts of disobedience, as Allah Most High says:

And He says:

That is, whatever prosperity, victory or guidance comes to you is a blessing Allah has bestowed upon you; and whatever sorrow, humiliation or evil befalls you is because of your sins and misdeeds. All things come to pass through Allah’s will, power and creation. The servant must therefore believe in Allah’s decree and predestination and have certainty in His law and commands.

Whoever considers the reality of divine predestination while disregarding the commands and prohibitions, the promises of reward and threats of punishment, resembles the polytheists. Whoever considers the commands and prohibitions but denies divine decree and predestination resembles the Magians. But whoever believes in both, praising Allah Most High when he does good and seeking His forgiveness when he does wrong, while knowing that this occurs by Allah’s decree and predestination, is among the believers.

When Adam—peace be upon him—sinned, he repented, and his Lord chose him and guided him. Iblīs, however, persisted and sought to justify himself, so Allah cursed him and banished him. Whoever repents follows Adam’s way, while whoever persists and invokes predestination as an excuse follows the way of Iblīs. Thus, the blessed follow their father, while the wretched follow their enemy, Iblīs.

We therefore ask Allah to guide us to the straight path, the path of those upon whom He has bestowed His favour: the prophets, the steadfastly truthful, the martyrs and the righteous. Amen, O Lord of all worlds.

## Page 3780

Is this hadith authentic? Did Allah take them Himself, or did He command one of the angels to take them? And what of the other hadith stating:

“When Allah created Adam, He showed him his descendants to the right and to the left, then said, ‘These are for the Fire, and I care not; and these are for Paradise, and I care not.’”

This is recorded in the Sahīh.

He replied—may Allah be pleased with him:

Yes, this meaning is well known through numerous reports from the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him. Among them is the report in Mālik’s Muwattaʾ, the Sunan of Abū Dāwūd and al-Nasāʾī, and elsewhere, from Muslim ibn Yasār—and, in another wording, from Nuʿaym ibn Rabīʿah—that ʿUmar ibn al-Khattāb was asked about the verse:

“And when your Lord took from the children of Adam, from their loins…”

—and the rest of the verse. ʿUmar then narrated from the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him. In another wording, he said that he had heard the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, being asked about it. The Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, said:

“Allah created Adam, then wiped his back with His right hand and brought forth descendants from him. He said, ‘I created these for Paradise, and they will perform the deeds of the people of Paradise.’ Then He wiped his back and brought forth descendants from him. He said, ‘I created

---

## Page 3781

these for the Fire, and they will perform the deeds of the people of the Fire.’ A man asked, ‘O Messenger of Allah, what, then, is the point of deeds?’ The Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, replied, ‘When Allah creates a man for Paradise, He causes him to perform the deeds of the people of Paradise until he dies performing one of their deeds, and thereby admits him to Paradise. When He creates a man for the Fire, He causes him to perform the deeds of the people of the Fire until he dies performing one of their deeds, and thereby admits him to the Fire.’”

In the hadith narrated by al-Hakam ibn Sufyān, from Thābit, from Anas ibn Mālik, he said that the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, said:

“Allah took a handful and said, ‘To Paradise, by My mercy.’ And He took a handful and said, ‘To the Fire, and I care not.’”

This hadith and others like it concern two matters.

The first is the prior divine decree: Allah, glorified be He, knew who would belong to Paradise and who would belong to the Fire before they performed their deeds. This is a truth in which one must believe. Indeed, the imams, including Mālik, al-Shāfiʿī and Ahmad, explicitly stated that whoever denies this has disbelieved. Rather, one must believe that Allah knew everything that would happen before it happened. One must also believe what He has told us: that He wrote it down and made it known before it came to pass. Thus, in Sahīh Muslim, ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAmr narrated that the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said:

“Allah decreed the destinies of all creatures fifty thousand years before He created the heavens and the earth, and His Throne was upon the water.”

In Sahīh al-Bukhārī and elsewhere, ʿImrān ibn Husayn narrated that the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said:

“Allah existed, and nothing else existed. His Throne was upon the water. He wrote everything in the Record and created the heavens and the earth.”

In another wording:

“Then He created the heavens and the earth.”

## Page 3783

, they will be enabled to perform the deeds of the wretched.’ Then he recited the words of the Most High:

‘As for the one who gives and fears Allah, and believes in the best reward, We will make easy for him the way of ease. But as for the one who withholds and considers himself self-sufficient, and denies the best reward, We will make easy for him the way of hardship.’”

It is also reported in the Sahīh:

“He was asked, ‘O Messenger of Allah, is it already known who will be among the people of Paradise and who will be among the people of the Fire?’ He replied, ‘Yes.’ He was then asked, ‘What, then, is the point of deeds?’ He said, ‘Perform deeds, for everyone will be enabled to do that for which he was created.’”

Thus the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, explained that Allah knows who will be among the people of Paradise and who will be among the people of the Fire, and that He has recorded this. He forbade them to rely on this record and abandon deeds, as those who deviate from the truth do. He said that everyone will be enabled to do that for which he was created: the blessed are enabled to perform the deeds of the blessed, and the wretched are enabled to perform the deeds of the wretched. This is among the clearest explanations possible.

Allah, glorified and exalted be He, knows things as they truly are. He has appointed causes through which things come about, and He knows that they will come about through those causes. For example, He knows that a man will have a child by having intercourse with a woman and causing her to conceive. If that man were to say, “If Allah knows that I will have a child, there is no need for intercourse,” he would be foolish, for Allah knows that the child will come into being through the intercourse He decrees.

Likewise, He knows that a person’s crops will grow through the water with which he irrigates them and the seeds he sows. If that person were to say, “If He knows that this will happen, there is no need to sow,” he would be ignorant and misguided, for Allah knows that it will happen through those means. Likewise, if Allah knows that one person will satisfy his hunger by eating, another will quench his thirst by drinking, and another will die by being killed, then the causes through which Allah knows these things will occur must necessarily take place.

---

## Page 3784

Likewise, if Allah knows that one person will be blessed in the Hereafter and another wretched, we say: That is because the latter performs the deeds of the wretched. Allah knows that he will become wretched through these deeds. To say, “He will be wretched even if he does not perform them,” would be false, for Allah admits no one to the Fire except on account of his sins. As the Most High says:

“I will surely fill Hell with you and all those among them who follow you.”

Thus He swore that He would fill it with Iblīs and his followers. Whoever follows Iblīs has disobeyed Allah Most High. Allah does not punish a servant for what He knows he will do until he actually does it. Thus, when the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, was asked about the children of the polytheists, he said:

“Allah knows best what they would have done.”

This means that Allah knows what they would have done had they reached maturity. It has been reported that a messenger will be sent to them on the Day of Resurrection: whoever obeys him will enter Paradise, and whoever disobeys him will enter the Fire. The obedience or disobedience that Allah knew of them will thereby become manifest.

Likewise, Allah created Paradise for those who believe in Him and obey Him. Whoever He has decreed to be among them, He enables to believe and obey. If someone says, “I will enter Paradise whether I am a believer or a disbeliever, if Allah knows that I am among its people,” he is fabricating a lie against Allah. For what Allah knows is that he will enter it through faith. If he has no faith, he is not the one whom Allah knows will enter Paradise. Rather, whoever is not a believer but a disbeliever is known to Allah as one of the people of the Fire, not one of the people of Paradise.

For this reason, He commanded people to supplicate, seek Allah’s help, and employ other such means. Whoever says, “I will neither supplicate nor ask, relying instead on divine decree,” is also mistaken, because Allah has made supplication

---

## Page 3785

and asking means of obtaining His forgiveness, mercy, guidance, help, and provision. If He decrees that a servant will obtain some good through supplication, it will not be obtained without supplication. Whatever Allah has decreed and known concerning His servants’ circumstances and ultimate outcomes, He has decreed through causes. He brings decreed events to pass at their appointed times. Nothing in this world or the Hereafter occurs without a cause, and Allah is the Creator of causes and their effects.

For this reason, some have said:

“Relying on causes is to associate partners with Allah, contrary to belief in His oneness; denying that causes have a causal role is a deficiency of reason; and disregarding causes altogether undermines the revealed Law.”

Causes alone do not necessarily produce their effects. When rain falls and seeds are sown, that alone is insufficient for plants to grow. There must also be a wind that fosters growth by Allah’s permission, and their failure to emerge must be averted. All the necessary conditions must therefore be fulfilled and all impediments removed, and all of this occurs by Allah’s decree and predestination. Likewise, a child is not born merely because semen is deposited in the vagina. How many men have ejaculated without fathering a child! Rather, Allah must will the child’s creation, so that the woman conceives and nurtures it in her womb, together with all the other conditions and the removal of impediments necessary to complete its creation.

The same applies to the Hereafter: a person does not attain blessedness through deeds alone; rather, deeds are a cause. For this reason, the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said:

“None of you will enter Paradise by his deeds.” They asked, “Not even you, O Messenger of Allah?” He replied, “Not even I, unless Allah envelops me in mercy and bounty from Him.”

Yet He has said:

“Enter Paradise for what you used to do.”

Here, the preposition bi- indicates causation—that is, “because of your deeds.” What the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, negated was bi- indicating exchange, as when one says, “I bought this in exchange for that.” In other words, deeds are not sufficient payment or a sufficient price for entering Paradise. Rather, there must also be Allah’s pardon

## Page 3786

and His bounty and mercy. Through His pardon He erases sins, through His mercy He brings good things, and through His bounty He multiplies blessings.

Another group began demanding recompense from Allah as a hired worker demands it from his employer, relying on their own ability, strength, and deeds, and as slaves demand it from their masters. These people are ignorant and misguided. Allah did not command His servants to do what He commanded out of any need for it, nor did He forbid them what He forbade out of stinginess. Rather, He commanded what benefits them and forbade what harms them. As He, glorified be He, said:

When a king commands his slaves to do something, he does so because he needs their service. They carry it out with strength that he did not create for them, and so they demand recompense for it. Allah Most High, however, has no need of any of His creation. If they do good, they do so for themselves; if they do evil, its consequences fall upon them. The good they earn is theirs, and the evil they earn counts against them.

“Whoever does righteousness—it is for his own soul; and whoever does evil—it is against it. And your Lord is not ever unjust to His servants.”

He is the One who gives and withholds, lowers and raises, honours and humiliates, enriches and impoverishes, leads astray and guides, and grants happiness and brings misery. ## Page 3796

Shaykh al-Islām—may Allah Most High have mercy on him—was asked about the goodness of Allah Most High’s will to create His creatures and bring beings into existence, and whether He creates for a reason or without one:

If it is said that He creates without a reason, this would be purposeless—exalted is Allah above that. If it is said that He creates for a reason, then if you say that this reason has always existed, it follows that its effect must also have always existed. If you say that it came into existence, it follows that it must itself have a cause, yet an infinite regress is impossible.

He replied:

All praise is due to Allah, Lord of all worlds. This is a weighty question, among the greatest questions people have discussed, among the most extensive in its ramifications and subsidiary issues, and among those occasioning the most doubts and perplexities.

It concerns Allah Most High’s attributes, names, actions, and rulings, including His commands, prohibitions, promises, and threats. It pertains to both His creation and His command, so everything in existence is connected to this question: all created things are connected to it, and it concerns the Creator, glorified is He. Likewise, all revealed laws—their commands, prohibitions, promises, and threats—are connected to it. It also concerns questions of divine decree and command, and questions of divine attributes and actions. These encompass the principal fields of human knowledge. Thus, jurisprudence, which concerns commands and prohibitions, is connected to this question.

---

## Page 3797

People have also discussed “the reasons underlying religious rulings, commands, and prohibitions,” such as the commands to affirm Allah’s oneness, be truthful and just, establish prayer, pay zakah, fast, and perform Hajj, and the prohibitions against associating partners with Allah, lying, wrongdoing, and indecencies. Did He prescribe these things for a wise purpose, a benefit, and a reason that called for them? Or was this solely a matter of His will and sheer volition? Are the reasons assigned by revealed law to be understood as motives and impetuses, or as indicators and signs? Is it compatible with wisdom for Allah to forbid affirming His oneness, truthfulness, and justice, and to command associating partners with Him, lying, and wrongdoing, or not?

People have also discussed Allah Most High’s freedom from injustice: is He free from it despite having the power to commit it, or is injustice intrinsically impossible and therefore incapable of occurring? They have discussed Allah’s love, pleasure, anger, and displeasure: do these mean His will, or are they the created reward and punishment, or are they attributes more specific than will?

They have disagreed concerning the disbelief, wickedness, and disobedience that occur on earth: does He will, love, and approve of them just as He wills and loves everything else that happens? Or do they occur independently of His power and will, while He is unable to guide someone who is astray or lead astray someone who is rightly guided? Or do they occur by His power and will, such that nothing occurs in His dominion that He does not will, and He has consummate wisdom in all that He creates, while He hates and abhors these things and detests those who commit them, neither loves corruption nor approves of disbelief for His servants, and does not will it by His religious will, which entails His love and pleasure, even if He wills it by His universal will, which encompasses whatever He has ordained and decreed?

The subsidiary questions arising from this fundamental issue are numerous; this is not the place to examine them exhaustively.

---

## Page 3798

Because of the conflicting considerations and ambiguities surrounding this fundamental issue, people have adopted the three possibilities mentioned in the question. Each has been upheld by groups of people, both Muslims and non-Muslims.

The first possibility:

This is the position of those who say that He created His creatures and prescribed His commands for no reason, motive, or impetus, but solely by His will and sheer volition. This is the position of many speculative theologians, jurists, and others who affirm divine decree and profess adherence to the Sunnah. Groups among the followers of Mālik, al-Shāfi‘ī, Ahmad, and others have held this view. It is also the position of al-Ash‘arī and his followers, and of many Zāhirī “opponents of analogical reasoning in jurisprudence,” such as Ibn Hazm and others like him.

One of their arguments is that if He created creation for a reason, He would be deficient without it and acquire perfection through it. For, with respect to Him, either the existence and nonexistence of that reason are equal, or its existence is preferable. If the former is true, He cannot act for its sake. If the latter is true, then its existence is established as preferable for Him; He would therefore acquire perfection through it and would consequently have been deficient before it.

Another of their arguments is what the questioner mentioned: if the cause were eternal, the effect would necessarily have to be prior as well. For although the final cause precedes the effect in knowledge and intention—as it is said, “What comes first in thought comes last in execution, and what comes first as a goal comes last in attainment,” and it is said that the final cause is what makes the agent an agent—there is no doubt that, in actual existence, it comes after the effect. Thus, whoever performs an act

---

## Page 3799

for an objective he seeks through that act attains that objective only after the act. If that objective, which is the cause, is assumed to be eternal, then the act must all the more be eternal.

Thus, if it were said that He acts for an eternal reason, this would entail that nothing ever comes into being, contrary to what is observed. If, however, it were said that He acts for a temporally originated reason, two untenable consequences would follow.

The first is that He would be a locus of temporal occurrences. For if the reason is separate from Him and produces no effect upon Him, its existence cannot be preferable to its nonexistence with respect to Him. If it is assumed to produce an effect upon Him, that effect would be temporally originated, and temporal occurrences would therefore subsist in Him.

The second untenable consequence is that this entails an infinite regress in two respects.

First, that temporally originated reason sought through the act is itself something Allah Most High brings into being through His power and will. If He brings it into being for no reason, this entails purposelessness, as explained above. If He does so for a reason, the same alternatives arise again. Thus, if everything He brings into being is brought into being for a reason, and that reason is itself something He brings into being, an infinite regress of temporal occurrences necessarily follows.

Second, that reason must be intended either for its own sake or for another reason. If it is intended for its own sake, it cannot have a temporal beginning, because Allah Most High does not delay bringing into being something He wills for its own sake and has the power to bring about. If it is intended for the sake of something else, the same argument applies to that other thing, and an infinite regress necessarily follows. These and similar arguments are advanced by those who deny that Allah Most High’s actions and rulings are based on reasons.

The second possibility:

This is the position of those who hold the final cause to be eternal, just as they hold the efficient cause to be

---

## Page 3800

eternal, as various groups of Muslims maintain—as will be explained—and as do those among the philosophers who affirm the eternity of the world. The fundamental premise of their position is that the Originator of the world is a complete cause that necessarily entails its effect, such that its effect cannot come after it.

Their strongest argument is as follows:

“If everything required for Him to act existed from eternity, then the effect must also have existed from eternity, because the effect of a complete cause cannot come after it. If it did, not all the conditions for the act would have existed from eternity. By a complete cause, we mean nothing other than that which necessarily entails its effect. Thus, if the effect is assumed not to accompany it, the cause would not be complete.

“If, however, the complete cause—that is, everything required for the act, constituting the fully sufficient cause of its existence and comprising all the conditions whose existence necessarily entails the existence of the act—did not exist in its entirety from eternity, then, if the effect subsequently came into existence, a new cause must have arisen. Otherwise, one of the two alternatives for a contingent thing would have been favored without a determining factor. If there is a newly arisen cause, the same argument applies to its coming into existence as applies to the first temporal occurrence, and an infinite regress necessarily follows.”

They say: “Denying the existence of a complete cause that necessarily entails its effect therefore entails either an infinite regress or a preference without a determining factor.”

Most of these philosophers also affirm a final cause for the act, identifying it with the efficient cause itself. Yet they contradict themselves: they affirm a final cause for Him and a final cause for His act, while also saying that He has no will, but rather produces effects by the necessity of His essence, not as an agent acting by choice. Their position is false on many grounds.

---

## Page 3801

One is as follows:

This position entails that nothing comes into being, and that whatever does come into being does so without being brought into being by an originator. Clearly, the falsity of this is more evident than the falsity of an infinite regress or of a preference without a determining factor. For a complete cause that necessarily entails its effect is accompanied by that effect, and no part of its effect can come after it. Thus, no temporal occurrence can arise from this complete cause. Yet there is nothing from which contingent things can proceed other than the intrinsically necessary being, whom these philosophers call a complete cause. If temporal occurrences cannot proceed from Him, and there is nothing else to bring them into being, it follows that they come into being without an originator.

(Moreover, suppose that something other than Him brought them into being. If it were intrinsically necessary, the same argument would apply to it as to the first necessary being. Their fundamental premise is that the intrinsically necessary being is a complete cause whose effect must accompany it. According to their position, therefore, no temporal occurrence can proceed from a complete cause, either through an intermediary or without one. For if that intermediary were a necessary concomitant of His existence, it would be eternal along with Him, making it impossible for temporal occurrences to proceed from it. If it came into being, the same argument would apply to it as to any other temporal occurrence.

If, on the other hand, the originator of temporal occurrences were assumed not to be intrinsically necessary, it would be contingent and dependent upon a necessitating cause to bring it into existence. Then, if it were said to have been brought into being, it would itself be one of the temporal occurrences. If it were said to be eternal, it would have a complete cause that necessarily entailed it, and temporal occurrences could not then arise from it. For neither a contingent being nor any of its attributes or acts can exist except through the intrinsically necessary being.

Thus, if temporal occurrences are assumed to arise from an eternal contingent being that is the effect of an eternal cause, the question is: has a cause arisen within it

---

## Page 3802

that entails their coming into being, or not?

If it is said that no cause has arisen, this entails a preference without a determining factor. If it is said that a cause has arisen, this entails an infinite regress, as explained above.

(The second argument demonstrating the falsity of their position is as follows:

The substance of the argument is that, unless there is an eternal cause, either an infinite regress or a preference without a determining factor must follow. Yet you consider an infinite regress possible. Indeed, their fundamental position is that these temporal occurrences form an infinite succession, one after another, and that the movements of the celestial sphere prepare receptive substrates for newly arising forms to emanate upon them from the eternal cause—whether you say that this cause is the active intellect or the Necessary Being, from whom they proceed through the intellects or other intermediaries. Since you consider an infinite regress possible, temporal occurrences could arise from something other than a cause that necessarily entails its effect, even if this involves an infinite regress. Indeed, this is better, in light of both revelation and reason, than your position.

For revelation states that Allah created the heavens and the earth in six days. This is agreed upon by the adherents of the religious communities: Muslims, Jews, and Christians.

If it is said that He created them through a cause that had come into being before that, this would be better, in light of revelation, than your claim that they are eternal and have existed with Him from all eternity. It would also be preferable on rational grounds, for reason provides no evidence that these celestial spheres are eternal that could stand against revelation. This rational argument establishes only that nothing comes into being except through a cause that has itself come into being. Thus, if it is said that Allah Most High created the heavens and the earth through something that had come into being before that, your rational argument contains nothing that disproves this.

(The third argument is as follows:

The coming into being of one temporal occurrence after another without limit is either rationally possible or impossible. If it is rationally impossible, it follows that all temporal occurrences

---

## Page 3803

have a beginning, as some speculative theologians maintain, and their claim that the movements of the celestial spheres are eternal is thereby invalidated. If, however, it is possible, then the coming into being of what Allah Most High has created, such as the heavens and the earth, could depend on prior temporal occurrences—just as you yourselves maintain concerning the animals, plants, minerals, rain, clouds, and other things that arise in this world. Thus, your argument fails on either assumption.

It may then be said:

Either you affirm that the Originator of the world acts with wisdom and for an intended end, or you do not. If you do not, your affirmation of a final cause is invalidated, as is what you say about the wisdom of the Creator Most High in creating animals and other creatures. (Furthermore, reality itself refutes this position, for the instances of wisdom found in existence are beyond numbering or enumeration. For example, He—glory be to Him—brings forth His blessings and mercy when His creatures need them: He brings rain in winter in the measure needed, and provides human beings with the faculties and organs they require in proportion to their needs. There are other such examples, which this is not the place to discuss at length.

If, however, you affirm that He acts for an intended wise purpose—which, in your terminology, is the final cause—you must necessarily affirm that He possesses will and volition. For to say that an agent performed a particular act for a particular wise purpose without intending that purpose is to affirm two contradictories together. These philosophers are among the most self-contradictory of people. Thus, they identify knowledge with the knower, knowledge with will, and will with power, and make similar assertions. Their views have been discussed at length elsewhere.

As for the third possibility, namely, that He brought created things into being and enjoined His commands for a wise purpose

---

## Page 3804

that is praiseworthy—this is the view of most people, both Muslims and non-Muslims. It is held by groups among the followers of Abū Hanīfah, al-Shāfi‘ī, Mālik, Ahmad, and others; by groups of speculative theologians among the Mu‘tazilah, Karrāmiyyah, Murji’ah, and others; by most scholars of hadith, Sufis, and Quranic exegetes; and by most ancient philosophers and many later philosophers, such as Abū al-Barakāt and others like him. These people, however, hold differing views.

(Some of them say:

The intended wise purpose is likewise something created and separate from Him. This is maintained by some of the Mu‘tazilah and Shī‘ah and those who agree with them.

They say:

The wise purpose in this is His benevolence towards creation, while the wise purpose in His commands is to recompense those subject to religious obligations with reward. They maintain that reason recognizes doing good to others as good and praiseworthy. He therefore created creation for this wise purpose, without any resulting effect upon Him, and without any act or attribute subsisting in Him.

Others replied to them:

Your position is self-contradictory. Doing good to others is praiseworthy because it has an effect upon the doer for which he deserves praise: either he perfects himself through it; he seeks praise and reward through it; he feels compassion and pain within himself and dispels that pain by doing good; or he finds pleasure, happiness, and joy in doing good. A noble soul rejoices, delights, and takes pleasure in the good that others receive from it. Thus, doing good to others is praiseworthy because the benefactor’s performance of these deeds has an effect upon him for which he deserves praise.

If, however, it is assumed that doing good and not doing it are entirely the same for the doer, there is no known basis for considering such an act good on his part. Rather, rational people regard such conduct as purposeless. Anyone who performs an act in which he himself finds neither pleasure nor

---

## Page 3805

advantage nor benefit of any kind, whether immediate or future, acts purposelessly and deserves no praise for it. You explained His acts in terms of purposes to avoid purposelessness, yet you fell into purposelessness yourselves. For a purposeless act is one that brings its doer no advantage, benefit, or gain. For this reason, neither Allah Most High, nor His Messenger (may Allah bless him and grant him peace), nor any rational person has enjoined anyone to do good to others, benefit them, or the like, except because of the benefit and advantage this brings to the doer. Otherwise, enjoining someone to perform an act that brings him no pleasure, happiness, benefit, or joy whatsoever, either immediately or in the future, is not commendable on the part of the one issuing the command.

This discussion gave rise to a dispute among the Mu‘tazilah, others, and those who agreed with them over “the rational discernment of moral goodness and badness.” The Mu‘tazilah and others affirmed this, as did those who agreed with them among the followers of Abū Hanīfah, Mālik, al-Shāfi‘ī, and Ahmad, as well as scholars of hadith and others. They also attributed this position to Abū Hanīfah himself. The Ash‘arīs denied it, as did those who agreed with them among the followers of Mālik, al-Shāfi‘ī, Ahmad, and others.

Both sides agreed that, when goodness is understood as an act’s being beneficial and congenial to its doer, and badness as its being harmful and uncongenial to him, these can be known through reason as well as through revealed law. Some among them supposed that the goodness and badness known through revealed law fall outside this meaning. This is not so. Rather, all the acts that Allah Most High has made obligatory or recommended are beneficial to those who perform them and serve their welfare. All the acts that Allah has forbidden are harmful to those who perform them and detrimental to their welfare. The praise and reward resulting from obedience to the Lawgiver benefit the doer and serve his welfare, while the blame and punishment resulting from disobedience to Him harm the doer and are detrimental to his welfare.

---

## Page 3806

The Mu‘tazilah affirmed goodness in the acts of Allah Most High, but not in the sense that any consequence of His acts accrues to Him. Their opponents, believing that an act can be good or bad only insofar as it has some consequence for its doer, denied this and said: “With regard to Allah Most High, what is bad is what is intrinsically impossible; every act conceived as possible is good.” For, according to them, there is no distinction between one thing He brings about and another with respect to Him.

The Mu‘tazilah, by contrast, affirmed goodness and badness without any consequence accruing to the doer that subsists in His essence. For, according to them, neither an attribute, nor an act, nor anything else subsists in His essence, although they may contradict themselves. They then began drawing analogies with what is good or bad on the part of a servant. Thus, they imposed upon Allah, glorified be He, the obligations they imposed upon the servant, and forbade Him things of the same kind as those they forbade the servant. They called this justice and wisdom, despite their reason’s inability to comprehend His wisdom and justice.

They affirm neither an all-encompassing will nor perfect power for Him. Thus, they do not acknowledge that He has power over all things, nor do they say, “Whatever Allah wills comes to pass, and whatever He does not will does not come to pass.” Nor do they acknowledge that He is the Creator of all things. They ascribe to Him forms of injustice from which He, glorified be He, has declared Himself free. For He said:

“Whoever does righteous deeds while being a believer need fear neither injustice nor loss.”

That is, he need not fear being wronged by being made to bear the sins of others, nor having his good deeds diminished. And He Most High said:

“My word cannot be changed, and I am never unjust to My servants.”

The Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) said in the hadith of the card, narrated by Imam Ahmad, al-Tirmidhī, and others:

“A man from my nation will be brought forward on the Day of Resurrection, and ninety-nine scrolls will be unrolled before him, each extending as far as the eye can see. He will be asked, ‘Do you deny any of this?’ He will reply, ‘No, my Lord.’ He will be asked, ‘Do you have any excuse? Do you have any good deed?’ He will reply, ‘No, my Lord.’ Then He will say, ‘Indeed you do!

---

## Page 3807

You have a good deed credited with Us, and you will not be wronged today.’ He said: A card will then be brought out for him bearing the words, ‘I bear witness that there is no god but Allah.’ The card will be placed in one pan of the balance and the scrolls in the other. The scrolls will rise, outweighed by the card.”

The Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) thus stated that this man would not be wronged, but would instead be rewarded for the monotheism he had professed, as Allah Most High says:

“Whoever does an atom’s weight of good will see it,
and whoever does an atom’s weight of evil will see it.”

Yet most of those who call themselves “upholders of justice” say that whoever commits a single major sin thereby nullifies all his good deeds and will remain in the Fire of Hell forever. Thus, they attribute to Allah what Allah and His Messenger have called injustice, despite their claim to declare Him free of injustice. Meanwhile, they call it injustice when He singles out whomever He wills for His mercy and bounty, and when He creates what He creates for the consummate wisdom inherent in it.

These matters are discussed at length elsewhere. Here, however, we have drawn attention to the main principles underlying people’s positions on this subject.

These Mu‘tazilah, together with those among the Shia who agree with them, hold that Allah, glorified be He, is obliged to do what is best for every servant in matters of religion. They disagree over whether He is obliged to do what is best for him in worldly matters. Their position is that He cannot do anything for a creature’s religious welfare other than what He has already done, and that He cannot guide someone who is astray, nor lead someone rightly guided astray.

As for the other groups who affirm that His acts have purposes—among the jurists, scholars of hadith, Sufis, and theologians such as the Karrāmiyyah and others, as well as the philosophers—they do not agree with them on

---

## Page 3808

this; rather, they say that He, glorified be He, does what He does for a wise purpose known to Him, glorified and exalted be He. His servants, or some of them, may know whatever He discloses to them of His wisdom, or they may not know it. His acts of general scope serve a general wisdom and mercy, such as His sending Muhammad (may Allah bless him and grant him peace), concerning whom He Most High says:

“We have sent you only as a mercy to the worlds.”

His sending him was among the greatest blessings bestowed upon creation, embodying the Creator’s supreme wisdom and His mercy towards His servants. As He Most High says:

“Allah has certainly bestowed a great favour upon the believers by raising among them a Messenger from their own midst, reciting His verses to them, purifying them, and teaching them the Book and wisdom.”

He Most High also says:

“Thus We have tested some of them through others, so that they may say, ‘Are these the ones Allah has favoured from among us?’ Does Allah not know best those who are grateful?”

And He says:

“Muhammad is no more than a messenger; messengers have passed away before him. If he dies or is killed, will you turn back on your heels? Whoever turns back on his heels will not harm Allah in the least, and Allah will reward the grateful.”

He Most High also says:

“Have you not seen those who exchanged Allah’s favour for disbelief?”

They said: “This refers to Muhammad (may Allah bless him and grant him peace).”

If someone says, “Yet some people were harmed by his message, such as those among the polytheists and the People of the Book who rejected him,” there are two answers to this.

The first is that he benefited them as far as possible. He reduced the evil they would have committed had it not been for the message, by presenting the proofs and signs that shook what was in their hearts, and through jihad and the jizyah tax, which frightened and humbled them until their evil diminished. Those of them whom he killed died before they could live longer in disbelief and thereby increase in it. This therefore diminished their evil. The messengers—may Allah’s blessings be upon them—

---

## Page 3809

were sent to secure and perfect benefits, and to prevent and reduce harms as far as possible.

The second answer is that any harm that occurred was negligible beside the benefit achieved. This is like rain whose benefits are widespread, even if it destroys some houses or hinders some travellers and people pursuing their livelihoods, such as cloth-bleachers and the like. Whatever brings widespread benefit and welfare is an intended good and a cherished mercy, even if some people suffer harm from it. This answer has been given by various groups of Muslims: speculative theologians, jurists and others among the Hanafīs, Hanbalīs and others, as well as the Karrāmiyyah and Sufis. It is also the answer given by many who engage in philosophy.

They say:

All the harm He brings into existence must involve a wise purpose. Allah Most High says:

“The work of Allah, who has perfected all things.”

And He says:

“Who has made good everything He created.”

Harm through which a desired wise purpose is achieved is not absolute evil, even if it is evil in relation to those harmed by it. Hence, neither the words of Allah Most High nor the words of His Messenger (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) attribute evil alone to Allah. Rather, evil is mentioned only in one of three ways: it is included within the generality of created things; it is attributed to the cause that produces it; or its agent is left unmentioned. When it is included within that generality, this conveys the all-encompassing nature of His power, will and creation, and encompasses the wisdom pertaining to the whole.

The first is exemplified by His saying, Most High:

“Allah is the Creator of all things,”

and similar passages. This category also includes Allah’s names that occur in pairs, such as the Giver and the Withholder, the Bringer of Harm and the Giver of Benefit, the Bestower of Honour and the Abaser, the Lowerer and the Raiser.

---

## Page 3810

so the name “the Withholder” is not used apart from its counterpart, nor “the Bringer of Harm” apart from its counterpart, because pairing them conveys an all-encompassing meaning. Every instance of mercy, benefit and welfare in existence comes from His bounty, Most High, while everything else comes from His justice. Every blessing from Him is bounty, and every affliction from Him is justice. As reported in the two Sahīh collections, the Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) said:

“Allah’s right hand is full, undiminished by expenditure, pouring forth night and day. Have you considered what He has spent since He created the heavens and the earth? It has not diminished what is in His right hand. In His other hand is justice; He lowers and raises.”

He thus explained that His right hand holds kindness towards creation, while His other hand holds justice and the balance by which He lowers and raises. His lowering and raising proceed from His justice, and His kindness towards His creation proceeds from His bounty.

As for leaving the agent unmentioned, an example is the statement of the jinn:

“And we do not know whether evil is intended for those on earth, or whether their Lord intends right guidance for them.”

Another is His saying, Most High, in Sūrat al-Fātihah:

“The path of those You have blessed, not of those who have incurred wrath, nor of those who have gone astray.”

There are other similar examples.

As for attributing evil to its cause, an example is His saying:

Another is His saying:

“So I intended to damage it,”

in contrast with His saying:

And His saying, Most High:

“Whatever good befalls you is from Allah, and whatever evil befalls you is from yourself.”

And His saying:

“Our Lord, we have wronged ourselves.”

And His saying, Most High:

“Why, when a calamity befell you, although you had inflicted twice as much, did you say, ‘Where has this come from?’ Say, ‘It is from yourselves.’”

There are many similar examples.

For this reason, none of Allah’s most beautiful names entails evil. Evil is mentioned only in what He brings about, as in His saying:

And His saying:

“Indeed, your Lord is swift in punishment, and indeed, He is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful.”

And His saying:

“Know that Allah is severe in punishment, and that Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful.”

He thus makes clear—glory be to Him—that His onslaught is severe, and that He is the All-Forgiving, the Most Loving.

“The Avenger” is not among Allah’s most beautiful names established in reports from the Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace). Rather, it occurs in the Quran only with qualifications, as in His saying, Most High:

“We shall indeed exact retribution from the criminals.”

And His saying:

“Indeed, Allah is Almighty, Possessor of Retribution.”

As for the hadith enumerating the most beautiful names, which includes “the Avenger” in the sequence “the Beneficent, the Accepter of Repentance, the Avenger, the Pardoner, the Most Compassionate,” those versed in hadith do not regard this enumeration as the words of the Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace). Rather, al-Walīd ibn Muslim related it from Sa‘īd ibn ‘Abd al-‘Azīz or from one of his other teachers.

For this reason, none of the compilers of the well-known collections transmitted it except al-Tirmidhī, who narrated it through al-Walīd ibn Muslim with one wording. Others narrated it with differences in the names and their order, showing that it is not the words of the Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace). All the other narrators who transmitted this hadith from Abū Hurayrah, then through al-A‘raj, then through Abū al-Zinād, did not specify the individual names. Rather, they related his saying (may Allah bless him and grant him peace):

“Allah has ninety-nine names, one hundred less one. Whoever enumerates them will enter Paradise.”

This is how the compilers of authentic collections, such as al-Bukhārī, Muslim and others, recorded it. However, an enumeration of the names was also transmitted through

---

## Page 3812

another chain of transmission, in the report of Muhammad ibn Sīrīn from Abū Hurayrah. Ibn Mājah narrated it, but its chain is weak. Hadith scholars know that it is not the words of the Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace). These are the only two reports attributed to the Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) that enumerate the most beautiful names, and both are transmitted through Abū Hurayrah. This is discussed at length in its proper place.

The purpose here is to draw attention to principles that help one understand this question, for it continues to weigh heavily upon human souls. If a servant knows, in general, that Allah has great wisdom in what He creates and commands, that suffices him. Then, as his knowledge and faith increase, aspects of Allah’s wisdom and mercy become apparent to him that astound his mind and demonstrate the truth of what Allah has declared in His Book, where He says:

“We will show them Our signs in the horizons and within themselves until it becomes clear to them that it is the truth.”

For the Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) said in an authentic hadith:

“Allah is more merciful to His servants than a mother is to her child.”

It is also reported from him in the two Sahīh collections that he said:

“When Allah created mercy, He created it in one hundred parts. He sent down one part, through which creatures show mercy to one another; even an animal lifts its hoof away from its young because of that mercy. He kept ninety-nine parts with Himself. On the Day of Resurrection, He will join this one to those and show mercy to His servants through them.”

Or words to that effect, as spoken by the Messenger of Allah (may Allah bless him and grant him peace).

Furthermore, these people—the majority of Muslims and others, such as the imams of the four schools and other early authorities and scholars—affirm His wisdom and do not deny it—as the Ash‘arīs and others like them have denied it

They enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong. Yet they went astray concerning divine decree, believing that affirming an all-encompassing will, comprehensive power, and creation extending to everything would necessarily impugn the Lord’s justice and wisdom. In this they were mistaken.

Opposing them were people among the scholars, devout worshippers, and practitioners of speculative theology and Sufism. They affirmed divine decree and believed that Allah is the Lord and Sovereign of all things; that whatever He wills comes to pass, and whatever He does not will does not come to pass; and that He is the Creator, Lord, and Sovereign of all things. This is good and correct. Yet they fell short regarding the divine commands and prohibitions, the promise of reward and threat of punishment. They went to such excess that their extremists fell into heresy, becoming like the polytheists who said:

“Had Allah willed, neither we nor our forefathers would have associated partners with Him, nor would we have forbidden

## Page 3815

anything.”

Although those Qadariyyah resemble the Magians in affirming an agent other than Allah—glorified is He—for what they consider evil, these others resemble the polytheists who said:

“Had Allah willed, neither we nor our forefathers would have associated partners with Him, nor would we have forbidden anything.”

The polytheists are worse than the Magians. Muslims unanimously agree that the Magians may retain their religion upon payment of the jizyah, and some scholars have held that marrying their women and eating their food are lawful. As for the polytheists, the Muslim community unanimously agrees that marrying their women and eating their food are forbidden. The position of al-Shāfiʿī, Ahmad—according to the well-known report from him—and others is that they may not retain their religion upon payment of the jizyah. The majority of scholars hold that the Arab polytheists may not do so, even though the Magians may. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, did not accept the jizyah from any of the polytheists. Rather, he said:

“I have been commanded to fight the people until they testify that none is worthy of worship but Allah and that I am the Messenger of Allah. If they say this, their lives and property are protected from me, except when its requirements warrant otherwise, and their reckoning rests with Allah, Mighty and Majestic.”

The point here is that whoever affirms divine decree and invokes it to invalidate the divine commands and prohibitions is worse than someone who affirms the divine commands and prohibitions but does not affirm divine decree. This is agreed upon by Muslims and adherents of other religions—indeed, by all creation. For whoever invokes divine decree and the witnessing of Allah’s universal lordship over all created beings, without distinguishing between what is commanded and what is forbidden, between believers and disbelievers, and between the obedient and the disobedient, believes in none of the messengers and none of the scriptures. To him, Adam and Iblīs are alike; Noah and his people are alike; Moses and Pharaoh are alike; and the first and foremost believers and the disbelievers of Mecca are alike. This error has become widespread among many practitioners of Sufism, asceticism, and worship, especially

They do not understand Allah’s exclusive right to worship, nor do they know that a deity is an object of worship and devotion, and that merely acknowledging Allah as the Lord of everything does not constitute affirmation of His oneness until one testifies that none is worthy of worship but Allah. ## Page 3818

For these polytheists acknowledged that Allah created the heavens and the earth and created them, and that dominion over all things rests in His hand. Indeed, they also acknowledged divine decree: the Arabs affirmed it in the pre-Islamic age, as is well known from their poetry and prose. Nevertheless, because they did not worship Allah alone, without partners, but worshipped others besides Him, they were polytheists worse than the Jews and Christians. Thus, anyone whose utmost attainment in monotheism and its realization amounts to this has attained nothing beyond the monotheism of the polytheists.

This is a matter of tremendous consequence: here feet have slipped, understandings have gone astray, and the religion of the Muslims has been altered. Here, too, many who claim the highest attainment in monotheism, realization, knowledge, and theological discourse have confused those who worship Allah alone with idolaters.

Everyone who believes in Allah and His Messenger knows that the Mu‘tazilah and the Qadarī Shiites, who affirm divine commands and prohibitions, promises of reward and threats of punishment, are better than those who make no distinction between the believer and the unbeliever, the righteous and the wicked, the truthful prophet and the lying pretender to prophethood, or Allah’s allies and His enemies, and who regard this as the utmost realization and the highest attainment in monotheism. These people fall under the designation “Qadariyyah” whom the early generations condemned. Indeed, they deserve condemnation more than the Mu‘tazilah and others like them.

As Abū Bakr al-Khallāl wrote in Kitāb al-Sunnah (The Book of the Sunnah): “Refutation of the Qadariyyah and their assertion that Allah compelled His servants to commit sins.” He related that al-Marwadhī said: “I said to Abū ‘Abd Allāh, ‘A man says that Allah compelled His servants.’ He replied, ‘Do not put it that way.’ He rejected this and said:

‘Allah leaves astray whom He wills and guides whom He wills.’”

He also related from al-Marwadhī that a man said, “Allah did not compel His servants to commit sins.”

## Page 3819

whereupon another man replied to him, “Allah did compel His servants,” intending thereby to affirm divine decree. This is a vast subject. The point here is that al-Khallāl and other scholars included those who affirm compulsion under the designation “Qadariyyah,” even when they did not invoke divine decree to justify sins. What, then, of those who do invoke it to justify sins?

Clearly, those who invoke divine decree to set aside commands and prohibitions fall more fully under Allah’s condemnation of the Qadariyyah than those who deny it, for the former’s misguidance is greater. This is why the Qadariyyah were associated with the Murji’ah in the statements of several of the early generations, and a hadith traced back to the Prophet has been narrated to this effect. Each of these two innovations undermines commands and prohibitions, promises of reward and threats of punishment. Thus, irjā’ weakens belief in the threats of punishment and makes light of obligatory duties and prohibitions

---

## Page 3821

and if a Qadarī invokes divine decree as an excuse, he supports the Murji’ah; but if he denies it, he and the Murji’ah stand at opposite extremes. The former goes to extremes in severity, leaving no room for the servant to seek Allah’s help in doing what he has been commanded and refraining from what he has been forbidden, while the latter goes to the opposite extreme.

It is well known that Allah Most High sent the messengers and revealed the scriptures so that the messengers would be believed in what they reported and obeyed in what they commanded. As He Most High says:

“We did not send any messenger except to be obeyed by Allah’s permission.”

And He Most High says:

“Whoever obeys the Messenger has indeed obeyed Allah.”

Belief in divine decree completes this. Whoever affirms divine decree but sets it against the divine command has thereby destroyed the very foundation. It is well known that anyone who sets aside the commands and prohibitions with which Allah sent His messengers is an unbeliever, as Muslims, Jews, and Christians all agree. Indeed, these people’s position is self-contradictory: none of them can live by it, no creature’s welfare can be maintained on its basis, and no two people can live together according to it. For if divine decree is a valid excuse, it is a valid excuse for everyone; otherwise, it is a valid excuse for no one.

Suppose someone wrongs a man, insults him, takes his wealth, corrupts his family, or does something else of this kind. Whenever that man blames or condemns the offender, or seeks his punishment, he invalidates the use of divine decree as an excuse.

Whoever claims that a gnostic, upon witnessing divine decree, is no longer bound by the divine command has uttered words of unbelief that neither Jews nor Christians would accept. Indeed, this is rationally impossible and inconceivable under divine law. A hungry person distinguishes bread from dust, and a thirsty person distinguishes water from a mirage. He desires what satisfies his hunger and quenches his thirst, rather than what does him no good, although all of these things are created by Allah Most High. Thus a living being—even if

---

## Page 3822

it be what it may—must distinguish between what benefits it, brings it comfort and joy, and what harms it, brings it misery and pain. This is the essence of divine commands and prohibitions: Allah Most High has commanded His servants to do what benefits them and forbidden them from what harms them.

People fall into “four categories” with respect to divine law and decree. The worst of creation are those who invoke divine decree as an excuse for themselves but do not accept it as an excuse for others. They appeal to it to justify sins and faults, yet find no reassurance in it when calamities strike. As one scholar said: “When obedient, you are a Qadarī; when disobedient, a Jabrī. You adopt whichever doctrine suits your desires.”

At the opposite extreme are the best of creation: those who patiently endure calamities and seek forgiveness for their faults. As Allah Most High says:

“So be patient. Indeed, Allah’s promise is true. And seek forgiveness for your sin.”

And He Most High says:

“No calamity befalls the earth or yourselves without being recorded in a Book before We bring it into being. That is surely easy for Allah.”

“So that you may neither grieve over what you have missed nor exult over what He has given you.”

And He Most High says:

“No calamity befalls except by Allah’s permission. And whoever believes in Allah, He guides his heart.”

One of the early generations said: “This is a man who is struck by a calamity and knows that it is from Allah, so he is content and submits.”

He Most High says:

“And those who, when they commit an indecency or wrong themselves, remember Allah and seek forgiveness for their sins—and who forgives sins except Allah?—and do not knowingly persist in what they have done.”

Allah Most High relates that when Adam, peace be upon him, had done what he did, he said:

“Our Lord, we have wronged ourselves. If You do not forgive us and have mercy on us, we will surely be among the losers.”

And He relates that Iblīs said:

“Because You have led me astray, I will surely make evil appealing to them on earth, and I will lead them all astray.”

Thus, whoever repents resembles

---

## Page 3823

his father Adam, while whoever persists in sin and invokes divine decree as an excuse resembles Iblīs.

In the hadith recorded in the two Sahīhs concerning the debate between Adam and Moses, peace be upon them, Moses said to Adam:

“You are Adam, the father of humankind. Allah created you with His hand, breathed into you of His spirit, and taught you the names of all things. Why did you cause us and yourself to be expelled from Paradise?”

Adam replied:

“You are Moses, whom Allah chose for His message and to whom He spoke, and for whom He inscribed the Torah with His hand. How many years before I was created did you find it written concerning me: ‘Adam disobeyed his Lord and went astray’?”

He replied: “So many years.” The narration states: “Thus Adam prevailed over Moses in argument.”

This hadith is recorded in the two Sahīhs on the authority of Abū Hurayrah. It has also been narrated with a good chain of transmission on the authority of ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him.

Adam, peace be upon him, prevailed over Moses only because Moses blamed him for what he had done on account of the calamity that had befallen them through his eating from the tree. He was not blaming him on account of Allah’s right that had been violated by the sin. Adam had already repented of that sin, as Allah Most High says:

“Then Adam received words from his Lord, and He accepted his repentance.”

And He Most High says:

“Then his Lord chose him, accepted his repentance, and guided him.”

Moses, peace be upon him—and even those below Moses in rank—knows that after repentance and forgiveness, no blame for the sin remains. Adam knew Allah too well to invoke divine decree as an excuse for sin, and Moses, peace be upon him, knew Allah Most High too well to accept such an argument. If it were a valid argument for sin, it would also have been a valid argument for Iblīs, Adam’s enemy; for Pharaoh, Moses’ enemy; and for every disbeliever and evildoer. Allah’s commands and prohibitions would thereby have been rendered void.

Rather, divine decree was a valid argument for Adam against Moses only because Moses blamed another for a calamity that had befallen him through that person’s action, when that calamity had already been decreed for him.

## Page 3824

Allah Most High has said:

In the two Sahīhs, ‘Ā’ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, said:

When Allah’s sacred limits were violated, nothing could withstand his anger until he had exacted retribution for Allah’s sake.”

“If Fātimah, the daughter of Muhammad, were to steal, I would cut off her hand.”

Thus, in matters of Allah’s commands and prohibitions, he would hasten to obey and enforce the prescribed punishments upon those who transgressed Allah’s limits, undeterred by anyone’s blame in fulfilling his duty to Allah. But when someone harmed him or fell short in fulfilling his rights, he would pardon that person and not hold him accountable, mindful of divine decree.

This is the path of those whom Allah has blessed: the prophets, the steadfastly truthful, the martyrs, and the righteous. What excellent companions they are!

This is obligatory regarding decreed calamities that occur without human agency, such as natural disasters, or through an act for which punishment is no longer possible, such as Adam’s action, peace be upon him. There is no basis for blaming him under revealed law—because of his repentance—or in terms of divine decree, because the matter had been foreordained and decreed.

But when one person wrongs another, the wronged person may obtain just redress. If he pardons the offender, however, that is better for him, as Allah Most High says:

“And for wounds there is equal retribution. But whoever waives it as an act of charity, it will be an expiation for him.”

## Page 3825

As for the “third category,” they are those who take no account of divine decree, either in misdeeds or in calamities caused by human actions. Rather, they attribute all of this to the person concerned. When they do wrong, they seek forgiveness, and this is good. But when a calamity befalls them through someone’s actions, they do not consider the divine decree by which it was ordained for them. Nor do they say of someone who has fallen short in fulfilling their rights, “Leave him alone. Had something been decreed, it would have happened.” Moreover, that calamity may have come about because of their own sins, yet they take no account of those sins. Allah Most High has said:

“When a calamity befell you, although you had inflicted twice as much, did you say, ‘How has this happened?’ Say, ‘It is from yourselves.’”

And Allah Most High has said:

“Whatever calamity befalls you is because of what your own hands have earned.”

Also relevant are His words, Most High:

“Whatever good befalls you is from Allah, and whatever evil befalls you is from yourself.”

Many who affirm divine decree and many who deny it have disputed over this verse. The former say that all actions are from Allah, citing His words, Most High:

“Say, ‘All is from Allah.’”

The latter say that good is from Allah and evil is from yourself, citing His words:

“Whatever good befalls you is from Allah, and whatever evil befalls you is from yourself.”

The former may answer them by citing a fabricated reading of “from yourself,” with an a-vowel, giving it an interrogative meaning. Some of them instead supply an implied interrogative, yielding the meaning: “Is it, then, from yourself?” Others posit an implicit “they say” in the passage beginning with His words, Most High, “Whatever befalls you.” Thus they say that the verse is to be understood as: “What is the matter with these people that they can hardly

---

## Page 3826

understand any words?”—with “they say” supplied after it. They thereby distort both the wording and the meaning of the Quran, making what is Allah’s speech—His truthful speech—into the words of the hypocrites whose statements Allah condemned. Thus, both groups are ignorant of the meaning of the Quran and of the true implications of the position they defend.

As for the Quran, what is meant here by good and evil is blessings and calamities, not acts of obedience and disobedience. This is like His words, Most High:

“If good befalls you, it distresses them; but if evil befalls you, they rejoice in it. Yet if you are patient and mindful of Allah, their scheming will not harm you at all.”

Another example is His saying, Most High:

As He, Most High, also said:

That is, with blessings and calamities. This differs from His saying:

“Whoever comes with a good deed will have ten times its like, and whoever comes with an evil deed will be repaid only with its like.”

In this and similar passages, what is meant is obedience and disobedience. In each passage, there is something that clarifies the intended meaning of the expression. Thus, praise be to Allah Most High, there is no obscurity in the mighty Quran; rather, it is clear.

This is because, when He says “whatever befalls you,” “whatever touches you,” or similar expressions, it refers to something done to you by someone other than yourself. As He said:

“Whatever good befalls you is from Allah, and whatever evil befalls you is from yourself.”

And as He, Most High, said:

“If good befalls you, it distresses them.”

And He, Most High, said:

“But if evil befalls them because of what their own hands have sent ahead.”

## Page 3827

—up to His words:

“Wherever you may be, death will overtake you, even if you are in lofty, fortified towers. If good befalls them, they say, ‘This is from Allah’; but if evil befalls them, they say, ‘This is from you.’”

These are the words of the disbelievers and hypocrites. When victory or other blessings come to them, they say, “This is from Allah.” But when humiliation, fear or other calamities befall them, they say:

## Page 3828

He mentions something similar in the account of Moses and Pharaoh. He, Most High, says:

Similarly, He, Most High, says in Surah Yā Sīn:

Thus Allah, Most High, tells us that the disbelievers regarded the believers as an evil omen: whenever affliction befell them, they blamed the believers for it, while whatever good came to them they regarded as theirs from Allah, Mighty and Majestic. He, Most High, therefore said:

“What is the matter with these people that they can hardly understand what they are told?”

Allah, Most High, has sent down the finest discourse. Had they understood the Quran, they would have known that Allah commanded them to do what is right and forbade them to do what is wrong: He commanded good and forbade evil. Nothing in the message with which Allah sent His messengers is therefore a cause of evil. Rather, evil results from people’s sins. He, Most High, said:

“Whatever good befalls you is from Allah.”

That is, whatever victory, provision or well-being comes to you is from Allah, as a blessing He has bestowed upon you. Even if it comes through your righteous deeds, He is the One who guided you, helped you, eased your way to ease, bestowed faith upon you, made it pleasing to your heart, and made disbelief, wickedness and disobedience hateful to you.

At the end of the authentic hadith narrated by Abū Dharr from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, who relates it from his Lord, Blessed and Most High, He says: “O My servants, these are but your deeds, which I record for you

The corruption this would cause in religious and worldly affairs is self-evident to sound reason, which accords with what the Messenger brought.

Divine decree must therefore be believed in, not invoked as an excuse. Whoever does not believe in divine decree resembles the Magians; whoever invokes it as an excuse resembles the polytheists. Whoever acknowledges both Allah’s command and His decree, yet impugns His justice and wisdom, resembles Iblīs. For Allah relates that he challenged His wisdom and opposed Him with his own opinion and desire, saying:

“Because You have led me astray, I will surely make evil alluring to them on earth and mislead them all.”

Some of the People of the Book, as well as certain writers on religious doctrines, such as al-Shahrastānī, have related

Writers on religious doctrines draw many of their accounts from Muʿtazilite books, just as al-Ashʿarī and others drew the accounts they presented in their works on religious doctrines from Muʿtazilite books. For the Muʿtazilah were among the earliest and most prolific groups to write on this subject. Hence these doctrines are found transmitted in their wording.

They thus fabricated this debate, putting its words into the mouth of Iblīs, just as we have seen many of them compose a book or a poem in the voice of a Jew or someone else. Their purpose is to refute those who affirm divine decree. They say that Allah’s case against His creation can only be established by denying divine decree. The point here is that this noble verse is evidence against both groups:

It is evidence against those who invoke divine decree as an excuse, for Allah Most High states that He punished them for their sins. Had their argument been acceptable,

---

## Page 3831

He would not have punished them for their sins. It is also evidence against those who deny divine decree, for He, glory be to Him, states that good comes from Allah and that evil comes from the servant himself. The Qadariyyah agree that the servant brings his disobedience into being just as he brings his obedience into being. In their view, Allah brings neither into being; rather, He commands obedience and forbids disobedience.

According to them, Allah has bestowed no religious blessing upon His believing servants without bestowing its like upon the disbelievers. Thus, in their view, ʿAlī ibn Abī Tālib, may Allah be pleased with him, and Abū Lahab received equal religious blessings from Allah: the Messenger was sent to each, each was given the ability to act, and any impediment had been removed for each. Yet the former came to faith by himself, without Allah singling him out for a blessing through which he believed, while the latter disbelieved by himself, without Allah favoring that believer over him or granting the believer a special blessing on account of which he believed.

In their view, Allah made faith as beloved to disbelievers such as Abū Lahab and his like as He did to believers such as ʿAlī, may Allah be pleased with him, and his like. He adorned it in the hearts of both groups and equally made disbelief, wickedness, and disobedience hateful to both. Yet the believers hated what Allah had made hateful to them without receiving any blessing peculiar to them, while the disbelievers did not hate what Allah had made hateful to them.

Anyone who imagines that they hold, or reports them as holding, that obedience comes from Allah while disobedience comes from the servant is ignorant of their doctrine. None of the scholars of the Qadariyyah has said this, nor could he do so, for their fundamental position is that the servant’s performance of obedience is like his performance of disobedience: he performs both through a capacity he possesses, without Allah singling him out by creating in him a will or placing in him a power specific to either one. Thus, if they invoke this verse as evidence for their doctrine, they would be ignorant of their own doctrine, and the verse would be evidence against them

not in their favor; for Allah Most High says:

contradict their position, since they hold that good deeds and evil deeds come from the servant, not from Allah, glory be to Him.
