They said that the servant’s power has no effect on bringing about the act within its scope, nor on any of its attributes. Rather, Allah has established the customary pattern of creating that act concurrently with the servant’s power. Thus, the act is a creation on Allah’s part, through His originating it and bringing it into being, and an acquisition on the servant’s part, because it occurs concurrently with his power. They also said that the servant neither originates his acts nor brings them into existence. Yet despite this, they may say: “We do not uphold absolute compulsion. Rather, we affirm that the servant possesses a created power. An absolute proponent of compulsion is someone who affirms no power for the servant.”

---

## Page 3834

They then began to distinguish between the acquisition they affirmed and creation, saying:

“Acquisition means the concurrence of an act with created power, whereas creation is that which lies within the scope of eternal power.” They also said: “Acquisition is the act that occurs within the locus of the power to perform it, whereas creation is the act that occurs outside the locus of the power to perform it.”

Others replied:

“This establishes no distinction between saying that the servant acquired an act and saying that he performed it, brought it into existence, originated it, made it, did it, or similar expressions. For his performing, originating, doing, and making likewise fall within the scope of created power and occur within its locus.

“Moreover, this distinction has no real substance. Whether the act within the scope of a power occurs within that power’s locus or outside it has no bearing on the power’s actual influence upon it.”

This distinction rests upon “two principles.” The first is that Allah has no power to perform an act that subsists in His own being, and that His creation of the world is the world itself. Most rational people, Muslims and others alike, hold the contrary view.

The second is that whatever falls within the scope of the servant’s power can occur only within the locus where that power exists, and nothing within its scope can occur outside its locus. There is lengthy disagreement concerning this, which this is not the place to discuss.

Furthermore, if influence is explained as mere concurrence, it makes no difference whether the distinguishing factor is within the locus or outside it.

Their opponents also said:

“It is firmly rooted in human nature that whoever performs

---

## Page 3835

an act of justice is just, whoever commits injustice is unjust, and whoever tells a lie is a liar. If the servant does not perform his own acts of lying, injustice, and justice, but Allah performs them, it follows that He is the one characterized by lying and injustice.”

They said:

“This parallels what you and all others who affirm the divine attributes have said: it is firmly rooted in human nature that whoever has knowledge subsisting in him is knowledgeable; whoever has power subsisting in him is capable; whoever has motion subsisting in him is moving; whoever has speech subsisting in him is speaking; and whoever has will subsisting in him is willing. You have also said that if speech were created, it would be the speech of the locus in which He created it, just as with the other attributes. This consistent principle concerning those in whom attributes subsist has its counterpart in those who perform actions.”

They also said:

“The Quran abounds in passages attributing these actions to the servants, such as His words, Exalted is He:

‘As a reward for what they used to do,’

and His words:

‘Do whatever you will,’

and His words:

‘And say, “Work, for Allah will see your deeds,”’

and His words:

‘Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds,’

and other such passages.”

They also said:

“Revelation and reason agree that the servant is praised or blamed for his own action, which counts as a good or evil deed on his part. If it were nothing but someone else’s action, that other would be the one praised or blamed for it.”

This is not the place for a full discussion of this question. We shall, however, draw attention to some useful points concerning this difficult issue. Thus we say:

---

## Page 3836

The statement, “This person did this and did that,” is ambiguous, for “act” sometimes means the action itself and sometimes what the verbal noun denotes. Thus one says, “I did this; I do it; a doing,” and “I performed this work; I perform it; a working.” When “work” means the action itself, which is what the verbal noun denotes—as with a person’s prayer, fasting, and the like—the work here is the very thing done: the verbal noun and the act denote the same thing. But when what is intended is the result of one’s work—as with weaving cloth, building a house, and the like—the work here differs from the thing produced. Allah, Exalted is He, says:

“They made for him whatever he wished: sanctuaries, statues, basins as large as reservoirs, and firmly set cauldrons.”

He thus describes these manufactured objects as things made by the jinn. The same applies to His words, Exalted is He:

“Allah created you and what you make.”

According to the more correct of the two interpretations, mā means “that which,” referring to the idols they carve. As Allah, Exalted is He, says:

“Do you worship what you carve, when Allah created you and what you make?”

That is, Allah created you and created the idols you carve. The hadith narrated by Hudhayfah from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, is another example:

“Allah is the Creator of every craftsman and his handiwork.”

Nevertheless, the verse may be cited as evidence that Allah created the servants’ actions through another line of reasoning. One may say: If He is the Creator of the carved objects they make, He must also be the Creator of the configuration they produce in them. These objects become idols only through that configuration; without it, they would not be things made by them. If He is the Creator of that configuration, then He is the Creator of their actions.

The point is that the terms “act,” “work,” and “making” have various senses. Like “building,” “sewing,” and “carpentry,” they can denote either the action expressed by the verbal noun or the thing produced. Likewise, the terms “recitation,” “reading,” “speech,” and “utterance” can denote the very referent of

---

## Page 3837

the verbal noun or the actual utterance and speech produced by that action. Thus, “recitation” and “reading” may refer to the Quran itself that is read and recited, just as they may refer to the action denoted by the verbal noun.

The point here is that when someone says, “These actions are Allah’s act,” or “They are the servant’s act,” if he means that they are Allah’s act in the sense denoted by the verbal noun, this is false by the consensus of the Muslims and according to clear reason. But if someone says that they are Allah’s act, meaning that they are produced and created by Allah, like all other created things, this is true.

Some who hold this view say that Allah has no act subsisting in Him. They therefore make no distinction between His act and what He produces, or between His act of creation and what He creates. The majority, however, who distinguish between these things, say: These actions are created and produced by Allah; they are not His act itself. As for the servant, they are his act, subsisting in him. They are also something he produces, if “act” is used to mean the thing produced.

Thus, when someone who does not distinguish, with respect to the Lord, Exalted is He, between the act and the thing produced says that these actions are Allah’s act, the expression “Allah’s act” has no two distinct meanings for him. Consequently, they cannot be the servant’s act, still less something produced by him. Some of these people say that they are an act of both the Lord and the servant, thereby affirming one effect produced by two agents.

Most of the Muʿtazilah agree with these people that the act of the Lord, Exalted is He, can mean only what He produces, although they distinguish, in the servant’s case, between the act and the thing produced. For this reason, the dispute became intense

---

## Page 3838

and the issue became obscure to both groups, leaving them bewildered.

Those, however, who hold that the Lord’s creation of His creatures is not identical with the creatures themselves maintain that the servants’ acts are created like all other created things and are produced by the Lord like everything else He produces. They do not say that these acts are the Lord’s own act and act of creation; rather, they say that they are the servant’s own acts. On this understanding, the difficulty disappears. For lying, wrongdoing, and other such evils characterize the one whose acts they are—as when the servant performs them and they subsist in him. They do not characterize the One who created them, when He has made them attributes of another. Likewise, glorified is He, He is not characterized by the tastes, colors, smells, shapes, dimensions, movements, and other things He creates in others. When He creates a person’s color, He Himself does not take on that color. When He creates a foul smell, a bitter taste, an ugly form, or anything else that is loathsome, blameworthy, and repugnant, He is not characterized by these ugly, blameworthy, and loathsome created things, nor by evil acts. The evil of these acts means that they harm their doer, give cause for his blame and punishment, and bring him pain and torment. This affects the doer in whom they subsist, not the Creator who created them as the acts of another.

Furthermore, the majority, who affirm that He has wisdom in creating whatever is repugnant, harmful, and hurtful in the world, say that He has great wisdom in creating these evil acts that harm their doers, just as He has great wisdom in creating illnesses and sorrows.

As for those who say that His acts are not explained by underlying reasons, neither of these is so explained on their view.

---

## Page 3839

This is clarified by the fact that when Allah Most High creates blindness, illness, hunger, thirst, pain, weariness, and the like in a person, it is the servant who is ill, hungry, thirsty, and in pain. The harm, suffering, and unpleasantness inherent in these created things affect him; none of this affects Allah Most High. Likewise, the lying, wrongdoing, unbelief, and similar things He creates in him are harmful, repugnant, and hurtful. This is what it means to call them evil and reprehensible: they distress and harm the person who commits them. They may also distress and harm others, just as his illness, foul smell, and the like may distress and harm others.

This is further clarified by the fact that the Qadariyyah concede that Allah may create unbelief and wickedness in the servant as recompense, as in His words, Most High:

“We turn their hearts and eyes away, just as they did not believe in it the first time.”

And His words:

“In their hearts is a disease, so Allah has increased their disease.”

And His words:

“When they deviated, Allah caused their hearts to deviate.”

Now, it is well known that these created things are acts performed and acquired by the servant, for which he is recompensed and deserves blame and punishment, while they are created by Allah Most High. Thus, according to those who affirm divine decree, what He creates of the servants’ deeds in the first instance is, in this respect, no different from what He creates as recompense, even though the two differ in another respect. The Qadariyyah cannot distinguish between them on the grounds that one, but not the other, is Allah’s act, and that one, but not the other, is the servant’s act. Rather, they say that creation as recompense is fitting for Allah Most High because it is recompense for the servant, whereas initial creation is not fitting for Him because it is an initial action toward the servant

---

## Page 3840

involving something harmful to him. They maintain that it is not fitting for Him to harm a living being except because of a prior offence or with subsequent compensation. As for those who affirm divine decree, those among them who do not attribute purposes to His acts make no distinction between one created thing and another.

Those who affirm divine wisdom—and they are the majority—say:

Allah Most High has great wisdom in the suffering He creates in living beings, just as He has wisdom in everything else. We do not confine His wisdom to reward and compensation, for that would mean judging Allah Most High by analogy with an individual human being, and likening Allah’s wisdom and justice to that person’s wisdom and justice.

The “Muʿtazilah” liken Allah to His creation in His acts while denying His attributes. Among their corrupt principles is that they describe Allah in terms of what He creates in the world, since, according to them, no attribute or act subsists in Him. They therefore name Him on this basis and describe Him in terms of what He creates in the world. For example, they say that He speaks through speech He creates in another, and wills through a will He brings into existence without its inhering in any subject. They also say that His pleasure, anger, love, and hatred are the very reward and punishment He creates; and that if He were the creator of the servant’s wrongdoing and lying, He Himself would be the wrongdoer and liar. These and similar assertions are such that any rational person who reflects upon them recognizes their falsity as self-evident.

For this reason, the early generations and the leading scholars vehemently condemned them, especially when they openly proclaimed that the Quran was created. The early generations knew that this was, in reality, a denial of the speech of Allah Most High, and that if His speech were whatever He creates, it would follow that every created utterance was His speech. Thus, the speech He causes skins to utter on the Day of Resurrection, the glorification He causes mountains and pebbles to utter, the testimony of hands and feet, and the like would all be His speech. And if He is the Creator of every

---

## Page 3841

thing, then every utterance that exists would be His speech. This is the position of the Hulūliyyah among the Jahmiyyah, such as the author of al-Fusūs and his like. Hence they say:

“All speech in existence is His speech;
To us, its prose and verse are alike.”

Sound reason plainly establishes that when Allah Most High creates an attribute in a subject, it is an attribute of that subject. Thus, when He creates motion in a subject, that subject is what moves by it. When He creates a colour or an odour in a body, that body is what bears the colour or odour. When He creates knowledge, power, or life in a subject, that subject is what knows, possesses power, or lives. Likewise, when He creates will, love, or hatred in a subject, that subject is what wills, loves, or hates. When He creates an act for a servant, the servant is the one who performs it. Thus, if He creates lying, wrongdoing, or disbelief for him, the servant is the liar, wrongdoer, or disbeliever. If He creates prayer, fasting, or pilgrimage for him, the servant is the one who prays, fasts, or performs pilgrimage.

Allah Most High is not described by any of His created things; rather, His attributes subsist in His own Essence. This is consistent with the principles of the early generations and the majority of Muslims, both Ahl al-Sunnah and others. They maintain that Allah’s creation of the heavens and the earth is not the heavens and the earth themselves; rather, the act of creation is distinct from what is created. This is especially true of the position of the early generations, the leading scholars, and those of Ahl al-Sunnah who agreed with them in affirming Allah’s attributes and acts. For the Mu'tazilah and those Jahmiyyah and Qadariyyah who agreed with them challenged the consistency of this principle as upheld by those who did not maintain that the act of creation is distinct from what is created, such as al-Ash'arī and those who agreed with him. They said:

---

## Page 3842

“If you say that when an attribute subsists in a subject, that subject alone is described by it—as you have stated regarding motion, knowledge, power, and all other accidents—then your principle is contradicted by justice, beneficence, and other acts of Allah Most High. For He is called just on account of justice He creates in another, and beneficent on account of beneficence He creates in another. Likewise, He may be called a speaker on account of speech He creates in another.”

The majority of Ahl al-Sunnah and others respond by consistently upholding this principle. They say that He is just only by virtue of the justice that subsists in His own Essence, and beneficent by virtue of the beneficence that subsists in His own Essence. As for the created benefit received by the servant, it is the effect of that beneficence. Likewise, He is the Most Merciful, the Bestower of Mercy, by virtue of the mercy that is His attribute; whatever mercy He creates is an effect of that mercy.

A term denoting an attribute sometimes refers to the attribute itself, as denoted by the verbal noun, and sometimes to its object, as denoted by the passive participle. Thus, “creation” sometimes refers to the act of creating and sometimes to what is created. “Mercy” likewise refers to either. Similarly, “command” may refer to His commanding—the verbal noun in the sequence “he commanded, he commands, commanding”—and sometimes to what is brought about by it, as in His saying, Most High:

“Allah’s command is a decree determined.”

Likewise, the word “knowledge” may refer to what is known, and “power” to the object of power. There are numerous similar examples.

Among the proofs Imām Ahmad and other leading scholars of the Sunnah cited to establish that Allah’s speech is uncreated was the Prophet’s saying, peace be upon him:

“I seek refuge in the perfect words of Allah,”

and similar expressions. They said that refuge is not attained through anything created. Comparable to this is the saying of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“O Allah, I seek refuge in Your pleasure from Your wrath, in Your pardon from Your punishment, and in You from You.”

---

## Page 3843

Whoever reflects on this subject and others like it will find that the people of innovation and misguidance gain the upper hand over a group professing adherence to the Sunnah and guidance only because that group has itself adopted some other innovation or error—especially when it has agreed with its opponents on that point. They then argue against it on the basis of those concessions and press their implications until, if they can, they draw its members out of the religion as easily as a hair is drawn from dough. This is what the esoteric Qarmatians, the philosophers, and others like them have done to certain groups of Muslims.

The “Muʿtazilah” gained the upper hand over the “Ashʿarīs” and others who affirm the divine attributes and decree through their agreement with them in denying acts subsisting in Allah Most High. They thereby undermined the very principle their opponents had used against them to establish that Allah’s speech is uncreated: namely, that when speech or anything similar is created in a subject, the corresponding description applies to that subject.

They also gained the upper hand over them through this concession on the “question of divine decree,” forcing them into holding that the very evil deeds committed by the servant are acts of Allah, the Lord of the worlds, rather than of the servant. They then affirmed an acquisition that has no reality, for no intelligible distinction exists between acquisition and action in terms of the relation of power to its object. Hence people began to ridicule those who held this view, saying:

“Three things have no reality: al-Nazzām’s leap, Abū Hāshim’s states, and al-Ashʿarī’s acquisition.”

They also forced them to explain the efficacy of power upon its object as mere customary conjunction. Yet customary conjunction occurs between anything and its necessary concomitant, and between the object of power and power itself. There is therefore no more reason to regard one as exerting an effect upon the other than the reverse. It also occurs between an effect and its cause

---

## Page 3844

that is separate from it, even though, in his view, the servants’ power does not extend beyond its locus. Thus, when they saw the contradictions inherent in this position, Qādī Abū Bakr resorted to one view, Abū Ishāq al-Isfarāyīnī to another, and Abū al-Maʿālī al-Juwaynī to yet another. This is discussed at length in its proper place; the purpose here is merely to draw attention to it.

Among the subtle points in this discussion is that expressions such as “causal efficacy,” “compulsion,” and “provision” are general terms. If someone asks, “Does the servant’s power have an effect upon its object or not?” he should first be told that the term “power” encompasses two kinds:

The first is the capacity recognized by the Law, which enables action and forms the basis for commands and prohibitions. (The second is the capacity determined by the divine decree, which necessarily brings about the act and is simultaneous with it: the act does not lag behind this capacity.

The first is what is mentioned in the words of Allah Most High:

“Pilgrimage to the House is a duty owed to Allah by those who are able to make their way to it.”

If this ability were the capacity simultaneous with the act, pilgrimage to the House would be obligatory only upon those who actually performed it. Someone who did not perform pilgrimage would therefore not be disobedient for abandoning it, whether he had provisions and a mount and was capable of performing pilgrimage or not.

The same applies to the Prophet’s words—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—to ʿImrān ibn Husayn:

“Pray standing; if you cannot, then sitting; and if you cannot, then on your side.”

Likewise, Allah Most High says:

“So fear Allah as much as you are able.”

And the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—said:

“When I command you to do something, do as much of it as you are able.”

Had he meant an ability that exists only alongside the act, he would effectively have said, “Do as much of it as you actually do.” Thus, someone who did nothing would not be disobedient

---

## Page 3845

to him. This is the ability referred to in works of jurisprudence and in common usage.

People disagree over what the terms “ability” and “power” denote. Some recognize only this ability and maintain that ability must precede the act. Others recognize only an ability that accompanies the act. You will find many jurists contradicting themselves: when discussing the matter with speculative theologians who affirm divine decree and maintain that ability exists only alongside the act, they agree with them. Yet when discussing jurisprudence, they affirm the prior ability that forms the basis for commands and prohibitions.

From this distinction arises “the question of imposing duties beyond one’s capacity.” Capacity means ability, and the term admits of more than one meaning. Allah has never imposed any duty upon anyone without the ability recognized by the Law, which forms the basis for commands and prohibitions. Thus, according to this interpretation, He does not impose duties beyond one’s capacity. As for the capacity that exists only alongside the act, all commands and prohibitions impose duties beyond one’s capacity in this sense, for Muslims agree that this capacity is not a prerequisite for any command or prohibition.

The same applies to their disagreement over whether the servant has the power to act contrary to what Allah knows will occur. If “power” means the power recognized by the Law, which forms the basis for commands and prohibitions—like the ability mentioned in the words of Allah Most High:

“So fear Allah as much as you are able”—

then everyone whom Allah commands and forbids possesses ability in this sense, even if Allah knows that he will not obey Him. If, however, power is understood as “determined by the divine decree,” existing only alongside the act, then anyone whom Allah knows will not perform the act does not possess this power.

---

## Page 3846

Another example is people’s disagreement over “command and will”: does Allah command what He does not will, or does He command only what He wills? The term “will” admits of more than one meaning. It may refer to His universal will, which encompasses all events, as in the Muslims’ saying, “Whatever Allah wills happens, and whatever He does not will does not happen.” Likewise, Allah Most High says:

“Whoever Allah wills to guide, He opens his breast to Islam; and whoever He wills to lead astray, He makes his breast tight and constricted, as though he were ascending into the sky.”

And Noah, peace be upon him, said:

“My advice will not benefit you, even if I wish to advise you, if Allah wills to lead you astray.”

There is no doubt that Allah commands His servants to do things He does not will in this sense. As Allah Most High says:

“Had We willed, We would have given every soul its guidance.”

This indicates that He has not given every soul its guidance, although He has commanded every soul to follow its guidance. Similarly, the scholars agree that if someone swears by Allah that he will repay his creditor tomorrow, if Allah wills; or return property entrusted to him or property he has wrongfully seized; or perform the noon or afternoon prayer, if Allah wills; or fast Ramadan, if Allah wills—or do some other thing Allah has commanded—then he does not break his oath if he fails to do what he swore to do, even though Allah commanded him to do it. This is because he said, “If Allah wills.” Thus, it is known that Allah did not will it, although He commanded it.

As for His legislative will, it means love and approval and is inseparable from His command. As Allah Most High says:

“Allah wills to make things clear to you, guide you to the ways of those before you, and turn to you in forgiveness.”

This is also the meaning intended when Muslims say of someone committing an indecency, “This person is doing something Allah does not will.” That is, He neither loves nor approves of it; rather, He forbids and dislikes it.

Likewise, the term “compulsion” admits of more than one meaning. It may mean forcing someone to act without

---

## Page 3847

their consent, as when it is said that a father compels a woman to marry. Allah Most High is far too exalted and great to compel in this sense, for He creates in the servant willingness and choice concerning what he does. In this respect, that is not compulsion.

“Compulsion” may also mean creating the beliefs and intentions within souls, as in the statement of Muhammad ibn Kaʿb al-Qurazī: “Al-Jabbār (the Compeller) is He who compels His servants to what He wills.” Likewise, in the supplication transmitted from ʿAlī, may Allah be pleased with him:

“Compeller of hearts according to their innate dispositions, whether wretched or blessed.”

Compulsion in this sense is affirmed. Since the term “compulsion” admits of more than one meaning, the eminent imams prohibited affirming or denying it without qualification.

Likewise, the term “provision” admits of more than one meaning. It may refer to what Allah has made lawful or granted someone ownership of. Unlawful things are therefore not included in provision in this sense, as in His words, Most High:

“And they spend out of what We have provided for them.”

And His words, Most High:

“And spend out of what We have provided for you before death comes to one of you.”

And His words:

“And one whom We have provided with good provision from Us, from which he spends secretly and openly.”

There are other similar passages. “Provision” may also refer to whatever a living creature benefits from, even where neither lawful permission nor ownership has been granted. In this sense, it includes unlawful things, as in His words, Most High:

“There is no creature on earth whose provision is not upon Allah.”

And in his words, peace be upon him, in an authentic hadith:

“Then his provision, deeds and lifespan are recorded, and whether he will be wretched or blessed.”

Since the terms “compulsion,” “provision” and others like them admit of more than one meaning, the imams prohibited affirming or denying them without qualification, as previously reported from al-Awzāʿī, Abū Ishāq al-Fazārī and other imams.

---

## Page 3848

Likewise, the term “causal efficacy” admits of more than one meaning. Capacity stands in relation to what it enables as a causal means does to its effect, a cause to what it causes, and a condition to what is conditional upon it. If “capacity” means the capacity recognized by the revealed law, which makes the act possible and precedes it, then it is a condition for the act, one of its causal means, and an incomplete cause of it. If, however, “capacity” means the capacity that accompanies the act and necessarily entails it, then it is a cause of the act and a sufficient causal means.

It is well known that nothing among created things is, by itself, a complete cause and sufficient causal means for events, in the sense that its existence necessarily entails their occurrence. This belongs exclusively to the will of Allah Most High: whatever Allah wills occurs, and whatever He does not will does not occur. As for created causal means—such as fire in burning, the sun in illumination, and food and drink in satisfying hunger and quenching thirst—none of these produces the event by itself. Rather, another causal means must join it. Even then, there are impediments that prevent the two from producing their effect. Thus, every causal means depends upon the presence of the requisite conditions and the absence of impediments. Nothing among created things produces anything entirely by itself.

This makes clear to you the error of the philosophizers who said:

“From one, only one proceeds.”

They drew an analogy with natural effects, such as things that are heated or cooled, and the like. This is mistaken, for heating requires two things: first, an agent, such as fire; and second, a recipient, such as a body capable of receiving heat and being burned. Otherwise, when fire comes into contact with a salamander or a ruby, it does not burn it. Likewise, the sun’s rays depend upon a body facing the sun, onto which the rays are reflected; and they are obstructed by clouds, roofs, and other

---

## Page 3849

such things. Thus, this “one” that they have conceived in their minds has no existence in external reality. This has been explained at length elsewhere. The conceptual “one” affirmed by the philosophers—such as existence stripped of attributes, immaterial intellects, the universals from which they claim species are composed, conceptual matter and form, and similar things—has no existence in external reality. Such things exist only in minds, not as concrete entities. They are even further removed from existence than the indivisible atom affirmed by some speculative theologians. This “one” has no reality outside the mind, and neither does that atom, as has been explained in its proper place.

The point here is that if “causal efficacy” means the presence of a condition for an event, or of a causal means whose production of the event depends upon another causal means and the absence of impediments—all of which Allah Most High creates—then this is true. In this sense, the servant’s capacity does indeed have causal efficacy in bringing about what it enables. But if “causal efficacy” means that the agent independently produces the effect, with neither a helper sharing in its production nor an obstacle preventing it, then nothing created has causal efficacy. Rather, Allah alone is the Creator of everything, without partner or equal. Whatever Allah wills occurs, and whatever He does not will does not occur.

“Whatever mercy Allah opens up for people, none can withhold; and whatever He withholds, none can release after Him.”

“Say, ‘Call upon those whom you claim to be gods besides Allah. They do not possess even an atom’s weight in the heavens or on earth, nor do they have any share in either, nor does He have any helper from among them.’”

“Intercession is of no avail with Him except for those He permits.”

“Say, ‘Have you considered those you invoke besides Allah? If Allah intended harm for me, could they remove His harm? Or if He intended mercy for me, would they

---

## Page 3850

withhold His mercy?’ Say, ‘Allah is sufficient for me. In Him do those who trust put their trust.’” There are many similar passages in the Quran. Once the ambiguity and multiple meanings of “causal efficacy” are understood, the misconception is dispelled and the balanced position between the two groups becomes clear.

Whoever says that the believer and the unbeliever are equal in the causes conducive to faith that Allah has bestowed upon them; that Allah has not specially granted the believer any capacity or volition through which he came to believe; and that, when the servant acts, he gains no assistance from Allah or volition that he did not have before the act—his position is plainly false.

These people may be told: The servant’s action is itself one of the contingent things that come into being. Thus, every argument establishing that Allah Most High brought something else into being also establishes that Allah brought this action into being. The servant’s becoming an agent after not having been one is a contingent occurrence. If this contingent occurrence could arise without a necessarily existent originator to bring it into being and give precedence to its existence over its nonexistence, the same would be possible for other things, thereby invalidating the proof establishing the Creator’s existence.

There is no doubt that many speculative theologians who uphold affirmation and believe in divine decree conceded to the Muʿtazilah that an agent possessed of power and choice can favor one of two alternatives within his power over the other without a determining factor. On “the question of bringing the world into being,” they said that the agent possessed of power and choice—or the eternal will, whose relation to all events and times is the same—favored certain kinds of contingent things at the time it favored, without any cause arising to necessitate that preference. They claimed that an agent possessed of power and choice can favor one alternative without a determining factor, or that the eternal will can favor one alternative without any further determining factor. At this point, objections were raised against them by their opponents among the adherents of religious traditions and the philosophers who hold that Allah brings events into being

---

## Page 3851

through acts subsisting in Himself and that Allah created the heavens and the earth and all that is between them in six days, as well as by those who maintain the eternity of the world. They said:

“What you have said is self-evidently false. To admit this possibility entails that events can arise without a cause and that one alternative can prevail without a determining factor. This closes the door to establishing the Creator’s existence.”

Then these affirmers of divine decree used this argument against those who deny divine decree, saying:

“For the servant’s action to come into being after not existing, there must be an originating and fully determining cause other than the servant, since whatever proceeds from the servant is itself also brought into being. When that originating and fully determining cause exists, the servant’s action must necessarily exist.”

What they have said is true and constitutes a decisive argument against the Qadariyyah and the Muʿtazilah. Yet they undermined it and contradicted themselves concerning the acts of the Lord, blessed and exalted is He. There they claimed that self-evident reason distinguishes between the action of an agent possessed of power and the operation of a cause that necessitates its effect by its very essence. If this distinction is valid, their argument against the Muʿtazilah fails, and the Qadariyyah’s position has not been refuted. If it is invalid, their account of Allah’s bringing the world into being and creating it is false. And this account is indeed false.

For the principle that the existence of a contingent thing cannot prevail over its nonexistence without a fully determining factor is known through the innate disposition as a self-evident necessity and cannot be challenged. It is universal, admitting no exceptions. The distinction mentioned is therefore invalid. This invalidates their claim that the creation of the world is the world itself, and that it came into being after not existing without any newly arising cause.

Whoever says that the servant’s power and the other causes through which Allah Most High has created things are not causes, or that their existence is no different from their nonexistence, and that there is nothing beyond a mere conjunction

---

## Page 3852

based on habit, like the association of evidence with what it indicates, has denied the causes, wise purposes, and underlying reasons present in Allah’s creation and His revealed law. Such a person recognizes no power of sight in the eye distinguishing it from the cheek, no power of understanding in the heart distinguishing it from the leg, and no power of burning in fire distinguishing it from earth. These people deny the inherent natures and dispositions of physical bodies.

One learned man said:

“Some people argued against the existence of causes, powers, and inherent natures, making themselves a laughingstock among people of sound reason.”

Moreover, these people say that one should not say that one’s hunger was satisfied by bread or one’s thirst quenched by water. Rather, one should say, “My hunger was satisfied upon eating it, and my thirst was quenched upon drinking it.” For, according to them, Allah creates satiety, the quenching of thirst, and other such occurrences when the things habitually associated with them are present—not through those things.

This contradicts the Quran and the Sunnah, for Allah Most High says:

“It is He who sends the winds bearing glad tidings before His mercy, until, when they carry heavy clouds, We drive them to a lifeless land, then send down water thereby and bring forth thereby every kind of fruit”—to the end of the verse.

Allah Most High also says:

“And the water Allah sends down from the sky, thereby giving life to the earth after its death and spreading throughout it every kind of creature.”

Allah Most High also says:

“Fight them; Allah will punish them by your hands.”

He also says:

“Say, ‘Are you awaiting anything for us but one of the two best outcomes? We, however, await for you that Allah should afflict you with punishment from Himself or at our hands.’”

He also says:

“And We sent down blessed water from the sky, thereby causing gardens and grain for harvest to grow.”

Allah Most High also says:

“It is He who sends down water from the sky, and thereby We bring forth vegetation of every kind.”

Allah Most High also says:

“Do you not see that Allah sends down water from the sky, and thereby We bring forth fruits of varying colours?”

Allah Most High also says:

“It is He who sends down water from the sky; from it you drink, and from it grows vegetation among which

## Page 3853

you pasture your livestock.”

“Through it He causes crops, olives, date palms, grapes, and every kind of fruit to grow for you.”

Allah Most High also says:

“Indeed, Allah is not ashamed to set forth a parable”—up to His words—“Through it He leads many astray and guides many.”

He also says:

“There has come to you from Allah a light and a clear Book.”

“Through it Allah guides those who seek His pleasure to the ways of peace.”

There are many such passages in the Quran. The same is true of the hadiths of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, such as his saying:

“Whenever any of you dies, be sure to inform me so that I may offer the funeral prayer for him, for through my prayer for him Allah will bring blessing and mercy.”

He also said, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“These graves are filled with darkness for their occupants, and through my prayer for them Allah will bring light.”

There are many such examples.

Comparable to those who deny the causes decreed in Allah’s creation are those who deny the means prescribed in His commands. Such are those who suppose that if the good things attained through supplication, righteous deeds, and other such means are decreed, they will occur without those means; and if they are not decreed, those means will not bring them about.

These people are like those who said to the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, “Should we not then give up deeds and rely on what has been written?” He replied, “No. Act, for everyone will be enabled to do that for which he was created.”

It is also reported in the Sunan collections that he was asked, “O Messenger of Allah, what do you say about medicines we use to treat ourselves, healing recitations we ask others to recite over us, and precautions we take? Can they ward off anything of Allah’s decree?” He replied, “They are part of Allah’s decree.”

Hence some scholars have said: Reliance on causes compromises monotheism by associating partners with Allah

---

## Page 3854

and denying the causal role of causes distorts reason; disregarding causes altogether undermines the revealed Law. Allah, glorified be He, created causes and their effects and made one thing a cause of another. If someone says, “If this is decreed, it will happen without the cause; otherwise, it will not happen,” the answer is that it is decreed to occur through the cause, not without it. As the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Allah created people for Paradise; He created them for it while they were still in their fathers’ loins. And He created people for the Fire; He created them for it while they were still in their fathers’ loins.”

He also said, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“Act, for everyone will be enabled to do that for which he was created. Those destined for bliss will be enabled to do the deeds of those destined for bliss, while those destined for misery will be enabled to do the deeds of those destined for misery.”

In the two Sahīh collections, Ibn Masʿūd, may Allah be pleased with him, said: The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace—the truthful one whose truthfulness is confirmed—told us:

“The creation of each of you is brought together in his mother’s womb for forty days as a drop of fluid. Then he becomes a clot for a similar period, then a lump of flesh for a similar period. Then the angel is sent to him and commanded to record four things. He is told, ‘Write down his provision, his deeds, his lifespan, and whether he will be wretched or blessed.’ Then the soul is breathed into him.”

He said:

“By Him in whose hand is my soul, one of you may do the deeds of the people of Paradise until only a cubit stands between him and it; then the written decree overtakes him, and he does the deeds of the people of the Fire and enters it. And one of you may do the deeds of the people of the Fire until only a cubit stands between him and it; then the written decree overtakes him, and he does the deeds of the people of Paradise and enters it.”

---

## Page 3855

Thus the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, explained that one person enters Paradise through the deeds he performs and with which his life ends, while another enters the Fire through the deeds he performs and with which his life ends. As he said, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“Deeds are judged by their endings.”

This is because all good deeds are nullified by apostasy, and all sins are forgiven through repentance. Similarly, if someone fasts but breaks his fast before sunset, or prays but deliberately breaks his state of ritual purity before completing the prayer, his act of worship is invalidated.

In sum, the position of the early generations of this community and its leading scholars is what Allah sent His messengers with and revealed His Books to convey. They believe in Allah’s creation and His command, His decree and His revealed Law, His decrees governing creation and His religious rulings, and His universal and legislative will. As He said in the first verse:

“Whoever Allah wills to guide, He opens his heart to Islam; and whoever He wills to lead astray, He makes his heart tight and constricted, as though he were ascending into the sky.”

Noah, peace be upon him, said:

“My advice will not benefit you, even if I wish to advise you, if Allah wills to lead you astray.”

Concerning His legislative will, Allah Most High said:

“Allah intends ease for you and does not intend hardship for you.”

He also said:

“Allah wishes to make things clear to you, guide you to the ways of those before you, and accept your repentance. And Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise.”

And He said:

“Allah does not intend to impose hardship upon you, but He intends to purify you and complete His favor upon you.”

While acknowledging that Allah is the Creator, Lord, and Sovereign of everything, and that He created all things through His power and will, they also acknowledge that there is no deity worthy of worship except Him and that none other deserves worship. They obey Him and His messengers, love Him, place their hope in Him, fear Him, rely upon Him, and turn to Him in repentance. They ally themselves with His allies and oppose His enemies. They acknowledge His love for what He has commanded and for His believing servants

---

## Page 3856

and His pleasure in them, His hatred of what He has forbidden and of the disbelievers, and His wrath and loathing toward them. They also acknowledge what has been widely reported from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“Allah rejoices more at the repentance of His repentant servant than a man who lost his mount, carrying his food and drink, in a desolate, deadly wilderness. He searched for it but could not find it, then took a midday nap beneath a tree. When he awoke, there was his mount with his food and drink upon it! Allah rejoices more at His servant’s repentance than this man rejoices at recovering his mount.”

He is their God whom they worship and their Lord whom they ask, as Allah Most High says:

“All praise is for Allah, Lord of all worlds,”

through to His words:

“You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help.”

Thus, He is the One worshipped and the One whose help is sought. Worship combines perfect love with perfect humility.

They love Him more deeply than any lover loves their beloved, as Allah Most High says:

“Yet among people are those who take others as equals to Allah, loving them as they should love Allah. But those who believe are stronger in their love for Allah.”

Whatever else they love, they love only for His sake. As reported in the two Sahīh collections, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Whoever possesses three qualities will taste the sweetness of faith: that Allah and His Messenger are dearer to him than everything else; that he loves someone only for Allah’s sake; and that he hates returning to disbelief, after Allah has saved him from it, as much as he hates being thrown into the Fire.”

In al-Tirmidhī and elsewhere, it is reported:

“The firmest bonds of faith are love for Allah’s sake and hatred for Allah’s sake. Whoever loves for Allah’s sake, hates for Allah’s sake, gives for Allah’s sake, and withholds for Allah’s sake has perfected his faith.”

He, glorified be He, loves His believing servants. The perfection of love is intimate friendship, which Allah bestowed upon Abraham and Muhammad, may Allah bless them both and grant them peace. For Allah took Abraham as an intimate friend. And it has been widely reported

---

## Page 3857

from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, through several authentic chains of transmission, that he said:

“Allah has taken me as an intimate friend, just as He took Abraham as an intimate friend.”

He also said:

“If I were to take an intimate friend from among the people of the earth, I would take Abū Bakr as an intimate friend. But your companion is Allah’s intimate friend.”

He meant himself. Thus, the early generations of this community, its leading scholars, and all the people of the Sunnah and those with knowledge of Allah agreed that Allah Himself is loved and loves. The Jahmiyyah and their followers denied this love.

The first to deny it was al-Ja'd ibn Dirham, the teacher of al-Jahm ibn Safwān. Khālid ibn ‘Abd Allāh al-Qasrī offered him as a sacrifice at Wāsit, saying:

“O people, offer your sacrifices! May Allah accept your sacrifices, for I am sacrificing al-Ja'd ibn Dirham. He claims that Allah did not take Abraham as an intimate friend and did not truly speak to Moses. Exalted is Allah, far above what al-Ja'd says!”

Then he descended and slaughtered him. This is the foundation of the faith of Abraham, whom Allah made a leader for mankind. Allah Most High says:

“And when Abraham was tested by his Lord with certain commands, which he fulfilled, He said, ‘I will make you a leader for the people.’”

He also says:

“Who is better in religion than one who submits himself to Allah, does good, and follows the faith of Abraham, devoted to Allah alone? And Allah took Abraham as an intimate friend.”

Whoever says that loving Allah means loving to draw near to Him contradicts himself, for loving to draw near to Him follows from loving Him. Whoever loves Allah Himself loves to draw near to Him, while someone who does not love Him Himself cannot love to draw near to Him. As for someone who obeys Him and complies with His command only for some other end, in reality he loves only the end for which he acts, and has

---

## Page 3858

made obedience to Allah a means to that end. It is established in an authentic hadith that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“When the people of Paradise enter Paradise, a caller will announce: ‘People of Paradise, Allah has a promise for you that He wishes to fulfil.’ They will ask: ‘What is it? Has He not brightened our faces, made our scales heavy, admitted us to Paradise, and saved us from the Fire?’ Then the veil will be lifted, and they will look upon Him. Nothing He has given them will be dearer to them than looking upon Him. This is the additional reward.”

He thus explained that looking upon Him is dearer to them than all the pleasures they enjoy. Their love of looking upon Him follows from their love for Him: they love to look upon Him only because they love Him. Every believer finds in his heart love for Allah, tranquillity in remembering Him, delight in knowing Him, and pleasure and joy in remembering Him and speaking intimately to Him. This grows stronger or weaker, increases or decreases, according to people’s faith. The more complete a person’s faith, the more complete his delight in these things.

For this reason, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said in the hadith narrated by Ahmad and others:

“Of the things of your world, women and perfume have been made dear to me.” Then he said: “And my greatest delight has been placed in prayer.”

He would also say:

“Bring us comfort through prayer, Bilāl.”

This is discussed at length elsewhere. The point here is that His believing servants love Him, and He, glorified and exalted, loves them. Their love for Him is in proportion to their doing what He loves. Thus, in Sahīh al-Bukhārī, Abū Hurayrah narrates that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Allah Most High says: ‘Whoever shows enmity towards a close servant of Mine has openly challenged Me to war. Nothing by which My servant draws near to Me compares to fulfilling what I have made obligatory upon him. My servant continues to draw near to Me through voluntary acts of worship until I love him. When I love him, I am his hearing with which he hears, and his sight with which he sees

---

## Page 3859

and his hand with which he grasps, and his foot with which he walks. Through Me he hears, through Me he sees, through Me he grasps, and through Me he walks. If he asks Me, I will surely give him, and if he seeks My protection, I will surely protect him. I have never hesitated over anything I am going to do as I hesitate over taking the soul of My believing servant: he dislikes death, and I dislike causing him distress, yet death is inevitable for him.’”

He has thus made clear that when a servant draws near to Allah through the voluntary acts He loves, after fulfilling the obligatory duties, Allah loves him. Allah’s love for His servant is therefore proportionate to the servant’s doing what Allah loves. His love for the worship and obedience offered to Him follows from His love for Himself. His love for that worship and obedience is the reason He loves His believing servants; thus, His love for the believers follows from His love for Himself.

Although the believers praise and extol their Lord, they cannot fully praise Him. Rather, He is as He has praised Himself. As related in an authentic hadith, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, used to say:

“O Allah, I seek refuge in Your pleasure from Your wrath, in Your pardon from Your punishment, and in You from You. I cannot praise You as You deserve; You are as You have praised Yourself.”

It is also authentically established that he said:

“No one loves praise more than Allah; for that reason, He has praised Himself.”

Al-Aswad ibn Sarīʿ said to him, “I have praised my Lord with words of praise.” He replied, “Your Lord loves praise.”

He loves His servants’ praise of Him, yet His praise of Himself is greater than their praise of Him. He loves their extolling Him, yet His extolling Himself is greater than their extolling Him. The same holds for His love for Himself and His exaltation of Himself. He, glorified be He, knows Himself better than anyone else does, and He possesses attributes of perfection beyond the grasp of created minds. Majesty is His lower garment, and grandeur is His cloak. It is also authentically reported from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace,
