## Page 3860

that he recited from the pulpit:

“They have not esteemed Allah as He deserves. On the Day of Resurrection, the whole earth will be in His grasp, and the heavens will be folded in His right hand. Glory be to Him!”

He said: “Allah grasps the earth and folds up the heavens in His right hand, then shakes them and says: ‘I am the King! I am the Most Holy! I am the Source of Peace! I am the Giver of Security! I am the Guardian! I am the One who originated the world when it was nothing! I am the One who will bring it back!’” Another narration states: “The Lord glorifies Himself—glorified be He.”

Thus He praises, extols, and glorifies Himself, glorified and exalted be He. He is self-sufficient, needing no one else; rather, everything besides Him is in need of Him:

“All who are in the heavens and the earth ask of Him; every day He is engaged in some affair.”

He is the One, the Eternal Refuge, who neither begets nor is born, and to whom none is equal.

When He rejoices at the repentance of one who repents, loves those who draw near to Him through voluntary acts of worship, is pleased with the earliest forerunners, and so forth, it is not permissible to say that He thereby needs another or is made perfect by anything besides Himself. For He is the One who created these people, guided them, and helped them until they did what He loves, is pleased with, and rejoices in. These things He loves came about only through His power, His will, and His creation. His is the sovereignty, with no partner; to Him belongs all praise in this world and the Hereafter; His is the judgment, and to Him you will be returned.

This and similar evidence is cited by the majority, who affirm that His actions have a wisdom relating to Himself, which He loves and is pleased with, and for the sake of which He acts.

---

## Page 3861

They said:

There are several answers to the claim, “This entails that He is made perfect by something other than Himself, and thus was deficient beforehand.”

First: this objection is countered by the very effects He produces. Whatever answer is given concerning those effects also answers this objection. In the observable world, we know of no agent who is not perfected through his action.

Second: they said that His perfection consists in His always being able to act with wisdom. Were He supposed to be incapable of that, He would be deficient.

Third: the claim that He is made perfect by something other than Himself is false. For that comes about only through His power and will, with no partner sharing in it; thus, He has no need of another in this regard. To say that He is perfect by virtue of His action, in which He needs no other, is like saying that He is perfect by virtue of His attributes or His very essence.

Fourth: regarding the claim that He was deficient beforehand, if this means the absence of what has newly come about, we do not concede that its absence before the time at which wisdom required its existence constitutes a deficiency. If His being deficient is intended to mean something else, that is denied. Rather, the absence of something at a time when wisdom does not require its existence is an aspect of perfection, just as its existence at the time when wisdom requires it is perfection. Not everything’s absence, then, is a deficiency; rather, the absence of what ought to exist

---

## Page 3862

is deficiency, just as the existence of what ought not to exist is deficiency. Thus, it is clear that the existence of these things when wisdom requires their absence is the deficiency—not their absence.

For this reason, the Lord, exalted is He, is described by affirmative attributes that embody His perfection, and by negative attributes that likewise necessarily imply His perfection. The absence of whatever is negated of Him is therefore an aspect of perfection, just as the presence of whatever is rightly affirmed of Him is an aspect of perfection. Once this is understood concerning attributes, the same applies to actions and the like. Not every addition the mind conceives is an aspect of perfection; rather, many additions detract from the perfection of that to which they are added, as can be understood in the case of many existing things. For a human being, the presence of certain things at one time may constitute a deficiency and a fault, while at another time it constitutes perfection and is praiseworthy, just as something may harm him at one time and benefit him at another.

(Fifth: If we suppose one who is able to bring about temporal events for a wise purpose and another who is unable to do so, it is self-evident to reason that the one who is able is more perfect. Yet temporal events can exist only as things that come into being; they cannot be beginningless. If the ability to bring this about is more perfect, and what this ability produces can only be something that comes into being, then its existence is perfection, while its absence beforehand contributes to complete perfection. For the absence of what is impossible, which is a prerequisite for the existence of perfection, is itself an aspect of perfection.

They are divided here into three groups:

One group says that His will, love, pleasure, and the like are beginningless: He has always been pleased with those whom He knows will die as believers, and He has always been displeased with those whom He knows will die

---

## Page 3863

as disbelievers, as is held by some among the Kullābiyyah, the scholars of hadith, the jurists, and the Sufis. Their position therefore does not entail an infinite regress on account of temporal events inhering in Him. However, the majority oppose them concerning the wise purpose He loves, just as they oppose them concerning His will.

They say to them: “If His will is beginningless and has always existed, and its relation to all times and temporal events is the same, then singling out one time rather than another for something to come into being, and one effect rather than another, is a selection without a determining factor.”

The former reply: “It is the nature of will to select.”

Their opponents say to them: “Selection in general belongs to its nature. But selecting this particular thing over that particular thing is not something necessarily entailed by will. Rather, there must be a cause that necessitates one of the two being willed rather than the other. A person finds within himself that he selects through his will, but he knows that he wills this rather than that only because of a reason that calls for this selection. Otherwise, if all the possible objects of will were equal in every respect, it would be impossible for the will to single out one rather than its counterparts, for that would be preference without a deciding factor. Once this is admitted as possible, the way to establishing the existence of the Maker is closed.”

They say: “Anyone who reflects on this and examines it thoroughly will recognize its truth. Only someone who blindly follows another’s statement without considering its reality disputes it.”

Likewise, the majority say to them: “If Allah Most High, in His beginningless eternity, is pleased with, loves, and rejoices in what He brings into being, even before He brings it into being, then, when He does bring it into being, does doing so realize a wise purpose that He loves, is pleased with, and rejoices in? Or has nothing come about beyond what existed in beginningless eternity? If you say, ‘Nothing has come about beyond what existed in

---

## Page 3864

beginningless eternity,’ the reply is: ‘That was already present without the effects He brought into being, so those effects could not have been brought about in order to attain it.’ Thus, just as your position entails that effects come into being without a cause that Allah Most High brings about, it also entails that He produces them without a wise purpose that He loves and is pleased with.”

They say: “Your position therefore entails denying His will concurrent with the act, His love, and His wise purpose, without which the act cannot occur.”

(The second group say: “The wise purpose relating to Him is realized through His will and power, just as the act occurs through His will and power.” They say: “Even if this inheres in His Essence, it is like all the other attributes and acts of which He has informed us inhering in His Essence.”

The Muʿtazilah deny that attributes and acts inhere in Him. They call attributes “accidents” and acts “temporal events,” and say: “Neither accidents nor temporal events inhere in Him.” Those who do not understand the true nature of their position therefore imagine that they are declaring Allah Most High free of imperfections, defects, and deficiencies.

There is no doubt that Allah must be declared free of every defect, imperfection, and deficiency. For He is the Most Holy, the Flawless, the Self-Sufficient, the Master who is perfect in every attribute of perfection, with a perfection whose reality creation can comprehend. He is free of every imperfection, and creation cannot comprehend the fullness of this transcendence. Every perfection established for an existent being that entails no imperfection belongs more rightfully to the Creator Most High, who possesses it more perfectly. Every imperfection from which a created being is declared free is something from which the Creator has a greater right to be declared free, and from which He is more fittingly held to be exempt.

We have transmitted through several routes, including those of ʿUthmān ibn Saʿīd al-Dārimī, Abū Jaʿfar al-Tabarī, Abū Bakr al-Bayhaqī, and others, the explanation narrated by ʿAlī ibn Abī Talhah from Ibn ʿAbbās concerning the words of the Most High, “the Self-Sufficient.” He said: “The Master whose mastery is perfect, and the Noble One who is perfect

---

## Page 3865

in His nobility, the Great One who is perfect in His greatness, the Wise One who is perfect in His wisdom, the Self-Sufficient who is perfect in His self-sufficiency, the Compeller who is perfect in His might, the All-Knowing who is perfect in His knowledge, and the Forbearing who is perfect in His forbearance. He is perfect in every aspect of nobility and mastery. He is Allah, Mighty and Majestic. This description befits Him alone. He has no equal, and there is nothing like Him. Glory be to Him, the One, the All-Subduing.”

This explanation is reliably transmitted from ʿAbd Allāh ibn Abī Sālih, from Muʿāwiyah ibn Sālih, from ʿAlī ibn Abī Talhah al-Wālibī. It is said, however, that he did not hear the commentary directly from Ibn ʿAbbās. Nevertheless, statements of this kind are reliably transmitted from the early generations. It is reported that Saʿīd ibn Jubayr said: “Al-Samad is the One who is perfect in His attributes and acts.”

It is also reliably transmitted that Abū Wāʾil Shaqīq ibn Salamah said: “Al-Samad is the Master whose mastery has reached its utmost perfection.” These statements and others like them do not contradict what many of the early generations—including Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyib, Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, Mujāhid, al-Hasan, al-Suddī, al-Dahhāk, and others—said: that al-Samad is the One who has no interior cavity. This is transmitted from Ibn Masʿūd, and from ʿAbd Allāh ibn Buraydah on the authority of his father, either as a Companion’s statement or as a report traced back to the Prophet. Both explanations are true, as has been discussed at length elsewhere.

In ordinary language, the term “accidents” may be understood to refer to ailments and the like that befall a person. Likewise, the terms “temporal events and newly introduced things” may be understood to refer to what a person introduces

---

## Page 3866

in the form of blameworthy deeds and innovations that are not prescribed, or the illnesses and the like that befall a person. Allah, Glorified and Exalted, must be declared free of anything beyond these that involves any deficiency—how much more, then, must He be declared free of these things themselves! Yet when the Muʿtazilah said that He is free of accidents and temporal events, their sole intention was to deny His attributes and acts. According to them, no knowledge, power, will, mercy, love, pleasure, joy, creating, beneficence, justice, approach, coming, descent, rising over, or any other attribute or act of His subsists in Him.

The vast majority of Muslims disagree with them on this. Some groups dispute their position regarding the attributes but not the acts; others dispute it regarding some attributes but not others. Some dispute their position regarding the beginningless act, saying that His act is beginningless even though what it produces comes into existence, analogous to the position held by some concerning the will. These positions, their proponents, and their arguments are discussed at length elsewhere.

The purpose here is to indicate the main lines of people’s responses to the aforementioned question. When people say to this second group:

“If you affirm wisdom that comes into existence after not having existed, you must accept an infinite regress,”

they reply: “The question of this wisdom coming into existence is like that of all the other things He has brought into existence. We are addressing someone who concedes to us that He brought things into existence after they had not existed. Thus, if we say that He brought them into existence with a wisdom that has come into existence, he would have no right to

---

## Page 3867

say, ‘This entails an infinite regress.’ Rather, we say to him: ‘The question of wisdom coming into existence is like that of the effect that comes into existence and gives rise to that wisdom. Whatever answer you give concerning the latter is our answer concerning the former.’”

When the second group thus prevailed over the first, a third group—comprising leading scholars of hadith, jurists, Sufis, and theologians—said to them:

“This is a dialectical argument that binds your opponents to their own concessions; you have not provided a satisfying answer. You have neither scriptural nor rational evidence that rules out this infinite regress. Rather, infinite regress is of two kinds, as is circular dependence:

“First: an infinite regress of causes and their effects. This is impossible by common agreement.

“Second: an infinite regress of conditions and effects. There are two well-known positions among Muslims and others concerning whether this is possible. Groups among the theologians, hadith scholars, and philosophers hold it to be possible. Among them are the early generations and the imams who say that Allah has always spoken whenever He wills, and that acts and other things connected with His will and power have always subsisted in Him.

“They have explained that the arguments their opponents use to deny an infinite regress of effects and to establish the impossibility of an infinite past are weak. These include the argument based on putting two sets into correspondence despite one being larger than the other, the argument from even and odd numbers, and similar arguments. They have demonstrated their invalidity and refuted their proponents by invoking future events, numerical orders, and the objects of Allah’s knowledge together with

---

## Page 3868

the things within His power, and other matters discussed in detail in their proper place. Circular dependence is of “two kinds”: circular dependence involving priority is impossible. This means that one thing cannot exist until after another, while the other cannot exist until after the first. This is circular dependence among causes. As for circular dependence involving coexistence and concomitance—where one thing exists only together with another, and the other exists only together with the first—this concerns conditions and similar things that are mutually relative or mutually entailing. Circular dependence of this kind is possible.

These are the main outlines of the answers people have given to this question. They comprise several positions:

The first is the position of those who hold that neither His acts nor His rulings are based on reasons.

The second is the position of those who explain them by reference to things distinct and separate from Him, among the effects He brings into being.

The third is the position of those who explain them by reference to beginningless things subsisting in Him.

The fourth is the position of those who explain them by reference to things subsisting in Him and connected with His power and will, but who hold that their kind has a beginning.

The fifth is the position of those who explain them by reference to things connected with His will and power. If the act that gives rise to wisdom belongs to a kind that has a beginning, then the wisdom is likewise. If, however, it is supposed that speech or action connected with His will subsists in Him, and that this has always been so, then the wisdom is likewise. Thus, the kind is beginningless, even though its individual instances come into being.

The question can also be answered through an exhaustive division, as follows:

There is no doubt that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, brings into being effects that did not previously exist. The possibilities are that newly occurring acts must have a beginning, and that they may extend without limit into the past, just as they extend without limit into

---

## Page 3869

the future. If they must have a beginning, then events can come into being without forming an infinite regress. Thus, if someone says, “If He acted for a reason that came into being, the explanation of how that reason came into being would be the same as the explanation of how its effect came into being, necessitating an infinite regress,” the answer, on this assumption, is that events must have a beginning. If He performs an act for a wisdom that comes into being, both the act and its wisdom come into being. A reason that comes into being need not itself have another reason that comes into being, unless it is possible for events to have no beginning. If events may have a beginning, this objection falls away; how much more so if both must have a beginning.

If, on the other hand, it is said:

“Events may extend infinitely into the past, just as they extend infinitely into the future according to Muslims, the other religious communities, and the vast majority of humanity. Only certain adherents of innovation have disputed the latter: those who maintain that Paradise and Hell will cease to exist, as al-Jahm ibn Safwān maintains, or that the movements of the people of Paradise will cease, as Abū al-Hudhayl maintains. These two held that events, as a kind, must have an end, just as, in their view, they must have a beginning. Most of those who agreed with them that events must have a beginning disagreed with them about their having an end, saying that they have a beginning but no end. A third group said that they have neither a beginning nor an end. These three positions are well known among Muslim groups.”

The point here is that an answer is available on either assumption. Whoever allows that events may extend infinitely into the past allows an infinite regress of events and says: “This is an infinite regress of effects and conditions, not an infinite regress of causes and agents that produce effects. It is only the latter that is impossible, not the former.”

---

## Page 3870

and says that there is no proof that the latter is impossible, as maintained by groups among both the early and later scholars of kalām and hadith. Whoever holds that events must have a beginning says of the coming into being of the reason what he says of the coming into being of the effect, since there is no difference between them in this respect.

Among the answers that exhaust the possibilities is the following:

Allah’s act of creation either may or may not be explained in terms of a reason. If it may not, this is the first formulation. On this assumption, it is not called pointless. If someone does call it pointless, that designation does not undermine what has been established. For our discussion assumes that explaining it in terms of a reason is impossible. If that is impossible, this conclusion must be affirmed, whatever anyone may call it.

If, however, it may be explained in terms of a reason, then either it may be explained by a reason that comes into being, or it may not. If it is said that this is not possible, it follows that the reason is eternal, while on this assumption the effect cannot be eternal. For we are discussing the supposition that an effect which comes into being may be explained by an eternal reason. If it is said that it may be explained by a reason that comes into being, that position can be maintained.

Then it may be said that events may be explained by a finite reason belonging to the agent, so that it does not follow that something which comes into being subsists in Him—something that must subsist in Him for a wise purpose, even though that purpose is within His power and intended by Him. If the former is maintained, it follows that the reason which comes into being is separate from Him. On this basis, it also follows that the agent brings events into being after they did not exist, for a reason that comes into being in something other than Him, without any cause coming into being that necessitates the first event, and without anything that comes into being subsisting in the originator.

But if it is said: “Rather, it is not possible to

---

## Page 3871

bring events into being without a purpose pertaining to Him; rather, that which constitutes the cause and wisdom behind their coming into being must subsist in Him,” then this must be affirmed.

It must then be said either that this entails an infinite regress or that it does not. If it is said that it does not, then no infinite regress follows, and the objectionable consequence is avoided. If it is said that an infinite regress necessarily follows, then, on this supposition, an infinite regress is not objectionable. For the supposition is that His acts may be explained by a reason that comes into being, and that this entails an infinite regress. It is well known that what is possible cannot entail something impossible. If it did, it would be impossible on account of something else, even if possible in itself. Yet the supposition is that it is possible without qualification, with no impossibility involved. Whatever is possible without qualification, with no impossibility involved, cannot entail something whose existence is impossible. Thus, on this supposition, an infinite regress is not impossible.

This answers the objection without committing to any particular position. Rather, we show that no objectionable consequence actually arises. The objection, however, rests on six premises: that pointlessness necessarily follows, and that it is ruled out; that the effect must be eternal, and that this is ruled out; and that an infinite regress necessarily follows, and that it is ruled out.

The proponent of the first position says: “I do not concede that pointlessness necessarily follows.” The proponent of the second position says: “I do not concede that the effect must be eternal.” The proponent of the third position says:

---

## Page 3872

“I do not concede that an infinite regress necessarily follows,” or he says: “I do not concede that an infinite regress of effects is impossible.” These, then, are four challenges that must be considered. They cannot all be invalid; at least one must be sound. Whichever is sound answers the objection, which is the intended purpose. This is because the rational division exhausts the possibilities in the alternatives mentioned. Whoever finds one of these alternatives tenable adopts it. Elsewhere, we have discussed at length the foundations of this issue, its implications, and people’s positions on it. Our purpose here is to defend the Muslims collectively, for this objection is among those raised against people by the proponents of the eternity of the world. We have given several answers to it in our writings responding to the specious argument of those who maintain that the world is eternal.

Among their answers is the following:

This objection does not apply exclusively to the world’s coming into being. Rather, it applies to every event that comes into being in existence. That things come into being is witnessed, perceived by the senses, and agreed upon by rational people. Thus, whatever objection someone raises against the heavens and the earth having been created with a beginning, an equivalent objection can be raised against him concerning events that are directly witnessed. We have indicated the kinds of arguments advanced by each group in this discussion. However, an exhaustive treatment would exceed the scope of these pages and would not be appropriate here.

---

## Page 3873

Whoever understands what has been written will find this subject opened up to him and will be able to attain a full understanding of questions of this kind. For it is by discussing them gradually, stage by stage, that the intended aim is achieved. Otherwise, if firm assent to positions is thrust upon the heart before one has mastered their proofs, the reasoning behind them, and the answers to objections against them, one will be more inclined to reject and disbelieve them than to affirm them.

For this reason, difficult questions must be discussed by presenting the evidence for each position and the objections raised against it by the opposing side, until the truth becomes clear through the reasoning that establishes it, for those whom Allah wills to guide.

“Whoever Allah does not grant light has no light.” “Allah speaks the truth, and He guides to the way.” Allah, glorified is He, knows best and is most wise. All praise belongs to Allah, Lord of all worlds. May Allah’s blessings and peace be upon Muhammad, his family, and his Companions.

He was also asked:

The term “will” has two possible meanings: it may refer to His willing what He creates, or to His love and approval of what He commands.

“Whatever good befalls you is from Allah, and whatever evil befalls you is from yourself.”

Many people think that the good and evil mentioned in this verse refer to acts of obedience and disobedience.

## Page 3877

Then “those who affirm divine decree” cite His saying, “All is from Allah,” as evidence, but their argument is countered by His saying:

This is further clarified by the fact that every good thing and blessing that reaches the servant comes only from Allah. Every evil and calamity that is warded off from him or lifted from him is prevented only by Allah and removed only by Allah. Even when the means by which these things come about operate through His creatures, Allah, glorified be He, is the Creator of all those means. This applies whether the means consist of the movement of a living being acting by its own choice and intention—as with what He, Most High, brings about through the movements of angels, jinn, human beings, and animals—or the movement of an inanimate thing through the natural properties Allah has placed within it or through an external force that compels it to move, as with the movement of winds, waters, and the like. Allah is the Creator of all of this. There is no might or power except through Him. Whatever He wills comes to pass, and whatever He does not will does not come to pass.

All hope must therefore be placed in the Lord, all trust in Him, and all supplication directed to Him. If He wills something and facilitates it, it will come about and be made easy, even if people do not will it. If He does not will it and does not facilitate it, it will not come about, even if people will it.

This would be obligatory even if one of the causes were independently sufficient to produce the desired outcome. For if it were assumed to be independently sufficient to produce that outcome—though this could only be by Allah’s will and His making it possible—then it would be obligatory to

---

## Page 3882

place one’s hope in none but Allah, put one’s trust in Him alone, ask of Him alone, seek help from Him alone, and appeal to Him alone for deliverance. To Him belongs all praise, to Him all complaints are addressed, and He alone is sought for help and deliverance. There is no might or power except through Him. How much more so, then, when no cause can independently produce the desired outcome! Rather, other causes must join it, and obstacles and counteracting factors must also be removed before the intended result can be achieved.

Every cause has something that assists it and something that opposes it. Unless its assisting factor supports it and its opposing factor is averted, it will not produce its result. Rain alone does not make plants grow without the air, soil, and other things that work alongside it. Then the crop cannot fully develop unless destructive blights are kept away from it. Food and drink provide nourishment only through the organs and faculties placed within the body, and all of these together are of no benefit unless harmful factors are averted.

As for a created being who gives to you or supports you—notwithstanding that Allah creates within him the will, power, and action—what he does cannot be accomplished without many causes beyond his control that assist him in achieving his aim, even if he is a king whose commands are obeyed. Whatever opposes or obstructs these assisting causes must also be averted. Thus, the desired outcome can be achieved only when the causal basis is present and impediments are absent. Every particular cause is merely one component of that causal basis; no single thing in existence constitutes it on its own. Even if one calls a particular cause the “causal basis” and calls everything else that assists it “conditions,” this is merely a disagreement over terminology.

In that case, one would say:

The causal basis and the conditions must be present, and impediments must be absent. As for there being among created things a complete cause that necessarily entails its effect, this is false.

## Page 3883

And whoever truly understands this will find the door to understanding Allah’s oneness opened to him. Whoever places his trust in an angel, a prophet, a righteous man, or anyone similar for intercession or supplication should be told:

This too is merely one cause among others. The one who intercedes or supplicates does so only by Allah’s will and power. Moreover, those who obey Him intercede only for someone with whom He is pleased. As the Exalted says:

“They intercede only for those with whom He is pleased.”

No one intercedes with Him except by His permission—permission pertaining to His universal decree. For intercession, being an act performed by His servants, occurs only by His will and power. He is not like a created being approached by an intercessor whose intercession takes place independently of the might and power of the one being approached. Rather, He, glorified be He, creates the intercessor’s intercession, just as He creates all other changes. There is no might or power except through Him.

The word hawl (might) encompasses a change from one state to another, whether through movement, volition, or something else. Thus, the intercessor has no power to bring about any change, in intercession or anything else, except through Him. Furthermore, those who obey Him and whose intercession is accepted intercede only for those with whom He is pleased. They do not ask Him for anything that He does not love to be asked for. Indeed, even the angels—His own angels—are as He says of them:

“They say, ‘The Most Merciful has taken a son.’ Glory be to Him! Rather, they are honored servants.

“They do not precede Him in speech, and they act by His command.

“He knows what is before them and what is behind them. They intercede only for those with whom He is pleased, and they stand in awe of Him.”

## Page 3884

What proceeds from them is either speech or action. In speech, they do not precede Him; rather, they do not speak until He speaks, and they intercede only for those with whom He is pleased. We must likewise conduct ourselves toward Him and His messengers: we must not speak about religion until He has spoken, nor put ourselves ahead of Allah and His Messenger, nor worship Him except as He has commanded. A higher degree still is to do nothing except what He has commanded, so that all our actions are either obligatory or recommended.

If this is the case with causes such as these, what of someone who places his trust or hope in other causes—heavenly bodies, for example—or in the actions of human beings, such as kings, leaders, companions, friends, slaves, followers, and others?

Among the things that should be understood is the statement made by a group of scholars:

“Placing one’s reliance in causes is a form of associating partners with Allah that violates His oneness. Denying that causes are causes is a deficiency in reason, while disregarding causes altogether undermines the revealed law. True trust and hope combine what is required by belief in Allah’s oneness, reason, and the revealed law.”

The explanation is this: looking to a cause means that the heart depends on it, places hope in it, and relies upon it. Nothing in creation deserves this, for nothing acts independently: it necessarily has cooperating causes and opposing forces. Moreover, despite all this, unless the One who ordains causes makes it operate, it will not operate.

This is among the things that demonstrate that Allah is the Lord and Sovereign of everything, and that the heavens, the earth, all that lies between them, the celestial spheres, and everything they contain have a Creator and Governor distinct from them. For you will find that whatever proceeds from a celestial sphere, a heavenly body, an angel, or anything else cannot independently bring about anything

---

## Page 3885

that comes into being. Rather, it requires others to cooperate with it and assist it, and even then it encounters opposing and obstructing forces. One of the greatest examples of this is the “starless ninth sphere.” Many metaphysical philosophers, astrologers, and others suppose that its motion causes all events, and their knowledge of the causes of events goes no further than this motion. They either regard it as known to the Necessary Existent through the mediation of an intellect or a soul, or without such mediation; or else they deny that it is an effect and regard it as necessarily existent in itself. This claim of theirs is among the most utterly unsound, although, despite their intelligence, they fail to recognize this, and many people do not know how to refute them on this point.

Anyone who looks at the sky knows that its motion is not the cause of all celestial motions. It is often said that, through its easterly motion, all the spheres within it move from east to west. Yet each sphere also has another motion peculiar to it, contrary to this motion: the sphere of the fixed stars, and the spheres of the sun, the moon, and the other celestial bodies that recede, run their courses, and disappear from view. These differing motions do not arise from that motion—they run counter to it—nor are their spheres effects of that ninth sphere. Even if we suppose that events are brought about by the motion of the heavenly bodies and the various configurations formed through trines, squares, sextiles, conjunctions, and the like, it is well known that those

---

## Page 3886

different configurations are not effects of the motion of the ninth sphere. Rather, its motion is part of the cause, just as the motion of each sphere is part of the cause. The celestial configuration arises from the combined effect of two motions or several different motions. If we suppose that the nine spheres come into conjunction, they have seven motions—or, according to them, even more, depending on the additional spheres whose existence is inferred from the different motions, such as the badrī spheres and others that account for the direct and retrograde motions of the heavenly bodies and their other movements. Accordingly, anyone who makes the motion of the ninth sphere the cause of all events contradicts what is known to these philosophers and astrologers, and to every rational person.

Even supposing that it causes the motion of all the spheres, it does not independently bring about clouds, thunder, lightning, rain, vegetation, or the conditions of animals and minerals. For the motions of these bodies do not all derive from the motions of the spheres. Rather, they possess powers and causes that produce other motions in them, just as every sphere that initiates motion has a motion that does not derive from another sphere.

All motions are either “natural,” “voluntary,” or “forced.” Forced motion depends on the agent imposing it. Natural motion is motion of which the moving body has no awareness, such as the downward movement of earth. Voluntary motion is motion of which the moving being is aware, such as the movement of an animal. Thus, whatever among these bodies moves by an inherent nature or will has the source of its motion within itself. As for whatever is moved by force, the created agent imposing that force does so only because the body possesses a capacity to receive it; and this is a property that does not derive

---

## Page 3887

from the agent imposing the force. Thus, even when combined, the motions of the spheres do not independently move these bodies, although they may form part of the cause, just as we observe that the sun forms part of the cause of the growth, moisture, dryness, and similar conditions of certain bodies. Moreover, even supposing that they are causes, there are things that impede and counteract them. For every conceivable cause has something that can impede it, whether voluntary, natural, or otherwise. Supplication, charity, and righteous deeds, for example, are among the greatest means of averting calamities descending from heaven. This is why we have been commanded to perform them during eclipses and other heavenly signs that may cause punishment. As the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“The sun and the moon are not eclipsed because of anyone’s death or birth. Rather, they are two of Allah’s signs through which He instils fear in His servants. When you see that, hasten to prayer.”

During an eclipse, he, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, commanded prayer, remembrance of Allah, seeking forgiveness, charity, and the emancipation of slaves.

Once it is understood that, when you examine observable beings individually—the ninth sphere and everything else—you find that none independently brings about anything whatsoever, but that events necessarily require other causes, even if the being in question forms part of a cause, and that these causes also face other opposing factors, it becomes clear that none of these things can rightly be said to bring about observable events. Still less can any of them be said to originate bodies whose motion differs from its own and counteracts what its motion would bring about. For a thing does not necessitate what opposes it and runs counter to it. If, among moving bodies, there is something whose effects run counter to what the ninth sphere necessarily produces and entails

---

## Page 3888

and oppose it, neither can be the cause of the other. For an effect cannot oppose its cause, just as it cannot produce its cause. Likewise, a thing cannot be its own opposite or produce itself. Its being opposed to itself would entail its existence depending on its own existence, making it both existent and nonexistent. Its producing itself, given that a cause precedes its effect, would likewise entail its being both existent and nonexistent.

It is known that if the events and motions arising from the powers of bodies do not originate from the “ninth sphere,” and it imparts to them only accidental motion, then there is all the more reason that the bodies themselves and their powers should not originate from it. This establishes that the mover of the spheres and other observable bodies, and the originator of these bodies through another cause, is a Lord distinct from them. He is the One who originated them in their different forms and set them in motion with their different motions. This is what was to be established.

Moreover, even if these heavenly bodies form part of the cause of certain events, they do so only in some circumstances, not others. When they appear above the earth, their light and influence become manifest; when they set, their light and influence cease. They then cease to be either a cause or part of a cause. This is why Allah’s intimate friend, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“I do not love those that set.”

When they set, their influence upon us ceases altogether, leaving no semblance of a justification on which anyone attached to them can rely. The Lord who is invoked and asked, in whom hope and trust are placed, must be the self-subsisting Sustainer who sustains His servant at all times and in every circumstance. As He said:

“And put your trust in the Ever-Living, who does not die.”

And He said:

“Allah—there is no deity except Him, the Ever-Living, the Sustainer of all existence.”

Thus this and other forms of

---

## Page 3889

reflection and contemplation establish that the servant should place his hope in Allah alone and rely upon Him alone. As for fearing nothing but his own sin, this follows from the knowledge that no calamity befalls him except because of his sins. This is known through the signs in the world around us and within ourselves, and through what Allah has revealed in His Book, as explained at length elsewhere. We have also explained the underlying reason for this in greater detail than this discussion allows.

This bears out what is established in the authentic hadith narrated by Abū Dharr from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, reporting that his Lord said:

“My servants, it is only your deeds that I record for you and then recompense you for in full. Whoever finds good, let him praise Allah; and whoever finds otherwise, let him blame no one but himself.”

He thus explained that the servant should praise Allah for whatever good he finds, for Allah is the One who bestowed it upon him, and that he should blame no one but himself for whatever evil he finds.

It is also authentically reported that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“The best supplication for forgiveness is for the servant to say: ‘O Allah, You are my Lord; there is no deity except You. You created me, and I am Your servant. I remain true to Your covenant and promise as far as I am able. I seek refuge in You from the evil of what I have done. I acknowledge before You Your blessings upon me, and I acknowledge my sin. So forgive me, for no one forgives sins but You.’”

The words, “I acknowledge before You Your blessings upon me,” express recognition and acknowledgment of His blessings, while the words, “and I acknowledge my sin,” express acknowledgment of sin. Hence one of the early generations said:

“Each morning I find myself between a blessing and a sin, so I wish to respond to the blessing with gratitude and to the sin by seeking forgiveness.”

Gratitude, however, follows the blessing, whereas reliance and hope precede it, as Allah’s intimate friend said:

“So seek from Allah

---

## Page 3890

provision, and worship Him and be grateful to Him.”

In his sermon, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Praise be to Allah. We seek His help and forgiveness, and we seek refuge in Allah from the evils of our souls and from our evil deeds.”

He thus combined praising Allah, seeking His help, and asking His forgiveness. It has therefore become clear that placing one’s reliance on causes constitutes associating partners with Allah, contrary to His oneness, and is wrongdoing and ignorance. This is the condition of someone who invokes another besides Allah and relies upon him.

As for their statement, “To deny that causes are causes is a deficiency in reason,” this is indeed so, and it also undermines the revealed Law. Many speculative theologians have denied causes altogether, treating their existence as no different from their absence. Those naturalists, by contrast, regarded them as causes that necessarily produce their effects, while the Muʿtazilah distinguished between the actions of living creatures and other occurrences. All three views are false, for Allah says:

“He is the One who sends the winds as glad tidings before His mercy. When they bear heavy clouds, We drive them to a lifeless land and send down water through them, bringing forth thereby every kind of fruit.”

And He, Most High, says:

“And the water Allah sends down from the sky, giving life thereby to the earth after its death.”

And He, Most High, says:

“Through it Allah guides those who seek His pleasure to the paths of peace.”

And He, Most High, says:

“Through it He leads many astray and guides many.”

There are many similar passages. Whoever says that effects occur in the presence of causes, but not through them, contradicts the wording of the Quran. Moreover, sensory experience and reason testify that these are causes and recognize the difference between the forehead and the eye, in that one possesses a faculty absent from the other; likewise, between bread and pebbles, in that one provides nourishment while the other does not.

As for their statement, “To disregard causes altogether undermines the revealed Law,” it also undermines reason. The actions of servants are among the strongest causes of the outcomes attached to them. Thus, whoever regards

---

## Page 3891

those who believe and do righteous deeds as those who spread corruption on earth, or treats the God-fearing like the wicked, is among the most ignorant of people and the most deeply steeped in disbelief. Rather, the worship, supplications, knowledge and deeds that Allah has commanded are among the greatest causes of the acts of worship linked to them. Likewise, the disbelief, wickedness and disobedience He has forbidden are among the greatest causes of the misery attached to them.

Nevertheless, the best of creation said:

“None of you will enter Paradise by virtue of his deeds.”

They asked, “Not even you, O Messenger of Allah?”

He replied, “Not even me, unless Allah envelops me in His mercy and bounty.”

And when he told them, “There is not one of you whose place in Paradise and whose place in Hell is not already known,” they asked, “O Messenger of Allah, should we not then rely on what has been written and abandon deeds?”

He replied, “No. Act, for everyone will be enabled to do that for which he was created. Whoever is among the people of bliss will be enabled to perform the deeds of the people of bliss, and whoever is among the people of misery will be enabled to perform the deeds of the people of misery.”

Likewise, supplication and reliance upon Allah are among the greatest causes of the outcomes for which Allah has made them causes. Whoever says, “Whatever has been decreed for me will come to me, whether I supplicate or not, and whether I rely upon Allah or not,” is like someone who says, “Whatever bliss or misery has been allotted to me will come to me, whether I believe or not, and whether I obey or disobey.” It is well known that this is misguidance and disbelief, although the former statement is not as misguided as the latter: the connection between attaining one’s aims and supplication and reliance upon Allah is not like the connection between bliss in the Hereafter and faith. Yet there is no doubt that whatever Allah has made supplication a cause of is comparable to that for which action has been made

---

## Page 3892

a cause—namely, righteous action. He, glorified is He, is able to bring about the outcome without this cause, and He may bring it about through another cause.

Likewise, whoever abandons the prescribed means of securing benefits or warding off harm, whether commanded as an obligation or as a recommendation, undermines the revealed Law and departs from sound reason. This is where they went wrong: they abandoned the means they were commanded to take, thinking that this perfected their reliance upon Allah. Yet reliance upon Allah is coupled with worship in His words:

“So worship Him and rely upon Him.”

Worship consists in doing what has been commanded. Whoever abandons the prescribed worship while relying upon Allah is no better off than someone who worships Him without relying upon Him. Rather, both disobey Allah by abandoning part of what they have been commanded to do.

Reliance upon Allah includes relying upon Him to help one do what He has commanded, and relying upon Him to grant what lies beyond one’s own power. Seeking help concerns the performance of deeds, whereas reliance upon Allah is broader than that: it includes relying upon Him to secure benefit and ward off harm. Allah Most High says:

“If only they had been content with what Allah and His Messenger gave them and had said, ‘Allah is sufficient for us. Allah will give us of His bounty, and so will His Messenger. Indeed, to Allah we turn in hope.’”

And Allah Most High says:

“Those to whom people said, ‘The people have gathered against you, so fear them,’ but this only increased them in faith, and they said, ‘Allah is sufficient for us, and He is the best Disposer of affairs.’”

Whoever does not do what he has been commanded is not seeking Allah’s help in doing it. Thus, he has abandoned worship and seeking help to perform it, also abandoning reliance upon Allah in this respect. Another person relies upon Allah without doing what has been commanded; this is blameworthy helplessness. As related in Sunan Abī Dāwūd: “Two men took their dispute

---

## Page 3893

to the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and he ruled against one of them. The man against whom he ruled said, ‘Allah is sufficient for me, and He is the best Disposer of affairs.’ The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said, ‘Allah blames helplessness, so you must act prudently. Then, if something overcomes you, say: Allah is sufficient for me, and He is the best Disposer of affairs.’”

In Sahīh Muslim, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, is reported to have said:

“The strong believer is better and more beloved to Allah than the weak believer, though there is good in both. Strive for what benefits you, seek Allah’s help, and do not give in to helplessness. If something befalls you, do not say, ‘Had I done such and such, such and such would have happened.’ Rather, say, ‘Allah has decreed, and He has done what He willed,’ for ‘if only’ opens the door to Satan’s work.”

A person is not commanded to look to divine decree when considering the actions he is commanded to perform, but rather when calamities befall him that he has no means of averting. Whatever befalls you, whether through human actions or otherwise, bear it patiently, be content, and submit. Allah Most High says:

“No calamity befalls except by Allah’s permission. And whoever believes in Allah, He guides his heart.”

One of the early generations—either Ibn Masʿūd or ʿAlqama—said: “This is the man whom a calamity befalls, who knows that it is from Allah, and so is content and submits.”

This is why Adam said to Moses, “Do you blame me for something Allah decreed for me forty years before I was created?” Thus Adam prevailed over Moses in argument. For Moses had said to him, “Why did you cause us and yourself to be expelled from Paradise?” He blamed him for the calamity that resulted from his action, not for its being a sin. That is why Adam invoked divine decree in his argument against him. As for the notion that the blame concerned the sin itself, as various groups of people suppose, this is not what the hadith means, because Adam, peace be upon him, had already repented of the sin, and one who repents of sin

---

## Page 3894

is like one who has no sin, and all agree that one who has repented may not be blamed.

Moreover, Adam invoked divine decree in his argument, yet no one may invoke divine decree to justify sin, as Muslims, adherents of all other religions, and all other rational people agree. If this were acceptable, anyone could commit whatever occurred to him—killing people, seizing their wealth, or perpetrating any other form of corruption on earth—and invoke divine decree as his excuse. Yet the very person who invokes divine decree will not accept this excuse from someone who wrongs him. He thus contradicts himself, and a position’s inconsistency demonstrates its invalidity. The invalidity of invoking divine decree as an excuse is therefore evident even to the most elementary reason.

Whoever supposes that belief in divine decree consists in believing that Allah is the Creator of His servants’ deeds—as supposed by the polytheistic antinomians, who acknowledge divine decree but not divine commands, and the Magian Qadarites, who acknowledge divine commands but not divine decree—or supposes that, given this, imposing religious obligations is unintelligible, but that the Lawgiver is obeyed in this solely because of the divine will, and that Allah acts; and makes this his argument concerning deeds, without including reasons appropriate to commands and prohibitions, but instead denies the benefits, merits, and purposes that the revealed law contains for people in this life and the Hereafter; reduces that law to a mere attribution, without any correspondence or congruity between cause and effect; and denies that deeds have qualities by virtue of which they are good and commanded, or evil and forbidden, invoking divine decree as his argument for this and maintaining that, since the Lord is the Creator, all of this is impossible—

---

## Page 3895

then he is mistaken and astray. The invalidity of his position is self-evident and established by what rational people agree upon. The Quran, the Sunnah, and scholarly consensus likewise demonstrate its invalidity.

For people generally believe in divine decree and say that aggressors must be punished—even the insane and animals are disciplined to curb their aggression, although their actions are decreed—and that all human beings pardon their aggression, although their actions are decreed.

The servant must therefore be patient and should be content with the afflictions decreed for him. He should seek forgiveness for sins and faults, not invoke divine decree to excuse them, and give thanks for the blessings and gifts Allah has decreed for him. Thus he combines gratitude, patience, and seeking forgiveness with belief in divine decree and the revealed law. And Allah knows best.

---

## Page 3896

What do the esteemed scholars, the imams of religion—may Allah be pleased with them all—say concerning the words of Allah Most High:

“Our word to a thing, when We intend it, is only that We say to it, ‘Be,’ and it is.”

If the one addressed already exists, then bringing into existence what already exists is impossible. But if it does not exist, how can addressing something nonexistent be conceived?

And concerning His words, exalted is He:

“I did not create the jinn and mankind except to worship Me.”

If the particle lām indicates the eventual outcome, that outcome has not come about. If it indicates purpose, this would entail that none of His creatures should fail to worship Him, yet that is not the case. How, then, can this difficulty be resolved?

And concerning the reports and verses enjoining contentment with Allah Most High’s decree, and the Prophet’s words—may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“The Pen has dried concerning what is to be.”

And concerning the meaning of His words, exalted is He:

“Call upon Me; I will respond to you.”

If supplication, too, concerns what is destined to occur, what benefit is there in commanding it, when it must inevitably occur?

Shaykh al-Islām Abū al-ʿAbbās Ahmad ibn Taymiyyah—may Allah have mercy on him—replied:

All praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds.

---

## Page 3897

As for the “first question,” it rests on two principles:

The first is the distinction between the address that brings things into being and the address that imposes obligations. Through the former, He, glorified is He, does not require any action from the addressee. Rather, He Himself brings the addressee into being and creates it through that address, without any action, power, will, or existence on the addressee’s part. Through the latter, He requires the one commanded to perform an act or refrain from it, exercising power and will—although all of this occurs through Allah’s might and power, for there is no might or power except through Allah.

People have disagreed over this latter address: may something nonexistent validly be addressed on condition that it comes into existence, or may it validly be addressed only after it exists? They do not disagree, however, that the ruling conveyed by the address applies to it only after it exists. Likewise, they have disagreed over the former: is it an actual address, or is it an expression of His power and the swiftness with which He brings things into being through that power? The former is the well-known view among those who identify with the Sunnah.

The second principle concerns whether something nonexistent is a thing while it does not exist. Certain groups among the theologians of the Muʿtazilah and the Shīʿah have held that it is a thing outside the mind—an entity and a distinct reality. They have claimed that essences are neither made nor created, and that their existence is something additional to their essential reality. Certain groups among the philosophers, the Ittihādiyyah (advocates of union), and other heretics have likewise adopted this view.

---

## Page 3898

The view held by the vast majority—and by the affirmationist theologians and those who identify with the Sunnah and the community—is that, before it exists, the nonexistent is nothing at all outside the mind: neither a thing, nor an entity, nor a distinct reality. Nor are there two things outside the mind, one being its essential reality and the other its existence, additional to that reality. Allah brought the entities themselves—that is, their essences—into being. Everything other than Him, glorified and exalted is He, is created, made, brought into being, and originated by Him.

Among those who hold this view, however, some say that the nonexistent is not a thing at all, and that it is called a thing only because it is established in knowledge; the designation is therefore figurative. Others say that it undoubtedly has an established reality and an existence in knowledge, and that, in respect of this reality and existence, it is a thing and an entity.

These people do not distinguish between existence and being established, as those who say that the nonexistent is a thing do. Nor, in holding that the nonexistent is not a thing, do they distinguish between the possible and the impossible, as the latter do. They all agree that the impossible is not a thing; their disagreement concerns only the possible. The principal argument of those who regard it as a thing is simply that it is established in knowledge. In this respect, it can properly be singled out as something intended, created, spoken of, commanded, prohibited, and so forth.

They say that such specific relations cannot pertain to sheer nonexistence. If, then, the distinction is drawn specifically between existence as concrete reality and existence as reality in knowledge, the confusion in this matter disappears.

---

## Page 3899

Concerning His words, exalted is He:

“When We will something, all We say to it is, ‘Be!’ and it is.”

That thing is known before it is brought into being and before this address is directed to it; in this respect, it has already been ordained and decreed. For Allah, glorified and exalted is He, speaks and writes whatever He wills of what He knows. Thus, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said in the hadith narrated by Muslim in his Sahīh from Abd Allāh ibn Amr:

“Allah decreed the destinies of all creatures fifty thousand years before He created the heavens and the earth.”

In Sahīh al-Bukhārī, Imrān ibn Husayn relates that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Allah was, and nothing was with Him. His Throne was upon the water, and He wrote everything in the Record, then created the heavens and the earth.”

In Sunan Abī Dāwūd and elsewhere, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, is reported to have said:

“When Allah first created the Pen, He said to it, ‘Write.’ It asked, ‘What shall I write?’ He said, ‘Whatever will happen until the Day of Resurrection.’”

These and similar texts show that, before a created thing is created, it is known, spoken of, and written down. It is therefore a thing in respect of its existence in knowledge, speech, and writing, even though its reality—its concrete existence—is not established outside the mind; rather, it is pure nonexistence and sheer negation. These are the four well-known levels of existence. Allah, glorified and exalted is He, mentioned them in the first surah He revealed to His Prophet, saying:

“Read in the name of your Lord who created—created man from a clinging clot. Read! And your Lord is the Most Generous, who taught by the pen—taught man what he did not know.”

We have discussed this at length elsewhere. Accordingly, the address is directed to that toward which the will is directed and to which is connected

---

## Page 3900

His power, and which He creates and brings into being, as He says:

“When We will something, all We say to it is, ‘Be!’ and it is.”

Thus, that to which “Be!” is said is the very thing that is willed. When it is willed, before it is created, it is already established and distinct in knowledge and decree. Otherwise, the thing willed and created would not be distinguished from anything else. This provides the answer to the alternatives posed in the question.

The questioner says: “If that which is addressed exists, then bringing into being what already exists is impossible.”

The reply is: This is so if it already exists in external reality with the very existence in question. Undoubtedly, what is nonexistent does not exist, nor does it have any established reality in itself. But as for what is known and willed, and is a thing in knowledge, will, and decree, its existence in external reality is not impossible. Indeed, no created thing comes into existence until after it exists in knowledge and will.

The questioner also says: “If it is nonexistent, how can addressing the nonexistent be conceivable?”

The reply is: If what is meant is addressing something while it is nonexistent with words that it understands and obeys, this is impossible. For the one addressed must be capable of understanding and acting, whereas it is inconceivable that something nonexistent should understand and act. Thus, it is impossible to address it with a command imposing an obligation while it is nonexistent, in the sense of requiring it to understand and act during its nonexistence. Likewise, it is impossible to address something nonexistent in external reality with a creative command, in the sense of supposing that it is something already established in external reality and is being addressed with the command to be.

---

## Page 3901

As for a thing that is known, mentioned, and written down, if addressing it with a creative command is like directing the will toward it, this is not impossible; rather, it is possible. Indeed, a person finds something similar within himself: he conceives of something he wishes to do, then directs his will and desire toward that intended and desired thing he has conceived. Its realization depends on his ability. If he has the power to bring it about, it comes about with resolute will and desire; if he is incapable, it does not. A person may say, “Let such-and-such be,” or use similar expressions of demand, but the realization of what he seeks depends on his power to accomplish it. Allah, glorified is He, has power over all things. Whatever He wills comes to pass, and whatever He does not will does not come to pass. Thus, when He wills a thing, His command is only to say to it, “Be!” and it is.

Section

As for the second question, the questioner says:

“In the words of the Exalted,

‘I did not create jinn and mankind except to worship Me,’

if this lām—the particle ‘to’—denotes the eventual outcome, that outcome has not come about. If it denotes purpose, it would follow that none of the created beings could fail to worship Him. Yet this is not the case. How, then, can this difficulty be resolved?”

The reply is:

This lām is not what grammarians call the lām of outcome or eventual result. No one has maintained that it is here, given the questioner’s observation that this outcome did not come about—except

---

## Page 3902

according to those who interpret “worship Me” as “know Me,” meaning the knowledge enjoined upon both believer and unbeliever. But this is a weak view. Some people have made this claim concerning His words near the end of Sūrat Hūd:

“And for that He created them.”

Some of the Qadarīs claimed that this lām denotes outcome or eventual result: that is, their eventual outcome was mercy or disagreement, even though the Creator did not intend it. They likened this to His words:

“Then Pharaoh’s household picked him up, only for him to become an enemy and a source of grief to them,”

and to the poet’s words:

“Bear children for death, and build for ruin.”

This interpretation is also weak here, because the lām of outcome is used only of someone who does not know how matters will ultimately turn out, and who therefore performs an act whose outcome he does not know—as was the case with Pharaoh’s household. But as for one who knows the outcomes and consequences of actions, it is inconceivable that he should perform an act without knowing its outcome. If he knows that his act has a particular outcome, he does not intend by it something he knows will not occur, for that would be wishful thinking, not willing.

Rather, the lām here has its familiar meaning: it is the lām meaning “in order to,” the lām of purpose. When it is omitted, the verbal noun it governs in the genitive takes the accusative as an expression of purpose. This purpose is called the final cause: it precedes the act in knowledge and will, but follows it in existence and realization. This cause is the intended, sought-after objective of the act. However, it should be understood that will in the Book of Allah is of two kinds:

---

## Page 3903

The first is the creational will: the will that necessarily entails the occurrence of what is willed. Of this it is said, “Whatever Allah wills comes to pass, and whatever He does not will does not come to pass.” This is the will referred to in such statements as His words:

“Whomever Allah wills to guide, He opens his heart to Islam; and whomever He wills to lead astray, He makes his heart tight and constricted.”

And His words:

“My advice will not benefit you, even if I wish to advise you, if Allah wills to lead you astray.”

And Allah Most High says:

“Had Allah willed, they would not have fought one another, but Allah does whatever He wills.”

And Allah Most High says:

“Why, when you entered your garden, did you not say, ‘What Allah wills! There is no power except through Allah’?”

There are other similar passages.

This will is what the lām signifies in His words:

“They will continue to differ, except those upon whom your Lord has mercy; and for that He created them.”

The early generations said: “He created one group for disagreement and another for mercy.” Since mercy here was the will, and there it was creational, what was willed through it came to pass: some people differed, while others were shown mercy.

As for the second kind, it is the religious, legislative will. It consists in loving and approving what is willed, loving and being pleased with those who fulfill it, and rewarding them with the best. Thus Allah Most High says:

“Allah intends ease for you and does not intend hardship for you.”

And Allah Most High says:

“Allah does not intend to place any hardship upon you, but He intends to purify you and complete His favor upon you.”

And He says:

“Allah intends to make things clear to you, guide you to the ways of those before you, and turn to you in forgiveness. Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise.”

“Allah intends to turn to you in forgiveness, but those who follow their desires want you to stray far away.”

“Allah intends to lighten your burden, for mankind was created weak.”

This will does not necessarily entail the occurrence of what is willed unless the first kind of will also pertains to it. Thus there are four categories:

---

## Page 3904

The first is that to which both kinds of will pertain: righteous deeds that actually occur. Allah wills them by His religious, legislative will, commanding, loving and approving them; and He wills them by His creational will, so they occur. Otherwise, they would not occur.

The second is that to which only the religious will pertains: righteous deeds that Allah commands, but the disbelievers and the wicked disobey that command. All these deeds are objects of His religious will, and He loves and approves them whether they occur or not.

The third is that to which only the creational will pertains: events that He decrees and wills but has not commanded, such as permissible acts and sins. He has not commanded, approved or loved them, for He does not command indecency, nor does He approve disbelief for His servants. Were it not for His will, His power and His creation of them, they would not occur or come into existence. Whatever Allah wills comes to pass, and whatever He does not will does not come to pass.

The fourth is that to which neither kind of will pertains: permissible acts and sins that do not occur.

Accordingly, what the lām signifies in His words:

“I did not create jinn and mankind except to worship Me”

is this religious, legislative will. What is intended by this will may or may not occur. The meaning is that the purpose He loves and approves for them, and which they have been commanded to fulfill, is worship. This is the deed for which He created His servants: it brings about their perfection and well-being, through which they become pleasing and beloved to Him. Whoever does not fulfill this purpose therefore lacks what is loved, approved and intended for him by the religious will, wherein lie his happiness and salvation, and lacks

---

## Page 3905

his perfection and well-being—a deprivation that entails his corruption and punishment. As for the claims that worship is resolve or innate disposition, these are two weak and unsound views whose flaws are evident in many respects.

Section

As for the third question, he asks concerning the reports and verses about contentment with Allah’s decree:

“If sins occur apart from Allah’s decree, that is impossible and undermines belief in His oneness. But if they occur by the decree of Allah Most High, does not disliking and hating them amount to disliking and hating the decree of Allah Most High?”

The answer is that neither the Book of Allah nor the Sunnah of His Messenger contains any verse or hadith commanding people to be content with every decreed and predestined human action, whether good or evil. This is a fundamental principle that requires careful attention. People must, however, be content with what Allah has commanded; no one may resent what He has commanded. Allah Most High says:

“But no, by your Lord, they will not believe until they make you judge in their disputes, then find within themselves no discomfort at your judgment and submit completely.”

Allah Most High also says:

“That is because they followed what angered Allah and disliked His good pleasure, so He rendered their deeds worthless.”

And He says:

“If only they had been content with what Allah and His Messenger gave them and had said, ‘Allah is sufficient for us. Allah will give us of His bounty, and so will His Messenger. To Allah alone we turn in hope.’”

The mention of the Messenger here makes it clear that this giving is religious and legislative, not creational and decretal. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, also said in

---

## Page 3906

the authentic hadith:

“He has tasted the sweetness of faith who is content with Allah as his Lord, Islam as his religion, and Muhammad as his Prophet.”

A person should be content with the afflictions Allah decrees for him that are not sins, such as being tried with poverty, illness, humiliation, or harm inflicted by others. Patience in the face of affliction is obligatory. Contentment with it is prescribed, but is it obligatory or recommended? The followers of Ahmad and others hold “two views” on this; the sounder view is that it is recommended, not obligatory.

It is well known that the strongest bonds of faith are love for Allah’s sake and hatred for Allah’s sake. Allah has commanded us to enjoin what is right, love it, be pleased with it, and love those who practise it; and to forbid what is wrong, hate it, be displeased with it, hate those who practise it, and strive against them with our hands, tongues, and hearts. How, then, could we imagine that there is nothing among created things that we should hate and dislike? After mentioning various prohibitions, Allah Most High says:

“The evil of all this is hateful in the sight of your Lord.”

If Allah dislikes these things, although He is the One who decreed them, how could those whom He has commanded to dislike and hate them fail to do so? He is the One who says:

“And He has made disbelief, wickedness, and disobedience hateful to you. Those are the rightly guided.”

Allah Most High also says:

“That is because they followed what angered Allah and disliked His good pleasure, so He rendered their deeds worthless.”

Allah Most High says:

“So when they angered Us, We exacted retribution from them.”

And Allah Most High says:

“Allah became angry with them and cursed them.”

Allah Most High also says:

“They hide from people, but they cannot hide from Allah. He is with them when they plot by night to say things that do not please Him.”

He thus states that some of what is actually said does not please Him.
