## Page 3907

Allah Most High also says:

“Allah has promised those among you who believe and do righteous deeds that He will surely make them successors in the land, as He made those before them successors, and will surely establish for them their religion which He has approved for them.”

He says:

“And I have approved Islam as your religion.”

And He says:

“If you are grateful, He approves it for you.”

He thus makes clear that He approves the religion He has commanded. If He approved everything, that religion would have no special distinction. The two Sahīh collections report that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“No one has greater jealousy than Allah over His male or female servant committing unlawful sexual intercourse.”

He also said:

“Allah is jealous, and the believer is jealous. Allah’s jealousy is over a servant doing what He has forbidden him.”

Jealousy necessarily entails disliking and hating that which occasions it. This is a vast subject.

Section

As for the “fourth question,” it is his statement: “If the Pen has dried after recording all that is to occur, what is the meaning of His saying, ‘Call upon Me; I will answer you’? If supplication is also among the things destined to occur, what is the benefit of commanding it when it must inevitably occur?”

The answer is this: supplication brings about an answer just as other righteous deeds bring about reward, and just as other causes bring about their effects. Whoever says that supplication is merely a sign and indication that what is sought and requested will be obtained, rather than a cause of it; or that it is purely an act of worship with no effect on whether the desired outcome occurs or not—rather, whatever is attained through supplication is attained

---

## Page 3908

without it—has adopted one of two weak views. For Allah has made the answer dependent upon supplication as an effect depends upon its cause, as in His saying:

“Your Lord says, ‘Call upon Me; I will answer you.’”

The two Sahīh collections report that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“No Muslim calls upon Allah with a supplication involving neither sin nor the severing of family ties but that He grants him one of three things through it: either He hastens the fulfilment of his supplication, stores up an equivalent good for him, or averts an equivalent evil from him.” They said, “O Messenger of Allah, then we shall supplicate abundantly!” He replied, “Allah has still more to give.”

Thus, He made these gifts dependent upon supplication, just as the promised reward and recompense depend upon performing the commanded deed. ‘Umar ibn al-Khattāb said: “I do not concern myself with the answer; rather, I concern myself with supplication. When I am inspired to supplicate, the answer comes with it.” There are many similar statements.

Moreover, observable reality demonstrates and clarifies this, just as it demonstrates the same relationship in the case of all other causes. Allah, glorified is He, has told us of this in passages such as His saying:

“Noah certainly called upon Us, and how excellent We are at answering!”

And His saying, Most High:

“And the man of the fish, when he went away in anger, thinking that We would not constrain him. Then he called out in the darkness, ‘There is no god but You. Glory be to You! Indeed, I have been among the wrongdoers.’”

“So We answered him and saved him from distress. And thus do We save the believers.”

And His saying:

“Who is it that answers the distressed when he calls upon Him, removes hardship, and makes you successors on the earth?”

And His words, Most High, concerning Zechariah:

“My Lord, do not leave me childless, though You are the best of inheritors.”

“So We answered him, granted him John, and made his wife fertile for him.”

He also says, Most High:

“When they board a ship, they call upon Allah, devoting their worship sincerely to Him. But when He delivers them safely to land, they immediately associate partners with Him.”

And He says, Most High:

“And among His signs are the ships on the sea, like mountains.”

“If He wills, He stills the wind, leaving them motionless on its surface. Indeed, in that

---

## Page 3909

are signs for everyone who is steadfast and grateful.”

“Or He may destroy them for what they have earned, though He pardons much.”

“And those who dispute Our signs will know that they have no escape.”

He thus tells us that, if He wills, He destroys them. His taking them to task for their sins and His pardoning many of those sins are accompanied by the realization among those who dispute His signs that they have no escape. For in such circumstances, the person who raises specious objections against the proofs of the Lord’s lordship, power, will, and mercy knows that he has no escape from the plight in which he finds himself. This is like His saying in another verse:

“Yet they dispute about Allah, while He is mighty in retribution.”

Knowledge that arises in the soul through compelling circumstances is firmer and more deeply rooted than knowledge produced by mere syllogistic reasoning—which vanishes from people’s minds in such circumstances: Is the Lord a cause whose effects follow necessarily from His essence, so that He does not Himself originate events and cannot bring anything into being or change the world, such that He could be invoked and petitioned? Does He know things both in detail and in general, and have the power to alter circumstances, so that He may be asked to bring about a change from one state to another? Or is He not so, as certain philosophizers and other misguided people claim?

Thus, alongside punishment and pardon from the Possessor of Majesty, those given to disputation and argument come to know that they have no escape from what He has inflicted upon those who disputed His signs, for He is mighty in retribution. We have discussed this and similar matters elsewhere, together with the doctrines and religious beliefs connected with them. The point here is to recognize that supplication and petition are a means of attaining what is sought and requested

---

## Page 3910

—its presence is not equivalent to its absence in this respect, nor is it merely a sign, as the Quran and Sunnah demonstrate. Certain groups among Muslims and others have disputed this, although the vast majority of humankind—Muslims, Jews, Christians, Sabians, Magians, and polytheists—acknowledge it.

Yet some polytheists and Sabians among the Peripatetic philosophizers who follow Aristotle, together with his followers among the philosophizers of the religious communities—such as al-Fārābī, Ibn Sīnā, and those who follow their path, including those who blend this with speculative theology, Sufism, and jurisprudence—and others like them, explain supplication’s effect in attaining what is sought in the same way that they explain the effects of other contingent, created things: celestial and natural forces, and the powers of the soul and intellect. They attribute the results of supplication to the influence of human souls, without affirming that the Creator, glorified be He, has detailed knowledge of this or the power to change the world, or that, had He willed to do otherwise than He did, He could have done so. In their view, He is therefore unable to gather a human being’s bones and re-form his fingertips. Yet He, glorified be He, is the Creator of those souls and their powers. There is no might or power except through Allah.

As for his statement:

“If supplication is something that is going to occur, what benefit is there in commanding it, when it must inevitably occur?”

The reply is:

The supplication that is commanded does not necessarily occur. Rather, when Allah commands His servants to supplicate, some obey Him: their supplication is answered, and they attain what they seek. This indicates that what was foreknown and decreed was both the supplication and its answer. Others disobey Him and do not supplicate, so they do not obtain what was made dependent upon supplication. This indicates that neither the supplication nor its answer was among what was foreknown and decreed. Thus, the supplication that occurs is that

---

## Page 3911

which was foreknown to occur, while the supplication that does not occur is that which was foreknown not to occur.

If it is asked, “What, then, is the benefit of commanding supplication that is foreknown to occur?” the reply is:

The command itself, like other causes, is a cause of compliance with what is commanded. Supplication is a cause that repels affliction: if it is stronger than the affliction, it repels it; if the cause of the affliction is stronger, it does not repel it, but lessens and weakens it. This is why prayer, supplication, seeking forgiveness, giving charity, and freeing slaves have been enjoined at times of eclipses and other signs. And Allah knows best.

## Page 3912

Shaykh al-Islām—may Allah Most High have mercy on him—was asked:

“Do divine decrees entail wisdom or not? If they entail wisdom, has Allah willed that people do what they actually do? And if His will has preceded their actions, what does it mean for there to be an excuse under these circumstances? Please give us a ruling; may you be rewarded.”

He replied:

All praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds. Our Lord, glorified and exalted is He, encompasses everything in knowledge, power, and rule; His mercy and knowledge embrace all things. There is not an atom in the heavens or the earth, nor any meaning whatsoever, that does not testify to Allah Most High’s complete knowledge and mercy and His perfect power and wisdom. He did not create creation without purpose, nor has He done anything in vain. Rather, He is wise in His actions and His words—glorified and exalted is He. Some aspects of His wisdom He has disclosed to some of His creatures, while knowledge of others He has reserved for Himself.

His will is of “two kinds”: the will pertaining to command and legislation, and the will pertaining to decree and ordainment.

The first kind pertains only to acts of obedience, not sins, whether those acts occur or not. As He says:

“Allah intends to make things clear to you, guide you to the ways of those before you, and accept your repentance.”

And He says:

“Allah intends ease for you and does not intend hardship for you.”

---

## Page 3913

And as for the second kind—the will pertaining to decree—it encompasses all beings and every event. In this sense, rather than the first, Allah has willed that His creatures do what they actually do. As He, Most High, says:

“Whoever Allah wills to guide, He opens their heart to Islam; and whoever He wills to lead astray, He makes their heart tight and constricted.”

And He says:

“My advice will not benefit you, even if I wish to advise you, if Allah wills to lead you astray. He is your Lord.”

Likewise, Muslims say: “Whatever Allah wills happens, and whatever He does not will does not happen.” There are many similar examples.

This will encompasses acts of obedience and disobedience that actually occur, but not those that do not occur. The first will, by contrast, encompasses acts of obedience whether they occur or not. The blessed person is one from whom Allah wills, by His decree, what He wills for him through His legislation. The wretched servant is one for whom He wills, by His decree, what He does not will for him through His legislation. Judgment proceeds in accordance with these two wills. Whoever views deeds with both these eyes sees clearly; whoever considers divine decree without divine legislation, or divine legislation without divine decree, sees with only one eye. Such were the Quraysh, who said:

“If Allah had willed, neither we nor our forefathers would have associated partners with Him, nor would we have forbidden anything.”

Allah Most High said:

“Likewise, those before them denied the truth until they tasted Our punishment. Say, ‘Do you have any knowledge that you can produce for us? You follow nothing but conjecture, and you do nothing but lie.’”

These people believed that everything Allah willed to exist and occur—this being His decretive will—He had also commanded and approved, without regard to His legislative will. Then they saw that their associating partners with Him without any revealed authorization was among the things Allah had willed to exist. They therefore said: “Then He must have approved and commanded it.” Allah said:

“Likewise, those before them denied”—the revealed laws, with their commands and prohibitions—“until they tasted Our punishment. Say, ‘Do you have any

---

## Page 3914

knowledge that you can produce for us?’”—that Allah has prescribed associating partners with Him and forbidding what you have forbidden.

“You follow,” in this matter, “nothing but conjecture”—namely, your supposition that whatever He has decreed, He has also prescribed. “And you do nothing but lie”—that is, you lie and fabricate, thereby setting His law aside.

“Say, ‘Allah’s is the conclusive argument’”—against His creatures, for He sent them messengers who called them to worship Him alone and follow His law. Nevertheless, had He willed, He would have guided all creatures to follow His law. Yet He bestows His favor upon whomever He wills, guiding them out of His grace and kindness, and withholds it from whomever He wills. For one who bestows a favor may either bestow it or refrain from doing so. His withholding His favor from those He deprives of it is just and equitable, and He has consummate wisdom in doing so.

He punishes His creatures for contravening His command and His legislative will, even though their doing so occurs by His decretive will. For just as disobedience occurs by divine decree, so too does its punishment. Likewise, He, glorified be He, may decree that a servant suffer illnesses that bring pain: the illness is by His decree, and the pain is by His decree.

If a servant says, “It was already willed that I should sin, so I will not be punished,” this is like a sick person saying, “It was already willed that I should become ill, so I will not feel pain”; or saying, “It was already willed that I should eat something hot, so my constitution will not become overheated”; or, “It was already willed that the blow should be struck, so the person struck will not feel pain.” Besides being ignorance, this does not benefit the person who says it. Rather, invoking divine decree as an excuse is a second sin for which he will also be punished.

It was Iblīs who invoked divine decree as an excuse when he said:

“Because You have led me astray, I will surely make evil appealing to them on earth.”

Adam, by contrast, said:

“Our Lord, we have wronged ourselves. If You do not forgive us and have mercy upon us, we will surely be among the losers.”

When Allah wills blessedness for someone, He inspires him to say what Adam—peace be upon him—said, or words to that effect.

---

## Page 3915

and whoever He wills to be wretched invokes Iblīs’s excuse or something similar. He is thus like someone seeking refuge from scorching ground in fire.

His likeness is that of a man into whose house a spark flies. Sensible people tell him, “Put it out before it burns down the house!” But he begins saying, “Where did it come from? The wind carried it here, and I am not to blame for this fire.” He continues offering such excuses until the fire blazes up, spreads, and burns down the house and everything in it.

Such is the condition of someone who attributes his sins to divine decree rather than counteracting them by seeking forgiveness and offering apologies. Indeed, his condition is worse, because he himself committed the sin, whereas he had no part in causing the spark.

May Allah, glorified be He, grant us, you, and all our brothers success in doing what He loves and is pleased with. For obedience to Him can only be attained through His help, and disobedience to Him can only be avoided through His protection. And Allah knows best.

## Page 3916

He was asked—may Allah sanctify his soul—about divine decrees:

“Do they embody wisdom or not? If they embody wisdom, has He willed what people will do or not? If His will has already preceded their actions, what does it mean for an excuse to exist in such circumstances?”

He replied:

All praise is due to Allah, Lord of all worlds. Yes, Allah has perfect wisdom in His decrees and ordainments, even if He has not made it known to His servants. For Allah possesses knowledge that He has taught His servants—or whomever He wills among them—and knowledge that He has not taught His servants:

“They encompass nothing of His knowledge except what He wills. His Kursī extends over the heavens and the earth, and preserving them does not tire Him.”

He, glorified be He, has willed what His servants will do by His creative will. Thus, the Muslims agree that whatever Allah wills happens, and whatever He does not will does not happen. As He says:

“Whoever Allah wills to guide, He opens his heart to Islam; and whoever He wills to lead astray, He makes his heart tight and constricted.”

And as He says:

“They will continue to differ,”

“except those to whom your Lord has shown mercy; and for this He created them.”

And as He says:

“If Allah had willed, they would not have fought one another, but Allah does whatever He wills.”

And as He says:

“Allah makes firm those who believe

---

## Page 3917

with the firm word in this worldly life and in the Hereafter. Allah leads the wrongdoers astray, and Allah does whatever He wills.”

Yet He has not willed acts of disobedience from those who commit them in the sense of commanding or legislating them, loving or approving them, or prescribing them as religion. Rather, this latter kind of will is as expressed in His words, Exalted is He:

“Allah intends ease for you and does not intend hardship for you.”

And His words, Exalted is He:

“Allah wishes to make things clear to you and guide you to the ways of those before you.”

“Allah wishes to turn to you in mercy, but those who follow their desires wish you to deviate far from the right path.”

“Allah wishes to lighten your burdens, for mankind was created weak.”

And He, Exalted is He, says:

“Allah does not intend to impose hardship upon you, but He intends to purify you.”

And He, Exalted is He, says:

“I did not create the jinn and mankind except to worship Me.”

By drawing distinctions and explaining matters in detail, confusion is removed and error dispelled. I have discussed this at appropriate length in several places in my writings on fundamental principles, for this is not the place to elaborate on it.

As for the questioner’s words, “What does it mean for an excuse to exist?” the person who is excused, and knows that he is excused, is someone unable to perform an act despite wishing to do so. Examples include a sick person unable to stand in prayer, fast, or take part in jihad, and a poor person unable to spend, and similar cases. Such people are neither obligated to perform these acts nor punished for omitting them. The same applies to those unable to hear and understand, such as a child, a person of unsound mind, and someone whom the call to Islam has not reached.

---

## Page 3918

As for someone who has been made to love committing evil deeds, to choose them and to approve of them, and who consequently commits them, he is neither forced to act against his will nor coerced into doing what he willingly accepts. How, then, can he be called excused? Rather, he should be called deluded. But explaining this fully requires discussing the wisdom underlying creation and command. This is discussed in its proper place, and there is no room for it here. Allah knows best, and may Allah bless Muhammad.

be accompanied by something that exists. Thus, when a person lacks knowledge, his soul naturally impels him, for it is alive (*), and voluntary movement is inseparable from life. Hence the names that most truthfully describe a person are al-Hārith and al-Humām. The hadith states:

and so on. Another hadith states:

Such being its condition, if Allah guides the soul, He teaches it what benefits it and what harms it, so that it desires what benefits it and abandons what harms it. Allah, glorified be He, has favoured the children of Adam with two things that form the foundation of happiness:

“I created My servants as pure monotheists,”
and the hadith continues. Thus, if left to its natural disposition, the soul would love Allah and worship Him without associating anything with Him. It is corrupted, however, by those devils among humans and jinn who make evil alluring to it. Allah Most High says:
“And when your Lord took from the children of Adam—from their backs—their descendants,”
and the verse continues. The explanation of this verse is set out at length elsewhere.

Second: Allah Most High has granted people general guidance through the reason He has endowed them with, the scriptures He has sent down to them, and the messengers He has sent to them. Allah Most High says:

up to His words:
“what he did not know.”

Within every person, therefore, is that which calls for recognizing the truth and loving it. Allah has guided each person to kinds of knowledge through which he can attain happiness in the Hereafter, and has placed a love for this within his natural disposition.

## Page 3921

But a person may turn away from seeking knowledge of what benefits him. This turning away is a privation. Yet will and movement are inseparable from the soul, for it possesses natural life. Its happiness, however, lies in living a beneficial life by worshipping Allah. Whenever it fails to live this life, it is dead, while the natural life it possesses becomes a cause of its torment. Thus, it is neither alive and enjoying life nor dead and relieved of torment. Allah Most High says:

“Then he will neither die therein nor live.”

The recompense corresponds to the deed: since, in this world, he neither lived a beneficial life nor was dead and without sensation, his condition in the Hereafter is likewise.

If the soul knows the truth and desires it, this is part of Allah’s complete favour upon it. Otherwise, its very nature necessarily leads it to have an object of desire and worship other than Allah, as well as evil objects of desire. This state arises from its failure to know Allah and worship Him, and this is a privation.

The Qadariyyah acknowledge this, and acknowledge that Allah created man with a will. However, they regard him as possessing will only potentially, as a capacity—that is, as capable of willing this or that. As for his actually willing this particular thing or that particular thing, they hold that this is not created by Allah. They are mistaken. Rather, Allah is the Creator of all of this, and He is the One who inspired the soul with its wickedness and its piety. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, used to say:

“O Allah, grant my soul its piety,”

and so on.

---

## Page 3922

As for its final cause:

He created it only for a wise purpose in light of which it is good, even though it is evil in relative terms. If evil is attributed to Him in isolation, someone might imagine the doctrine of Jahm ibn Safwān: that Allah created pure evil containing no good for anyone, with no wise or merciful purpose. The Quran, the Sunnah, and reasoned reflection refute this.

For example, saying, “Muhammad and his community shed blood and spread corruption on earth,” would disparage them and would be false. But saying, “They fight so that Allah’s word may be supreme, and kill those who prevent them from achieving that,” would praise them and would be true.

Likewise, the following statement is true and constitutes praise of the Lord: “The Lord Most High is Wise and Merciful. He has perfected everything He created, and He is the Most Merciful of those who show mercy. Good is in His hands, and evil is not ascribed to Him. He does nothing but good. Whatever He has created of pain in some living creatures, or of their blameworthy deeds, contains great wisdom and immense blessing.”

But saying, “He creates evil containing no good or benefit for anyone, with no wisdom or mercy in it, and punishes people without their having sinned,” would not praise Him, but rather the opposite.

We have already explained some of the wisdom and mercy in the creation of Hell, Iblīs, and evil deeds; what we do not know is greater still. Allah, glorified and exalted be He, deserves praise, love, and contentment with Him, both for who He is and for His beneficence. Praise for His beneficence is praise in gratitude, while praise for who He is is unqualified praise.

Elsewhere, we have explained that whatever He has created is a blessing for which He deserves thanks. It is among His favours. Hence He says at the end of Sūrat al-Najm:

“Then which of your Lord’s favours will you doubt?”

---

## Page 3923

And in Sūrat al-Rahmān He mentions:

“Everyone upon the earth will perish,”

and similar statements, after which He says:

“Then which of your Lord’s favours will you both deny?”

A group of scholars offered the following explanation—the wording is al-Baghawī’s. Then, after citing His words,

“They will go back and forth between it and scalding water,”

he said: “Everything Allah, Mighty and Majestic, mentions from His words, ‘Everyone upon the earth will perish,’ onwards consists of admonitions. This is a blessing, because it deters people from sins.”

Others, including al-Zajjāj and Ibn al-Jawzī, explained these verses as meaning: “Then which of your Lord’s favours will you both deny?”—referring to these things, for they are all blessings: they point you to His oneness, and through them He provides you with what sustains you. This is what they said concerning Sūrat al-Rahmān.

Regarding His words,

“Then which of your Lord’s favours will you doubt?”

they said: “Which of your Lord’s blessings, pointing to His oneness, do you call into question?” Another explanation is: “You doubt and dispute.” Ibn ‘Abbās said: “You deny.”

I say: The word tatamārā (“you dispute”) incorporates the meaning of tukadhdhib (“you deny”); hence He made it transitive with tā. It follows the tafā‘ul pattern, derived from mirā (disputation). One says, “We disputed about the crescent moon,” and, “Disputing about the Quran is disbelief.” Such disputation can involve denial and casting doubt.

It is also said that, since the address was directed to them, He said tatamārā (“you dispute”), meaning yatamārawna (“they dispute”), rather than tamtarī (“you doubt”), because the tafā‘ul form involves two parties.

Concerning His words,

“And that a person will have only what he strives for,”

they said: “It has been said that this refers to al-Walīd ibn al-Mughīrah.” For He said:

“Or has he not been informed of what is in the Scriptures of Moses,”

“and of Abraham, who fulfilled his obligations,”

“that no bearer of burdens will bear the burden of another?”

[Then He turned to address him, saying: “And that a person will have only what he strives for.”] (*)

Likewise, He said:

“He created man from clay like pottery,”

“and He created the jinn from a smokeless flame of fire.”

“Then which of your Lord’s favours will you both deny?”

Thus, everything He has created contains kindness towards His servants for which He is to be thanked, and He has in it a wise purpose that pertains to Him

## Page 3924

for which He deserves to be praised in His own right. Thus, all created things contain blessings for His servants—including humankind and jinn, addressed in His words:

“Then which of your Lord’s favours will you both deny?”

This is because they are signs through which His servants are guided, pointing to His oneness and the truthfulness of His prophets. Hence He says immediately afterwards:

“This is a warner like the warners of old.”

Some say this refers to Muhammad; others say it refers to the Quran. The two are inseparable. The meaning is: this is a warner who warns of what the earlier messengers and scriptures warned of. His words, “like the warners of old,” mean that it is of their kind. The greatest blessing is therefore the blessing of faith, and every created thing is among the signs through which something of this blessing is attained. Allah Most High says:

“There is certainly a lesson in their stories for people of understanding.”

And He says:

“As insight and a reminder for every servant who turns to Him.”

Whatever befalls a person, if it pleases him, is an evident blessing. If it distresses him, it is also a blessing, because it expiates his sins and he is rewarded for bearing it patiently. It is also a blessing because it contains wisdom and mercy unknown to the servant:

“Perhaps you dislike something which is good for you, and perhaps you love something which is bad for you,”

and the rest of the verse. Both kinds of blessing require patience as well as gratitude. In adversity, the need for patience is obvious. As for the blessing of prosperity, it requires steadfastness in obedience amid that prosperity. As one of the early generations said: “We were tested with adversity and remained patient; we were tested with prosperity but did not remain patient.” This is why most of those who enter Paradise are the poor. However, since prosperity brings pleasure and adversity brings pain, gratitude has commonly been associated with prosperity, and patience with adversity. Allah Most High says:

“And if We give man a taste of mercy from Us, then withdraw it from him”

—up to His words—

“Except those who remain patient and do righteous deeds,”

and the rest of the verse.

---

## Page 3925

Moreover, those enjoying prosperity have greater need of gratitude, while those facing adversity have greater need of patience. Gratitude is obligatory for the former, and patience for the latter. Patience in prosperity, however, may be recommended, and gratitude may be recommended for someone facing adversity. Gratitude and patience can be combined amid both pain and pleasure, though this is a state many find difficult. A fuller discussion belongs elsewhere.

The point is that Allah Most High bestows blessings through all of this, even if most people do not recognize it at first. Allah knows, and you do not know. A person’s sins, however, come from himself. Nevertheless, when accompanied by a good outcome, even these are a blessing. They are also a blessing for someone else because of the lessons he draws from them. An example of this is the saying:

“O Allah, do not make me a cautionary lesson for others, and do not let anyone else benefit more than I do from what You have taught me.”

Among the supplications in the Quran is:

“Our Lord, do not make us a trial for the wrongdoing people.”

Likewise, it says:

“And make us leaders for the righteous.”

Make us leaders for those who follow our example, and do not make us a trial for those who go astray through us.

In Arabic, ālā’ means blessings, which also imply power. In the Quran, Allah Most High mentions His signs that demonstrate His power and lordship, His signs that contain His blessings to His servants, and His signs that reveal His wisdom. These are inseparable. Yet the blessing of benefiting from food, drink, dwellings, and clothing is evident to everyone. Hence these are cited as evidence in Surah al-Nahl, also called “the Surah of Blessings,” as Qatāda and others stated.

On this basis, many people say that praise is broader than gratitude in terms of its grounds, since it may be offered for a blessing or for something else, whereas gratitude is broader in terms of its forms, since it is expressed

---

## Page 3926

through the heart, the tongue, and the hand. If, then, every created thing contains a blessing, praise can only be for a blessing. And praise belongs to Allah in every circumstance. Yet this is understood only by those who recognize the blessings within created things. The Jahmiyya and the Jabriyya are far removed from this, as are the Qadariyya, who say: “Wisdom concerns not Him, but only the benefit of created beings.”

Their position therefore leaves room only for gratitude, just as the position of the Jahmiyya leaves room only for power. Power devoid of blessing and wisdom displays nothing praiseworthy. The reality of their doctrine is that He does not deserve praise: His is sovereignty without praise. Likewise, according to the Mu'tazila, His is a kind of praise without sovereignty. According to the early generations, however, His are both sovereignty and praise in their entirety.

Allah Most High says:

“Allah bears witness that there is no deity except Him—as do the angels and those endowed with knowledge—while He upholds justice. There is no deity except Him, the Almighty, the All-Wise.”

He alone is worthy of worship, and to Him belong justice, might, and wisdom. These four are affirmed only by the early generations and their followers. Whoever falls short in knowledge of the Sunnah denies the Lord some of what is rightfully His.

The Jahmī-Jabrī affirms neither justice nor wisdom, nor His oneness as the sole object of worship; rather, he affirms only His oneness as Lord. The Mu'tazilī affirms neither His oneness as the sole object of worship, nor justice, might, or wisdom. Even if he says that he affirms some wisdom, understood as pertaining to others rather than Him, that is not wisdom. Anyone who acts, not for a purpose pertaining to himself but for one pertaining to another, is not wise in the judgment of all rational people.

Since praise is offered only for a blessing, it has been established that it is the foremost part of gratitude; it is therefore the beginning of gratitude and praise,

---

## Page 3927

and even when it is offered for both blessing and wisdom, gratitude expressed through deeds is for His blessing, and is worship of Him on account of His divinity, which encompasses His wisdom. Thus, all these matters fall within gratitude. This is why the Quran attaches such great importance to gratitude, rather than to praise alone, since praise is one form of gratitude. Praise, which is gratitude expressed in words, has been prescribed at the beginning of every address, together with the affirmation of Allah’s oneness. Thus, al-Fātiha combines gratitude with the affirmation of His oneness, and prescribed sermons must include both.

The enduring righteous deeds are of two kinds:

“Glory and praise be to Allah” expresses gratitude, declares His freedom from imperfection, and magnifies Him; “There is no deity except Allah” and “Allah is the Greatest” affirm His oneness and greatness.

[Allah Most High has said:

“So call upon Allah, sincerely devoting your religion to Him.”

“All praise belongs to Allah, Lord of all worlds.”] (*)

Is praise confined to matters of choice, as has been said regarding resolve, or is it broader in scope? This requires consideration, but this is not the place for it. An authentic report states that when the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, raised his head from bowing, he would say:

“Our Lord, to You belongs all praise, filling heaven, filling the earth, and filling whatever else You will. You are worthy of praise and glory—the truest words a servant has said, and we are all Your servants. None can withhold what You give, and none can give what You withhold; nor can worldly fortune avail its possessor against You.”

This is the wording of the hadith. Ahaqq (“truest”) is a superlative. Some have mistakenly said:

“What the servant says is true.”

This is not sound, for a servant speaks both truth and falsehood. Rather, it is what the Lord says that is true, as He has said:

“The truth—and I speak the truth.”

Ahaqq, however, is the predicate of an omitted subject: that is, “Praise is the truest thing a servant has said.” The hadith thus establishes that praise is the truest thing a servant has said, which is why it is obligatory in every prayer.

And man’s soul is naturally active in a manner that inevitably involves evil, in accordance with consummate wisdom and as an abundant blessing.

If it is asked, “Why, then, did He not create it differently?” the answer is that this would have meant creating a being other than man, and the wise purpose of his creation would not have been fulfilled. This was the angels’ question when they said:

“Will You place in it someone who will spread corruption there and shed blood?”

—through to His words—

“Indeed, I know what you do not know.”

He thus knew aspects of the wisdom in creating this being that the angels did not know. How, then, could individual human beings know them? And the human soul was created as the Most High has said:

“Indeed, man was created anxious,”

“distressed when evil touches him,”

“and withholding when good touches him.”

And He says:

He has thus given it a constitution that necessarily entails the existence of what is created from it, out of great wisdom and all-embracing mercy. This addresses the matter from the standpoint of its ultimate purpose, while evil is not attributed to Him, glory be to Him.

As for (the second aspect), concerning the cause: this evil exists only because of the absence of the knowledge and will that set the soul aright. The soul was created with an innate disposition that calls for knowing and loving Allah, and it has been guided to knowledge and deeds that help it achieve this. All of this comes from Allah’s grace and kindness. Yet when devils among mankind and jinn made evil deeds attractive to the sinful soul (*), it inclined towards them. This involved the absence of what is beneficial, which is the fundamental factor; the existence of this absence is not attributed to Allah Most High. What is said of these devils is the same as what is said of the soul: He created them for a wise purpose.

Since the absence of what sets the soul aright is one of the two causes, and pure evil is pure nonexistence—which is not a thing—whereas Allah is the Creator of everything, evil deeds therefore come from the soul insofar as it necessarily entails voluntary activity.

When a servant acknowledges that Allah is the Creator of his actions, if he does so in affirmation that Allah creates everything, affirming His perfect words and acknowledging his own need for Him, and that unless He guides him he will be astray, thus submitting to His might and wisdom—this is the state of the believers. But if he acknowledges this to use divine decree as an excuse, this sin is greater than the first, and this is a form of following Satan.

Some have raised a question here: nothing is decreed for the believer without its being good

for him, even though He has decreed that he commit sins? There are two answers to this:

His case is then as described in several reports:

Sin brings about the servant’s humility, submission, seeking of forgiveness, and recognition of his poverty and need before Allah, glory be to Him.

Among the lessons in His words, “is from yourself,” is that the servant should not place his trust in his own soul, for evil comes only from it. He should not occupy himself with blaming and censuring others, but should instead turn his attention to his sins and repent of them, seek refuge in Allah from the evil of his own soul and his evil deeds, and ask Allah to help him obey Him. Through this, good comes to him and evil is averted from him. This is why the most beneficial

supplication—the greatest and most perfect—is the supplication of al-Fātihah:

For when Allah guides a servant to this path, He helps him obey Him and refrain from disobeying Him, so that no evil befalls him, either in this world or in the Hereafter. His need for guidance is greater than his need for food and drink, and it encompasses countless kinds of needs. Were there not within people’s souls something of the same kind as that which was in the souls of those who denied the messengers—Pharaoh and those before him—we would have no need to draw lessons from people whom we do not resemble at all. And the Most High says:

And He says:

This is why the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said:

## Page 3932

“You will surely follow the ways of those before you, matching them exactly, so much so that if they entered a lizard’s burrow, you would enter it too.”

They asked, “O Messenger of Allah, the Jews and Christians?”

He replied, “Who else?”

He also said:

They asked, “O Messenger of Allah, the Persians and Romans?”

He replied, “Who else?”

Both hadiths are in the two Sahīh collections. During the expedition of Hunayn, the polytheists had a lote tree on which they hung their weapons. Some people said, “O Messenger of Allah, appoint for us a Dhāt Anwāt (tree with hanging objects), just as they have a Dhāt Anwāt.”

He, peace and blessings be upon him, said: “Allah is the Greatest! By Him in whose hand is my soul, you have said just what the companions of Moses said: ‘Make for us a god just as they have gods.’ These are recurring ways! You will surely follow the ways of those before you.”

The Quran has made clear that evil deeds come from the soul, even though they occur by Allah’s decree. The gravest of them are denying the Creator, associating partners with Him, and the soul’s desire to be a partner to Him—glory be to Him—or a god besides Him. Both of these latter ambitions have occurred: Pharaoh and Iblīs each sought to be worshipped and obeyed instead of Allah. What was in Pharaoh and Iblīs represents the utmost wrongdoing and ignorance, and within the souls of all other humans and jinn there is a share of this. Unless Allah helps and guides His servant, he will fall into some of what Pharaoh and Iblīs fell into, to the extent that he is able.

One of those possessed of spiritual insight said: “There is no soul that does not contain something of what was in Pharaoh’s soul. The difference is that he had the power and so revealed it, whereas others lacked the power and so concealed it.”

---

## Page 3933

This is because, when a person reflects and comes to understand himself and others, he sees that each individual wants to be obeyed and to gain ascendancy as far as he can. Souls are filled with a love of supremacy and leadership to the extent within their reach. Thus, you find a person befriending whoever agrees with his desires and opposing whoever goes against them. What he truly worships is whatever he desires and wants. Allah Most High says:

“Have you seen the one who takes his own desire as his god? Will you then be a guardian over him?”

To him, people are classified as they are by the unbelieving rulers among the Turks and others: “yāl, yāghī,” meaning “my friend” and “my enemy.” Whoever conforms to their desires is an ally, even if he is an unbeliever; whoever does not is an enemy, even if he is among the God-fearing. Such was Pharaoh’s condition.

Each such person wants his commands obeyed as far as possible, but he lacks Pharaoh’s ability to claim divinity and deny the Creator. Although these people acknowledge the Creator, when someone calls them to worship Allah in a way that entails ceasing to obey them, they oppose him, just as Pharaoh opposed Moses, peace be upon him.

Many people have enough reason and faith not to seek such extremes. Rather, their souls seek what is within their reach. If someone is a Muslim who commands obedience, he seeks to be obeyed in pursuing his aims, even when these involve sin and disobedience to Allah. Someone who obeys him becomes dearer to him and more esteemed than someone who obeys Allah but goes against his desires. This is one aspect of the condition of Pharaoh and all others who denied the messengers.

If he is a scholar or a religious teacher, he loves those who esteem him rather than those who esteem his peer. He may even hate his peer out of envy and transgression, as the Jews did when Allah Most High sent someone calling to the same message preached by

## Page 3935

the majority of Quran commentators. Ummah means a creed and a way, as Allah says:

“Indeed, we found our forefathers following a religion.”

A road is likewise called an imām (guide), because the person traveling along it is followed; similarly, the traveler heads toward it and makes for it. Ummah also means a teacher of goodness whom people follow. Allah made Abraham, peace be upon him, a leader and declared that he was an ummah. Allah Most High commanded the messengers to have one creed and religion and not become divided over it, as stated in the two Sahīh collections:

“We prophets have one religion.”

Allah Most High says:

“He has ordained for you of religion what He enjoined upon Noah”—to the end of the verse.

Thus, they affirmed one another and did not differ, despite the diversity of their prescribed laws. Whoever among those in positions of authority—rulers, scholars, and shaykhs—follows the Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, commands what he commanded, calls to what he called to, and loves anyone who calls to the same thing. Allah loves this, so he loves what Allah loves, because his aim is that Allah alone be worshipped and that all devotion be to Allah.

But whoever resents having a counterpart who calls to this seeks to be the one obeyed and worshipped. He shares something of the condition of Pharaoh and his like. Whoever seeks to be obeyed instead of Allah is in the same condition as Pharaoh. Whoever seeks to be obeyed alongside Allah wants people to take rivals besides Allah, loving them as they love Allah. Yet Allah, glorified is He, has commanded that none but He be worshipped, that all devotion be to Him alone, that allegiance and enmity be for His sake, that none but He be relied upon, and that help be sought only from Him.

Thus, one who follows the messengers commands people to do what the messengers commanded them, so that all devotion may be to Allah, not to himself,

---

## Page 3936

so if someone else enjoins the same, he loves and supports him and is pleased with him. If he does good to people, he does so only to seek the Face of his Lord Most High. He knows that Allah has favored him by making him a doer of good, and thus recognizes that his deeds are for Allah and accomplished with Allah’s help. This is mentioned in al-Fātihah:

“You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help.”

He therefore seeks neither recompense nor thanks from those to whom he has done good, nor does he remind them of his favors. He knows that it is Allah who has favored him by employing him in doing good. He must therefore thank Allah for easing his way to goodness, while the recipient must thank Allah for making available to him what benefits him.

Some people, however, do good to others so that they can hold their favors over them, or so that the recipients will repay them with obedience, reverence, or some other benefit. Such a person may remind someone of his favors, saying, “I did such-and-such for so-and-so, but he did not thank me,” or something similar. Such a person has neither worshipped Allah nor sought His help: he has neither acted for Allah nor acted with His help. He is therefore like someone who acts to be seen by others. Allah has nullified the charity of both those who hold their favors over others and those who give to be seen. He Most High says:

“O you who believe, do not nullify your charity with reminders of your generosity and hurtful conduct, like someone who spends his wealth to be seen by people and does not believe in Allah and the Last Day. His likeness is that of a smooth rock covered with dust: a downpour strikes it and leaves it bare. They can gain nothing from what they have earned. And Allah does not guide the disbelieving people.”

“And the likeness of those who spend their wealth seeking Allah’s pleasure and out of firm conviction within themselves is that of a garden on high ground: a downpour strikes it, and it produces twice its yield. If no downpour strikes it, then a light rain suffices. And Allah sees all that you do.”

Qatādah said: “‘Out of firm conviction within themselves’ means seeking reward of their own accord.”

Al-Shaʿbī said: “With certainty and belief within themselves.”

It has also been explained as meaning that they give willingly, certain of the reward and believing Allah’s promise, knowing that what they have given away is better for them than what they have kept.

I say: If the giver seeks reward from Allah, not from the recipient, he does not hold his favor over the recipient.

---

## Page 3937

(*)
The sixth distinction: The sins with which a person is tried, although created by Allah, are a punishment for his failure to do what Allah created him for and made part of his innate disposition. Allah created him to worship Him alone, and his innate disposition points to this. When he fails to do what he was created for and innately disposed to, he is punished by Satan making his acts of associating partners with Allah and disobedience appear attractive to him. He Most High says:

“Go! Whoever among them follows you, Hell will surely be your recompense—an ample recompense.”

Then, further on, He says:

“Indeed, you will have no authority over My servants.”

He Most High also says:

“Indeed, he has no authority over those who believe and put their trust in their Lord. His authority is only over those who take him as their ally”—to the end of the verse.

He Most High says:

“Indeed, when those who fear Allah are touched by a temptation from Satan, they remember, and at once they see clearly. But their brothers draw them further into error and never desist.”

It is thus clear that sincere devotion to Allah prevents Satan from gaining mastery over a person. As He Most High says:

“Thus We turned evil and immorality away from him. Indeed, he was one of Our chosen servants.”

Thus, his being inspired to wickedness was a punishment for him. Failure to perform good deeds is not an existing entity of which it could be said, “Allah created it.” Whoever reflects on the Quran will see that, in most passages where Allah mentions His creation of disbelief and sins, He presents it as recompense for that conduct. For example, He Most High says:

“Whomever Allah wills to guide, He opens his heart to Islam; and whomever He wills to lead astray, He makes his heart tight and constricted”—to the end of the verse.

He Most High says:

“When they deviated, Allah caused their hearts to deviate.”

He also says:

“But as for the one who is miserly, considers himself self-sufficient, and denies the best reward, We will ease him toward hardship.”

In these and similar passages, He mentions deeds with which He punished them for doing what was forbidden and abandoning what was commanded. They must necessarily act and exercise their will; so when they did not engage in good deeds, they were impelled

## Page 3938

toward evil deeds, as an act of justice from Allah. As the saying goes: “If you do not occupy your soul with truth, it will occupy you with falsehood.” Properly understood, this distinction cuts off the arguments of both Qadarī factions: those who deny divine decree and those who affirm compulsion.

To those who say, “He created them for that purpose, and punishing them is unjust,” the answer is: He only caused them to fall into those sins and sealed their hearts as a punishment. He did not wrong them; rather, they wronged themselves. To wrong someone means to deprive him of his due. Allah Most High says:

“Each of the two gardens yielded its fruit and fell short in nothing.”

Many of them concede that Allah creates deeds as recompense for earlier deeds. They say: “He creates the obedience of the obedient, but He does not create any sins in the first instance; rather, He creates them as recompense.” Thus they say: “The servant’s first act was not brought about by Allah.”

What we have explained, however, entails that Allah is the Creator of everything. Yet the first of these sins is a punishment for the servant’s failure to do what he was created for, and this absence is not ascribed to Allah. Thus, the first sin He brings about is a punishment for this absence. Subsequent sins may be punishment for something that has actually occurred, or punishment for persisting in that absence. As long as a person does not devote himself sincerely to Allah, he continues to associate partners with Him, and Satan is given mastery over him.

Then, when He, glorified be He, singles out someone for guidance by enabling him from the outset to do what he was created for, He does so out of His bounty. This entails no injustice and does not preclude justice. Hence Allah Most High says:

“Allah singles out for His mercy whom He wills.”

Likewise, He knows best concerning His bounty, just as He has singled out certain bodies

---

## Page 3939

with faculties not found in others. The absence of a faculty may give rise to actual illnesses in a person, alongside other manifestations of His wisdom. A proper understanding of this dispels the doubts surrounding this subject.

Among the passages that mention punishment for the absence of faith are His words, Most High:

“And We turn their hearts and eyes away, just as they did not believe in it the first time.”

This completes His statement:

“And what will make you realize that, even if it came, they would not believe?”

He thus states that this turning away happens to those who did not believe in it the first time. This is an absence of faith.

It may, however, be objected: “This comes after the Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, has called them. They have denied his message and abandoned faith, and these are things that actually occur.” Yet what necessitates punishment is the absence of faith; the things mentioned are conditions for punishment, as is the sending of the Messenger. A person may be distracted from faith by something that is permissible in itself, for which he deserves no punishment except because it distracted him from faith. Some maintain that the opposite of faith is abandoning it, that this abandonment is a positive act, and that faith has no opposite other than this.

The seventh distinction:

The evils that consist of calamities have no cause except a person’s sin, which comes from himself. The causes of whatever good comes to him, however, are innumerable, for it comes from Allah’s bounty, both through his deeds and apart from them. His deeds themselves are among Allah’s blessings upon him. Moreover, He, glorified be He, does not reward him merely in proportion to his deeds, but multiplies the reward. A person should therefore rely only upon Allah and turn only to Him.

He thus deserves unqualified, all-encompassing and complete gratitude. Others deserve gratitude only in return for the good Allah has brought about through them, as in the case of gratitude to one’s parents. Indeed, whoever does not thank people does not thank Allah. Yet neither anyone’s words nor his favors can justify thanking him by disobeying Allah, or obeying him in disobedience to Allah, for He alone is

---

## Page 3940

the Bestower of blessings.

He, Most High, says:

“Whatever blessing you have is from Allah.”

And He says:

“He has subjected to you whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth—all from Him.”

No one can match His recompense for obedience and gratitude, or for disobedience and disbelief. For this reason, no created being may be obeyed in disobedience to the Creator. He, Most High, says:

“We have enjoined upon man kindness to his parents. But if they strive to make you associate with Me that of which you have no knowledge, do not obey them”—to the end of the verse.

And in the other verse:

“But if they strive to make you associate with Me that of which you have no knowledge, do not obey them, but keep their company in this world with kindness.”

The point is that when a person recognizes that all blessings come from Allah, he places his trust and hope in Him, glorified be He; and when he understands the gratitude He deserves, which none other deserves … (1)

The cause of evil is confined to his own self. He thus recognizes where harm comes to him, seeks forgiveness and Allah’s help, and seeks refuge in Him from deeds he has not yet committed. As one of the early Muslims said:

“Let no servant place his hope in anyone but his Lord, nor fear anything but his sin.”

This contradicts the position of the Jahmiyyah, who say that He punishes without sin, and who fear Him even if they have not sinned. When a person believes His words:

“Whatever good befalls you is from Allah, and whatever evil befalls you is from yourself,”

he recognizes the falsity of this position.

The statement of Ibn ʿAbbās and others has already been cited: what befell them on the day of Uhud was because of their sins. He made no exception for anyone. This is one benefit of making the address specific: it prevents anyone from supposing that it is a general statement subject to exceptions.

## Page 3941

The eighth distinction:

When evil comes from the soul, it is vile and blameworthy. Its vileness is described in such statements as His words:

“Vile things are for vile people.”

The majority of the early Muslims said: “Vile words are for vile people.” Some said: “Vile words and deeds are for vile people.” He, Most High, also says:

“Allah sets forth a parable: a good word”—up to His words—“And the likeness of a vile word is that of a vile tree.”

And He says:

“To Him ascends good speech, and righteous deeds raise it.”

Words and deeds are attributes of the person who speaks and acts. Thus, when a soul is characterized by evil and vileness, it belongs only in a place suited to it. Whoever wishes to have snakes and scorpions live among people like cats will not succeed. Nor will anyone who wishes to make falsehood serve as a witness, an ignorant person a teacher, or a fool a ruler.

Vile souls are therefore unfit to dwell in the pure abode of Paradise. Rather, if a soul contains any vileness, it is purified and refined, as stated in the authentic collection:

“When the believers have been saved from the Fire, they will be detained on a bridge”—to the end of the hadith.

When a person knows that evil comes from his own soul, he will not expect complete happiness while evil remains within him. Rather, he will recognize the truth of His words:

“Whoever does evil will be recompensed for it.”

And His words:

“Whoever does an atom’s weight of good will see it, and whoever does an atom’s weight of evil will see it.”

He will know that the Lord’s actions follow the rule of justice and beneficence. In the authentic collection it is stated:

“Allah’s right hand is full”—to the end of the hadith.

He will also recognize the falsity of the position of the Jahmiyyah, who hold that reward and punishment have no underlying wisdom. He, glorified be He, has borne witness that there is no deity but Him, as have the angels and those endowed with knowledge, while He upholds justice. Their aim was to oppose

---

## Page 3942

the Mu'tazilah on divine decree and the threat of punishment. For this reason, some who affiliate themselves with the Sunnah, hadith, and adherence to the early Muslims followed Jahm’s approach. Likewise, concerning “faith and the threat of punishment,” they followed the approach of the extremist Murji'ah: Jahm and his followers.

Jahm became known for “two kinds” of innovation. One concerned (the divine names and attributes), in which he went to extremes in negation. The Bātiniyyah, the philosophers, and others agreed with him on this, as did the Mu'tazilah regarding the attributes, though not the names. The Kullābiyyah, together with those jurists and hadith scholars who agreed with them, followed him in denying the attributes connected with Allah’s will. The Karrāmiyyah and others agreed with him on the underlying principle: that an infinite succession cannot have continued eternally, and that He cannot have always spoken whenever He willed and acted whenever He willed, since events without a beginning are impossible. On the basis of this principle—denying the existence of an endless succession in the future—he maintained that Paradise and Hell would perish. Abū al-Hudhayl, the leading scholar of the Mu'tazilah, agreed with him on this, but held that movements would come to an end.

Thus, regarding the attributes, the Mu'tazilah are the effeminates of the Jahmiyyah. As for the Kullābiyyah regarding the attributes . . . (1) (*), and likewise the Ash'ariyyah. But, as Abū Ismā'īl al-Ansārī said:

“The Ash'ariyyah—the females—are the effeminates of the Mu'tazilah.”

Some people say, “The Mu'tazilah are the effeminates of the philosophers,” because they do not know that Jahm preceded them in adopting this principle, or because they are their effeminates in certain respects. Al-Shahrastānī states that they derived what they adopted from the philosophers, because he considers only the debates of his Ash'ari companions with them. This contrasts with the leading scholars of the Sunnah, whose debates were with the Jahmiyyah, who were known among

## Page 3943

the early Muslims for denying the divine attributes; this was what distinguished them from the other sects in the eyes of the early Muslims. The Mu'tazilah, however, were distinguished by their doctrine of an intermediate position between the two positions, introduced by 'Amr ibn 'Ubayd. He and his companions would sit apart from the community, so Qatādah and others would say:

“Those are the Mu'tazilah.”

This was after al-Hasan’s death. The innovation of the Qadariyyah had arisen earlier, after Mu'āwiyah’s death. This is why Ibn 'Umar, Ibn 'Abbās, and others spoke against them. Ibn 'Abbās died before Ibn al-Zubayr, while Ibn 'Umar died shortly after him. Soon afterwards, al-Hajjāj assumed the governorship of Iraq, in the seventies AH. People continued debating divine decree in the Hijaz, Syria, and Iraq. Most of this took place in Syria, Iraq, and Basra, and least in the Hijaz.

When the Mu'tazilah emerged and advocated the intermediate position between the two positions, they maintained that the threatened punishment would inevitably be carried out, that those who affirmed Allah’s oneness would remain in Hell forever, and that no one who entered the Fire would leave it. They coupled this with their doctrine concerning divine decree, as this completed their position.

At that time, people had not yet introduced any denial of the divine attributes. Then al-Ja'd ibn Dirham appeared, the first of them to do so. Khālid ibn 'Abd Allāh al-Qasrī slaughtered him as a sacrifice, saying:

“O people, offer your sacrifices! May Allah accept your sacrifices. I am sacrificing al-Ja'd ibn Dirham, for he claimed that Allah did not take Abraham as a close friend and did not speak directly to Moses. Exalted is Allah, far above what al-Ja'd says!”

Then he descended and slaughtered him. This took place in Iraq.

---

## Page 3944

Then Jahm emerged in the East, in Tirmidh, and it was from there that his doctrine spread. For this reason, the scholars of the Sunnah in the East spoke more extensively in refutation of their doctrine than those of the Hijaz, Syria, and Iraq. These included Ibrāhīm ibn Tahmān, Khārijah ibn Mus‘ab, ‘Abd Allāh ibn al-Mubārak, and others like them. Mālik, Ibn al-Mājishūn, and others also condemned them, as did al-Awzā‘ī, Hammād ibn Zayd, and others.

Their doctrine became widely known only at the time of the ordeal of Imam Ahmad and other scholars of the Sunnah. They grew stronger and more numerous during al-Ma’mūn’s rule, for he had spent some time in Khorasan and met with them. He then issued written orders for the inquisition from Tarsus in 218 AH, the year in which he died. Ahmad was returned to prison in Baghdad, where he remained until 220 AH. In that year, he underwent his ordeal under al-Mu‘tasim and debated them. When he refuted their arguments and explained that their demand that people agree with them, and their testing of them, constituted ignorance and injustice, al-Mu‘tasim wanted to release him. Some, however, advised him that the prudent course was to flog Ahmad, lest the dignity of the caliphate be undermined. When they flogged him, a public outcry arose; they became afraid and released him. Ibn Abī Du’ād had assembled for him deniers of the divine attributes from all the sects.

Scholars of the Sunnah, such as Ibn al-Mubārak, Ahmad, Ishāq, and al-Bukhārī, call all these people Jahmiyyah. Many later followers of Ahmad and others came to suppose that his opponents were the Mu‘tazilah. This was not so; rather, the Mu‘tazilah were one group among them.

The point here is that Jahm became known for two innovations: the first was denial of the divine attributes; the second was extremism concerning divine decree and irjā’. Thus he made

---

## Page 3945

faith nothing more than knowledge in the heart. He also held that human beings neither act nor possess any power. These are two matters in which the Mu‘tazilah went to extremes in opposing him. Al-Ash‘arī, however, agreed with his basic position, though he might dispute with him over wording. Jahm affirms none of the divine attributes, neither will nor anything else. Thus, when he says that Allah loves acts of obedience and hates sins, he means reward and punishment. Al-Ash‘arī, by contrast, affirms attributes such as will, and therefore had to address whether will is identical with love.

He said: “Allah loves sins and is pleased with them, just as He wills them.” Abū al-Ma‘ālī mentioned that he was the first to say this. Before him, the people of the Sunnah held that Allah does not love sins. This view spread among many Sufis, who agreed with Jahm on questions of human actions and divine decree while opposing him concerning the attributes. One example is Abū Ismā‘īl al-Ansārī, author of Censure of Speculative Theology. He is among those most vehement in condemning the Jahmiyyah for denying the attributes, and he wrote a book declaring the Jahmiyyah unbelievers. He also vehemently condemns the Ash‘arīs, even though they are among the closest of these groups to the Sunnah; at times, he would even curse them.

Someone asked him in the presence of Nizām al-Mulk, “Do you curse the Ash‘arīs?” He replied, “I curse whoever says there is no god in the heavens, no Quran in the physical copy, and no prophet in the grave.” He then rose and left him in anger.

Despite this, on the question of willing all that occurs and creating human actions, he goes further than the Ash‘arīs: he affirms neither causation nor wisdom. Rather, he says that the spiritual knower’s contemplation of the decree leaves him unable to approve of a good deed or disapprove of an evil one. By “decree,” he means the divine will, because, in his view, the spiritual knower is someone who reaches the station of fanā’ (annihilation), and good and evil deeds differ in how they affect the servant

---

## Page 3946

in that he is granted bliss for the one and punished for the other. Attending to this concerns the self’s own interests, whereas the station of annihilation involves nothing but contemplating what Allah wills. Since al-Ash‘arī affirmed the distinction between the two from the creature’s perspective, he was more rational than they were, for they claim that the spiritual knower makes no distinction.

They erred concerning both the servant and the Lord. As regards the servant, their position requires that all events be alike to him, which is utterly impossible. Thus, they set aside the distinction established by the Most Merciful and instead made distinctions based on instinct, caprice, and satanic influence. Consequently, many of them fell into sins, others into flagrant disobedience, and others into unbelief, even permitting the worship of idols. Many of them then proceed to the doctrine of oneness and openly profess the worship of everything that exists.

Our concern here is to discuss those who followed Jahm in denying wisdom, causation, and justice in the divine decree—this being his second innovation, unlike irjā’, which is also attributed to groups other than his. These people say:

“The Lord may do anything He has the power to do.”

This is why you find that their followers do not hold the commands and prohibitions, or the promises of reward and threats of punishment, in due reverence. Rather, they cast off all or some of this and strain to uphold their beliefs. For when they agree with Jahm and al-Ash‘arī that goodness and evil consist in a thing’s being commanded or forbidden—a distinction relating to the servant’s own interests—while claiming to have become oblivious to such interests, they sometimes say that complying with the commands and prohibitions belongs to the station of concealment. At other times they say:

“He does this for the sake of the inmates of the asylum”—meaning the common people—as the Maghribī shaykh puts it. They make various other claims of this kind.

---

## Page 3947

Even when someone who follows their path holds the commands and prohibitions in high regard, the most he can say is what is reported from al-Shādhilī:

“Unity is to be witnessed in your heart, while distinction is to be voiced upon your tongue.”

His words and those of others also contain statements, supplications, and devotional litanies that entail setting aside the commands and prohibitions. One example is the claim that Allah grants him more for disobedience than He grants him for obedience. Such claims imply that, in his view, Allah may treat those who commit evil deeds like those who believe and do righteous deeds—or even better. They also offer supplications that overstep proper bounds, as found in al-Shādhilī’s litany.

Others among their common followers consider it possible for Allah to honour a wicked person—even an unbeliever—with the miraculous gifts of the greatest of His close servants. They say:

“This is a gift and a bounty.”

They imagine these to be miraculous gifts bestowed upon Allah’s close servants, when in fact they are satanic phenomena of the kind found among sorcerers and soothsayers. Allah Most High says:

“And when a messenger from Allah came to them confirming what was with them, a party of those who had been given the Scripture cast the Book of Allah behind their backs, as though they did not know.”

“And they followed what the devils recited during Solomon’s reign. Solomon did not disbelieve, but the devils disbelieved, teaching people magic and what had been revealed to the two angels in Babylon, Hārūt and Mārūt. Yet the two would teach no one without first saying, ‘We are only a trial, so do not disbelieve.’ But they learned from them that by which they could separate a man from his wife. Yet they could harm no one thereby except by Allah’s permission. They learned what harmed them and did not benefit them. And they certainly knew that whoever purchased it would have no share in the Hereafter. Wretched indeed was that for which they sold themselves, if only they knew.”

“And had they believed and feared Allah, a reward from Allah would have been better, if only they knew.”

---

## Page 3948

The Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) also said:

“You will surely follow the ways of those before you, as closely as one arrow feather matches another, so that even if they entered a lizard’s burrow, you would enter it too”—to the end of the hadith.

Although the Muslims have received Allah’s Book, the Quran, many of those who profess to belong to their ranks and whom Satan has led astray have turned away, casting Allah’s Book behind their backs and following what the devils recite. They do not honour those whom the Quran commands them to befriend, nor do they treat as enemies those whom the Quran commands them to oppose. Instead, they revere anyone they see performing extraordinary feats of the kind that sorcerers and soothsayers perform with the devils’ assistance—feats brought about through what the devils recite. Some of them recognize that this comes from the devils, yet exalt it out of their own desire and prefer it to the way of the Quran. Such people are unbelievers, like those of whom Allah Most High says:

“Have you not seen those who were given a portion of the Scripture? They believe in superstition and false gods, and say of the disbelievers, ‘These are better guided than the believers.’”

“Those are the ones whom Allah has cursed; and whoever Allah curses, you will never find anyone to help him.”

They resemble those of whom Allah Most High says:

“And when a messenger from Allah came to them confirming what was with them”—up to His words—“but the devils disbelieved.”

Others do not recognize that this comes from the devils. Groups among those versed in speculative theology and religious learning, as well as devotees and Sufis, may fall into this. They have even deemed the worship of heavenly bodies and idols permissible because of the extraordinary phenomena they have witnessed in connection with them, which the devils help them bring about. Through these phenomena, they achieve some of their aims involving wrongdoing and acts of obscenity. Thus they paid no heed to their associating partners with Allah or their disbelief in Him and His Book if

---

## Page 3949

they attained those ends. Nor did they hesitate to teach this to people and exalt it for the authority or wealth they might gain, even though they knew it to be disbelief and associating partners with Allah, and called others to it. Indeed, they came to harbour doubts and misgivings about what the Messenger (peace and blessings be upon him) brought, and to believe that, for a beneficial purpose, he addressed the masses with claims that had no underlying reality—as some heretical esotericists maintain. Some from both groups adopted this view. This is one way in which they resembled the Persians and Romans. The Persians venerated lights and prostrated themselves before the sun and fire, while the Romans, before Christianity, were polytheists who worshipped heavenly bodies and idols. These people are worse than those who resembled the Jews and Christians;

[for those imitated the People of the Book in matters that had been altered or abrogated, whereas these imitated people who had no scripture.

He—may Allah Most High have mercy on him—also said: Souls are naturally endowed with immediate knowledge of the Creator who created the heavens] (*), and that He created the heavens and the earth, none of which mankind created. Thus Moses said to Pharaoh, when Pharaoh asked him:

“What is the Lord of all worlds?”

He replied: “The Lord of the heavens and the earth and everything between them, if you would be certain.”

And Pharaoh said:

“Who, then, is the Lord of you both, O Moses?”

He replied: “Our Lord is He who gave everything its form, then guided it.”
