## Page 4006

had fasted, and standing in prayer would be obligatory only for someone who had stood. The meaning would then be: “Those who fast the month must feed a needy person.” Yet the verse was revealed when they were given a choice between fasting and feeding the needy during Ramadan.

The ability with which the act occurs may be described as the ability that accompanies the act and necessarily entails it—this is the second type. In this connection, they have cited the words of the Most High:

“Those whose eyes were veiled from My remembrance and who were unable to hear.”

And His words, Most High:

“Their punishment will be doubled. They were unable to hear, and they did not see.”

Similar to this are His words:

“Indeed, We have placed shackles around their necks, reaching up to their chins, so that their heads are forced up.”

“And We have placed a barrier before them and a barrier behind them, and covered them, so they cannot see.”

The ability denied here—whether its absence is being reported or brought about—is not the ability upon which commands and prohibitions depend. If that ability were absent, commands and prohibitions, promises and threats, praise and blame, reward and punishment would likewise cease to apply. Yet it is well known that these people, even in this condition, remain subject to commands and prohibitions, promises and threats. Thus, the ability denied here is not the ability required for commands and prohibitions, mentioned in His words:

“So fear Allah as much as you are able.”

It may, however, be said that the ability here is like the ability denied in al-Khidr’s words to Moses:

“You will never be able to bear patiently with me.”

For if this ability that is denied meant merely ability concurrent with the act, in the case of both those who act and those who refrain, there would be no difference between these censured people and the believers

---

## Page 4007

nor between al-Khidr and Moses. For in every case, whether a person acts or refrains, ability concurrent with the act is not present before the act. The Quran indicates that this ability is denied only of the one who refrains, not of the one who acts. Thus, it is understood to be opposed to the impediments within a person that prevent his heart from willing and performing the act. In any event, this ability is absent in someone for whom it has been written that he will not act—indeed, this has been decreed for him.

Once this distinction is understood, it becomes clear that both unrestricted assertions are erroneous and constitute innovation: the assertion that a person cannot do anything other than what he has done, or anything contrary to what Allah knows and has decreed; and the assertion that those who act and those who refrain have the same ability, with no particular ability distinguishing the former from the latter.

For this reason, the early generations of the Muslim community, its leading scholars, and the majority of the schools of speculative theology agreed that Allah has power over what He knows and has declared will not occur, and over that which cannot proceed from Him because He does not will it, not because He lacks the power to do it. Only certain misguided groups among the Jahmiyyah, the Qadariyyah, and the Sabian philosophers disagreed. They claim that what is possible through His power is confined to what actually exists, restricting His power to what He has willed and knows will exist, to the exclusion of what He has declared will not occur. This was the position preferred by al-Nazzām and al-Aswārī. Likewise, some claim that no world other than this one is within His power, and that nothing within His power could guide one who is astray.

Yet Allah, Most High, has said:

“Does man think that We will not gather his bones?
Yes indeed, We are able to make even his fingers level.”

Yet He, glorified be He, does not make his fingers level. And He, Most High, has said:

“Say: He is able to send upon you

---

## Page 4008

punishment from above you or from beneath your feet, or divide you into factions and make you taste one another’s violence.”

It is established in the Sahīh that Jābir reported:

“When this verse was revealed—‘Say: He is able to send upon you punishment from above you’—the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said, ‘I seek refuge in Your Face.’ At ‘or from beneath your feet,’ he said, ‘I seek refuge in Your Face.’ At ‘or divide you into factions and make you taste one another’s violence,’ he said, ‘These two are less severe.’”

Allah, Most High, has also said:

“Had We willed, We would have given every soul its guidance.”

Those among the speculative theologians who attribute to Ahl al-Sunnah wa-l-Jamāʿah the statement that a person has no power to do anything other than what he has done—that is, anything contrary to what Allah knows—are mistaken insofar as they attribute to them an unrestricted denial of ability. They are, however, correct insofar as they attribute to them the denial of that particular ability which distinguishes the one who acts from the one who refrains. This is one of the underlying issues in their dispute over whether it is permissible to impose obligations beyond a person’s capacity.

Those who say that ability exists only concurrently with the act, so that one who refrains has no ability whatsoever, say that everyone who disobeys Allah has been charged by Allah with something beyond his capacity. They may likewise say that all people have been charged with what they cannot do.

Those who say that the ability to act is the same as the ability to refrain say that people have been charged only with that for which they all possess equal capacity, power, and ability: the one who acts has no particular ability distinguishing him from the one who refrains. Thus, to state without qualification that a person has been charged with what he cannot do is like stating without qualification that he is compelled to perform his actions

---

## Page 4009

—for denying the ability to perform what is commanded is comparable to affirming compulsion to commit what is forbidden—and like stating without qualification that a person has the power and ability to act contrary to what Allah knows and has decreed.

The early generations of this community and its leading scholars rejected all these unqualified statements, especially since both the affirmative and the negative positions contain falsehood, even though they also contain truth. Rather, sound expressions should be used without qualification: those transmitted in the revealed texts. Ambiguous expressions that admit different meanings must be explained in detail.

The same approach must be followed in all other matters concerning the foundations of religion. What is established by the words of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, His Messenger, and the consensus of the community’s early generations must be treated as the definitive authority. Newly introduced expressions, with their opposing affirmations and negations, each containing both truth and falsehood, must be treated as ambiguous formulations requiring clarification; neither side may be asserted without qualification.

Elsewhere, we have recorded statements from al-Awzāʿī, Sufyān al-Thawrī, ʿAbd al-Rahmān ibn Mahdī, Ahmad ibn Hanbal, and other leading scholars expressing their disapproval of affirming compulsion without qualification, and likewise prohibiting its unqualified denial.

Similarly, regarding the imposition of obligations beyond a person’s capacity, the leading scholars did not affirm either position without qualification.

Abū Bakr ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz, al-Khallāl’s companion, said in his Book of Divine Decree, which forms the introduction to his Kitāb al-Muqniʿ:

“We have received no statement from Abū ʿAbd Allāh on this question that we might follow. People have differed over it: some affirmed the imposition of obligations beyond a person’s capacity, while this was denied by

---

## Page 4010

others, who rejected it.”

He said:

“Our position on this is that the Quran attests to the correctness of what we maintain: that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, requires His creatures to perform acts of obedience both within and beyond their capacity.”

Then, at the end of the section, he said:

“Someone might challenge our position, saying: ‘If Allah may impose upon a servant what is beyond his capacity, then He may require a blind person to work with colours, a paralysed person to walk, and someone without hands to grasp things, and so forth.’ He should be answered as follows: Ibn ʿAbbās said concerning the words of the Exalted:

‘We shall gather them on the Day of Resurrection on their faces’:

‘This means that they will walk on their faces.’ Ibn ʿAbbās’s explanation of walking on their faces thus disposes of every objection they have raised.”

He then said:

“Abū al-Hasan—meaning al-Ashʿarī—has provided sufficient clarification of these matters in the statements we previously quoted from him.”

Al-Qādī Abū Yaʿlā, after quoting the statements of Abū al-Hasan—meaning Abū al-Hasan al-Ashʿarī—said:

“He distinguished between what a person can do, with no intrinsic impossibility involved, which may therefore be imposed as an obligation, and what is impossible, which may not.”

He said:

“The apparent wording of Abū al-Hasan al-Ashʿarī leaves open both possibilities regarding that which cannot possibly exist: may it validly be imposed as an obligation or not?”

He said:

“The correct position is the distinction we have set out. This concerns, first, what a person cannot do because it is intrinsically impossible, such as a command to do the impossible: combining two opposites, making something that came into existence beginningless, or making something beginningless come into existence. It also includes what a person cannot do because of incapacity, such as a paralysed person who cannot stand or a mute person who cannot speak. Obligations of this kind may not be imposed.

“And (the second category: what a person cannot do, neither because it is intrinsically impossible nor because he is incapable of it, but

---

## Page 4011

because he leaves it undone and occupies himself with its opposite. For example, a disbeliever is required to believe while in a state of disbelief, since he is neither incapable of believing nor is belief impossible for him. He is like someone unable to acquire knowledge because he is occupied with earning a living.)”

This position stated by al-Qādī Abū Yaʿlā is that of the majority of jurists and theologians, and of the majority of Imam Ahmad’s followers. Al-Qādī also cited al-Ashʿarī’s explicitly stated position—as reported by al-Qādī himself. He mentioned that Abū Bakr ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz quoted Abū al-Hasan’s statements on this matter, just as an author quotes Abū al-Hasan’s statements on the matter and quotes the statements of those who agree with him and of his associates. For Abū al-Hasan was among the theologians who affiliated themselves with Imam Ahmad and the other imams of the Sunnah, as he stated in his books.

Among Abū al-Hasan’s followers, some agreed with the very position stated by al-Qādī, such as Abū ʿAlī ibn Shādhān and his followers. Others disagreed with him, such as Abū Muhammad al-Labbān, al-Rāzī, and various groups. They said that it is permissible to impose an obligation to do the impossible, such as combining two opposites, or to do something beyond one’s capacity.

The third position, stated by Abū Bakr ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz, is that anything possible may be imposed as an obligation, even if it is impossible in the ordinary course of things, such as walking on one’s face or a blind person adding dots to a copy of the Quran.

Abū ʿAbd Allāh ibn Hāmid, the teacher of al-Qādī Abū Yaʿlā, mentioned in his work on foundational principles the two positions of “drawing a distinction and allowing it without qualification” held by Ahmad’s followers. He said:

---

## Page 4012

Section

For no such command has occurred, even if it can be conceived. This resembles matters for which the revealed Law has issued no command: issuing commands to children and those lacking reason, commanding the blind to see, the poor to provide maintenance, or someone with a disabling infirmity to journey to Mecca. The revealed Law has prescribed none of these things. Had it prescribed them, believing in them and affirming their truth would have been obligatory. Thus, statements concerning this should not be qualified.

He said:

A group of our companions held that one may speak without qualification of the permissibility of imposing obligations beyond one’s capacity, whether on someone with a disabling infirmity, a blind person, or others. This is the position of Jahm and Burghūth.

(The second aspect)

The faculties are sound, but capacity is lacking because of the absence of enabling grace and acceptance. This is permissible, with no contrary position. What this means is that an obligation may be imposed on someone who, as determined in Allah’s knowledge, will not perform it. The Muʿtazilah rejected this. The evidence for it is Allah’s statement to Iblīs:

“What prevented you from prostrating to what I created with My two hands?”

And His words:

“From prostrating when I commanded you?”

And other such verses. Thus, He issued a command despite His prior knowledge that Iblīs would not perform the act. The command therefore concerned something that Allah had foreknown he would be unable to do.

(The second position)

This is also transmitted from Abū al-Hasan. Abū al-Maʿālī al-Juwaynī claimed that most of Abū al-Hasan’s answers inclined toward it and that many of his followers approved it.

---

## Page 4013

and Abū al-Hasan refrained from answering this question in al-Mūjaz. Abū al-Maʿālī initially preferred this position, but later retracted it and declared categorically that imposing obligations beyond one’s capacity is impossible. The first position is that of Ibn ʿAqīl, Abū al-Faraj Ibn al-Jawzī, Abū ʿAbd Allāh al-Rāzī, and others. This (second position) is the view of Abū Ishāq al-Isfarāyīnī, Abū Bakr Ibn Fūrak, Abū al-Qāsim al-Ashʿarī, and al-Ghazālī. Abū Ishāq al-Isfarāyīnī claimed that it was the view of his teacher, Abū al-Hasan, and of the people of truth. As for al-Qādī Abū Bakr, he affirmed its permissibility in some of his books, but most of his discussions distinguish between imposing an obligation on someone incapable of fulfilling it and imposing it on someone capable of refraining from it, as is the position of the majority.

There is also (a third position) on this question, mentioned by Abū Bakr ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz: it is permissible to impose an obligation to do anything possible, even if it is impossible in the ordinary course of things, such as walking on one’s face or a blind person adding dots to a written copy of the Quran, but not something impossible, such as combining two opposites.

The decisive clarification of “this question” is that the dispute concerns two fundamental issues. The first concerns the obligations actually imposed, whose occurrence in the revealed Law Muslims unanimously acknowledge: requiring all of Allah’s servants to do what Allah and His Messenger have commanded them, namely, to believe in Him and fear Him. Is this, or any part of it, to be called imposing obligations beyond one’s capacity?

Those who maintain that capacity exists only together with the act say that the disobedient person has been charged with something beyond his capacity. They also say that everyone was charged with an obligation at a time when he lacked the capacity to fulfil it. Likewise, whoever claims that prior knowledge and the prior recording of something prevent

---

## Page 4014

one from being able to do otherwise says: “If someone is charged with doing the contrary of what is known beforehand, he has been charged with something beyond his capacity.” Likewise, whoever holds that an accident does not endure for two successive moments says that the capacity preceding an act does not endure until the act occurs.

In reality, this is not a dispute over whether the acts Allah has commanded or forbidden fall within the scope of religious obligation. Rather, it concerns whether those acts lie beyond a person’s capacity when he refrains from performing them, and before he performs them. We have already explained that capacity is of two kinds, and that the unqualified assertion that capacity exists only together with the act contradicts what appears in the Quran and Sunnah and what the early generations of this community and its leading scholars agreed upon—just as an unqualified assertion of compulsion does.

Nevertheless, some groups affiliated with the Sunnah have made this unqualified assertion in their refutations of the Qadariyyah. They include followers of Imam Ahmad and other leading scholars of the Sunnah, such as Abū al-Hasan, Abū Bakr ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz, Abū ʿAbd Allāh ibn Hāmid, al-Qādī Abū Bakr, al-Qādī Abū Yaʿlā, Abū al-Maʿālī, Abū al-Hasan ibn al-Zāghūnī, and others. Yet the majority of scholars, including Abū al-ʿAbbās ibn Surayj, Abū al-ʿAbbās al-Qalānisī, and others, have rejected this unqualified assertion. This rejection has also been transmitted from Abū Hanīfah himself, and it is what the statements of all the imams entail. For this reason, Abū Ishāq ibn Shāqlā refrained from making that unqualified assertion.

He related both positions on the matter, saying—as reported from him by al-Qādī Abū Yaʿlā:

“Does capacity exist together with the act or before it? One side argues that prayer, pilgrimage, and jihad may not be enjoined upon someone who lacks the capacity to perform them.

---

## Page 4015

and the other side argues that an act is something created by Allah, Mighty and Majestic: when He creates an act in a person, that person performs it.”

Likewise, anyone who maintains that a person has only one capacity, enabling him both to act and to refrain from acting, and that when acting he needs no assistance from Allah Most High to enable him to act, and who equates Allah’s favor upon the believer and the unbeliever, the righteous and the wicked, is in error. Such people belong to the Qadariyyah, from whom he turned away during those well-known days. Their position was that, while performing a righteous deed, a person has no need of Allah Most High beyond what he had already received before acting (1), and that Allah Most High has bestowed no greater favor upon those who believe in Him and obey Him than upon those who disbelieve in Him and disobey Him. This position is unquestionably wrong. Hence, Ahl al-Sunnah wa-l-Jamāʿah have unanimously judged those who hold it to be misguided.

Beyond this, much of their disagreement over these matters is verbal, while some concerns conceptual distinctions—for example, their dispute over whether an accident endures, upon which they based their view of whether capacity endures. Yet the best formulations and conceptual distinctions are those that accord with the Quran, the Sunnah, and the consensus of this community’s early generations and leading scholars. What is required is to make the texts of the Quran and Sunnah the authoritative foundation that must be followed and whose wording may be used without qualification; to withhold disputed expressions, whether affirming or denying them, pending clarification and detailed explanation; and to prohibit

> **Footnotes:**
> (1) Thus in the original.

---

## Page 4016

unqualified denial of what Allah and His Messenger have affirmed, and unqualified affirmation of what Allah and His Messenger have denied.

The second principle concerns matters agreed to be beyond a person’s capacity, but concerning which there is disagreement over whether they may be imposed as obligations. These fall into two categories: what is impossible in the ordinary course of things, such as walking on one’s face, flying, and the like; and what is intrinsically impossible, such as combining two opposites. As previously mentioned, there are three views on whether imposing such obligations is rationally admissible. As for whether this occurs in the Sharīʿah or is admissible under it, the scholars who transmit the Sharīʿah agree that nothing of this kind occurs in it. Several scholars have reported a consensus on this, including Abū al-Hasan ibn al-Zāghūnī, who said:

“Section: Imposing obligations beyond one’s capacity. This is of two kinds:

(First): Imposing an obligation beyond one’s capacity because of incapacity, the opposite of ability. Examples include requiring someone unable to stand to stand, or requiring a blind person to write and add dots to a written text, and similar cases. Such obligations may not be imposed, and consensus has been established on this. This is because the absence of capacity in these cases is treated as equivalent to impossibility and inconceivability, placing the act beyond one’s power. Imposing such an obligation is therefore inadmissible.

(Second): Imposing an obligation beyond one’s capacity, but not because of incapacity, the opposite of ability. An example is imposing an obligation on a disbeliever whom Allah already knew would not welcome the obligation, such as Pharaoh and Abū Jahl

---

## Page 4017

and others like them. This is permissible. The Muʿtazilah held that imposing obligations beyond one’s capacity is impermissible.” He said: “This issue serves as a foundation for the present one.”

I say:

This consensus is that of the jurists and the scholars, for a group of speculative theologians held that requiring what is intrinsically impossible does occur in the Sharīʿah. This was the view of al-Rāzī and a group before him. They claimed that the obligations imposed on Abū Lahab and others fall into this category, since he was required to believe the revealed reports, which included the report that he would not believe. This is mistaken. For if, after the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—has called someone to faith, Allah declares that he will not believe and will burn in the Fire, then the decree of punishment has become binding upon him. Like someone who sees the angels at the moment of death, he is no longer addressed by the Messenger with these two contradictory demands.

Likewise, whoever maintains that imposing an obligation on someone incapable of fulfilling it necessarily occurs, citing His words:

“On the Day when a shin will be laid bare, and they will be called to prostrate but will be unable to do so,”

contradicts this consensus. The substance of the consensus is that this does not occur in the Sharīʿah. Moreover, such an address serves only to demonstrate their inability, as punishment for their failure to prostrate while they were sound and able. They are punished for neglecting worship when they were capable of it by being commanded to perform it when they are incapable. An address of punishment and recompense is of the same kind as a creative command: the capacity of the person addressed is not a condition, since the aim is not for him to perform the act. Once these types and categories are made clear, confusion and ambiguity disappear.

---

## Page 4018

Shaykh al-Islām—may Allah sanctify his soul—said:

In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Bestower of Mercy.

All praise belongs to Allah. We praise Him, seek His help, ask for His guidance and forgiveness, and seek refuge in Allah from the evil within ourselves and from our evil deeds. Whomever Allah guides, none can lead astray; and whomever He leads astray, none can guide. I bear witness that none is worthy of worship except Allah alone, without partner, and I bear witness that Muhammad is His servant and Messenger. May Allah bestow abundant blessings and peace upon him and his family.

Chapter

On the Prophet’s statement—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—“Thus Adam prevailed over Moses in argument,” when Adam invoked the divine decree against him; and an explanation that this concerns calamities, not sins. Allah has commanded patience and piety: this relates to patience, not piety. He said:

“So be patient; indeed, Allah’s promise is true, and seek forgiveness

---

## Page 4019

for your sin.” He thus commanded patience in the face of calamities and seeking forgiveness for faults. The descendants of Adam have fallen into confusion over this issue—the conflict between the divine command and decree. We have discussed this at length elsewhere.

The point here is that the two Sahīh collections record the hadith narrated by Abū Hurayrah from the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—who said:

“Adam and Moses disputed. Moses said, ‘O Adam, you are the father of mankind, whom Allah created with His own Hand, into whom He breathed of His spirit, and before whom He made His angels prostrate. Why, then, did you cause us and yourself to leave Paradise?’

“Adam replied, ‘You are Moses, to whom Allah spoke directly and for whom He wrote the Torah. How long before I was created do you find these words written in it: “Adam disobeyed his Lord and went astray”?’

“He replied, ‘Forty years.’”

The Prophet said, “Thus Adam prevailed over Moses in argument.”

This is also narrated through ‘Umar ibn al-Khattāb with a good chain of transmission. Many people have assumed that Adam invoked the prior divine decree to absolve himself of blame for the sin. Because of this assumption, they then divided into three groups:

One group rejected this hadith, including Abū ‘Alī al-Jubbā’ī and others, because it is self-evident that this contradicts what the messengers brought. There is no doubt that this cannot be the intended meaning of the hadith. The Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—indeed, all the prophets and their followers, must be held above making the divine decree an excuse for anyone who disobeys Allah and His Messenger.

---

## Page 4020

Another group interpreted it in ways that are manifestly invalid. Some said that Adam prevailed over Moses in argument only because he was his father, and a son does not blame his father. Others said that the sin occurred under one revealed law, whereas the reproach was made under another. Others said it was because the reproach came after repentance. Still others said that this matter differs between this world and the Hereafter.

(A third group) made this hadith their principal basis for absolving those who disobey Allah and His Messenger of blame. Yet they could not apply this consistently: even in their own everyday affairs, those who do things that harm themselves and others must be blamed.

Some of them, however, began invoking this argument when it served their own desires and purposes, but not the desires of others. As has been said of such people: “When obeying, you are a Qadarī (proponent of free will); when sinning, you are a Jabrī (proponent of compulsion). Whichever doctrine suits your desires is the one you adopt.” When one of them sins, he begins invoking the divine decree as an excuse; yet if someone else sins or wrongs him, he will not excuse him. Such people are unjust transgressors.

Others among them say: “This applies to the people of spiritual reality, who have witnessed Allah’s oneness in lordship and lost all awareness of anything other than Allah. They therefore see no agent but Allah. Such people do not regard a good deed as good or an evil deed as evil, for they attribute no action to any created being; rather, they see no agent but Allah. This is unlike someone who regards himself as acting: he is blamed and punished.”

This is the view of many later Sufis who claim to possess spiritual reality. They may regard this as the ultimate realization and the highest attainment of spiritual knowledge and affirmation of Allah’s oneness. This is also the view of a group of scholars.

---

## Page 4021

Abū al-Muzaffar al-Samʿānī said:

“As for the debate between Adam and Moses concerning this matter, it was permissible for them to engage in it because they were two eminent prophets granted special knowledge of realities and permission to uncover hidden mysteries. Their position was unlike that of other people, who were commanded to remain within the limits set for them and to remain silent about what had been concealed from them. The statement, ‘Thus Adam prevailed over Moses in argument,’ does not invalidate the obligation of obedience or dispense with obligatory deeds. Rather, it means giving greater weight to one of two considerations and giving the cause precedence in rank over the means. Wisdom may indeed lie in giving greater weight to the significance of one of two considerations. It is in this sense that the statement, ‘Thus Adam prevailed over Moses in argument,’ should be understood. This became evident in Adam’s case. Allah Most High said:

‘Indeed, I will place a successor on earth.’”

He went on to say:

“It thus followed that Adam could not continue dwelling in Paradise unless he refrained from approaching the tree, because of the prior decree written for him that he would leave it. On this basis he gained the upper hand over Moses in their debate. In this sense, the judgment was in his favour against Moses, hence the statement: ‘Thus Adam prevailed over Moses in argument.’”

I say: This is why Shaykh ʿAbd al-Qādir—may Allah sanctify his soul—says: “Many men, when they come to divine ordainment and decree, hold back. But a window into it was opened for me, and I countered the decrees of the True One with truth and for truth. The true man is one who contends with the decree, not one who simply conforms to it.”

He—may Allah be pleased with him—held the divine commands and prohibitions in great reverence, urged adherence to them, and forbade invoking the decree as an excuse. His teacher, Hammād al-Dabbās, did likewise. This was because of what they observed among

---

## Page 4022

many spiritual wayfarers: their acquiescence in the decree in opposition to the divine commands and prohibitions. The servant is commanded to strive in Allah’s cause and to counter decreed acts of disobedience with whatever acts of obedience he can perform. He thus counters what is decreed but forbidden with what is decreed and commanded by Allah Most High. This is Allah’s religion, with which He sent the messengers, from the first to the last—may Allah’s blessings be upon them all.

Many philosophers resemble these people, as in Ibn Sīnā’s statement about witnessing the secret of divine decree. Al-Rāzī endorses this, for he was an absolute determinist. In general, this notion circulates in the minds of many of the elite among scholars and worshippers, let alone ordinary people, yet it contradicts the religion of Islam.

Some of these people say: “Al-Khidr was absolved of blame only because he witnessed the reality of divine decree.”

One of their shaykhs used to say: “Even if I killed seventy prophets, I would not be in the wrong.”

Some carry their position through as consistently as possible, saying: “Anyone who is able to do something and does it incurs no blame. If it happens that he acts contrary to another person’s purpose, that person will contend with him, and the stronger of the two will defeat the other. Whichever of them is favoured by the decree is in the right insofar as he prevails; otherwise, there is no such thing as wrongdoing.”

Among these are the “monists,” who say: “Existence is one.” Then they say:

---

## Page 4023

“Some of it is superior to the rest, and what is superior deserves to be lord over what is inferior.”

They also say that Pharaoh was truthful when he said:

“I am your lord most high.”

This is the view of a group of heretical, philosophizing Sufi monists, such as al-Tilimsānī. The doctrine of universal union, known as “the unity of existence,” is held by Ibn ʿArabī al-Tāʾī, his companion al-Qūnawī, Ibn Sabʿīn, Ibn al-Fārid, and others like them. They disagree, however, about resurrection and recompense, just as they disagree over whether existence is something distinct from the entities themselves. These people have gone astray in several respects, including their failure to distinguish between the existence of the Creator and that of created beings.

As for witnessing divine decree, the response is this: there is no doubt that Allah Most High is the Creator and Sovereign of everything. Divine decree is Allah’s power—as Imam Ahmad said—and He decrees everything that comes to pass. Yet this does not negate the reality of commands and prohibitions, promises of reward and threats of punishment, or the fact that some actions benefit those who perform them, bringing them bliss, while others harm those who perform them, bringing them punishment.

We do not deny what all things have in common with respect to divine will, lordship, and their beginnings. But we affirm a further distinction with respect to wisdom, divine commands, and ultimate outcomes. For the good final outcome belongs to the God-fearing, not to those devoid of piety.

Allah Most High says:

“Or should We treat those who believe and do righteous deeds like those who spread corruption in the land? Or should We treat the God-fearing like the wicked?”

And He Most High says:

“Then shall We treat the Muslims like the criminals?”

Since this is so, the distinction essentially consists in this: some things are agreeable and beneficial to a person, bringing him pleasure, while others are contrary and harmful to him, bringing him pain. This brings us back

---

## Page 4024

to the distinction between pleasure and pain, and the causes of each. This distinction is known through sense perception, reason, and revealed law, and is agreed upon by earlier and later generations alike. Indeed, even animals recognize it; rather, it exists in all created beings. When we affirm the distinction between good deeds and evil deeds—which is the distinction between good and bad—it ultimately comes back to this.

People of sound reason agree that some actions are agreeable to a person while others are contrary to his interests. When these are described by saying, “This is good and this is bad,” goodness and badness in this sense are, by their unanimous agreement, knowable through reason.

They disagree, however, over goodness and badness in the sense of an action being grounds for blame and punishment: can this be known through reason, or only through revealed law? One cause of their disagreement was their assumption that this category was distinct from the first, whereas it actually falls within it. Nothing is good except in the sense of being agreeable, and nothing is bad except in the sense of being contrary to one’s interests. Praise and reward are agreeable, while blame and punishment are contrary to one’s interests. Thus, these are particular instances of the agreeable and its opposite.

The discussion therefore concerns certain kinds of good and bad, not all of them. Undoubtedly, some kinds can be known only through revealed law. The disagreement, however, concerns things whose badness is known to people generally, such as injustice, lying, and the like.

The disagreement concerns several matters. One is whether an action possesses a quality by virtue of which it becomes good or bad, and that rational goodness consists in its conformity to the knower’s interests, while rational badness is the opposite. Does revealed law, then, add anything beyond

---

## Page 4025

that? Another point of disagreement is whether punishment in this world and the Hereafter can be known through reason alone. A fuller discussion of this belongs elsewhere.

Some have posited a third category of goodness and badness, claiming agreement on it: an action’s being an attribute of perfection or deficiency. Most earlier scholars who discussed this question did not mention this category. Some later scholars, however, did mention it, such as al-Rāzī, who adopted it from the philosophers. Upon examination, this category is no different from the first. The perfection a person acquires through certain actions ultimately comes back to what is agreeable or contrary to his interests—that is, pleasure or pain. The soul takes pleasure in what perfects it and suffers from deficiency. Thus, perfection and deficiency ultimately come back to what is agreeable and what is incompatible. This is discussed at length elsewhere.

(The point here) is that the distinction between good actions, through which the person performing them experiences pleasure, and evil actions, through which he experiences pain, is a matter of sensory perception recognized by all animals.

Thus, if someone who claims insight into the reality of divine decree, annihilation in the oneness of divine lordship, and istilām claims that he remains in ‘ayn al-jam‘ (undifferentiated awareness), such that he does not distinguish between what causes pain and what gives pleasure, his claim is known to be false—if he understands what he is saying. Otherwise, he is astray, speaking of something whose reality he does not understand. This is usually the case with those who speak about this. For one of these people may experience this state—“the experience of annihilation in the oneness of

---

## Page 4026

divine lordship”—and perceives no distinction so long as he remains in this state. For a time, he may lose awareness of what gives rise to distinctions, and so imagine this annihilation to be a praiseworthy spiritual station, regarding it either as the ultimate goal or as something necessary for those following the spiritual path. This is mistaken. An occasional failure to distinguish between what brings pleasure and what brings torment is like failing to distinguish between sleep, forgetfulness, heedlessness, and absorption in one thing to the exclusion of another. It neither removes the distinction that actually exists nor prevents awareness of it when the cause of that awareness is present.

Any one of these people must inevitably become hungry or thirsty. He will not treat bread and drink alike, nor bitterly salty water and sweet, fresh water. Rather, he must distinguish between them and say, “This is wholesome, and this is not.” This is precisely the distinction underlying everything Allah and His Messenger have commanded and forbidden: they have commanded wholesome speech and deeds and forbidden what is foul.

Once it is understood that this distinction means that some things are beneficial and bring pleasure and bliss, while others are harmful and bring pain and torment, some of these things are perceived through the senses, while others people grasp through reason in worldly affairs. Thus, they recognize what brings them benefit in this world and what brings them harm. This belongs to the faculty of reason that distinguishes human beings, for it perceives consequences of actions that the senses cannot perceive. In the Quran, the term “reason” encompasses that by which one secures benefit and wards off harm.

---

## Page 4027

And Allah Most High sent the messengers to perfect human nature, so they showed people how to attain bliss in the Hereafter and escape its torment. The distinction between what is commanded and what is forbidden is thus like the distinction between Paradise and Hell, pleasure and pain, and bliss and torment. Whoever fails to perceive this distinction is excused if a cause for which he bears no blame has deprived him of reason. Otherwise, he is held accountable for the evil he has committed and the good he has neglected.

There is no doubt that some people may lose their reason in certain states. Others deliberately engage in things that deprive them of reason, such as drinking wine or listening to enrapturing sounds. The effects of such listening may become so powerful that its participants become intoxicated and devils attach themselves to them. They then kill one another during these intoxicating listening sessions, just as wine drinkers kill one another when drunk. Many people familiar with such spiritual states know this, yet some of them say that the person killed is a martyr.

The correct assessment is that the person killed resembles someone killed while drinking wine, for they entered a state of intoxication not sanctioned by the religion. Most of them, however, believe that this is one of the spiritual states of Allah’s pious friends. A person killed among them is therefore like someone killed during civil strife. He is not like the one who deliberately killed him, nor is he in every respect like someone killed unjustly.

If it is asked, “Does this annihilation suspend religious responsibility?” the answer is: If someone experiences something for which he is excused, and it deprives him of the reason by which he distinguishes between things, he is like someone asleep, unconscious, or intoxicated without incurring sin—for example, someone who became intoxicated before wine was prohibited, had wine poured into his mouth, or, according to the majority of scholars, was coerced into drinking it. If, however, the intoxication results from something forbidden, this is a matter of well-known disagreement among the scholars.

---

## Page 4028

Those who report utterances from Abū Yazīd and others expressing individual union with God and denying distinction, while excusing him for them, say that he lost his reason, to the point that he said: “I am the Truth,” “Glory be to me,” and “There is nothing in this robe but Allah.”

They say that when love overpowers someone whose heart is weak, he becomes so absorbed in his Beloved that he loses awareness of his love; in the One he finds, that he loses awareness of his ecstasy; and in the One he remembers, that he loses awareness of his remembrance—until he who once did not exist is annihilated, and He who has always existed remains.

They recount that someone threw himself into the water, and the man who loved him threw himself in after him. The first said, “I fell in, but why did you fall in?” He replied, “Absorbed in you, I lost awareness of myself, so I thought that you were me.”

Such a state, in which someone loses the ability to distinguish between the Lord and the servant, and between what is commanded and what is forbidden, is neither knowledge nor truth. At most, it reflects an impairment of the reason by which he distinguishes between these things. The most that can be said in his favor is that he may be excused—not that his words express true realization.

Yet some Sufis who claim true realization regard this as realization and affirmation of divine oneness, as did the author of Manāzil al-Sā’irīn (Stations of the Wayfarers), Ibn al-‘Arīf, and others. Likewise, some have regarded universal union as realization and affirmation of divine oneness, such as Ibn ‘Arabī al-Tā’ī.

Some have supposed that al-Hallāj belonged to the former category, and they then divided into two groups.

“One group” says that he fell into that state of annihilation and was therefore inwardly excused, but that his execution was obligatory on outward grounds. They say, “The killer is a fighter in Allah’s cause, and the slain is a martyr.” They also relate that one of the spiritual masters said, “He stumbled; had I lived in his time, I would have taken him by the hand.” They regard his state as akin to that of those who experience istilām and annihilation.

---

## Page 4029

And “a second group”—those who regard the state of annihilation in affirming Allah’s oneness in lordship as correct and say that it is the ultimate goal—say: “Rather, al-Hallāj had attained the highest degree of true realization and affirmation of divine oneness.” These, in turn, divide into two factions concerning his execution.

“One faction” says that he was unjustly killed and that executing him was impermissible. They are hostile to the Sharia and its adherents because they executed al-Hallāj. Some are hostile to jurists and scholars as a whole, saying: “They killed al-Hallāj.” These are like those who say: “We have a Sharia, and we have a spiritual reality that contradicts the Sharia.”

Those who speak this way do not discern what is meant by the word “Sharia” in the speech of Allah and His Messenger and in the speech of other people. Nor do they discern what is meant by “reality,” “truth,” “taste,” “ecstasy,” or “affirmation of divine oneness” in the speech of Allah and His Messenger and in the speech of other people. Indeed, some think that the divine Law simply means whatever a judge rules. Some of these make no distinction between a knowledgeable, just judge, an ignorant judge, and an unjust judge. Rather, whatever a judge rules, they call Sharia.

There is no doubt that the actual reality that Allah and His Messenger love may differ from a judge’s ruling. As the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“You bring your disputes before me, and some of you may be more eloquent in presenting their case than others. I judge only on the basis of what I hear. So if I rule in anyone’s favor at the expense of his brother’s rights

---

## Page 4030

whatsoever, he must not take it, for I am only allotting him a portion of the Fire.”

A judge rules according to the evidence and admissions he hears, while the other party may have arguments he has not presented, and so forth. Thus, the Sharia as it actually stands concerns the underlying reality, whereas the judge’s ruling is enforced outwardly.

In many matters, the underlying reality may differ from what appears to some people. The story of Moses and al-Khidr is an example. What al-Khidr did served a beneficial purpose and was an ordinance Allah had commanded him to carry out; it did not contravene Allah’s Law. But because Moses did not know the underlying reality, it appeared to him that this was impermissible. When al-Khidr explained matters to him, he agreed with him. Thus, this did not contravene the divine Law.

Regarding such matters, it may be said that the underlying reality can differ from outward appearances, and this is correct. However, calling the inward aspect “reality” and the outward aspect “Sharia” is a matter of terminological convention. Some people use “reality” for the inward aspect in general, and “Sharia” for outward matters.

This is like the term “Islam”: when paired with faith, it refers to outward deeds, while “faith” refers to the faith within the heart, as in the hadith of Gabriel. Thus, when the two are brought together in the expression “the ordinances of Islam and the realities of faith,” this is a valid statement. But whenever

---

## Page 4031

either term is used on its own, it includes the other. Thus, anyone whose observance of the Sharia lacks an inward reality is not a true believer, and anyone whose inward reality does not accord with the Sharia with which Allah sent Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, is not a Muslim, let alone one of Allah’s God-fearing allies.

The term “Sharia” may also refer to the conclusions reached by jurists through their independent judgment, while “reality” may refer to what Sufis inwardly taste and experience in their hearts. Undoubtedly, both groups exercise their own judgment: sometimes they are right, and sometimes they are mistaken. Neither is permitted deliberately to oppose the Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. The judgments of the two groups may agree; otherwise, neither group is obliged to follow the other unless the latter presents evidence from the Sharia that makes agreement with it obligatory.

Some people portray al-Hallāj as having been executed on the basis of a juristic judgment that contradicted the inward reality experienced by these Sufis. Many people believe this, but it is not so. Rather, he was executed for unbelief, and both groups agreed to his execution. This included his claim that he could produce something better than the Quran to rival it, and his claim that anyone who missed the Hajj could build a house, circumambulate it, and give a sum he prescribed in charity, thereby discharging the obligation of Hajj. There were other matters as well that constitute unbelief by the agreement of the Muslims who bear witness that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah: their scholars, worshippers, jurists, fuqarā’, and Sufis.

And (a group says): “He was executed because he divulged the secret of divine oneness and spiritual realization—a secret not

---

## Page 4032

to be divulged; for this is one of those secrets discussed only with a select few, to be kept concealed rather than recounted.” They recite:

Whoever among men divulges the secret meets death as his lot,
and his blood goes unavenged.
They divulged the secret, so their blood may be shed;
thus may the blood of those who divulge it be shed. (1)

What these people say is essentially like someone saying that what the Christians say about the Messiah is true, and that the same holds for other prophets and allies of Allah, but that it cannot be stated openly because the bearer of the Sharia has not permitted it.

The words of the author of Manāzil al-Sā’irīn (The Stations of the Wayfarers) and others like him point to this, as does his conception of divine oneness, concerning which he said:

No one has affirmed the oneness of the One,
for everyone who affirms His oneness denies Him.
The affirmation of His oneness by one who speaks of His attributes
is a borrowed thing that the One has annulled.
His affirmation of His own oneness is His affirmation of oneness;
and the description offered by one who describes Him is for someone.

For what these people are really saying is that the one affirming oneness is the very One whose oneness is affirmed; that it is the Real who speaks the affirmation of oneness through the servant’s tongue; and that none affirms His oneness but He Himself. Thus, the One whose oneness is affirmed can only be the one affirming it.

They distinguish between Pharaoh’s statement:

“I am your most exalted lord,”

and al-Hallāj’s statements, “I am the Real” and “Glory be to me.” For Pharaoh said this while conscious of himself, and so spoke about himself. As for those experiencing the annihilation of self-awareness, they lost awareness of themselves, and the one speaking through their tongues was someone other than themselves.

> **Footnotes:**
> (1) Thus in the original.
> Shaykh Nāsir ibn Hamad al-Fahd states (p. 76):
> These are two separate verses, each independent of the other.
> The first is in the basīt metre and reads:
> “Whoever among men divulges the secret, being slain is his lot … and his blood goes unavenged.”
> Shaykh al-Islām (may Allah have mercy on him) cites it in al-Jawāb al-sahīh, 4:497.

> “If they divulge the secret, their blood may be shed … and likewise the blood of those who divulge it may be shed.”

---

## Page 4033

This is an error into which many later Sufis fell. Hence al-Junayd—may Allah have mercy on him—refuted them when he was asked about divine oneness and replied: “It is distinguishing the Eternal from the created.” Al-Junayd, the foremost master of the Sufis, thus explained that affirming divine oneness is incomplete unless one distinguishes between the eternal Lord and the created servant—not as these people claim, making the two one and the same. These are the proponents of particular, restricted union and indwelling. As for those who advocate universal, unrestricted indwelling and union, they say that He Himself is everywhere, or that He is the very existence of created beings. They have been discussed at length elsewhere.

And (the point here is that al-Hallāj did not confine himself to any one of these categories. Rather, he made statements that, by agreement among the various groups of Muslims, constitute disbelief and warrant execution, as has been explained elsewhere. Likewise, most of the spiritual masters repudiated and censured him, including al-Junayd, ʿUmar ibn ʿUthmān al-Makkī, and Abū Yaʿqūb al-Nahrajūrī. Those among them who were uncertain about his case did not know what he had actually said—except for those who advocated indwelling and union, whether unrestrictedly or in a particular instance: such a person supposes that this was al-Hallāj’s position and defends it. Hence Ibn Sabʿīn’s sect included a number of men of wrongdoing, among them al-Hallāj.

The great majority of Sufi masters and scholars held that al-Hallāj was not one of the righteous spiritual masters. Rather, he was a heretic, and his asceticism had various motives that would take too long to describe. Nor was he among those who experienced the annihilation of self-awareness in “the oneness of divine lordship”; rather, he had

---

## Page 4034

learned sorcery and had devils serving him, besides other matters detailed elsewhere.

In any case, when Adam and Eve ate from the tree, Adam had neither lost his reason nor experienced the annihilation of self-awareness in contemplation of the all-encompassing divine decree. Nor did he invoke that in his argument against Moses. Rather, he said: “Why do you blame me for something Allah decreed for me before I was created?” Thus, he appealed to the prior divine decree, not to his failure to distinguish between what was commanded and what was forbidden.

Section

With this understood, we say: the correct understanding of the account of Adam and Moses is that Moses blamed Adam only for the calamity that his action had brought upon him and his descendants—not on the grounds that someone who fails to obey a command is a sinner and disobedient. Hence he said: “Why did you cause us and yourself to leave Paradise?” He did not say: “Why did you disobey the command? Why did you sin?”

When calamities befall people, whether through human actions or otherwise, they are commanded to submit to the divine decree and acknowledge Allah’s lordship, as the Exalted says:

“No calamity befalls except by Allah’s permission. And whoever believes in Allah, He guides his heart.”

Ibn Masʿūd, or someone else, said: “This is a man who is struck by a calamity and knows that it is from Allah, so he is content and submits.” In an authentic hadith, the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—said: “Strive for

---

## Page 4035

what benefits you, seek Allah’s help, and do not give up. If something befalls you, do not say, ‘If only I had done such-and-such, this or that would have happened.’ Rather, say, ‘Allah has decreed, and He has done what He willed,’ for ‘if only’ opens the door to Satan’s work.”

He thus commanded a person to strive for what benefits him—namely, obedience to Allah and His Messenger—for nothing benefits people more than obedience to Allah and His Messenger. He also commanded him, when a decreed calamity befalls him, not to focus on the decree or grieve over fruitless suppositions, but to say: “Allah has decreed, and He has done what He willed.” He should not say: “If only I had done such-and-such, this would have happened,” imagining something that did not occur and wishing that it had. This only produces futile regret and sorrow, whereas submission to the decree is what benefits him. As someone said: “Matters are of two kinds: those about which something can be done, so do not give up; and those about which nothing can be done, so do not be distraught.”

The rightly guided leaders, among the shaykhs and others, have always counselled people to do what is commanded, refrain from what is forbidden, and patiently endure what is decreed—even when the calamity results from a human action.

Suppose a man spent his wealth on sins until he died, leaving no wealth to his children, or wronged people in such a way that they came to hate his children and deny them what they gave to others like them. This would be a calamity for the children, brought about by their father’s actions. If one of them said to his father, “You did this to us,” the son would be told: “This was decreed

---

## Page 4036

for you, and you are commanded to bear patiently whatever befalls you.” The father has disobeyed Allah through his wrongdoing and squandering, and he is blameworthy for it. The prior decree does not exempt him from Allah’s condemnation and punishment. If, however, the father has sincerely repented, and Allah has accepted his repentance and forgiven him, he may no longer be condemned or blamed in any way: neither with regard to Allah’s right, since Allah has forgiven him, nor on account of the calamity his actions brought upon others, since he had not wronged them and that calamity had been decreed for them.

This is analogous to “the story of Adam”: Adam did not wrong his children; rather, they were born only after his descent from Paradise. Only Adam and Eve descended, with no children accompanying them, so it cannot be said that their sin extended to their children. Their children came into being after their descent to earth. Thus, Adam had not wronged his children in any way that entitled them to blame him. Their being in this world rather than Paradise was something decreed for them, for which they had no right to blame Adam. As for Adam’s sin, he had repented of it.

Allah Most High said:

“Adam disobeyed his Lord and went astray.”

“Then his Lord chose him, accepted his repentance, and guided him.”

He also said:

“Then Adam received words from his Lord, and He accepted his repentance.”

He therefore no longer deserved condemnation or punishment. Moses knew better than to blame him, on account of Allah’s right, for a sin that he knew Adam had repented of. Moses himself had also repented of a sin he had committed, and he said:

“You are our Protector, so forgive us and have mercy upon us. You are the best of those who forgive.”

Adam likewise knew better than to invoke the decree to argue that a sinner is not to blame. How could he do so, when he knew that Allah had cursed Iblīs because of

---

## Page 4037

his sin, which had also been decreed for him? Adam had repented of his sin and sought forgiveness. Had invoking the decree been of any avail to him before his Lord, he would have invoked it rather than repenting and seeking forgiveness.

It is related in Israelite traditions that he invoked the decree. Even if such a report were plausible, it would not be affirmed as true; how much less so when it contradicts the fundamentals of Islam—indeed, the fundamentals of revealed law and reason. Certainly, if he mentioned the decree while also repenting, that is possible. Yet nothing of this appears in what Allah has told us about Adam. Nor is it permissible to cite Israelite traditions as evidence in religion, except where their content is established by Allah’s Book or the Sunnah of His Messenger. For the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“When the People of the Book relate something to you, neither affirm nor deny it.”

Furthermore, if invoking the decree had been of any avail to him, why was he expelled from Paradise and sent down to earth?

If it is asked, “But he had repented, so why was he sent down to earth after repenting?” the answer is: repentance may require righteous deeds to complete it. A person may therefore be tested after repenting, to see whether he remains steadfast in obedience. Allah Most High said concerning someone who repents of apostasy:

“Except those who repent afterwards and mend their ways, for Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful.”

Concerning those who conceal knowledge, He said:

“Except those who repent, mend their ways, and make the truth clear. Those are the ones whose repentance I will accept, for I am the Accepter of Repentance, the Most Merciful.”

He also said:

“If any of you does wrong out of ignorance, then repents afterwards and makes amends, He is indeed All-Forgiving, Most Merciful.”

And concerning slander, He said:

“Except those who repent afterwards and mend their ways

---

## Page 4038

for Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful.” He also said:

“Except those who repent, believe, and do righteous deeds: Allah will replace their evil deeds with good deeds. And Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful.”

“And whoever repents and does righteous deeds truly turns to Allah in repentance.”

He also said:

“Indeed, I am Most Forgiving to whoever repents, believes, and does righteous deeds, then remains rightly guided.”

When Kaʿb ibn Mālik and his two companions repented, the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, ordered the Muslims—even their wives—to shun them for eighty nights.

Concerning the Ghāmidī woman, when he had her stoned, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“She has repented so sincerely that, were a collector of unlawful tolls to repent in the same way, he would be forgiven. Have you found anything better than her giving up her own life for Allah?”

Allah has also told us of His acceptance of the repentance of the Children of Israel, when Moses said to them:

“O my people, you have certainly wronged yourselves by taking the calf for worship. So repent to your Creator and kill one another. That is better for you in the sight of your Creator.”

If Allah Most High may test His servant with good and ill, prosperity and adversity, revealing whether he responds with gratitude and patience or ingratitude and anguish, and with obedience or disobedience, then one who repents has all the more reason to be tested. Adam was therefore sent down to earth as a test, and Allah enabled him to obey Him after his descent. His condition after descending was thus better than it had been before.

This is quite different from what would follow if invoking the decree had been of any avail to him: he would then have been entirely free of blame, and there would have been no repentance requiring that he be subjected to a trial.

Furthermore, Allah has related in His Book the punishments inflicted upon the disbelievers, such as the people of

---

## Page 4039

Noah, Hūd, and Sālih, the people of Lot, the inhabitants of Midian, and Pharaoh and his people. Each of these events shows that no one can invoke the divine decree as an excuse. Moreover, the punishments Allah has prescribed for those who wage war, whether disbelievers or Muslims, the execution of apostates, and the punishment of those who commit fornication or adultery, thieves, and drinkers of intoxicants all make this clear.

Section

It has thus become clear that Adam prevailed over Moses in argument when Moses sought to blame the one who had caused their affliction. This is what the Quran and Sunnah teach. Allah Most High says:

“No calamity befalls except by Allah’s permission. And whoever believes in Allah, He guides his heart.”

He also says:

“No calamity befalls the earth or yourselves but it is in a Record before We bring it into being. Indeed, that is easy for Allah.”

This applies equally to calamities that come from heaven and those caused by human actions. Allah Most High says:

“Be patient with what they say, and withdraw from them graciously.”

“Messengers before you were indeed rejected, but they patiently endured rejection and harm until Our help came to them.”

In Sūrat al-Tūr, He says, after His words:

“So remind them, for by your Lord’s grace you are neither a soothsayer nor a madman. Or do they say, ‘A poet—we await the misfortunes of time to befall him’? Say, ‘Wait, then; I too am waiting with you.’”

—and continuing to His words—

“Or do they say, ‘He has made it up’? Rather, they do not believe.”

—and continuing to His words—

“Or do you ask them for payment, so that they are burdened with debt? Or do they possess knowledge of the unseen, which they are writing down? Be patient with your Lord’s judgment, for you are under Our Eyes

---

## Page 4040

and glorify your Lord with praise when you rise.”

Allah Most High also says in Sūrat Nūn:

“Or do you ask them for payment, so that they are burdened with debt? Or do they possess knowledge of the unseen, which they are writing down? So be patient with your Lord’s judgment, and do not be like the companion of the whale, who called out in anguish.”

Its meaning has been explained as: “Be patient with whatever is decreed for you.” Another explanation is: “Bear their harm patiently in anticipation of your Lord’s judgment, which is coming.” The first is more correct.

Allah’s judgment is of two kinds: creation and command. The first concerns the calamities He decrees; the second concerns what He commands and forbids. The servant is commanded to exercise patience with both. He must patiently observe what he is commanded and what he is forbidden, carrying out the commands and refraining from what is prohibited. He must also bear patiently whatever Allah has decreed for him.

Some Quran commentators say: “This verse is abrogated by the verse of the sword.” This would be a tenable interpretation if the verse contained a prohibition on fighting: that prohibition would then be abrogated, not every form of patience. How could all forms of patience be abrogated, when the verse here neither prohibits nor prescribes fighting? Rather, patience with Allah’s judgment is obligatory and has always remained so. When he is commanded to engage in jihad, he must “also” be patient with Allah’s judgment, for fighting them brings ordeals more severe than their verbal abuse, as he experienced on the days of Uhud and the Trench. At such times, he must be patient and carry out the jihad he has been commanded to undertake.

---

## Page 4041

The point here is His saying:

“Be patient with your Lord’s judgment.”

The harm they have inflicted upon you is among the things decreed for you, so be patient with His judgment, even though they have wronged you. This patience is greater than patience with what befell the prophets and what was done to them. He also says:

“So be patient with your Lord’s judgment, and do not be like the companion of the whale, who called out in anguish.”

And He says:

“And remember the man of the whale, when he went away in anger, thinking We would not constrain him, then called out in the darkness.”

Whether his anger was directed at his people or at his Lord, it concerned something decreed for him. In showing patience, he was being patient with his Lord’s judgment, which He had ordained and decreed, even if his distress arose only from people’s rejection of him.

The messengers said to their peoples:

“Why should we not put our trust in Allah when He has guided us to our ways? We will surely bear patiently whatever harm you inflict upon us. And in Allah let those who trust put their trust.”

Moses spoke to his people when Pharaoh had declared:

“We will kill their sons and spare their women, and we have absolute power over them.”

“Moses said to his people, ‘Seek help from Allah and be patient. Indeed, the earth belongs to Allah; He grants it as an inheritance to whomever He wills of His servants. And the final outcome is for those who fear Him.’”

And He says:

“So be patient. Indeed, Allah’s promise is true, and seek forgiveness for your sin.”

Allah Most High also says:

“As for those who emigrated for Allah’s sake after being wronged, We will surely grant them a good dwelling in this world, but the reward of the Hereafter is greater, if only they knew.”

“Those who are patient and put their trust in their Lord.”

These people were wronged and patiently endured the injustice inflicted upon them. The occasion of this verse’s revelation concerned those who emigrated to the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. Yet it applies generally to everyone who possesses these qualities.

---

## Page 4042

An “emigrant,” in the fundamental sense, is someone who abandons what Allah has forbidden, as is authentically reported from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. Thus, whoever abandons evil and is wronged by people for forsaking disbelief, wickedness and disobedience, to the point that they drive him out—not someone who merely abandons certain worldly things—and patiently endures their wrongdoing, Allah will surely grant him a good dwelling in this world, while the reward of the Hereafter is greater. Such was Joseph, the man of truth: he shunned indecency, even though this compelled him to leave his home and remain in prison after being wronged. Then Allah established him in the land, allowing him to settle wherever he wished.

Those who confronted the disbelievers said:

“Our Lord, pour upon us patience.”

And He says:

“If there are twenty steadfast among you, they will overcome two hundred. And if there are one hundred among you, they will overcome a thousand of those who disbelieve, because they are a people who do not understand.”

“Now Allah has lightened your burden, knowing that there is weakness in you. So if there are one hundred steadfast among you, they will overcome two hundred. And if there are a thousand among you, they will overcome two thousand by Allah’s permission. And Allah is with the steadfast.”

And He says:

“How many a small company has overcome a large company by Allah’s permission! And Allah is with the steadfast.”

All of this is patience with the actions of created beings that have been decreed. Allah, glorified be He, praises in His Book those who are ever patient and grateful. In several places, the Most High says:

“Indeed, in that are signs for everyone who is ever patient and grateful.”

Patience and gratitude concern what the Lord decrees for His servant of prosperity and adversity, blessings and calamities, and the good and ill with which He tests him. He must therefore meet calamities with patience and blessings with gratitude. These blessings include the good deeds Allah enables him to perform, as well as blessings beyond his own actions. Thus, he recognizes the divine decree when he performs acts of obedience and when Allah bestows blessings upon him, and so gives thanks to Him

---

## Page 4043

and recognizes it when calamities befall him, and so remains patient. As for his sins, he seeks forgiveness and repents, as Allah says:

“So be patient; indeed, Allah’s promise is true. And seek forgiveness for your sin.”

But whoever reverses this—seeing the divine decree in his sins and his own agency in his good deeds—is among the greatest offenders. Whoever sees his own agency in both is a Qadarī. Whoever sees the divine decree in both, yet neither acknowledges his sin nor seeks Allah’s forgiveness, is of the same kind as the polytheists.

The believer, however, says:

“I acknowledge Your favor upon me, and I acknowledge my sin, so forgive me.”

As Allah says in the authentic divine hadith:

“My servants, these are only your deeds, which I record for you and then repay you for in full. Whoever finds good, let him praise Allah; whoever finds otherwise, let him blame no one but himself.”

Our Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, followed the command to endure patiently the harm inflicted by people. In the two Sahīh collections, ʿĀ’ishah said:

“The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, never struck a servant of his, an animal, or anything else with his hand, except when fighting in Allah’s cause. He never took revenge for any personal wrong done to him, unless Allah’s sacred limits were violated. When Allah’s sacred limits were violated, nothing could withstand his anger until he had exacted retribution for Allah’s sake.”

Anas said: “I served the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, for ten years. Never did he say about anything I had done, ‘Why did you do it?’ or about anything I had not done, ‘Why did you not do it?’ Whenever a member of his household reproached me for something, he would say, ‘Leave him alone, leave him alone. Had something been decreed, it would have happened.’”

In the Sunan collections, it is reported “from Ibn Masʿūd—may Allah be pleased with him—that he mentioned to the Prophet

---

## Page 4044

may Allah bless him and grant him peace, the words of someone who had offended him. He replied, ‘Leave us be. Moses suffered greater harm than this, yet he remained patient.’”

He would patiently endure the harm inflicted upon him by disbelievers, hypocrites, and even some believers, as Allah Most High says:

“That was causing the Prophet discomfort, but he was too shy to tell you.”

He would mention that this had been decreed.

The believer is commanded to bear patiently what has been decreed. Thus Allah says:

“If you are patient and mindful of Allah, their schemes will not harm you at all.”

Piety consists in doing what is commanded, avoiding what is forbidden, and patiently bearing their harm. Then, where Allah permits retaliation, He says:

“If you retaliate, retaliate only to the extent of the harm you have suffered. But if you are patient, that is certainly better for those who are patient.”

“And be patient; your patience is only through Allah. Do not grieve over them, nor be distressed by their schemes.”

He thus declares that the Prophet’s patience is through Allah: Allah is the One who helps him remain patient. Patiently enduring hardships without taking revenge upon the wrongdoer is difficult for the soul. Yet his patience is through Allah, just as Allah commanded that it be for His sake when He said:

“Be patient for the sake of your Lord.”

There, however, He expressed this as a command, because the Prophet is commanded to be patient for Allah’s sake, not for anyone else’s. Here, He expressed it as a statement:

“Your patience is only through Allah.”

For patience, like every other event, occurs only through Allah. Yet it may or may not occur. Whatever is not through Allah cannot occur, and whatever is not for Allah’s sake neither benefits nor endures.

It is not said, “Be patient through Allah,” since patience can only be through Allah. Rather, it is said, “Seek Allah’s help and be patient.” Thus, we seek Allah’s help to remain patient.

---

## Page 4045

Just as a person is commanded to acknowledge the divine decree and Allah’s oneness in lordship when calamities strike, he is also commanded to do so when Allah blesses him by enabling him to perform acts of obedience. Before performing them, he should recognize his need and utter dependence upon Allah’s assistance, and truly embody the words:

“You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help.”

He should offer supplications asking Allah to help him perform acts of obedience, such as:

“Help me to remember You, thank You, and worship You well.”

“O Turner of hearts, keep my heart steadfast upon Your religion. O Director of hearts, direct my heart to obedience to You and Your Messenger.”

“Our Lord, do not let our hearts deviate after You have guided us. Grant us mercy from Yourself; You are indeed the Bestower.”

“Our Lord, grant us mercy from Yourself and guide us rightly in our affairs.”

And likewise:

“O Allah, inspire me to follow right guidance and protect me from the evil of my own soul.”

The foremost and best of these supplications is:

“Guide us to the straight path—the path of those You have blessed, not of those who have incurred Your anger, nor of those who have gone astray.”

This is the best of supplications and the one people are most duty-bound to make, for it encompasses the servant’s well-being in religion, in this world, and in the Hereafter. The same applies to supplication for “repentance,” for it includes asking Allah to inspire the servant to repent. Likewise, the supplication of “istikhāra” seeks to have the servant taught what he does not know and to have it made easy for him.

The same is true of the supplication the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, would offer when he rose to pray at night. It is recorded in the Sahīh:

“O Allah, Lord of Gabriel, Michael, and Isrāfīl, Originator of the heavens and the earth, Knower of the unseen and the seen, You judge between Your servants concerning that over which they differed. Guide me concerning that over which there is disagreement

---

## Page 4046

to the truth, by Your permission. Indeed, You guide whom You will to a straight path.”

Likewise, there is the supplication that includes:

“Grant us such fear of You as will keep us from disobeying You, such obedience to You as will bring us to Your Paradise, and such certainty as will ease for us the calamities of this world.”

The same applies to asking for certainty and well-being, as in the hadith of Abū Bakr, and to the words, “O Allah, set right my heart and my intention.” Likewise, Allah’s intimate friend, Abraham, and Ishmael said:

“Make us both submissive to You, and from our descendants a nation submissive to You.”

There are many such supplications expressing the servant’s utter need for Allah to grant him faith and righteous deeds. This is an expression of need and a seeking of Allah’s help before the desired good is attained. Once it is attained, whether through supplication or otherwise, the servant recognizes Allah’s favor in it and assumes a state of gratitude and servitude to Allah, acknowledging that it came through His grace and kindness, not through the servant’s own power and strength.

Recognizing the divine decree in acts of obedience is among the most beneficial things for the servant, while being heedless of it is among the most harmful. For then he becomes a Qadarī, denying Allah’s favor upon him in granting him faith and righteous deeds. Even if he is not a Qadarī in belief, he is a Qadarī in his spiritual state. This breeds self-conceit, arrogance, claims of strength, a sense that his deeds constitute a favor he has bestowed, and the belief that those deeds entitle him to a reward from Allah.

Thus, someone who remains conscious of his servitude despite his sins and acknowledges them—without invoking the divine decree to justify them—is better than someone who regards his obedience as proceeding from himself rather than from Allah’s kindness to him. Those sinners, by virtue of the faith they possess, are better than obedience devoid of this faith.

---

## Page 4047

As for someone who sins yet considers himself entirely free of sin because Allah is the agent, but regards himself as the agent when he obeys, he is the worst of creation. As for the person who regards himself as the agent in both cases and the person who regards his Lord as the agent in both cases and sees no sin on his own part, the latter has a worse outcome than the Qadarī, while the Qadarī has a worse starting point than he does, as explained at length elsewhere.

In this regard, people fall into “four categories”: those who become angry for their Lord’s sake but not their own; those who do the reverse; those who become angry for both; and those who become angry for neither. Likewise, in their recognition of the divine decree, they fall into “four categories”: those who regard a good deed as Allah’s doing and an evil deed as their own; those who do the reverse; those who regard both as their Lord’s doing; and those who regard both as their own doing.

These four categories concerning awareness of Allah’s lordship correspond to those four categories concerning awareness of His right to worship. The latter classification concerns what people do for Allah and for themselves, while the former concerns what they do through Allah and through themselves. The pure category is to act for Allah through Allah’s help, acting neither for oneself nor through one’s own power.

Our concern here is to classify people with respect to what they do for Allah. The highest state is that of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and those who follow him: they patiently endure the physical and verbal harm people inflict upon them, while striving in Allah’s cause. They punish, become angry, and exact retribution for Allah’s sake, not their own. They punish because Allah commands that the person in question be punished and retribution must be exacted from him, as in fighting the disbelievers and enforcing the prescribed punishments.
