When the proof became clear against him, he said, ‘Allah may speak, but His speech is created.’ We said, ‘The speech of human beings is also created. You have thus likened Allah to His creation when

---

## Page 4135

you claimed that His speech is created. According to your doctrine, there was a time when He did not speak, until He created speech. You have thus combined disbelief with likening Allah to His creation. Exalted is Allah above such a description! Rather, we say: Allah has always spoken whenever He wills. We do not say that He existed without speaking until He created speech.’”

He then cited the remainder of his statement. He thus made clear that human speech is created: Allah created it. This is even more forceful than his explicit affirmation that people’s actions are created, although he explicitly affirmed both.

He also said:

“If you wish to know that the Jahmī lies about Allah when he claims that He is everywhere and is not in one place to the exclusion of another, say: ‘Did Allah not exist when nothing else existed?’ He will say, ‘Yes.’ Then ask him, ‘When He created His creation, did He create it within Himself or outside Himself?’ He must then adopt one of three positions.

“First, if he claims that Allah created creation within Himself, he commits disbelief by claiming that jinn, human beings, and devils are within Him.

“If he says, ‘He created them outside Himself and then entered into them,’ this too is disbelief, since he claims that He entered a desolate, filthy, foul place.

“If he says, ‘He created them outside Himself and did not then enter into them,’ he has abandoned his position entirely. This is the position of Ahl al-Sunnah.”

Ahmad thus made clear that human speech is created, and explicitly stated in several places that people’s actions are created. His explicit statement concerning their speech is more forceful, since the specious arguments concerning it are more apparent.

Thus, whoever says that

---

## Page 4136

human speech or actions are eternal is an innovator who opposes the Book, the Sunnah, and the consensus of the early generations of this Ummah and its imams.

Section

As for adding “if Allah wills” to statements about known and certain past matters—for example, saying, “This is a tree, if Allah wills,” “This is a human being, if Allah wills,” “The sky is above us, if Allah wills,” “There is no deity worthy of worship except Allah, if Allah wills,” or “Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah, if Allah wills”; or refusing to say categorically, “Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah,” or “This is a tree”—this is an innovation contrary to reason and religion.

We have heard of no one among the people of “Islam” doing this except a group of those affiliated with Shaykh Abū ‘Amr ibn Marzūq. Neither the shaykh nor his sensible followers held this view.

However, someone well informed told me that, after his death, two of his followers, Hāzim and ‘Abd al-Malik, fell into a dispute. Hāzim introduced this innovation of adding “if Allah wills” when speaking about past matters known with certainty, and ceased making categorical assertions about them. ‘Abd al-Malik opposed him in this, agreeing with the Muslim community and the imams of the religion. As for “Shaykh Abū ‘Amr,” he was too sensible to become involved in this sort of

---

## Page 4137

nonsense, for he possessed knowledge and religious devotion, although the previously mentioned view that human actions, both good and evil, are eternal is attributed to him. Some of them have shown me this in his own handwriting.

It has been said that he retracted this view. He followed the approach of Shaykh Abū al-Faraj al-Maqdisī al-Shīrāzī, and it was reported of him that he would withhold judgment, saying, “They are decreed and ordained,” and say no more. Shaykh Abū al-Faraj was one of the followers of Judge Abū Ya‘lā. However, Judge Abū Ya‘lā did not approve of such views; rather, he categorically affirmed that human actions are created. Had he heard anyone hesitate to affirm that disbelief, wickedness, and disobedience are created—let alone say that a person’s actions, both good and evil, are eternal—he would have rebuked him in the strongest terms.

Nevertheless, there are passages in the Judge’s writings in which his statements are inconsistent and contradictory. In one passage, he made a statement from which those who agreed with him developed unsound conclusions. A scholar may make an erroneous statement, and his followers then derive numerous further conclusions from it, as happened regarding the questions of “utterance,” “human speech,” “faith,” and “human actions.”

None of the early generations and imams—Imam Ahmad and others—said that human speech is uncreated, nor did they say that it is eternal, or that human actions are uncreated or eternal. Nor did they say that faith is eternal or uncreated. Neither did they say that people’s utterance of the Quran is created or uncreated. However, they prohibited declaring without qualification

---

## Page 4138

that faith is created or that utterance of the Quran is created, because this encompasses attributes of Allah Most High, and because such wording suggests that the Creator’s very speech is created and that this very word is created. They also prohibited saying, “The letters of the alphabet are created,” because these assertions entail that the Quran is not Allah’s speech and that He did not speak to Moses.

Then some people came and asserted the opposite without qualification. Some said, “My utterance of the Quran is uncreated.” Imam Ahmad and other imams declared those who said this to be innovators. Likewise, some asserted without qualification that faith is uncreated, until this came to be understood as meaning that the “human actions” constituting faith are uncreated. Others then went further, saying, “Human speech consists of letters that are uncreated; therefore, it is uncreated.” Still others said, “All human actions, then, are uncreated.”

The more an innovation is developed and its implications are drawn out, the uglier and more abhorrent it becomes, ultimately leading its proponent to contradict what is necessarily known through reason and religion. We have discussed this at length and explained people’s inconsistencies concerning it in the question of the Quran and other matters.

This is similar to the innovation introduced by some people who claimed that the letters of the Quran are not part of Allah’s speech

---

## Page 4139

and that Allah’s speech is nothing but a meaning subsisting in His essence, comprising command, prohibition, and report. This claim is invalid according to sound reason and authentic transmitted evidence. A single meaning cannot constitute the command to perform every commanded act and the report from every informant; nor can the Torah, the Gospel, and the Quran have one and the same meaning. They say: “When that speech is expressed in Arabic, it becomes the Quran, and when expressed in Hebrew, it becomes the Torah.” This is mistaken: the Torah can be expressed in Arabic, yet its meanings are not those of the Quran; and the Quran can be expressed in Hebrew, yet its meanings are not those of the Torah.

The first to introduce this position was Ibn Kullāb. Nevertheless, he and those who followed him in it, such as al-Ashʿarī and others, also say: “The Quran is truly preserved in hearts, truly recited by tongues, and truly written in the codices.”

Some of them illustrate this by saying that it is preserved in hearts just as Allah is known in hearts, recited by tongues just as Allah is mentioned by tongues, and written in the codices just as Allah is written in the codices. This is a mistaken account of the actual position of Ibn Kullāb and al-Ashʿarī. In their view, the Quran is a meaning expressed in words, and realities have four levels of existence: existence in external reality, in knowledge, in speech, and in writing. Thus, knowledge of the meaning does not occupy the second level, nor is its presence in a book like the presence of concrete entities in a book. These people have therefore made the position of Ibn Kullāb and al-Ashʿarī even more repugnant.

---

## Page 4140

Then groups among their followers followed a proponent of this school, maintaining that the Quran is merely a meaning subsisting in Allah’s essence, and that its letters are not part of Allah’s speech; rather, Allah created them in the air, or Gabriel or Muhammad composed them. To this they added that the Quran codex contains nothing but ink and paper. They disregarded their predecessors’ statement that it points to Allah’s speech and must therefore be respected, having seen that merely pointing to something does not entail a duty of respect. The same applies to whatever points to the Creator who speaks: all existing things point to Him, yet they need not be held sacred.

These people thus began to desecrate the Quran codex, even trampling it underfoot. Some of them write Allah’s names with excrement to strip Allah’s names and verses written in the codices and on paper of their sanctity. Muslims have agreed that anyone who treats the Quran codex with contempt—for example, by throwing it into a privy or kicking it to insult it—is an unbeliever whose blood may lawfully be shed.

Religious innovations begin as a handspan, then grow as they are followed until they extend to cubits, miles, and parasangs. This answer does not allow for a detailed discussion of this subject; it has been discussed at length elsewhere.

Those who attach the qualification “if Allah wills” to these past matters established with certainty are ignorant, misguided innovators. One of them argues in support of this as follows. When told, “This is a tree,” he replies, “If Allah wills to turn it into an animal, He can do so.”

---

## Page 4141

He should then be told: “It is certainly a tree now.” But if you say that it has changed, this is like a human being who is first a drop of fluid, then a clinging clot, then a morsel of flesh, then flesh, and then comes to life. Once the spirit has been breathed into him, he is certainly alive; and if Allah wills to cause him to die, He does so. Allah’s ability to transform His creatures from one state to another does not prevent them from actually being, at any given time, in the state in which He has created them. The sky is the sky by Allah’s will, power, and creation; a human being is a human being by Allah’s will, power, and creation; and a horse is a horse by Allah’s will, power, and creation. If Allah wills to change whatever He wishes, He changes it through His will—if He so wills—His power, and His creation.

Neither the Quran nor the Sunnah uses the qualification “if Allah wills” concerning the past, but rather concerning the future, as in His words:

“Never say of anything, ‘I will do that tomorrow,’ unless you add, ‘If Allah wills.’”

And His words:

“You will surely enter the Sacred Mosque, if Allah wills.”

And the words of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“And we, if Allah wills, will join you.”

He also said:

“Solomon said, ‘Tonight I shall go in to seventy women, each of whom will bear a horseman who will fight in Allah’s cause.’ His companion told him, ‘Say: “If Allah wills,”’ but he did not say it. Only one of them gave birth, and she bore half a child.” He said: “Had he said, ‘If Allah wills,’ they would all have fought as horsemen in Allah’s cause.”

He also said, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“Whoever swears an oath and says, ‘If Allah wills,’ may do it if he wishes, or refrain if he wishes.”

This is because a person swears an oath concerning the future: that he or someone else will do something, or that he or someone else will not do something. He therefore says, “If Allah wills,” because whatever Allah wills happens, and whatever He does not will does not happen. If the act occurs, Allah has willed it, so the person has not broken his oath. If it does not occur, Allah has not willed it, so the person has not broken his oath. This is because he only committed himself to it if Allah willed it. Thus, if Allah does not will it, he has not committed himself to it and does not break his oath.

---

## Page 4142

The practice of “qualifying one’s profession of faith with ‘if Allah wills’” is also reported from Ibn Masʿūd and other early Muslims and leading scholars. This was not because they doubted anything they were obliged to believe, for doubt concerning that is disbelief. Rather, they used this qualification out of fear that they had not fulfilled faith’s obligations and truly realized it. Allah Most High has said:

“And those who give what they give while their hearts are fearful.”

The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said: “This is the man who fasts, prays, and gives charity, yet fears that it will not be accepted from him.”

They also used this qualification because they did not know their ultimate fate, and the faith that benefits a person is the faith upon which he dies. They used it out of fear of declaring themselves pure, and for other similarly sound reasons.

The same applies to someone who qualifies statements about righteous deeds, saying, for example, “I prayed, if Allah wills.” All such qualifications concern actions that are not known to have been performed as commanded and accepted. Thus, the qualification concerns either something whose true reality is unknown, or a future matter made conditional upon Allah’s will, to make clear that all matters depend upon His will. As for qualifying a known past event in this way, this is an innovation contrary to reason and religion.

---

## Page 4143

He also said—may Allah have mercy on him:

Section

As for “the question of reason’s judgment of good and evil,” there is a well-known disagreement among Ahl al-Sunnah wa-l-Jamāʿah within the four schools and beyond. The Hanafīs and many Mālikīs, Shāfiʿīs, and Hanbalīs affirm that reason can judge good and evil. This is also the position of the Karrāmiyyah and the Muʿtazilah, and of most groups among Muslims, Jews, Christians, Magians, and others. Many Shāfiʿīs, Mālikīs, and Hanbalīs deny this, as do the Ashʿarīs.

Nevertheless, the adherents of the Sunnah agree in affirming divine decree: Allah has power over all things and is the Creator of everything, including His servants’ deeds and all else; whatever He wills comes to pass, and whatever He does not will does not come to pass. The Muʿtazilah and other Qadarites disagree on this.

Denying divine decree is a reprehensible innovation. Some people have supposed that anyone who affirms that reason can judge good and evil denies divine decree and joins the Muʿtazilah in questions of al-taʿdīl and al-tajwīz. This is mistaken. Rather, most Muslims do not agree with the Muʿtazilah on that. Nor do they agree with the Ashʿarīs in denying

---

## Page 4144

wisdom and causes. Rather, most Muslim groups affirm divine decree and say that Allah is the Creator of everything, including His servants’ deeds and all else. They also say: Whatever Allah wills comes to pass, and whatever He does not will does not come to pass.

As for acknowledging that Allah knew and recorded His servants’ deeds before they performed them, only the extremists among the Qadarites and others have denied this. Most Qadarites, whether Muʿtazilīs or others, acknowledge that Allah knew what His servants would do before they did it. They also believe what the truthful and trusted one reported: that Allah determined the destinies of His creatures before creating them.

Thus, it is established in Sahīh Muslim, on the authority of ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAmr, that the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said:

“Allah determined the destinies of His creatures fifty thousand years before He created the heavens and the earth, and His Throne was upon the water.”

In Sahīh al-Bukhārī and elsewhere, ʿImrān ibn Husayn reports that the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said:

“Allah existed, and nothing existed before Him. His Throne was upon the water. He recorded everything in the Record and created the heavens and the earth.”

In another wording: “Then He created the heavens and the earth.”

In the two Sahīh collections, ʿAbd Allāh ibn Masʿūd said:

“The Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him—the truthful and trusted one—told us: ‘The creation of each of you is brought together in his mother’s womb for forty days as a drop of fluid, then he becomes a clinging clot for a similar period, then a lump of flesh for a similar period. Then the angel is sent to him and commanded to record four things. He is told: Write down his provision, his lifespan, his deeds, and whether he will be wretched or blessed. Then the soul is breathed into him. By Him in whose hand is my soul, one of you may indeed perform the deeds of the people of Paradise until only a cubit separates him from it; then what has been written overtakes him, and he performs the deeds of the people of the Fire and enters the Fire. And a man may indeed perform the deeds of

---

## Page 4145

the people of the Fire until only a cubit separates him from it; then what has been written overtakes him, and he performs the deeds of the people of Paradise and enters Paradise.’” Reports like this are numerous.

Most Qadarites acknowledge this; only their extremists deny it, such as those mentioned to ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUmar in the hadith Muslim narrated at the beginning of his Sahīh. He was told:

“There are people among us who recite the Quran and seek knowledge, claiming that there is no divine decree and that events arise anew, without any prior decree.” He replied: “When you meet those people, tell them that I disavow them and that they have nothing to do with me.”

For this reason, the imams—such as Mālik, al-Shāfiʿī, and Ahmad—declared those who said that Allah did not know His servants’ deeds until they performed them to be disbelievers, unlike the other Qadarites.

The point here is that the vast majority of Muslims disagree with the Qadarites, whether Muʿtazilīs or others. The vast majority of Muslims also acknowledge the causes that Allah has established as causes in His creation and His commands, and acknowledge the wise purposes He intends in His creation and His commands.

They affirm what Allah says in the Quran:

“And the water Allah sends down from the sky, giving life thereby to the earth after its death.”

He also says:

“We sent down water through it, and brought forth through it fruits of every kind.”

There are many such passages in the Quran and Sunnah. This is the position of the majority of Muslims: they say that something was brought about through a particular cause. They do not say, as those who deny causes do, that it was brought about when those causes occurred, but not through them. These matters are discussed at length elsewhere.

---

## Page 4146

The point here is that the question of “moral goodness and badness” is not inseparably linked to the question of divine decree. Once this is understood, people hold three positions on moral goodness and badness: two extremes and a middle position.

One extreme is the position of those who affirm goodness and badness as inherent, inseparable properties of an act, regarding revealed law as merely disclosing those properties, not as giving rise to any of them. This is the position of the Muʿtazilīs—and it is weak.

If this is combined with drawing an analogy between the Lord and His creation, so that one says, “Whatever is good when done by a created being is good when done by the Creator, and whatever is bad when done by a created being is bad when done by the Creator,” the false doctrines of the Qadarites follow, along with their discussions of permissibility and justice. They liken the Creator to created beings, and created beings to the Creator, in their actions. This position is false, just as likening the Creator to created beings, and created beings to the Creator, in their attributes is false.

The Jews attributed to Allah deficiencies from which He is far exalted, thereby likening Him to created beings: they described Him as poor, miserly, and subject to weariness. This is false, for the Lord, exalted is He, is free of every deficiency and possesses perfection without any deficiency. In His perfect attributes, He is far exalted above any of His attributes resembling any attribute of created beings. No one is His equal in any of His attributes: neither in His knowledge, nor His power, nor His will, nor His pleasure, nor His anger, nor His creating, nor His rising above, nor His coming, nor

---

## Page 4147

His descending, nor any other attribute with which He has described Himself or His Messenger has described Him. Rather, the way of the early generations is to describe Allah as He has described Himself and as His Messenger has described Him, without distortion or denial, and without specifying how His attributes are or likening them to those of creation. They neither deny the attributes He has affirmed for Himself nor liken His attributes to those of created beings. Whoever denies them strips Him of His attributes, and whoever does so worships a nonentity. Whoever likens Him to creation equates Him with it, and whoever does so worships an idol. The way of the early generations is affirmation without likening, and declaring Allah free of imperfection without denying His attributes.

As the Exalted says:

“There is nothing like Him.”

This refutes those who liken Him to creation. His words:

“And He is the All-Hearing, the All-Seeing”

refute those who deny His attributes.

Allah’s actions cannot be likened to the actions of created beings. For created beings are His servants: they commit injustice and indecencies, and He is able to prevent them. Were He not to prevent them, that would be morally bad on His part, and He would be blameworthy for it. Yet this is not morally bad on the part of the Lord, exalted is He, because of the consummate wisdom and abundant blessing He has in it. This is according to the position of the early generations, the jurists, and the majority, who affirm wisdom in Allah’s creation and commands.

Whoever says that He creates nothing for a wise purpose and commands nothing for a wise purpose affirms nothing but sheer will, which gives preference to one of two identical alternatives over the other without any determining reason. This is the foundational principle of Ibn Kullāb and his followers, and it underlies the positions of both the Qadarites and the Jahmites.

As for the other extreme concerning “the question of moral goodness and badness,” it is the position of those who say:

---

## Page 4148

actions possess neither qualities that constitute moral judgments nor qualities that serve as grounds for such judgments. Rather, the One who has power has commanded one of two identical alternatives rather than the other out of sheer will, not for any wise purpose or to secure any benefit in creation and command.

They say that it is possible for Allah to command associating partners with Him and forbid worshipping Him alone, and possible for Him to command injustice and indecencies and forbid righteousness and piety. The judgments used to characterize rulings are merely matters of relation and attribution. In their view, what is right is not right in itself, nor is what is wrong wrong in itself.

Rather, when He says:

“He commands them to do what is right and forbids them from what is wrong, makes lawful for them what is wholesome and forbids them what is foul,”

its actual meaning, according to them, is that he commands them to do what he commands them to do, forbids them from what he forbids them, makes lawful for them what he makes lawful, and forbids them what he forbids. Indeed, with regard to commanding, forbidding, making lawful and prohibiting, they hold that nothing is in reality right or wrong, wholesome or foul—unless such descriptions refer to what accords with natural dispositions. Yet, according to them, this does not entail that the Lord loves what is right and hates what is wrong.

This position and its implications are also weak, contrary to the Book, the Sunnah, and the consensus of the early generations and the jurists, as well as to sound reason. For Allah has declared Himself free of indecency, saying:

“Indeed, Allah does not command indecency.”

Likewise, He has declared Himself free of treating good and evil alike. The Exalted says:

“Or do those who commit evil deeds think that We will make them like those who believe and do righteous deeds, equal in their life and their death

---

## Page 4149

? How evil is their judgment!” And He says:

“Shall We then treat the Muslims like the criminals? What is the matter with you? How do you judge?”

And He says:

“Or shall We treat those who believe and do righteous deeds like those who spread corruption on earth? Or shall We treat those who fear Allah like the wicked?”

Yet according to those who deny this, there is no difference between treating these two groups alike and favouring some over others. There is no more reason to declare Him free of one than of the other. This contradicts both the revealed texts and reason.

Allah Most High has also said:

“Allah knows best where to place His message.”

In their view, the relation of a messenger’s commission to the messenger is like that of the divine address to actions: it entails no quality, either before or after that relation is established. The jurists and the majority of Muslims, however, say: Allah prohibited forbidden acts, so they became forbidden, and made obligatory acts obligatory, so they became obligatory. Thus, there are two things here: first, making something obligatory or forbidden, which is Allah’s speech and address; and second, its being obligatory or forbidden, which is a quality of the act.

Allah Most High is All-Knowing, All-Wise. He knows the benefits that the rulings entail, and He commands and forbids with knowledge of the benefits and harms for His servants in commanding and forbidding, and in what is commanded and prohibited. He has established the ruling governing the act; its quality, however, may exist independently of the divine address, or may be established through it. The wisdom embodied in revealed laws is of three kinds:

(The first: An act may entail benefit or harm even if no revealed law has addressed it, just as it is known that justice serves the welfare of the world, whereas injustice

---

## Page 4150

brings about their ruin. Acts in this category are good or bad, and their badness may be known through reason and revelation; revelation does not confer on the act a quality it did not previously possess. Yet an act’s being bad does not necessarily mean that its perpetrator will be punished in the Hereafter if no revealed law has addressed it. This is where the extremists among those who affirm that moral goodness and badness can be known through reason have erred. They maintain that people will be punished for their evil deeds even if Allah has sent them no messenger. This contradicts the revealed text. Allah Most High says:

“We never punish until We have sent a messenger.”

And He says:

“Messengers bearing good tidings and warnings, so that people would have no argument against Allah after the messengers.”

And He says:

“Your Lord would never destroy towns until He had sent to their principal town a messenger reciting Our revelations to them. Nor would We destroy towns unless their people were wrongdoers.”

And He says:

“Whenever a group is cast into it, its keepers will ask them, ‘Did no warner come to you?’”

“They will say, ‘Yes, a warner did come to us, but we denied him and said, “Allah has revealed nothing; you are only in grave error.”’”

“And they will say, ‘Had we listened or used our reason, we would not have been among the inhabitants of the Blazing Fire.’”

In the two Sahīh collections, it is reported that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“No one loves to accept excuses more than Allah; for that reason He sent the messengers as bearers of good tidings and warnings.”

The texts indicating that Allah does not punish until after sending a messenger are numerous. They refute those advocates of rational knowledge of moral goodness and badness who say that people on earth are punished without a messenger having been sent to them.

(The second:
When the Lawgiver commands something, it becomes good, and when He forbids

---

## Page 4151

something, it becomes bad; the act thus acquires the quality of goodness or badness through the Lawgiver’s address.

The third:
The Lawgiver may command something to test whether the servant will obey or disobey Him, without intending that the commanded act actually be carried out. Thus, He commanded Abraham to sacrifice his son. When they both submitted and he laid his son down upon his forehead, the purpose was achieved, so He ransomed him with a sacrifice. Likewise, there is “the account of a leper, a bald man, and a blind man: when Allah sent someone to ask them for charity and the blind man responded, the angel said, ‘Keep your wealth, for you were only being tested. He is pleased with you and displeased with your two companions.’”

The wisdom thus arises from the command itself, not from the commanded act. The Muʿtazilah did not understand this category or the preceding one. They maintained that goodness and badness can belong only to what possesses those qualities independently of the Lawgiver’s command. The Ashʿarīs claimed that the entire revealed law falls under the category of testing, and that acts possess no quality of goodness or badness, either before the revealed law or as a result of it. The wise and the majority, however, affirmed all three categories, and this is the correct position.

---

## Page 4152

Shaykh al-Islām Taqī al-Dīn Abū al-ʿAbbās Ibn Taymiyyah, may Allah Most High have mercy on him, was asked about the servant:

Is he able to obey Allah if he wills to do so? If he wills to refrain from sin, is he able to refrain from it? When he does good, is he to attribute it to Allah, and when he does evil, to himself?

He replied:

Praise be to Allah. Yes, if the servant resolutely wills to perform the obedience Allah has required of him, he is able to do so. Likewise, if he resolutely wills to refrain from the sin forbidden to him, he is able to do so. Muslims and the followers of all other religions agree on this—even the leading Jabriyyah (determinists). Indeed, this is necessarily known to be part of the religion of Islam. It is disputed only by some extreme “Jabriyyah,” who maintain that the revealed law commands what is intrinsically impossible. They cite as evidence Allah’s command to Abū Lahab to believe in that which entails that he will not believe.

This position contradicts the consensus of the leading scholars of Islam, including the four imams and others, the leading scholars of hadith, the masters of Sufism, and others. It also contradicts the consensus of the leading theologians, whether proponents of negation or affirmation.

The consensus of the Muʿtazilah and those like them on this is evident. The same is true of the leading proponents of affirmation among the theologians:

---

## Page 4153

such as Abū Muhammad ibn Kullāb, Abū al-ʿAbbās al-Qalānisī, Abū al-Hasan al-Ashʿarī, Judge Abū Bakr al-Bāqillānī, Abū Bakr ibn Fūrak, Abū Ishāq al-Isfarāyīnī, the master Abū al-Maʿālī al-Juwaynī, and Abū Hāmid al-Ghazālī; likewise, Abū ʿAbd Allāh Muhammad ibn Karrām and his followers, such as Ibn al-Haysam, and the other theologians among the followers of Abū Hanīfah, such as Abū Mansūr al-Māturīdī and others. All these scholars and those like them agree on this. More than one scholar, including Abū al-Hasan ibn al-Zāghūnī, has reported the Muslims’ consensus on it. Only some among them disputed this, and Abū ʿAbd Allāh al-Rāzī followed them.

Their appeal to the account of Abū Lahab is an invalid argument. Allah commanded Abū Lahab to believe before the surah was revealed. When he persisted in his defiance, he deserved the threatened punishment, just as Noah’s people did when Noah was told:

“None of your people will believe except those who have already believed.”

Once he deserved the threatened punishment, Allah announced the punishment that would befall him. At that point, he was not under a command requiring him to believe.

The revealed law abounds with evidence that commanded acts are conditional upon ability and capacity. Thus the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said to ʿImrān ibn Husayn:

“Pray standing; if you cannot, then sitting; and if you cannot, then lying on your side.”

The Muslims agree that when someone praying is unable to fulfil some of the prayer’s obligations—such as standing, reciting, bowing, prostrating, covering the parts of the body that must be covered, facing the qiblah, or anything else—the obligations he is unable to fulfil are waived. He is obliged only to do what he would be able to do if he resolutely willed to do it. Likewise, they agree that inability to fast removes its obligation from people such as

---

## Page 4154

elderly men and women who cannot fast either at the prescribed time or later to make up missed days. They differed only over whether such people must compensate by feeding the needy. The majority, including Abū Hanīfah, al-Shāfi‘ī, and Ahmad, required this, whereas Mālik did not.

Likewise, they unanimously agree that Hajj is not obligatory for someone unable to perform it. Allah Most High says:

“Pilgrimage to the House is a duty owed to Allah by those who are able to undertake it.”

They differed, however, over whether this ability consists simply in possessing financial means, as held by al-Shāfi‘ī and Ahmad; or in being able to undertake it, even through physical ability alone, as held by Mālik; or whether both are necessary, as held by Abū Hanīfah. The former require a person prevented from performing Hajj (al-maghsūb) to appoint a proxy at his own expense, unlike the others.

Furthermore, it should be understood that, regarding the ability stipulated as a condition for commands and prohibitions, the Lawgiver does not consider mere capacity sufficient if exercising it entails harm. Rather, in many instances under the revealed law, someone who can perform an act only at the cost of suffering harm is treated as someone unable to perform it. Examples include purification with water, fasting during illness, standing in prayer, and other matters. This gives effect to the words of Allah Most High:

“Allah intends ease for you and does not intend hardship for you.”

And His words:

“He has placed no hardship upon you in religion.”

And His words:

“Allah does not intend to impose hardship upon you.”

In the Sahīh, Anas reports that when the Bedouin urinated in the mosque, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Do not interrupt him”—that is, do not interrupt his urination—“for you have been sent to make things easy, not to make them difficult.”

It is likewise reported in the Sahīh that when the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, sent Mu‘ādh and Abū Mūsā to Yemen, he told them:

“Make things easy, and do not

## Page 4155

make things difficult; give glad tidings, and do not drive people away. Be accommodating toward one another, and do not disagree.” Examples of this in the revealed law are too numerous to count.

Whoever claims that Allah has commanded His servants to do things they cannot do even when they firmly resolve to do them has lied about Allah and His Messenger. He is among the fabricators of whom Allah says:

“Indeed, those who took the calf for worship will incur wrath from their Lord and humiliation in the life of this world. Thus do We recompense the fabricators.”

Abū Qilābah said: “This applies to every fabricator in this community until the Day of Resurrection.”

Yet, while affirming this, you must also know that there is no power or strength except through Allah; that whatever Allah wills comes to pass, and whatever He does not will does not come to pass; and that Allah is the Creator of all things. He created His servants, their ability, their will, and their actions. He is the Lord and Sovereign of all things. Nothing occurs except by His will, permission, decree, predestination, power, and action. Will is mentioned in the Book of Allah in two senses:

The first is His religious will, as Allah Most High says:

“Allah intends ease for you and does not intend hardship for you.”

“Allah wishes to make things clear to you, guide you to the ways of those before you, and accept your repentance”—through to His words—“And Allah wishes to accept your repentance.”

Allah Most High also says:

“Allah does not intend to impose hardship upon you, but He intends to purify you and complete His favour upon you, so that you may be grateful.”

The second is His universal will, as Allah Most High says: “Whomever Allah wills to guide

## Page 4156

He opens his breast to Islam; and whomever He wills to lead astray, He makes his breast tight and constricted, as though he were climbing into the sky.” Allah Most High also says:

“Had Allah willed, they would not have fought one another, but Allah does whatever He wills.”

Noah said:

“My advice will not benefit you, even if I wish to advise you, if Allah wills to lead you astray.”

And He says:

“His command, when He wills something, is only to say to it, ‘Be,’ and it is.”

This is a valuable distinction. It also occurs in the Book of Allah regarding permission, command, words, prohibition, judgment, and decree, as we have explained elsewhere. Understanding it dispels serious misconceptions.

Among the sources of confusion and error is the disagreement over “ability”: must it accompany the act, or must it precede it?

The precise position upheld by the leading jurists is that the capacity stipulated as a condition for commands and prohibitions—the capacity discussed earlier—need not accompany the act. Allah has made Hajj obligatory only upon those capable of performing it. Any such person who fails to perform Hajj is sinful, by the agreement of the Muslims, yet in his case there has been no capacity accompanying the act. Likewise, everyone who disobeys Allah while subject to His commands and prohibitions possesses the capacity stipulated as a condition for those commands and prohibitions.

Capacity accompanying the act, however, exists only in someone who actually performs it. The person acting must resolutely will the act and be capable of it. When both are present, the act necessarily occurs.

For anyone who says that capacity is that which accompanies the act, it is the sum of what one desires of the act, including the will and other things. According to this terminology, it is said: if a person does not will the act, he is not

---

## Page 4157

capable of it.

It is now clear that a dispute of this kind is merely verbal. Whoever understands inability in this sense has made his meaning clear. If the matter is examined carefully and the question is asked, “Can a servant be incapable of doing what he has been commanded to do when he firmly wills to do it?” the truth becomes clear. Everyone can then see that when he wills to do what he has been commanded, he is not incapable of it, but capable. Whatever he remains incapable of doing even when he wills it, Allah has not charged him with doing, for Allah does not burden any soul beyond its capacity—that is, beyond what it can bear.

The servant must know that the good deeds he performs are due to Allah’s grace and mercy, and are among His blessings, as the people of Paradise say:

“Praise be to Allah, who guided us to this! We would never have been guided had Allah not guided us.”

Allah Most High says:

“But Allah has endeared faith to you and made it beautiful in your hearts, and has made disbelief, wickedness, and disobedience hateful to you. Those are the rightly guided.”

Allah Most High also says:

“What, then, of one whose breast Allah has opened to Islam, so that he follows a light from his Lord? Woe, then, to those whose hearts are hardened against the remembrance of Allah!”

And He says:

“Is one who was dead, whom We brought to life and gave a light by which to walk among people, like one who remains in darkness, unable to emerge from it?”

Allah Most High says:

“And thus We have revealed to you an inspiration by Our command. You did not know what the Scripture was, nor what faith was, but We made it a light by which We guide whom We will of Our servants.”

Likewise, he should attribute his evil deeds to himself, while knowing that Allah is the Creator of everything that exists: entities, attributes, movements, and states of rest. As Adam said:

“Our Lord, we have wronged ourselves. If You do not forgive us and have mercy upon us, we will surely be among the losers.”

Moses said:

“My Lord, I have wronged myself, so forgive me.”

And Allah’s intimate friend said: “And the One who, I hope, will

“We did not wrong them, but it was they who were the wrongdoers.”

“Their only cry when Our punishment came upon them was, ‘We were indeed wrongdoers.’”

There are many such passages in the Quran and Sunnah. In the authentic divine hadith narrated by Muslim and others from Abū Dharr, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, related that his Lord said:

“O My servants, I have forbidden injustice for Myself and have made it forbidden among you, so do not wrong one another.

“O My servants, if the first of you and the last of you, your humans and your jinn, gathered on a single plain and asked of Me, and I gave every one of them what he asked for, that would diminish My dominion no more than a needle dipped once into the sea diminishes it.

“O My servants, it is only your deeds that I record for you, then recompense you for in full. Whoever finds good, let him praise Allah; and whoever finds otherwise, let him blame no one but himself.”

This hadith makes clear that whoever finds good through righteous deeds should praise Allah, for He is the One who bestowed that blessing. But if he finds otherwise—either evil for which there is punishment, or futile activity

---

## Page 4159

that brings no benefit—let him blame no one but himself, for he is the one who has wronged himself. Everything that occurs does so by Allah’s power and will. Likewise, al-Bukhārī and others narrated from Shaddād ibn Aws that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“The foremost supplication for forgiveness is for the servant to say: ‘O Allah, You are my Lord; there is no deity except You. You created me, and I am Your servant. I remain faithful to Your covenant and promise as best I can. I seek refuge in You from the evil of what I have done. I acknowledge Your blessings upon me, and I confess my sin. So forgive me, for none forgives sins except You.’ Whoever says this in the morning with firm conviction and dies that day will enter Paradise; and whoever says it in the evening with firm conviction and dies that night will enter Paradise.”

His words, “I acknowledge Your blessings upon me,” encompass the blessing of good deeds and all other blessings. His words, “I confess my sin,” are an acknowledgment of his sin. This is the way of the believers.

Those other than them fall into three groups, making the division fourfold.

One group regard themselves as the creators and originators of good and evil deeds. They hold that Allah’s religious blessing upon the believer and the disbeliever is the same; that He has given the servant only a single capacity for either of two opposite acts; and that there is no guidance in Allah’s hand which He has bestowed specifically upon the believer, or which may be sought from Him through the servant’s words:

“Guide us to the straight path.”

They also hold that He has no power to guide someone who is astray or to lead someone who is guided astray. These are the Magian Qadariyyah.

And (another group strip the servant of his choice and capacity, and regard him as compelled in his movements

## Page 4160

like the movements of inanimate objects; they treat his voluntary and involuntary acts as being of the same kind, so much so that one of them says: “Everything Allah and His Messenger have commanded is something the servant has neither the power nor the capacity to do.” They thus strip him of capacity altogether, since they affirm for him only a single capacity concurrent with the act, and grant the sinner no capacity at all.

These and similar views are among “the doctrines of the determinist Qadariyyah,” whose position—like that of the first group—was rejected by the imams of guidance, such as Abd al-Rahmān ibn Amr al-Awzā‘ī, Sufyān ibn Sa‘īd al-Thawrī, Muhammad ibn al-Walīd al-Zubaydī, Abd al-Rahmān ibn Mahdī, Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Hanbal, and others.

If, in addition, they invoke divine decree to excuse sinners, claiming that they are thereby excused and deserve neither blame nor punishment, or regard their punishment as unjust, then they are disbelievers, just as anyone among the extreme Qadariyyah who denies Allah’s eternal knowledge is a disbeliever. If they hold that the reality of divine decree entails the abolition of commands and prohibitions, promises of reward and threats of punishment—as the antinomians do—then they are greater in disbelief than the Jews and Christians. They belong to the same category as the polytheists who said:

“‘Had Allah willed, neither we nor our forefathers would have associated partners with Him, nor would we have forbidden anything.’ Likewise, those before them denied the truth until they tasted Our punishment. For this position entails doing away with every command and prohibition

and it is self-evident, by both reason and religion, that this brings ruin to worldly affairs and the Hereafter.

As for (the fourth category:
it is the worst of all, as Shaykh Abū al-Faraj ibn al-Jawzī said: “When obeying, you champion free will; when sinning, you champion determinism. Whatever doctrine suits your desires, you adopt it.”

Such people are the worst of Satan’s followers. When such a person performs an act of obedience, he attributes it to himself and becomes so conceited that he nullifies his deed. When he commits a sin, he invokes divine decree as an excuse and appeals to divine ordainment. Yet this is a futile argument and an unacceptable excuse.

You see him refuse to submit to divine decree when a calamity befalls him through the actions of people or other causes. Yet when he wrongs himself or someone else, you see him invoke divine decree, saying: “The servant is helpless: neither capable nor excused.” He also says:

‘Beware, beware of getting wet!’”

But if someone else wrongs him to a lesser degree, or he merely imagines that someone has wronged him, he seeks revenge many times greater than the wrong. He will not excuse another person on the grounds of divine decree, although he used it to excuse himself, even though their situations are the same.

These principles, then, must be believed. As for discussing the reality that necessitates attributing sins to the servant, despite the all-encompassing nature of Allah’s creation

He replied:

All praise belongs to Allah, Lord of all worlds. The foundation of “this question” is to understand that the position of Ahl al-Sunnah wa-l-Jamā'ah—the people of the Sunnah and the united community—on this subject and others is what the Quran and Sunnah indicate, and what was upheld by the foremost pioneers among the Emigrants and the Helpers, and those who followed them in righteousness. It is that Allah is the Creator, Lord and Sovereign of all things. This encompasses all entities that subsist in themselves and the attributes inherent in them, including the deeds of His servants and everything else. Whatever He—glory be to Him—wills comes to pass, and whatever He does not will does not come to pass. Nothing, therefore, comes into existence except through His will and power. Nothing He wills is beyond Him; rather, He has power over all things, and He never wills anything without having the power to accomplish it.

He—glory be to Him—knows what has happened, what will happen, and how what has not happened would happen if it did. This includes the deeds of His servants and everything else. Allah ordained the destinies of created beings before creating them: He decreed their lifespans, their provisions and their deeds, and recorded all of this. He also recorded their ultimate outcome, whether bliss or wretchedness. Thus, they believe in His creation of all things

---

## Page 4165

and His power over all things, His willing of everything that comes to pass, His knowledge of things before they exist, and His decreeing and recording them before they exist.

The extreme Qadariyyah deny His prior knowledge and His prior recording. They claim that He commands and forbids without knowing who will obey Him and who will disobey Him; rather, events arise afresh—that is, without prior decree. This view first arose within Islam after the era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs and after the rule of Mu‘āwiyah ibn Abī Sufyān, during the conflict between Ibn al-Zubayr and the Umayyads, towards the end of the lives of ‘Abd Allāh ibn ‘Umar, ‘Abd Allāh ibn ‘Abbās and other Companions. The first person known to have openly expressed it in Basra was Ma‘bad al-Juhanī.

When the Companions learned of these people’s views, they disavowed them and rejected their doctrine. Thus, when ‘Abd Allāh ibn ‘Umar was told about them, he said: “When you meet those people, tell them that I disavow them and they disavow me.” There are likewise many statements concerning them from Ibn ‘Abbās, Jābir ibn ‘Abd Allāh, Wāthilah ibn al-Asqa‘, other Companions, those who followed them in righteousness, and the other leading scholars of the Muslims. Indeed, leading scholars such as Mālik, al-Shāfi‘ī, Ahmad ibn Hanbal and others declared that those who deny Allah’s prior knowledge are disbelievers.

Discussion of divine decree then became widespread, and most of them came to acknowledge prior knowledge and prior recording, while denying the all-encompassing scope of Allah’s will, creation and power. They supposed that His will meant nothing other than His command: whatever He wills, He has commanded, and whatever He does not will, He has not commanded. This committed them to saying that He may will what does not happen, and that what He does not will may happen. They also denied

---

## Page 4166

that Allah Most High is the Creator of His servants’ actions or has power over them, or that He singles out some of His servants for blessings that bring about their faith in Him and obedience to Him. They claimed that His blessing—which makes faith and righteous deeds possible—is the same for disbelievers such as Abū Lahab and Abū Jahl as it is for Abū Bakr, ‘Umar, ‘Uthmān and ‘Alī. They likened this to a man giving his children money and dividing it equally among them: one group then originated their own righteous deeds, while the other originated their own corrupt deeds, without Allah having singled out the believers for any special blessing. This is a false view.

Allah Most High has said:

Allah has commanded us to say in our prayers:

The people of Paradise will say:

Allah’s intimate friend, may Allah’s blessings and peace be upon him, said:

He also said:

And He has said:

The texts of the Quran and Sunnah and the statements of the early generations of the Muslim community that explain these

## Page 4167

principles are numerous, in addition to the many rational proofs supporting them.

Section

The early generations of the Muslim community and its leading scholars also agree that Allah’s servants are commanded to do what He has commanded them and forbidden to do what He has prohibited. They agree that His promise and warning, as expressed in the Quran and Sunnah, must be believed. They also agree that no one has any argument against Allah for neglecting an obligation or committing a forbidden act. Rather, Allah has the conclusive argument against His servants.

Whoever invokes divine decree to justify neglecting a command, committing a forbidden act, or rejecting what the revealed texts convey concerning promise and warning is further astray, more guilty of fabricating lies about Allah, and more opposed to Allah’s religion than those Qadariyyah. For those Qadariyyah are likened to the Magians, and reports describe them as the Magians of this Muslim community, as related from Ibn ‘Umar and others among the early generations. Hadiths to this effect have also been reported as traced back to the Prophet, may Allah’s blessings and peace be upon him, including reports narrated by Abū Dāwūd and al-Tirmidhī. However, a number of leading hadith scholars have challenged the authenticity of the reports traced back to the Prophet on this subject. This is discussed at length in its proper place.

The point here is that the Qadariyyah who deny divine decree resemble the Magians in affirming that someone other than Allah brings evil things into being independently of His will, power and creation.

---

## Page 4168

As for those who invoke divine decree to set aside commands, prohibitions, promise and warning, they resemble the polytheists of whom Allah said:

“Those who associate partners with Allah will say, ‘Had Allah willed, neither we nor our forefathers would have associated partners with Him, nor would we have forbidden anything.’ Likewise, those before them denied the truth until they tasted Our punishment. Say, ‘Do you have any knowledge that you can produce for us? You follow nothing but conjecture, and you do nothing but guess.’”

Allah Most High also said:

“Those who associate partners with Allah said, ‘Had Allah willed, neither we nor our forefathers would have worshipped anything besides Him, nor would we have forbidden anything without His authority.’ Those before them did likewise. Are the messengers responsible for anything other than conveying the message clearly?”

Allah Most High also said:

“When they are told, ‘Spend from what Allah has provided for you,’ the disbelievers say to the believers, ‘Should we feed those whom Allah could have fed, had He willed? You are plainly astray.’”

Allah Most High also said:

“They said, ‘Had the Most Merciful willed, we would not have worshipped them.’ They have no knowledge of that; they do nothing but guess.”

Those who invoke divine decree to set aside commands and prohibitions thus belong to the same category as the polytheists who rejected the messengers, and their condition is worse than that of the Magians. Their argument is invalid before their Lord; His wrath is upon them, and theirs will be a severe punishment.

Some of them imagine that Adam invoked divine decree before Moses to justify his sin, and that this is permissible for the elect among Allah’s allies who witness divine decree. This is a grave error. Moses reproached Adam only for the act of disobedience that affected his descendants as a result of his eating from the tree. He said:

“Why did you cause us and yourself to be expelled from Paradise?”

When calamities occur, the servant is commanded to turn to divine decree, for the servant’s happiness lies in doing what is commanded, avoiding what is forbidden, and submitting to what has been decreed. Allah Most High said:

## Page 4169

“No calamity befalls except by Allah’s permission. And whoever believes in Allah, He guides his heart.”

Ibn Masʿūd said: “This is the man who suffers a calamity, knows that it is from Allah, and so is content and submits.”

The fortunate person seeks forgiveness for his faults and patiently endures calamities, as Allah Most High said:

The wretched person, however, despairs when calamities strike and invokes divine decree to excuse his faults.

After all, Adam—may Allah’s blessings and peace be upon him—had repented of his sin, and his Lord had chosen and guided him. Moses was far too noble to reproach anyone for a sin of which he had repented and which Allah had forgiven, let alone Adam. Moses himself had also repented of what he had done, saying:

He also said:

And he said:

“You are our Protector, so forgive us and have mercy on us.”

Moses and Adam knew Allah far too well for either of them to suppose that divine decree excuses anyone who disobeys Him. They knew what had befallen Iblīs and others. Adam himself had been expelled from Paradise, and he and his wife had begun stitching together leaves from Paradise to cover themselves. Allah had punished the peoples of Noah, Hūd, Sālih and other nations. Allah has also prescribed punishment for transgressors and prepared Hell for the disbelievers. How, then, could divine decree excuse sin?

These people invoke divine decree only when they are following their desires without knowledge, and they do not apply their argument consistently. If divine decree were an excuse for people, it would follow that no one should be blamed, censured or punished, either in this world or in the Hereafter, and that no wrongdoer should ever face retribution. Rather, people would be allowed to do absolutely whatever they pleased. It is well known that no one’s welfare, either in this world or in the Hereafter, could conceivably rest on such a basis. Rather, it necessarily leads to universal corruption. And the proponent of

## Page 4170

this view can only be unjust and inconsistent. When someone else harms or wrongs him, he demands that the offender be punished and repays him, refusing to excuse him on the grounds of divine decree. Yet when he himself is the wrongdoer, he invokes divine decree in his own defence. Thus, no one invokes divine decree as an excuse except to follow his desires without knowledge; he is invariably defending falsehood, with no truth on his side. The polytheists likewise invoked it, and Allah Most High said:

For this reason, when anyone showed hostility towards these polytheists who invoked divine decree, they would confront him, fight him and punish him. They would not accept his argument if he said, “Had Allah willed, I would not have shown hostility towards you.” Rather, they continually condemned those who committed injustice and aggression, refusing to accept their appeal to divine decree. Yet when the truth came to them from their Lord, they began invoking divine decree to resist it. Thus, they sought to reject Allah’s commands and prohibitions by an argument they would not allow anyone to use against their own commands and prohibitions. Indeed, no rational person would allow such an argument to be used to deny his rights.

They therefore opposed their Lord and His messengers with an argument they would not allow to be used against any human being or anyone’s messengers. According to their position, a created being’s commands, prohibitions and rights carried greater weight than Allah’s commands, prohibitions and rights over His servants. Allah’s commands, prohibitions and rights over His servants were less inviolable in their eyes than a created being’s commands, prohibitions and rights over others. For Allah’s right over His servants is that they worship Him and associate nothing with Him, as is established in the two Sahīh collections, on the authority of Mu‘ādh ibn Jabal, who said:

“I was riding behind the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, on a donkey. He said, ‘O Mu‘ādh, do you know what Allah’s right over His servants is?’ I said, ‘Allah and His Messenger know best.’ He said, ‘His right

These polytheists were therefore among the most ignorant of people and the most hostile towards Allah and His Messenger. They sought to nullify His right, commands and prohibitions by an argument that neither they nor any rational person would allow to be used to nullify a created being’s rights, commands or prohibitions.
