Thus, the polytheists’ argument for associating partners with Allah, attributing offspring to Him, and invoking divine decree to reject His commands and prohibitions is invalid. These matters and related issues have been discussed at length elsewhere.

It is clear that the doctrine of the philosophers—such as Aristotle and his followers, who maintain that the world is eternal, that it emanates from a cause acting by the necessity of its own essence, and that it is generated from intellects and souls, and who worship the heavenly bodies above and fashion images of them below—involves greater disbelief and misguidance than that of the Arab polytheists. The latter acknowledged that Allah created the heavens, the earth and everything between them in six days by His will and power, yet they falsely attributed sons and daughters to Him without knowledge and associated with Him partners for which He had sent down no authority.

Likewise, the antinomians who dispense entirely with commands and prohibitions and invoke divine decree and predestination as their justification are worse than the Jews, Christians and Arab polytheists. Despite their disbelief, these groups acknowledge some form of commands and prohibitions, promises of reward and threats of punishment. Yet they had partners who prescribed for them a religion that Allah had not authorized.

By contrast, the antinomians who discard all religious laws are pleased only with what their own souls desire, and become angry only for the sake of what their own souls desire. They are not pleased for Allah’s sake, nor angry for Allah’s sake; they do not love for Allah’s sake, nor are they angry for Allah’s sake. They do not enjoin what Allah has commanded, nor do they

---

## Page 4173

forbid what He has forbidden, unless doing so serves their desires. They then act for the sake of those desires, not in worship of their Lord. Thus, they do not denounce the disbelief, wickedness and disobedience that occur in the world unless these conflict with their own aims. Their denunciation is then instinctive and satanic, not grounded in divine law and obedience to the Most Merciful. Consequently, their brethren, the devils, attach themselves to them and draw them further into error, never relenting. The devils may also appear to them in visible forms, speak to them and help them fulfil some of their desires, just as they used to do with the polytheists who worshipped idols.

Such people are numerous among groups that depart from the Book and Sunnah with which Allah sent His Messenger. They follow paths of worship and belief that are innovations in religion, without striving to conform to the Messenger or adhere firmly to the Book and Sunnah in their worship and beliefs. Consequently, desires and specious doubts proliferate among them, and the devils lead them astray. They come to resemble the polytheists in proportion to their distance from the Messenger. Just as the doctrine of the Qadariyyah, who resemble the Magians, must be rejected, rejecting the doctrine of these people is even more necessary, and refuting them still more warranted.

These people did not exist in the time of the Companions and those who followed them in righteousness. Religious innovations emerge successively, with the less serious appearing first. Thus, the innovations of the Khawārij and the Shīʿah arose towards the end of the era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs; then the innovations of the Murjiʾah and the Qadariyyah arose towards the end of the era of the Companions; then the innovation of the Jahmiyyah, who deny the divine attributes, arose towards the end of the era of the Successors. As for these antinomians, who discard commands and prohibitions and invoke divine decree to justify doing so, they are worse than all these groups, and emerged only after all of them.

---

## Page 4174

Section

Among the matters upon which the early generations of the Muslim community and its imams agreed is that people have a will and an ability, by which they do whatever Allah has enabled them to do. They affirmed this alongside their belief in divine decree and predestination: that Allah is the Creator of all things; that whatever He wills comes to pass, and whatever He does not will does not; and that He leads astray whom He wills and guides whom He wills. They also affirmed that people cannot will unless Allah wills.

As Allah Most High says:

“No! Indeed, it is a reminder. So whoever wills may heed it. But they will not heed it unless Allah wills”—to the end of the verse.

And He Most High says:

“Indeed, this is a reminder, so whoever wills may take a path to his Lord. But you cannot will unless Allah wills. Indeed, Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise.”

And He says:

“It is only a reminder to the worlds, for whoever among you wills to take a straight path. But you cannot will unless Allah, Lord of the worlds, wills.”

The Quran states that people believe and disbelieve, act, work, earn, obey and disobey, establish prayer, give zakah, perform Hajj and ʿumrah (the lesser pilgrimage), kill, commit unlawful sexual intercourse, steal, speak truthfully and lie, eat and drink, fight and wage war. None of the early generations or the imams said that a person neither acts nor chooses, nor has any will or ability. Nor did any of them say that he acts

---

## Page 4175

figuratively. Rather, those among them who used the terms “literal” and “figurative” agreed that a person truly acts, and that Allah Most High is the Creator of his very being, his attributes, and his actions.

The first known denial of this came from al-Jahm ibn Safwān and his followers. They are reported to have said that a person is compelled, has no action of his own at all, and has no ability whatsoever. Al-Jahm was extreme in his denial of the divine attributes: he denied that Allah Most High could be called by any name also applied to a person. Thus, He could not be called a thing, or described as living, knowing, hearing, or seeing, except figuratively. It is reported, however, that he called Allah Most High “Powerful,” because, in his view, a person has no power; thus, according to his position, this name involved no likening of Allah to a person.

He and his followers denied that Allah has wisdom in His creation and His commands, or that He has mercy. They said: “He acted solely by sheer will, unaccompanied by mercy.” It is reported that he denied that Allah is the Most Merciful of all who show mercy, and that he would go out to people afflicted with leprosy, look at them, and say: “Would the Most Merciful of all who show mercy do this to these people?” He would also say: “People are compelled to perform their actions; they have neither action nor choice.”

Al-Jahm and his doctrines concerning the denial of the divine attributes, compulsion, and irjā’ emerged toward the end of Umayyad rule, after the emergence of the Qadariyyah, the Mu'tazilah, and others. The Qadariyyah had appeared earlier, toward the end of the era of the Companions. When his doctrine emerged in opposition to that of the Qadariyyah, the early generations and the imams rejected it, just as they rejected the position of the Qadariyyah among the Mu'tazilah and others

---

## Page 4176

and declared both groups to be innovators. Even regarding the term “compulsion,” they objected both to those who said, “Allah compelled,” and to those who said, “Allah did not compel.” Reports to this effect are well known from al-Awzā‘ī, Sufyān al-Thawrī, ‘Abd al-Rahmān ibn Mahdī, Ahmad ibn Hanbal, and other early authorities and imams of this community. Abū Bakr al-Khallāl recorded some of these in his Book of the Sunnah, as did others who compiled the statements of the early generations.

Al-Awzā‘ī, al-Zubaydī, and others said that the word jabara (to compel) does not occur in the Quran or Sunnah; rather, the word found in the Sunnah is jabala (to endow with an innate disposition). This occurs in the authentic report in which the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, addressed al-Ashajj of ‘Abd al-Qays when the delegation of ‘Abd al-Qays came to him from Bahrain. They said:

“O Messenger of Allah, between us and you stands this tribe of the unbelievers of Mudar, and we can reach you only during a sacred month. Give us a clear, decisive instruction that we may act upon and enjoin upon those we have left behind.”

He said:

“I command you to believe in Allah. Do you know what faith is? To testify that none has the right to be worshipped except Allah and that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah, to establish prayer, to give zakat, and to pay one-fifth of whatever spoils you acquire.”

He also forbade them to prepare infused drinks in vessels in which the drink quickly becomes intoxicating. A man might even drink without realizing that he had drunk an intoxicant. This is unlike containers whose mouths are tied shut, which split open when the drink becomes strong. He prohibited al-dubbā’, meaning gourds; al-hantam, meaning earthenware vessels such as jars; al-muzaffat, meaning pitch-coated vessels; and al-naqīr, meaning hollowed-out wood.

It has been said, however, that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, subsequently permitted this after having prohibited it. Hence scholars differed over whether this prohibition was abrogated, holding two views

---

## Page 4177

well known among scholars, both of which are reported from Ahmad. The view that the prohibition was abrogated is the position of Abū Hanīfa and al-Shāfi‘ī, while the view that it was not abrogated is Mālik’s position. Mālik, however, prohibits only two types of vessels, for it is established in Sahīh al-Bukhārī that the Prophet prohibited those two types and permitted the other two after the earlier prohibition. Muslim, by contrast, narrated in his Sahīh that the prohibition was abrogated for all of them. This explains the differing positions reported from Ahmad: the hadiths conveying the prohibition are mass-transmitted, whereas the hadith conveying its abrogation is not of the same standing. Thus, people came to hold three views on the matter.

These men—the delegation of ‘Abd al-Qays—lived in Bahrain and embraced Islam willingly, as did the people of Medina. The first Friday prayer held in Islam took place in one of their villages in Bahrain.

The point is that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said to al-Ashajj of ‘Abd al-Qays:

“You possess two qualities that Allah loves: forbearance and deliberateness.”

He asked, “Are these two qualities that I acquired, or two qualities with which I was innately endowed?”

He replied, “Rather, they are two qualities with which you were innately endowed.”

He said, “Praise be to Allah, who endowed me with qualities that He loves.”

Al-Awzā‘ī, al-Zubaydī, and other early authorities therefore said that the term “jabl” (endowing with an innate disposition) occurs in the Sunnah, so one may say that Allah endowed someone with such-and-such an innate disposition. The term “jabr” (compulsion), however, does not occur. Al-Awzā‘ī, al-Zubaydī, al-Thawrī, Ahmad ibn Hanbal, and others objected to using the term “compulsion,” whether to deny or affirm it. This is because the term “compulsion” is ambiguous: one may say, “A father compelled his daughter to marry”

---

## Page 4178

and “A judge compelled a man to sell his property to pay his debt.” This means that he coerced him, not that he made him desire it, choose it, love it, or be content with it.

They said:

Whoever says that Allah Most High compels His servants in this sense is mistaken. Allah is far too exalted and majestic to compel anyone. Only someone unable to make another person desire an action, choose it, love it, and be content with it resorts to compelling him. Allah, glorified be He, is capable of doing so. He is the One who makes a person who desires an action, loves it, and is content with it have that desire, love, and contentment. How, then, can He be said to compel and coerce him as one created being compels another—as a ruler, judge, father, or anyone else compels those under his authority, whether rightfully or wrongfully? Their compelling others consists in coercing them to act, and coercion may be either rightful or wrongful.

(The former includes coercing those who refuse to fulfil their obligations into fulfilling them: for example, coercing a non-Muslim of harbī status to embrace Islam or pay the jizya in submission, being humbled; coercing an apostate to return to Islam; and coercing someone who has embraced Islam to establish prayer, give zakat, fast Ramadan, and perform pilgrimage to the House, as well as to repay debts he can afford to repay, return what has been entrusted to him when he is able to do so, and provide the maintenance incumbent upon him when he can afford it.

As for wrongful coercion, examples include coercing someone into disbelief or sinful acts. This compulsion, which is coercion, is something people exercise over one another because they cannot bring about willing and choosing in others’ hearts or make them agents

---

## Page 4179

of their own actions. Allah Most High is capable of bringing about a servant’s willing and choosing, and making him act through his own ability and will. He is too exalted and powerful to compel or coerce another into doing something He wishes him to do.

Rather, when He wills, He makes that person perform it of his own will. He is also capable of making him do something despite his aversion to it, so that he wills to do it and carries it out despite disliking it—just as a sick person may drink medicine despite disliking it. Allah Most High says:

“To Allah prostrates whoever is in the heavens and the earth, willingly or unwillingly.”

And He says:

“To Him has submitted whoever is in the heavens and the earth, willingly or unwillingly.”

Thus, whatever people do through their own will and choice, He is the One who makes them do it through their own will, whether they do it willingly or dislike it and do it reluctantly. He, glorified be He, does not coerce them into doing what they do not will, as one created being coerces another: he coerces him into something even though the other does not will it, yet he cannot make him will it and do it, whether with or without aversion.

This is why a servant may be said to have compelled another to act, whereas Allah is too exalted, majestic, and powerful to be described as compelling in this sense.

The word “compulsion” may also be used more broadly, encompassing anyone who overpowers another and has mastery over him, making him do what he wishes him to do—even if he himself brings about the other’s will and ability to do it. Concerning Allah’s name “al-Jabbār (the Compeller),” Muhammad ibn Kaʿb al-Qurazī said: “He is the One who compels

---

## Page 4180

His servants to do what He wills.” Similarly, it is reported that the Commander of the Faithful, ʿAlī ibn Abī Tālib, said in a transmitted supplication:

“O Allah, Spreader of all that is spread out, Creator of all that is raised aloft, Compeller of hearts according to their innate nature, the wretched and the blessed alike.”

Compulsion by Allah, understood in this sense, means mastery and power: He is able to do whatever He wills, compelling them to it and subduing them to it. He is not like a powerless created being who wills things that do not happen, while things happen that he does not will. His compulsion, mastery, and power include making His servants will what He wishes of them—whether they choose it willingly or will it despite disliking it—and making them carry it out.

This compulsion, which is His subduing through His power, is something none but He can exercise. It differs from the compulsion and coercion exercised by others in several respects.

One is that those besides Him lack the power to make His servants will what they want them to do or carry it out.

Another is that someone other than Him may compel and coerce another unjustly, whereas Allah Most High is just and does not wrong anyone by even an atom’s weight.

Another is that someone other than Him may be ignorant or foolish, not knowing what he does or what he is compelled to do, nor aiming at any wise purpose beyond that. Allah, however, is All-Knowing, All-Wise. In everything He has created and commanded, He has a profound wisdom arising from His knowledge, wisdom, and power.

---

## Page 4181

Section

Just as the early generations and leading scholars agree on belief in divine decree—that whatever Allah wills happens, whatever He does not will does not happen, and that He is the Creator of everything, including His servants’ deeds—and agree on affirming His commands and prohibitions, His promises and warnings, and that no one has any argument against Allah to justify neglecting a command or committing a forbidden act, they also agree that Allah is All-Wise, Most Merciful, the wisest of judges and the most merciful of those who show mercy.

It is authentically reported that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Allah is more merciful to His servants than a mother is to her child.”

Allah has made known His wisdom in His creation and commands through what He has revealed in His Book and the Sunnah of His Messenger.

Al-Jahm ibn Safwān and his followers deny His wisdom and mercy, saying: “The purposive ‘in order to’ does not apply to His acts or commands: He does nothing for a purpose and commands nothing for a purpose.” Many later speculative theologians who affirm divine decree, along with those who agree with them, have followed Jahm’s approach on many questions in this area, although they differed with him on some of

---

## Page 4182

those matters—whether their disagreement was merely verbal, unintelligible, or substantive. An example is the claim that the servant acquires his acts but does not truly perform them. Those who make this claim hold that acquisition is within the servant’s power, yet affirm for him a power that has no effect on the act within its scope. Hence, most rational thinkers have said: “This is contradictory and unintelligible speech. If power has no effect whatsoever on the act, its existence is no different from its absence, and it is not power at all. Rather, it merely accompanies the act, just as the agent’s other attributes—his height, breadth, and color—do.”

When these people were asked, “What is acquisition?” they replied: “It is what occurs in the agent and over which he has a created power, or what occurs in the locus of created power.” When asked, “What is power?” they replied: “That by which the movement of someone trembling is distinguished from the movement of someone acting by choice.”

Most rational thinkers therefore said to them: “The movement of someone acting by choice occurs through his will, unlike the movement of someone trembling; it also occurs through his power. If you make will alone the distinction, a person may will someone else’s act without performing it himself. If you mean that he has the power to perform it, then the question returns to the meaning of power. Power, as intelligibly understood, is an attribute by which an agent acts. No power can be affirmed for one who does not act, nor can there be a power whose existence or absence makes no difference to the agent.”

These followers of Jahm say that the servant does not truly perform his acts; rather, he truly acquires them. Alongside acquisition, they affirm a power that has no effect on it: its existence or absence makes no difference to acquisition, but it has been conjoined with it without having any effect on it. They further claimed that all the forces, natural properties, and higher and lower causes that exist

---

## Page 4183

are like the servant’s power: none has any effect on the events, acts, or effects with which it is associated. Rather, the Creator has conjoined one with another without any cause or wise purpose whatsoever.

They also said that obedience and disobedience stand in the same relation to reward and punishment: there is nothing in obedience that makes reward fitting, nor anything in disobedience that makes punishment fitting. Nor was there any wisdom in commands and prohibitions for the sake of which He commanded and prohibited. In sending the messengers, He did not intend mercy toward His servants or their welfare. Rather, He intended to grant bliss to one group and punish another, without any wise purpose. The means to this is His making commands and prohibitions, obedience and disobedience, signs of that outcome, without any cause or wise purpose. They also hold that He may command anything—even associating partners with Him, rejecting the messengers, injustice, and indecencies—and forbid anything—even worshipping Him alone, believing in the messengers, and obeying them.

Many of these, such as Abū al-Hasan and his followers, together with those later followers of Mālik, al-Shāfiʿī, and Ahmad who agreed with them—such as Ibn ʿAqīl, Ibn al-Jawzī, and others like them—say that the act of creation is the created thing, and that an act is the thing produced by it. They have made the servants’ acts acts of Allah, while an act, according to them, is the thing produced by it. On this basis, it cannot also be an act of the servant, lest a single act have two agents.

The majority, however, say that these acts are created and produced by Allah, while being acts of the servant that subsist in him. They are not acts of Allah subsisting in Him; rather, what He produces is distinct from His act. And the Lord

---

## Page 4184

Most High is not described by what He has created, but only by what subsists in Him. Thus, their position does not entail that the Lord is unjust. As for the others, when they say that He is described by created things distinct from Him, and is called just and Creator because of the existence of something distinct from Him that He created, they are held to the implication that He is unjust because He creates injustice distinct from Himself. For, among things distinct from Him, they do not distinguish between what is an attribute and act of another and what is not: according to them, all stand in the same relation to His power, will, and creation.

These people also affirmed without qualification that obligations beyond one’s ability may be imposed. Yet none of the early generations or the imams affirmed this without qualification, just as none of them affirmed compulsion without qualification. To say without qualification that He compels His servants is like saying without qualification that He imposes on them obligations beyond their ability. The latter denies their ability to do what they have been commanded, while the former denies that they are agents endowed with ability.

For this reason, the more moderate among them—such as Judge Abū Bakr ibn al-Bāqillānī and most of Abū al-Hasan’s followers, as well as the majority of the followers of Mālik, al-Shāfiʿī, and Ahmad ibn Hanbal, including Judge Abū Yaʿlā and others like him—make distinctions concerning the imposition of obligations beyond one’s ability, just as distinctions concerning compulsion were discussed earlier.

They say: imposing an obligation that is beyond the servant’s ability because he is incapable of it is not permissible. As for something said to be beyond his ability because he is occupied with its opposite, imposing it is permissible. This is because a person cannot be standing and sitting at the same time. While standing, he cannot also sit; yet he may be commanded to stand while sitting.

---

## Page 4185

and Muslims agree that this is permissible. Indeed, most commands and prohibitions are of this kind. But whether this is called imposing obligations beyond one’s ability is disputed.

It is said that a servant has the ability to act only when actually acting, and that ability exists only together with the act. This is the position of Abū al-Hasan al-Asharī and many speculative theologians who affirm divine decree. According to their position, everyone charged with an obligation is, at the time it is imposed, charged with something beyond his ability at that moment, although he may be able to perform it when he acts, through an ability that Allah creates for him at that time. His inability here, however, is due to his being occupied with the opposite action and lacking the ability that accompanies the act, not to his being incapacitated.

As for those who are incapacitated—the disabled person who cannot walk, the blind person who cannot see, and others like them—they have not been charged with what they are incapable of doing. All Muslim groups agree that obligations of this kind have not been imposed in the revealed Law, apart from a small handful of later scholars who claimed that such obligations do occur in it. They attributed this position to al-Asharī and most of his followers, but this is a mistaken attribution.

As for the rational permissibility of imposing such obligations, most of the Muslim community denied it without qualification. A group of those who affirm divine decree, comprising followers of Abū al-Hasan al-Asharī and those who agreed with them among the followers of Mālik, al-Shāfiī, and Ahmad—such as Ibn Aqīl, Ibn al-Jawzī, and others—held it to be rationally permissible.

A “third group” distinguished, with regard to rational permissibility, between what is possible in itself, which

---

## Page 4186

can conceivably exist in external reality, such as flight, and what is rationally impossible, such as combining two contradictories.

Those who claimed that obligations involving the intrinsically impossible have actually been imposed—such as al-Rāzī and others—argued that Allah charged Abū Lahab with believing, despite knowing and declaring that he would not believe. Thus, they argued, He required him to combine two contradictories: to perform the act and to affirm that he would not affirm it; his affirmation would be truthful if he did not affirm it. They also argued that he was charged with doing the contrary of what was known, and that the contrary of what was known is impossible. The obligation would therefore amount to requiring him to turn Allah’s knowledge into ignorance, which is intrinsically impossible.

These people treated the expression “beyond one’s ability” as a general term encompassing every act, since, according to them, ability exists only together with the act. They also included under it the contrary of what is known, what one is incapacitated from doing, and what is intrinsically impossible. They then presented some “ten arguments” to establish the permissibility of imposing obligations of this kind.

Once the matter is explained to them with these distinctions, however, it becomes clear that their claim that it is permissible to impose obligations that cannot be fulfilled owing to incapacity—whether the act is intrinsically impossible or possible—is false and unsupported by any evidence. As for the permissibility of charging a servant with acts of worship that he is able to perform—although they themselves say that he is able to perform them only when actually acting—everyone agrees that imposing such obligations is permissible. There is, however, both a terminological and a substantive dispute over whether this falls under what is “beyond one’s ability.”

Thus, what they have included under this designation comprises different categories: some involve disagreement over their permissibility or occurrence, and (others involve disagreement over their designation and characterization, not their occurrence.

---

## Page 4187

As for Abū Lahab and others being charged with believing, this is indeed true. If he is commanded to affirm everything the Messenger says, while it is also declared that he will not affirm him but will die a disbeliever, there is no contradiction in this, nor is he commanded to combine two contradictories. He is commanded to affirm everything the Messenger conveys, but this affirmation will not come from him. If he is told, “We have commanded you to do something, and we know that you will not do it,” this does not amount to requiring him to combine two contradictories.

If he says, “Affirming everything you say entails that I become a believer if I affirm you. Yet if I affirm you, I will not be a believer, because you have declared that I will not believe everything I am told,” he is answered:

“Had you affirmed us, this report would not have been included, nor would it have been reported that you would not believe. You are capable of affirming us, and, supposing that you did so, this report would not be made. It was made only because you yourself did not do what you were capable of doing—affirming us regarding this report. Thus, it came after your rejection and your failure to do what you had been capable of doing. We did not say this to you when we commanded you to affirm everything, which you were capable of doing.

“Even if you were told, ‘Believe, though we know that you will not believe this report,’ what you were commanded to believe is the declaration that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah. This you are capable of doing, but you do not do it. If you affirm our report that you will not believe, there is no contradiction here. It is, however, impossible to combine faith with affirming that report, for it has not occurred, and we have not commanded you to do this. Rather, we commanded you to have faith without qualification, which you are capable of, while also declaring that you will not do what you are capable of doing. We did not tell you, ‘Affirm both this and that at the same time.’ Rather, what is obligatory for you is

---

## Page 4188

affirmation without qualification; affirming this report is not then obligatory for you. Had you affirmed without qualification, it would have been impossible for us to make this report. Rather, this report was made only because we knew that you would not affirm without qualification.”

All of this assumes that Abū Lahab was made to hear this verse and commanded to affirm it; but that was not the case. When Allah revealed His words:

“He will burn in a Fire of blazing flame,”

it cannot be conceded to them that Allah commanded His Prophet to make Abū Lahab hear this statement and commanded Abū Lahab to affirm it. Indeed, no one can produce a report that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, commanded Abū Lahab to affirm that this surah had been revealed. Thus, the claim that he was commanded to affirm that he would not believe is false: no Muslim scholar has transmitted it. To attribute it to the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, is to speak without knowledge—indeed, it is a lie against him.

If it is said, “Faith was obligatory for Abū Lahab, and faith includes believing this,” the answer is:

We do not concede that, after this surah was revealed, the Messenger was obliged to convey it to him—or indeed any other surah. Rather, the decree of punishment had become binding upon him, just as it became binding upon Noah’s people when he was told:

“None of your people will believe except those who have already believed, so do not be distressed by what they have been doing.”

After that, the Messenger is no longer commanded to convey the message to them, for he has already conveyed it to them, but they disbelieved until the decree of punishment became binding upon those very individuals. Allah may inform the Messenger that a particular person will not believe, yet not command him to inform that person

---

## Page 4189

of that. Rather, he is commanded to convey the message to him, even though the Messenger knows that he will not believe, as with those of whom Allah says:

“Indeed, those against whom your Lord’s decree has become binding will not believe,”

“Even if every sign should come to them, until they see the painful punishment.”

And His words:

“Indeed, those who disbelieve—it is all the same to them whether you warn them or do not warn them—they will not believe.”

Some angels and some human beings, including prophets and others, may know that a particular individual among these people will not believe, even though they are commanded to convey Allah’s commands and prohibitions to him. This does not require him to combine two mutually contradictory things. What is required is contrary to what is known will occur. Allah does whatever He wills by His power. As for what He does not will, He knows that He will not do it and that He has the power to do it: were He to will it, He would do it. His knowledge that He will not do it does not preclude His having the power to do it.

As for the servants whom Allah knows will obey Him through their own volition, will, and ability—even though He is the Creator of all this—His creating it is all the stronger grounds for His knowing it before it comes into being. As the Most High says:

“Does He who created not know, while He is the Most Subtle, the All-Aware?”

As for the things He commands them to do which they do not do, it is known that these will not occur because they do not will them, not because they lack the ability to do them. Commanding them to do such things is not commanding them to do what lies beyond their ability. Rather, it is commanding them to do what they would be able to do if they willed it. Yet they do not do it because they do not will it.

Jahm and those of the Mu'tazilah who agreed with him shared the view that Allah’s will, love, and approval all have the same meaning. The Mu'tazilah then said that He does not love disbelief, wickedness, and disobedience, and therefore does not will them. They thus maintained that these occur without His will. But the Jahmiyyah said: “Rather, He wills

---

## Page 4190

that, and therefore He loves it and approves of it.” Abū al-Hasan and most of his followers agreed with them. Abū al-Maʿālī al-Juwaynī stated that Abū al-Hasan was the first to disagree with the early generations on this issue, making no distinction between will, love, and approval.

As for the early generations of this community, its leading scholars, the foremost authorities in jurisprudence, hadith, and Sufism, and many groups of speculative thinkers, such as the Kullābiyyah, the Karrāmiyyah, and others, they distinguish between these things. They say that Allah loves faith and righteous deeds and approves of them, just as He neither commands nor approves of disbelief, wickedness, and disobedience. He does not love them, just as He does not command them, even though He has willed them.

For this reason, the scholars who uphold the Sharia, both later and earlier, have agreed that if someone swears to perform an obligatory or recommended act—such as repaying a debt for which little time remains, or performing an act of worship for which little time remains—and says, “If Allah wills,” but then does not perform it, he has not broken his oath. This invalidates the position of the Qadariyyah. If, however, he says, “If Allah loves this and approves of it,” then he does break his oath, just as he would if he said, “If He encourages and urges it, or commands it as obligatory or recommended.” This refutes the Jahmiyyah and those who followed them, such as Abū al-Hasan al-Ashʿarī and those among the later scholars who agreed with him.

A detailed discussion of these matters belongs elsewhere. The purpose here is to answer this “question”: the difficulties mentioned arise only from the position of Jahm and those who agreed with him among the later followers of Abū al-Hasan al-Ashʿarī and others, and a group of the later followers of Mālik, al-Shāfiʿī, and Ahmad.

---

## Page 4191

As for the leading scholars among the followers of Mālik, al-Shāfiʿī, and Ahmad, and the great majority of the followers of Abū Hanīfah, they do not hold this position. Rather, they affirm what the early generations agreed upon: whatever He—glorified be He—wills occurs, and whatever He does not will does not occur. They distinguish between His will and His love and approval. They say that although disbelief, wickedness, and disobedience occur by His will, He neither loves nor approves of them; rather, He is displeased with them and hates them.

They also say that Allah’s intent, as mentioned in His Book, is of two kinds. One means His will concerning what He creates, as in His words:

“Whoever Allah wills to guide, He opens his heart to Islam; and whoever He wills to send astray, He makes his heart tight and constricted, as though he were climbing into the sky.”

The other means His love and approval of what He commands, even when He does not bring it into existence, as in His words:

“Allah intends ease for you and does not intend hardship for you.”

“Allah does not intend to place any burden upon you, but He intends to purify you and complete His favour upon you, so that you may be grateful.”

“Allah intends to make things clear to you, guide you to the ways of those before you, and turn to you in mercy. And Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise.”

“Allah intends to turn to you in mercy, but those who follow their desires intend that you should deviate far from the right path.”

“Allah intends to lighten your burdens, for humankind was created weak.”

This distinction resolves the dispute over whether a command necessarily entails intent. The Qadariyyah claim that it necessarily entails His will, which would mean that He willed what He commanded, yet it did not occur. The Jahmiyyah, however, say that it does not necessarily entail any kind of intent—neither His love for it nor His approval

---

## Page 4192

of it—unless it actually occurs. For whatever He wills occurs, and whatever He does not will does not occur. Likewise, according to them, whatever He loves and approves of occurs, and whatever He does not love or approve of does not occur. They interpreted His words:

“He does not approve of disbelief for His servants”

as referring to those who have not committed disbelief, or as meaning that He does not approve of it as a religion. Similarly, they say that He did not will it for those who have not committed it, or that He does not will it as a religion. For they agreed with the Jahmiyyah and the Qadariyyah that there is no distinction between love and will.

Yet Allah Most High says:

“If you disbelieve, Allah has no need of you, and He does not approve of disbelief for His servants. But if you are grateful, He approves of that for you.”

Thus He states that when His servants disbelieve, He does not approve of their disbelief. Likewise, He says:

“When they plot by night to say what He does not approve of.”

And He says:

“Allah does not love corruption,”

while also saying:

“And whoever He wills to send astray, He makes his heart tight and constricted.”

And (the decisive resolution is this: a command does not necessarily entail that the commanding Lord wills to create the commanded act, or intends to bring it about. Rather, He may command something that He does not create. His command does, however, necessarily entail that the Lord loves and approves of His servant’s performing it, in the sense that, if the servant performs it, He loves and approves of it. He intends it from the servant as one who commands intends the person commanded to do what he has commanded for that person’s benefit—even if He does not intend to create it or help the servant perform it, because of His wisdom in withholding that help. For His wisdom is perfect in what He creates and in what He does not create.

There is a difference between His intending to create the act Himself and make another its doer, showing him kindness and favour by helping him attain what benefits him, and His commanding another to do what is good for him and explaining what will benefit him if he does it—even though He Himself does not intend to help him, because of what is involved in withholding His assistance

---

## Page 4193

in terms of wisdom; for such assistance may entail something contrary to His wisdom. He hates and abhors the forbidden act that He has created, just as He abhors the evil beings and things He has created, such as devils and foul things. Yet He created them for a wise purpose that He loves and approves of.

We know that a person may wish to do something he does not love because it leads to something he loves. Thus, a sick person drinks unpleasant medicine because it leads to the recovery he loves, and a person performs tasks he dislikes because they lead to his desired goal. There is no contradiction between something being hateful to Him and His having created it for a wise purpose that He loves. Likewise, there is no contradiction between His loving something if it occurs and His not bringing it about; for bringing it about may entail losing something He loves more, or bringing into existence something more hateful to Him than its absence.

Section:

With this understood, we say:

As for the question, “How can a servant choose his actions while being compelled to perform them?” this objection applies only to the Jahmiyyah, who affirm compulsion without qualification and deny the servant’s power and choice, as well as the efficacy of his power in producing the act.

We have already explained that the unqualified use of the term “compulsion” was rejected by the leading scholars of the Sunnah, such as al-Awzāʿī, al-Zubaydī, al-Thawrī, ʿAbd al-Rahmān ibn Mahdī, and Ahmad ibn Hanbal

---

## Page 4194

and others. I know of none of the leading scholars who used it without qualification; indeed, I know of none of the Companions or those who followed them in righteousness who used it in “questions of divine decree and compulsion.”

None of the leading Muslim scholars—neither the four imams nor others: neither Mālik, Abū Hanīfah, al-Shāfi‘ī, Ahmad ibn Hanbal, al-Awzā‘ī, al-Thawrī, al-Layth, nor others like them—said that Allah imposes upon His servants obligations beyond their capacity. Nor did any of them say that a servant performs his act only figuratively, not in reality. Nor did any of them say that a servant’s power has no effect on his act or on his acquisition of it. Nor did any of them say that a servant possesses power only at the moment of acting, that the capacity to perform an act exists only alongside it, or that a servant has no capacity to perform an act before performing it.

Rather, their statements abundantly affirm what the Quran and Sunnah indicate: that someone may possess the capacity to act without actually acting. Thus Allah Most High says:

“Pilgrimage to the House is a duty owed to Allah by those who are able to undertake it.”

And He Most High says:

“But whoever is unable must feed sixty needy people.”

And the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said to ‘Imrān ibn Husayn:

“Pray standing; if you cannot, then sitting; and if you cannot, then on your side.”

They agreed that acts of worship are obligatory only upon those capable of performing them, and that a person may retain that capacity despite disobeying and failing to act—as with someone capable of fulfilling what he has been commanded concerning prayer and zakat

---

## Page 4195

and fasting and pilgrimage, yet does not perform them. By the consensus of the early generations of the Muslim community and its imams, such a person possesses the capacity to act. He deserves punishment for neglecting what he was commanded and was capable of doing but did not do—not for failing to do what was beyond his capacity.

They explicitly affirmed, as did Abū Hanīfah, Abū al-‘Abbās ibn Surayj, and others, that the capacity preceding an act enables either of two opposite courses of action, although, in their view, the servant also possesses capacity while acting. Thus, according to them, he possesses capacity both before and during the act. While acting, however, he cannot simultaneously perform the act and refrain from it. They therefore do not say that capacity exists only before the act, as the Mu‘tazilah say, or that it exists only alongside the act, as the proponents of compulsion say. Rather, the servant possesses capacity both before and during the act.

As for his statement:

“The scholars have explicitly stated that the servant performs them under compulsion.”

He is answered as follows:

None of the scholars of the early generations, the renowned imams of Islam, or the leading followers of the four imams explicitly stated this. Only some later scholars who followed the path of Jahm and those who agreed with him explicitly state it. This is not the position of the scholars of the Sunnah, nor even of their majority or their imams. Rather, the imams of the early generations count such people among the adherents of reprehensible innovations.

---

## Page 4196

Section

As for the questioner’s words in verse:

“For they have explicitly stated that he … is indeed compelled in his acts of will.”

He is answered as follows:

If compulsion regarding his willing means that Allah made him one who wills, then this is true. Yet calling this constraint, coercion, or compulsion is a contradiction in both wording and meaning. Someone who is constrained, coerced, or compelled is not willing, choosing, loving, and content; and someone who has been made to choose, love, and be content cannot be described as constrained, coerced, or compelled.

If it is said:

“What is meant is that he was made to will through Allah’s will and power, without any prior act of will on his part by which he chose to become one who wills.”

They are answered:

“This meaning is true, whether or not it is called compulsion. But it does not contradict his being one who chooses. For whoever has been made to will and choose has thereby been affirmed to possess will and choice. A thing does not contradict itself or what necessarily accompanies it. It is therefore inadmissible to ask: ‘How can someone who chooses have been made to choose, and someone who wills have been made to will?’”

If it is said:

“He is given a choice about being one who chooses.”

The reply is:

“The meaning of this is that Allah made him

---

## Page 4197

one who chooses, without any prior act of will on his part to become one who chooses, just as He made him capable, knowledgeable, alive, black or white, tall or short. It is well known that when Allah endows someone with a quality, this does not contradict his possessing that quality. When Allah gives him a quality, he possesses it because Allah has bestowed it upon him: whatever He wills comes to be, and whatever He does not will does not come to be. His being one who chooses, knows, and is capable is inseparably connected with Allah’s will and His making him so. Two inseparably connected things do not contradict one another; rather, they coexist and cannot be separated. Thus, the servant’s choice and what is termed ‘compulsion’—meaning that Allah made him one who chooses—are inseparably connected, not contradictory. There is nothing surprising about two inseparably connected things coexisting; what would be surprising is their contradicting one another.”

Section

As for the questioner’s words:

“For they have explicitly stated that he … is indeed compelled in his acts of will.
And that he is not truly the doer of his deeds … and this judgment is well known.”

He is answered as follows:

Those who explicitly state that he is not truly an agent are the Jahmiyyah—the followers of al-Jahm ibn Safwān—and those among later generations who agreed with them. This was never explicitly stated by any of the Companions or those who followed them

---

## Page 4198

in goodness, nor by the imams of the Muslims—neither the four imams nor anyone else. Rather, all those who employed the terms “literal” and “figurative” while following the early generations in this fundamental matter say that the servant is truly an agent. The leading scholars among the followers of the four imams—Abū Hanīfah, Mālik, al-Shāfiʿī, and Ahmad ibn Hanbal—and others explicitly affirmed this, and their books abound with such statements.

As for those who say that he is an agent only figuratively, and that the act does not subsist in the agent but is itself the thing brought about, their position necessarily implies that the servants’ acts have no agent: neither the Lord nor the servant. As for the servant, although the acts subsist in him, they hold that he is not their agent. As for the Lord, they hold that no act subsists in Him—neither these acts nor any others. Yet an agent, as intelligibly understood, is one in whom the act subsists, just as a speaker, as intelligibly understood, is one in whom speech subsists, and one who wills is one in whom will subsists. Likewise, one who is living, knowing, and capable is one in whom life, knowledge, and power subsist, and one who moves is one in whom motion subsists.

Thus, their affirmation of an agent in whom no act subsists is like the affirmation by their predecessors among the Jahmiyyah and Muʿtazilah of a speaker in whom no speech subsists, one who wills in whom no will subsists, one who knows in whom no knowledge subsists, and one who is capable in whom no power subsists. All of this is false, as they themselves have established in discussing “Allah’s speech” and the affirmation of “His attributes,” as has been explained at length in its proper place.

The principle on which they agreed with the imams of the Sunnah, and which they used as an argument against the Muʿtazilah, is this: when a quality subsists in a subject, the judgment it entails applies to that subject, and a name is derived from it for that subject; no name is derived from it for anything else. Its judgment applies to that subject and not to anything else. Similarly, when motion, blackness, whiteness, heat, or cold subsists in a subject, it is that subject which is

---

## Page 4199

moving, black, white, hot, or cold, and not anything else.

They said: Likewise, when speech and will subsist in a subject, that subject is the one who speaks and wills, and not anything else.

They said: Thus, a speaker can only be a speaker through speech that subsists in him, and one who wills can only do so through a will that subsists in him. Likewise, one can only be living, knowing, and capable through life, knowledge, and power that subsist in him. The consistent implication of this is that one can only be an agent through an act that subsists in him. For this reason, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, sought refuge in Allah Most High’s attributes, acts, and very Self, saying:

“O Allah, I seek refuge in Your pleasure from Your displeasure, in Your protection from Your punishment, and in You from You. I cannot adequately praise You; You are as You have praised Yourself.”

This is among the evidence that the imams, including Ahmad ibn Hanbal and others, cited to establish that Allah’s speech is not created. They said: He sought refuge in it, and refuge is not sought in anything created.

Section

As for the questioner’s statement:

“Hence the act has no effect on … what befalls the agent,”

if he means that the act has no effect on the praise, blame, reward, or punishment that the agent receives, this is said only by those who deny causes, such as Jahm and those who

---

## Page 4200

agree with him. The early generations and the imams, however, agree in affirming causes and wise purposes in both creation and command.

In matters of “command,” for example, the jurists say: The causes establishing inheritance are “three”: kinship, marriage, and the bond of patronage established by manumission. They disagree over a pact of alliance, a person’s embracing Islam at another’s hands, and both parties being enrolled in the dīwān (state register). Some, such as Abū Hanīfah, regard these as causes of inheritance; others, such as Mālik and al-Shāfiʿī, do not. Two positions are reported from Ahmad.

Similarly, they say: Possessing the minimum threshold of wealth is a cause for zakah becoming obligatory; purely intentional, wrongful killing is a cause for retaliatory execution; and theft is a cause for amputation.

The jurists’ position is that a cause has an effect on its consequence and is not merely a sign. Only a group of speculative theologians who built upon Jahm’s position maintain that it is merely a sign. Some jurists also use the same language, but most jurists who do so contradict themselves: at times they adopt the position of the early generations and the imams, and at other times they adopt the position of these theologians.

Likewise, the jurists agree with the early generations in affirming wisdom and that rulings are prescribed for wise purposes. The same applies to wisdom in “creation.” The Quran is full of this concerning “creation and command”

---

## Page 4201

and is full of statements that He creates things through causes, contrary to the followers of Jahm, who say that He acts when those causes occur, not through them. Thus, the Exalted says:

“He sent down water from the sky and thereby revived the earth after its death.”

And He says:

“We sent down blessed water from the sky, and with it caused gardens and grain for harvest to grow, and lofty palm trees bearing clustered fruit, as provision for His servants; and with it We revived a lifeless land.”

And He says:

“It is He who sends the winds bearing good tidings before His mercy, until, when they carry heavy clouds, We drive them to a lifeless land, sending down water thereby, and with it bringing forth fruits of every kind.”

And He says:

“Through it Allah guides those who seek His pleasure to the ways of peace.”

And He says:

“Fight them; Allah will punish them at your hands.”

There are many similar passages. As for the use of the lām of purpose (“so that”) concerning creation and command, it is exceedingly frequent. This is discussed at length in its proper place. The rational and scriptural arguments of those who deny wisdom and purpose have been set out at length and their invalidity demonstrated, just as the invalidity of the arguments of the Muʿtazilah and the Qadariyyah has been demonstrated.

Accordingly, actions are causes of praise and blame, reward and punishment. The jurists who affirm causes and rulings have divided the discourse of the Law and its rulings into “two categories”: prescriptive discourse, and declarative, informative discourse, such as designating something as a cause, a condition, or an impediment. Those who deny this objected, saying: “If by something’s being

---

## Page 4202

a cause you mean that the ruling applies when it exists, then there is no additional ruling here. If you mean something else, that is denied.”

The reply to them is that causes possess attributes appropriate to the ruling, on account of which the ruling was prescribed; it was also prescribed because it leads to a wise purpose. As the Exalted says:

“Indeed, prayer restrains one from shameful and evil deeds, and the remembrance of Allah is greater.”

And the Exalted says:

“Satan only seeks to sow enmity and hatred among you through intoxicants and gambling”—to the end of the verse.

Likewise, those who say that the servant’s ability has no effect on his actions are these very followers of Jahm who deny causes. By contrast, the position of the early generations, their followers, the leading scholars of Ahl al-Sunnah, and the majority of Muslims who affirm divine decree and oppose the Muʿtazilah is to affirm causes. They affirm that the servant’s ability accompanying his action has an effect, just as all other causes have effects on what they produce. Allah Most High created both causes and their effects.

Causes do not produce their effects independently. Rather, they require other causes to assist them, and they also have opposing factors that impede them. An effect does not come about until Allah creates all its causes and wards off the opposing factors that counteract it. He, glorified be He, creates all of this by His will and power, just as He creates all other created things.

The servant’s ability is thus one cause among others. His action does not come about through that ability alone; a firm resolve must accompany it. If by ability one means the strength inherent in a person, then impediments must also be removed, such as the removal of

---

## Page 4203

fetters, confinement, and the like, as well as whatever blocks the way, such as an enemy or anyone else.

Section

The Exalted’s words,

“But you do not will unless Allah wills,”

do not indicate that the servant does not perform his own voluntary action, that he lacks the ability to perform it, or that he has no will. Rather, they indicate that he does not will it unless Allah wills. This verse refutes both groups: the determinist Jahmiyyah and the Mu'tazilite Qadariyyah. For the Exalted says:

“For whoever among you wills to take a straight path.”

He thus affirms that the servant has a will and acts. Then He says:

“But you do not will unless Allah, Lord of all worlds, wills.”

He thereby makes clear that the servant’s will is dependent upon Allah’s will. The first verse refutes the Jabriyyah, while this one refutes the Qadariyyah, who say that the servant may will what Allah does not will, just as they say that Allah wills what they do not will.

If, in accordance with their principle, they say, “What is meant here by willing is commanding, and the meaning is that they do not will to do what Allah has commanded if Allah has not commanded it,” the reply is that the context of the verse makes clear that this is not what is meant. Rather, the meaning is that, after you have been commanded to perform an action, you do not will to perform it unless Allah wills. For the Exalted mentions commands and prohibitions, promises and warnings, and then says:

“Indeed, this is a reminder, so whoever wills may take a path to his Lord. But you do not will unless Allah wills.”

His words, “But you do not will,” negate their willing in the future. Likewise, His words, “unless Allah wills,”

---

## Page 4204

make their willing dependent upon the Lord’s will in the future, for the particle an (“that”) gives the imperfect verb an exclusively future sense. Thus, the meaning is: “unless He wills thereafter,” whereas the command precedes that. This is like someone saying, “I will not do this unless Allah wills.”

The early generations and the jurists agreed that if someone swears, saying, “I will certainly pray tomorrow, if Allah wills,” or “I will certainly repay my debt tomorrow, if Allah wills,” and tomorrow passes without his repaying it, he has not broken his oath. If willing meant commanding, he would have broken his oath, because Allah has commanded him to do that. This is among the arguments advanced against the Qadariyyah, to which they have no answer. For this reason, some of them departed from the long-established consensus and said that he does break his oath.

Furthermore, His words,

“But you do not will unless Allah wills,”

are intended to praise and extol the Lord by making clear His power and His servants’ need for Him. If the intended meaning were, “You do not act unless He commands you,” then the same would apply to every command, and this would not be among the Lord’s distinctive attributes for which He is praised. If, instead, the meaning were that they act only in obedience to His command, this would be praise of them, not of Him.

---

## Page 4205

Section

As for his words:

“And all things; then, were it conceded …
the Creator would have no decree.”

If he means that admitting that the servant truly performs his own acts, or accepting similar statements of the early generations, necessarily entails denying divine decree, then this alleged entailment is rejected. If, however, he means that conceding that the servant can will what Allah has not willed would entail that Allah’s will does not encompass prohibited and permissible acts, then this follows by common agreement. Indeed, it would entail that His will does not, in reality, encompass any of His servants’ acts, just as it would entail denying His power over all their acts and denying that He creates any of them. This negates divine decree in the sense of willing, power, and creation.

As for divine decree in the sense of His determining those acts within Himself, knowing them, speaking of them, and recording them, its denial clearly follows only from the position of those who deny foreknowledge. Most of the Qadariyyah do not deny it. Yet if they allow numerous events to occur apart from His will, power, and creation, they affirm that numerous events in the world are brought about by someone other than Him, while He is unable to bring them about. In that case, they cannot appeal to His words,

“Does He who created not know?”

---

## Page 4206

as evidence that He knows them, for, according to them, He did not create them. Their fellow Qadariyyah may dispute His knowledge of these acts before they occur, and they cannot use this verse as evidence against them. They may also argue that His knowing these acts while commanding the contrary of what He knows will occur entails imposing obligations beyond one’s capacity, since the contrary of what is known is impossible; He therefore does not know them. They would thus compel them to deny prior determination.

Section

As for his words:

“Or, if He does decree, this would entail …
its coming into being—a rejected view.”

He seems to mean—and Allah knows best—that if Allah does determine these acts and know them, then His knowing and determining them after they occur entails that knowledge of them arises after their occurrence. It would follow that the Lord neither knows His servants’ acts nor determines them until they have been performed. This is a rejected and false position. The early generations—the Companions and those who followed them in righteousness—and all other Muslim scholars agreed that it is false. Indeed, they declared anyone who upheld it to be an unbeliever. The Quran and Sunnah, together with rational evidence, demonstrate its falsity.

For Allah has foretold His servants’ deeds before they occur. Indeed, He has made them known to whomever He wills among His angels and others. The Most High says:

“And when your Lord said

---

## Page 4207

to the angels, ‘I will place a successor on earth.’ They said, ‘Will You place in it one who will spread corruption there and shed blood, while we glorify You with praise and proclaim Your holiness?’ He said, ‘Indeed, I know what you do not know.’”

The angels thus concluded that human beings would spread corruption and shed blood before Allah created humankind. Yet they had no knowledge except what Allah had taught them, as they said:

“We have no knowledge except what You have taught us.”

Then He said:

“Indeed, I know what you do not know.”

This encompassed what would later transpire involving Adam, Iblīs and their descendants, and the consequences that would follow.

This verse also indicates that He knew Adam would leave Paradise, for had Adam not left Paradise, he would not have become a successor on earth. Allah commanded him to dwell in Paradise and not to eat from the tree, saying:

“And We said, ‘O Adam, dwell in Paradise, you and your wife, and eat freely from it wherever you wish. But do not approach this tree, lest you become wrongdoers.’”

The Most High also said:

“So We said, ‘O Adam, this is indeed an enemy to you and your wife. Do not let him drive you both out of Paradise, lest you suffer hardship.”

“Indeed, there you will neither go hungry nor be unclothed,”

“nor will you thirst there or suffer the sun’s heat.’”

He forbade Adam to let Iblīs drive him out of Paradise. This was a prohibition against obeying Iblīs, which would cause his departure. Yet He had already known that Adam would leave Paradise, and that he would leave it only because he obeyed Iblīs and ate from the tree, for He had previously said:

“I will place a successor on earth.”

For this reason, some of the early generations said that He had decreed Adam’s departure from Paradise before commanding him to enter it, through His words:

“I will place a successor on earth.”

After this, He said:

“And We said, ‘Go down, as enemies to one another. On earth you will have a place to dwell and provision for a time.’”

---

## Page 4208

And the Most High said:

“He said, ‘Go down, as enemies to one another. On earth you will have a place to dwell and provision for a time.’”

“He said, ‘There you will live, there you will die, and from there you will be brought forth.’”

This foretells their future enmity toward one another and other matters.

The Most High also said:

“Indeed, those against whom your Lord’s word has come into effect will not believe, even if every sign should come to them.”

And He said:

“Indeed, those who disbelieve—it is all the same to them whether you warn them or do not warn them—they will not believe.”

This foretells the future and states that they will not believe.

The Most High also said:

“I will surely fill Hell with you and all those among them who follow you.”

And He said:

“But My word has come into effect: ‘I will surely fill Hell with jinn and human beings together.’”

This is an oath He swears concerning that, and He is truthful and faithful to His oath. His truthfulness necessarily entails His knowledge of what He has sworn to do; it also proves that He has the power to do it. It may also be adduced as evidence that He is the Creator of His servants’ acts. For if their acts were beyond His power, He could not fill Hell. Rather, that would be up to them: if they wished, they would disobey Him, and He would fill it; if they wished, they would obey Him, and He would not fill it.

It may, however, be said that He knew they would disobey Him and therefore swore to recompense them for that. One possible response is that His knowledge of the future before it comes to pass necessarily entails His creation of it. For He, glorified be He, does not acquire knowledge from others as angels and human beings do. Rather, His knowledge is inseparable from His very being. Thus, if His acts were outside His power and will, it would not necessarily follow that He knew them as He knows His creatures. A fuller discussion of this belongs elsewhere.

---

## Page 4209

The Most High said concerning the hypocrites:

“Had they gone forth with you, they would only have increased your confusion and hastened about among you, seeking to sow discord among you.”

This foretells the sins they would commit before they committed them.

The Most High also said:

“Say to those Bedouins who remained behind, ‘You will be called to face a people of great military might; you will fight them, or they will submit.’”

This foretells that someone would call them to wage jihad against those people. His calling them is itself one of the acts of Allah’s servants. There are many such examples in the Quran. Indeed, even individual created beings—angels, prophets, and others—can have knowledge of the future acts of Allah’s servants. How, then, could the Lord of all worlds lack such knowledge?

The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, foretold future acts of his nation and others, in accounts too numerous to recount at length. For example, he foretold that through his son al-Hasan, Allah would reconcile two great groups of Muslims; that a renegade faction would break away at a time of division among the Muslims and would be killed by whichever of the two factions was closer to the truth; that some people would turn back on their heels after him; and that the caliphate upon the prophetic way would last thirty years and then become kingship.

He also declared that no one upon the mountain was other than a prophet, a man of unwavering truthfulness, or a martyr—and most of those present did indeed become martyrs. On the day of Badr, he foretold the deaths of the leading men of Quraysh before they were killed. He foretold the emergence of the Dajjāl, the descent of Jesus, peace be upon him, at the white minaret east of Damascus, and Jesus’ killing him at the gate of Ludd. He also foretold the emergence of Gog and Magog, and the emergence of the Khārijites, concerning whom he said:

“From the stock of this man will emerge people whose prayer will make any one of you regard his own prayer as insignificant, and his fasting

## Page 4210

in comparison with theirs. They recite the Quran, but it does not pass beyond their throats. They pass out of Islam as an arrow passes through its quarry. The Muslims did indeed fight these Turks and others when they emerged. Such reports from His Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, are too numerous to recount. Yet he knows only what Allah has taught him. If he knows many of the deeds that Allah’s servants will perform, what, then, of the One who created him and taught him what he did not know? No one encompasses any of His knowledge except what He wills, and no one—whether a prophet or anyone else—knows anything except what Allah has taught him.

Al-Khidr said to Moses:

“I possess knowledge from Allah that He has taught me and that you do not know, and you possess knowledge from Allah that He has taught you and that I do not know.”

When a sparrow dipped its beak into the sea, he said to him:

“My knowledge and yours have diminished Allah’s knowledge no more than this sparrow has diminished this sea.”

It is He, glorified be He, who said concerning Moses:

“And We wrote for him on the Tablets instruction concerning all things and a detailed explanation of all things.”

The point is that denying Allah’s knowledge of events—including the deeds of His servants and other things—before they occur is false. Yet the extremists among the Qadariyyah deny this knowledge.

## Page 4211

As for His words, exalted is He:

“We appointed the direction of prayer you formerly faced only so that We might know who follows the Messenger and who turns back on his heels,”

and His words:

“So that We might know which of the two groups more accurately reckoned the length of their stay,”

and similar passages, these refer to knowledge of its object after that object comes into existence. This is the knowledge upon which praise and blame, reward and punishment depend. The former kind is knowledge that something will occur. That knowledge alone entails neither praise nor blame, neither reward nor punishment, for these follow only after the deeds have actually occurred.

It is reported that Ibn ‘Abbās explained this as meaning: “So that We might see.” Likewise, the Quran commentators said: “So that We might know it as actually existing, after having known that it would come to exist.”

Speculative thinkers hold two well-known positions concerning what newly arises here. Some say: “What newly arises is merely a relation and connection between knowledge and its object, and this relation has no positive existence.” Others say: “Rather, what newly arises is knowledge of the thing’s occurrence and existence, and this knowledge differs from knowing that it will occur.”

The same applies to His words:

“And say, ‘Act, for Allah will see your deeds, as will His Messenger and the believers.’”

Here He states that seeing will newly occur. Some have therefore said that this is a relation without positive existence; others have said that what newly arises has positive existence. These two positions, those who have advocated each, and the arguments of both sides have been discussed at length elsewhere.

The great majority of the early Muslims and the leading authorities of the Sunnah and hadith hold that what newly arises has positive existence, as the revealed text indicates. Denying this was one of the reasons Ahmad ibn Hanbal shunned al-Hārith al-Muhāsibī, for he held

---

## Page 4212

the view of Ibn Kullāb. He sought to avoid anything with positive existence newly arising and affirmed the implications of that position. He thus contradicted texts of the Quran and Sunnah and reports from the early Muslims in ways that made his innovation manifest, leading Imām Ahmad to shun him and warn against him.

It has, however, been said that al-Hārith retracted that position.

The later followers of Mālik, al-Shāfiʿī, Ahmad ibn Hanbal and Abū Hanīfah hold two positions: some follow the approach of Ibn Kullāb and his followers, while others follow that of the leading authorities of the Sunnah and hadith. This is discussed at length in its proper place.

The point here is that Allah’s knowledge and His recording of His servants’ deeds precede those deeds. This is true, whereas the view that this knowledge and recording newly arise is a rejected position, as the poet stated—if that is indeed what he meant. Nothing in this conflicts with Allah’s commands and prohibitions. His being the Creator of His servants’ deeds does not conflict with commanding and prohibiting; how much less, then, does His prior knowledge! Nor does any of this imply that the servant is compelled, possessing neither power nor action, as the Jahmī determinists claim.

As for his words:

“Nor should it be said, ‘Allah’s knowledge is of what is chosen’ …
for what is chosen is recorded.”

## Page 4213

they involve presenting an objection from the Qadariyyah and their answer to it. They may say: “We affirm that He knows. In saying this, we have not denied divine decree; rather, we have affirmed it in the sense of knowledge, while denying that the Lord Most High wills all events and creates His servants’ deeds.” The poet says: “What the servant chooses has already been recorded, so he cannot do otherwise; compulsion therefore follows.”

This answer may be challenged as follows: the consequence here stands on the same footing as that which entails it. His knowledge that the servant will choose something accords with His recording that the servant will choose it, and altering knowledge is a greater matter than altering what is recorded.

It may also be said that he intended the recording to form part of the statement being rejected: one should not say, “He knew what the servant would choose and recorded it”—meaning that prior knowledge and recording suffice for belief in divine decree. These alone do not suffice for belief in divine decree. This is part of the argument advanced by those who affirm compulsion.

They say: “Anything contrary to what is known is impossible, so commanding it is commanding the impossible. For if the commanded act were to occur, knowledge would necessarily become ignorance.”

The answer to them is that “impossible” is an ambiguous term. If they mean that anything contrary to what is known will not happen or come to pass, this is correct. But requiring something that will not occur does not amount to requiring something the agent is incapable of doing. An agent may refrain from an act because he is incapable of it, or he may refrain because he does not will it. He is thus charged only with what he is capable of, even though the Lord knows

---

## Page 4214

that it will not occur, just as He knows that what He does not will will not occur, even though, if He willed it, He would do it.

To the objector’s statement, “If it occurred, knowledge would turn into ignorance,” the reply is:

This is correct. It indicates that the act will not occur, but it does not indicate that the person charged with it is incapable of it—that he could not perform it even if he willed to. It does not occur because he does not will it, not because he lacks the ability to do it. The same applies to those things within the Lord’s power which He would do if He willed, although He knows that He will not do them. It is not permissible to say that He is unable to do them, as some extremists among the people of innovation have claimed. Rather, He, glorified be He, has said:

“Does man think that We will not assemble his bones? Yes indeed! We are able even to restore his fingertips.”

And He, Most High, has said:

“Say: He has the power to send punishment upon you from above you or from beneath your feet, or to divide you into factions.”

Yet it is established in the two Sahīh collections, on the authority of Jābir:

“When His words, ‘Say: He has the power to send punishment upon you from above you,’ were revealed, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said, ‘I seek refuge in Your Face.’ At ‘or from beneath your feet,’ he said, ‘I seek refuge in Your Face.’ At ‘or to divide you into factions and make some of you taste the violence of others,’ he said, ‘These two are less severe.’”

Thus, some of the things He has declared Himself capable of will not occur—namely, sending punishment upon the Muslim community from above them or from beneath their feet. Others will occur—namely, dividing them into factions and making some of them taste the violence of others, as is established in the Sahīh

from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, who said:

In several places in the Quran, He mentions things that will not occur, stating that, had He willed, He would have done them. For example, He says:

“Had We willed, We would have given every soul its guidance.”

And He says:

And He says:

“Had your Lord willed, He would have made mankind one community.”

These and similar verses make clear that, had He willed to do things that have not occurred, He would have done them. This indicates that He has power over what He knows will not occur. For if He lacked the power to do it, He would not do it even if He willed it, since doing it is possible only with the power to do so. Thus, when He declares—and He is truthful in what He declares—that He would do it if He willed, it is known that He has the power to do it, even though He, glorified be He, knows that it will not occur. It is also known that what is contrary to what is known may nevertheless lie within one’s power.

If it is said to be impossible, this is an impossibility arising from the Lord’s not willing it, not from its being intrinsically impossible or beyond His power. The term “impossible” is ambiguous, as explained earlier. As for what is called impossible in the sense that it will not occur, even though
